High-intensity training refers to high effort,\h\h low volume, and lower frequency training.\h We'll cover the precise details shortly. But often, high-intensity training is contrasted\h to high volume and perhaps more frequent training,\h\h the training style many iconic figures\h during the Golden era of bodybuilding,\h\h such as Arnold, are known to\h have performed and recommended. As Arnold describes in his 80s\h Encyclopedia of modern bodybuilding,\h\h he believed “you need to do at\h least 5 sets in order have the\h\h volume of training necessary to fully\h stimulate the available muscle fiber." In this video, we're going deep\h into high-intensity training to\h\h figure out if it's truly the\h optimal muscle-building way,\h\h as well as compare it to higher volume\h and more frequent training regimes. Numerous different variations of\h high-intensity training exist,\h\h and famous bodybuilders such as Mike Mentzer and\h Dorian Yates were known to train in this style. However, many folks (including Mentzer and Yates)\h\h credit Arthus Jones for popularising\h high-intensity training in the 1970s.\h\h The term “high-intensity training" appears\h as early as 1973 in an article by Jones.\h\h Jones’ further writings on the topic can be\h found in his numerous magazine and book writings. Who was Arthus Jones? He founded Nautilus, a company that\h manufactured training machines,\h\h machines designed to match the\h strength curves of a muscle. Jones was far from the typical\h man. He travelled extensively.\h\h His motto was "younger women, faster\h airplanes, and bigger crocodiles". A Nautilus building in\h Florida was home to a Gomek,\h\h an 18-foot saltwater crocodile\h Jones wanted to grow to record size. He ran businesses that imported wild animals and\h\h is believed to have owned a zoo in\h Louisana after the 2nd world war. We noted many variations of\h high-intensity training exist.\h\h But 3 common themes are consistent\h throughout all variations. The first is the emphasis on training\h to failure and sometimes even beyond. Arthus Jones instructed in\h his Nautilus Bulletin books,\h\h "a set is properly finished only when\h additional movement is utterly impossible,\h\h curl until you can't even begin to bend your\h arms, squat until you can't start up from\h\h the low position, press until you cannot move\h the bar away from your shoulders and chest". Mike Mentzer's stated in his book "working to this\h point of failure, when another rep is impossible\h\h despite the greatest effort, ensures you pass\h through the break-over point, a point in the\h\h set below which growth cannot be stimulated,\h and above which growth will be stimulated". The second common theme is performing a low number\h of sets per exercise, typically only one set. In another Arthus Jones' book, he says "how\h many sets of the exercise? one. Additional\h\h sets usually serve no purpose and may produce\h a state of overtraining with some subjects". A quote by Dorian Yates reads "One set at\h extreme intensity does the muscle-building job". The third main common theme is\h the low frequency of training. Arthur Jones initially advocated for three\h full-body weekly workouts, but later amended to\h\h training each muscle only once or at most twice\h per week, he states "how many weekly workouts,\h\h not more than two, and some people will produce\h better results from only one weekly workout.\h\h More is not always better, and in the\h case of exercise is usually worse". Mike Mentzer echoed this, recommending 96-120\h hours of rest between training sessions.\h\h In fact, Mentzer also states in his book he had a\h\h number of personal clients who\h trained once every 10-14 days. All three themes are closely connected. High-intensity advocates suggest when\h training with true maximal effort\h\h (as you do when training failure), you can\h only perform so much volume (hence the one\h\h set recommendations), and only so frequently\h too (hence the low-frequency recommendations. As Arthus Jones describes “The secret, if\h there is one, is high-intensity. And when\h\h you actually train with high-intensity,\h you don’t need a lot of volume.” Likewise, Mike Mentzer states “If you’re\h skeptical [of Heavy Duty’s low volume],\h\h your subconscious child is telling you\h that more is better. In some cases,\h\h that’s true. More money is better than\h less. But you can’t take that principle\h\h and blindly apply it to exercise and\h expect to get anything out of it.” Heavy duty was the name of Mike\h Mentzer's high-intensity training style. Now we have a good understanding\h of what high-intensity training is,\h\h is this method of training truly superior\h for muscle hypertrophy and strength? A few stories exist of individuals allegedly\h gaining an incredible amount of muscle mass with\h\h high-intensity training in a short time, with the\h Colorado experiment being the most fascinating. 63 lbs of muscle in 28 days\h through high-intensity training?\h\h Allegedly the infamous\h Colorado experiment found this. The experiment took place in 1973,\h at the Colorado State University\h\h under the supervision of Dr. Elliot Plese. In this experiment, Casey Viator\h (a successful bodybuilder,\h\h who was actually the youngest ever AAU\h Mr. America winner at the age of 19)\h\h trained high-intensity style for 28 days,\h while Arthus Jones himself trained for 22 days. The program is believed to look like this,\h at least something along these lines. One set was performed to failure in the\h prescribed rep ranges, and all exercises\h\h were performed with no rest between them. All\h exercises were performed on Nautilus machines too. The findings were published in the\h September ironman magazine in 1973. Viator gained 63.21lbs of muscle\h and Arthu 15.44lbs of muscle. Incredible results, but are\h they too good to be true? Likely, I’d argue yes. In the 4 months before this experiment, Casey\h Viator was believed to not have trained at all,\h\h as he was recovering from\h a serious accident at work. Similarly, Jones was believed to not have trained\h in the 4 months preceding the Colorado experiment,\h\h yet he had training experience in the past and\h\h at one point was believed to\h have been a muscular 205lbs. As a result, muscle memory (the phenomenon\h where your body can quickly rebuild lost muscle)\h\h is certainly confounding this experiment. Aside from this, Casey at least was clearly\h a gifted individual for putting on mass,\h\h so genetics are a consideration,\h something Arthus Jones did make clear. I think the use of anabolics\h cannot be ruled either. Now, Arthus Jones was opposed to anabolics,\h something he expressed many times in his writings. In a report on the Colorado experiment,\h Jones is reported to have said\h\h "the use of so-called growth drugs\h is neither necessary nor desirable." Moreover, in a T-nation article by Ellington\h Darden, someone who worked with Arthus Jones,\h\h it’s reported Jones hired someone to shadow\h Casey to ensure no anabolics were used. Despite all this, I still think it’s impossible\h to rule out the possibility of anabolics,\h\h even if Casey did not use during the 28 days,\h prior use can presumably still influence things. Aside from the Colorado experiment,\h Ellington Darden also put forth other\h\h accounts of individuals gaining abnormal amounts\h\h of muscle mass with high-intensity\h training in the T-nation article. Furthermore, I also came across\h an article by Tim Ferris,\h\h the author of the popular 4-hour work\h week, describing how he used Arthur\h\h Jones's high-intensity style training\h to put on 34lbs of muscle in 4 weeks. So what are we to make of all these accounts? Do they prove high-intensity training is\h the ultimate muscle hypertrophy system? In my view, no. As alluded to, many plausible confounders exist.\h The anecdotal data are also difficult to verify,\h\h and none of these experiments\h COMPARE how high-intensity\h\h training differs from other training methods. Something that does compare how different\h training methods compare is experimental research. With each of the three themes\h of high-intensity training,\h\h we can examine what the experimental\h research says about them. In my opinion, this is a much better way to\h evaluate the efficacy of high-intensity training. We noted training to failure is one theme\h in all high-intensity training protocols.\h\h Recall Jones' and Mentzer's statements. But is training to failure truly needed\h to maximize hypertrophy and strength? Starting with hypertrophy, in 2021,\h\h Grgic et al. conducted a meta-analysis\h of all the available evidence. For the unaware, a meta-analysis statistically\h combines all the current evidence on a topic,\h\h thus increasing statistical power\h and reliability when done well. Based on 7 studies (collectively\h comprising 130 men and 89 women),\h\h there was no difference in muscle growth between\h training to failure and not training to failure. After independently assessing the involved\h studies, most had the non-failure training\h\h groups leave 3 to 0 repetitions in reserve (that\h is, they stopped 3 to 0 reps away from failure),\h\h thus it seems training with this\h is similar to training to failure. Having said this, a subgroup analysis of\h studies done on trained individuals only\h\h did find training to failure to be\h better than not training to failure. However, a major limitation is only 2 studies\h were involved in this subgroup analysis, and both\h\h of these may not necessarily suggest training to\h failure in trained individuals is truly superior. In the one study by Karsten et al.,\h they found leaving 5 reps in reserve\h\h was inferior to training to failure,\h thus this study only suggests training\h\h to failure may be better than leaving 5 reps\h in reserve. It does not tell us how leaving\h\h 3 to 0 reps in reserve could compare\h to failure training in trained folks. The other study included in the subgroup\h analysis was by Pareja-Blanco et al.,\h\h and it found failure training was better for\h overall hypertrophy versus non-failure training.\h\h However, this was a velocity-based study,\h they had subjects terminate their sets once\h\h their lifting velocity decreased by a certain\h percentage, so it’s difficult to know what reps\h\h in reserve the non-failure training group used.\h But based on some data provided, it seems the\h\h non-failure group may have been training with\h 5 or more reps in reserve. For example, this\h\h group seemed to perform only around 5 reps with\h a 70% one-rep max load, fairly far from failure. Thus, again, this study does not inform us of how\h\h leaving 3 to 0 reps in reserve\h may compare to failure training. Fortunately, since this analysis by Grgic et al.\h in 2021, a study by Santanielo et al. has emerged. These researchers ultimately established\h\h in men with an average of 5.1\h years of training experience,\h\h leaving mainly 3 to 0 repetitions in reserve was\h similar to training to failure for hypertrophy. Thus, trained folks may also experience optimal\h\h gains while stopping 3 to\h 0 reps away from failure. Mechanistically, I'd argue\h these findings make sense. When we think about what causes muscle\h growth, training to failure probably does\h\h not provide any more benefit than\h stopping 3 to 0 reps from failure. Allow me to explain. Back in 2010, Brad Schoenfeld published a famous\h paper postulating that mechanical tension,\h\h muscle damage, and metabolic stress\h are all drivers of muscle hypertrophy. Fast forward to 2019, Brad\h Schoenfeld teamed up with\h\h Wackerhage and others to create an updated paper. They detail how the evidence behind metabolic\h stress and muscle damage being drivers of\h\h hypertrophy is not clear cut. Many cases exist\h where more metabolic stress or more muscle damage\h\h are not associated with more hypertrophy. Conversely, the evidence seems to\h demonstrate mechanical tension as\h\h the most likely and potent hypertrophy stimulus. In other words, we have solid\h reasons to believe mechanical\h\h tension is the primary driver of hypertrophy. And when we understand what precisely mechanical\h tension is, there's evidence training to failure\h\h does not produce higher levels versus\h stopping 3 to 0 reps shy of failure. Let's dive into this a little further. Mechanical tension is equal to the\h force generated by muscle fibers. \h Components within muscle\h fibers, called mechanosensors,\h\h detect forces produced by the muscle fiber and\h transduces these forces into a signaling cascade\h\h that results in muscle protein synthesis (which\h are the proteins that make our muscles bigger). The concept of motor units helps us\h understand overall mechanical tension further. A motor unit refers to a single motor neuron\h (that originates from the spine) and the\h\h multiple muscle fibers it innervates.\h When the single motor neuron sends an\h\h electrical signal through to the muscle fibers\h it innervates, those muscle fibers produce force. Within a whole muscle,\h different motor units exist,\h\h and their characteristics lie across a spectrum. On one end are low threshold motor units, and\h on the other end are high threshold motor units. Typically, a low-threshold motor unit consists of\h a small motor neuron that innervates slow-twitch\h\h muscle fibers that produce low amounts of force\h but are highly fatigue resistant. Due to this,\h\h low-threshold motor units are described as\h highly fatigue resistant but low force-producing. A high-threshold motor unit generally consists of\h a large motor neuron that innervates fast-twitch\h\h muscle fibers that produce high amounts of\h force but are highly fatigable. Therefore,\h\h high-threshold motor units are described\h as high-force producing but very fatigable. For maximizing overall mechanical tension (and\h thus the stimulus for overall muscle growth),\h\h we’d want to recruit as many motor\h units as possible during an exercise\h\h (from the low-threshold motor units all the\h way up to the high-threshold motor units). We'd also want each of the motor units\h to be producing decent amounts of their\h\h respective force capacities for a fair duration. Here’s the main points: Firstly, It’s not clear when you\h reach maximal motor unit recruitment,\h\h and the motor unit literature indicates\h this can differ between muscles. However, the literature indicates this is\h likely achieved a while before failure. For instance, one study suggests maximal\h motor unit recruitment for the shoulder\h\h and trap muscles may be obtained\h 3-5 repetitions before failure. Secondly, by the time you’ve reached failure,\h\h many motor units are likley past-producing\h their highest forces and are just fatiguing. Remember, it’s tension (analogous to force)\h\h that’s categorized as a prime stimulus for muscle\h hypertrophy. The idea that more motor unit fatigue\h\h is beneficial for muscle hypertrophy is\h not supported by the current literature. A motor unit modeling study by Potvin and\h Fuglevand demonstrates our points nicely. Their model included 7 different motor\h units, ordered in terms of thresholds. Motor unit 1 was the lowest threshold motor unit,\h\h while motor unit 120 was the\h highest threshold motor unit. The graph on-screen depicts the\h contribution of each motor unit to A-50%\h\h maximal isometric contraction held until failure.\h The total contraction lasted 100 seconds. Except for motor unit 120,\h all of the other motor units\h\h were recruited from the start of the contraction. Motor units 1, 20, 40, and 60 produced steady low\h forces throughout the full contraction duration.\h\h This makes sense, these would be\h considered the low-threshold motor units\h\h (which produce low forces but\h are highly fatigue resistant). Motor unit 80, a higher-threshold motor\h unit, produced its most force for the\h\h set at the start of the contraction,\h where it thereafter gradually fatigued. Motor unit 100, a higher-threshold motor\h unit, continued to increase its force\h\h contribution up until the 65-second\h mark, and thereafter began to fatigue. Motor unit 120, the highest-threshold motor unit,\h\h was recruited at the 70-ish second\h mark, and steeply increased its force\h\h contribution up until the 95-ish second\h mark, where it then steeply fatigued. This data demonstrates motor unit recruitment,\h as well as the maintenance of at least\h\h decent amounts of force production\h from the individual motor units,\h\h is achieved before failure.\h At the point of failure,\h\h no additional motor units nor enhancements\h in individual motor units force occurred. This probably explains why\h leaving 3 to 0 repetitions\h\h in reserve is sufficient for muscle growth. I should restate this data was from\h modeling isometric contractions. Recruitment patterns and strategies\h likely differ between isometric and\h\h the isotonic contractions that\h occur during typical exercises. Yet, I’m unaware of any reason to\h believe the main points (that failure\h\h offers no additional motor unit recruitment or\h enhancements in individual motor units force)\h\h would not also be the same\h with isotonic contractions. Moving on, is training to failure\h needed to max strength gains? The Grgic et al. meta-analysis found based\h on 15 studies (collectively comprising 265\h\h men and 129 women), there was no difference in\h gains between failure and non-failure training. A subgroup analysis also found the results\h stayed true for trained individuals. After independently assessing\h the studies, most of them\h\h seem to have had subjects leave between 5\h to 0 repetitions in reserve. So training\h\h with 5-0 reps in reserve may be similar to\h failure training for producing strength gains. Making this section clear, training\h to failure does not seem to promote\h\h additional hypertrophy or strength adaptations. Recall that high-intensity folks advocate low\h volumes, typically only one set per exercise. Does the literature support this recommendation? In 2017, a meta-analysis by Schoenfeld et\h\h al. combined the results of 15 studies\h comparing low to high volume training. Of the 15 studies, 14 had the low volume\h groups train with 1 set per exercise,\h\h while the high volume groups\h trained with 3 sets per exercise. It was found high volume was better than\h low volume for increasing muscle mass. Since 2017, three additional studies\h published also indicate performing\h\h 3 sets per exercise produces more\h muscle growth than performing 1 set. Why is this? It seems the higher volume attained with 3 sets\h\h ultimately stimulates the anabolic\h pathways within muscle fibers more. Demonstrating this, a 2010 study\h by Burd et al. compared fed-state\h\h myofibrillar protein synthesis\h after training with either 3\h\h or 1 set of reps to failure on the leg\h extension with a 70% one-rep max load. Performing 3 sets resulted not only in\h a greater fed-state myofibrillar protein\h\h synthesis amplitude but also a longer\h duration versus performing the 1 set. What about strength adaptations, how do\h low and high volumes compare for this? For this, we have a 2017\h meta-analysis by Ralston et al. They combined 9 studies comparing\h low vs high volumes for strength.\h\h 7 of the 9 studies had the low volume\h groups train only one set per exercise,\h\h and the high volume groups\h train with 3 sets per exercise. It was found strength gains were\h greater with the high volumes,\h\h indicating that 3 sets per exercise\h produce greater strength than 1 set. So overall, the current literature indicates\h\h that 1 set per exercise does not\h maximize size or strength gains. Another point mentioned by some high-intensity\h folks is that sets should never be added. Arthus Jones' stated, "never perform more\h than three sets of any one exercise". Mike Mentzer states "the tendency among\h enthusiastic bodybuilders is to add more\h\h sets to their workouts, etc., etc", "this tendency\h must be kept in check and avoided at all costs". Yet, some data suggests in trained individuals,\h\h modestly increasing weekly sets performed for\h a muscle group may accelerate muscle growth. A study by Aube et al. had\h trained men train the back\h\h squat and leg press with a variety of set numbers. After 8 weeks of training, the researchers\h divided the subjects into a high,\h\h moderate, or low responder group in terms\h of how much they grew their anterior thigh. Remember, the subjects were trained and had been\h consistently training before the study commenced. It was found those who grew their anterior thigh\h the most in the high responder group had increased\h\h their weekly set numbers the most relative to\h what they were performing before the study. Another study by Scarpelli et al. found in\h trained men, having them perform 20% more\h\h weekly sets for their quadriceps relative\h to what they performed before the study,\h\h produced larger vastus lateralis growth versus\h performing a prescribed number of 22 weekly sets. Collectively these data indicate\h for trained individuals,\h\h modestly increasing weekly\h set numbers (perhaps by 20%)\h\h can be effective for accelerating muscle gains,\h and may be a useful tool in the event of plateaus. The final main common theme of high-intensity\h regimes is lower frequency training. We noted Jones' ultimately recommended training\h each muscle group no more than twice per week,\h\h with perhaps better results from only one. Mike Mentzer recommended 96-120 hours of rest\h between training sessions. In fact, recall\h\h Mentzer also states he had a number of personal\h clients who trained once every 10-14 days. What does the literature\h say on training frequency? A range of studies has examined when keeping\h all other weekly training variables equal\h\h (including the number of sets performed\h for a muscle group each week),\h\h whether higher or lower\h frequency training is better. A 2019 meta-analysis by Schofield et\h al. combined 13 studies that did this\h\h and established similar muscle growth between\h lower and higher training frequencies. Out of the 13 studies included, 11\h had subjects train with a total of 12\h\h weekly sets per muscle group or fewer. So when training with a total of 12\h or fewer weekly sets per muscle group,\h\h lower and higher training frequencies\h seem to be similarly effective. As one illustration of this, Gomes et\h al. recruited 23 trained men with an\h\h average bench press one-rep max of 103kg\h and an average squat one-rep max of 132kg. A lower frequency group trained their\h muscle groups at a once per week frequency,\h\h while a higher frequency group trained their\h muscle groups at a five times per week frequency. Both groups accumulated 10\h weekly sets per muscle group. After 8 weeks of training, lean mass\h gains were similar between both groups. Now, when performing higher training\h volume (more than 12 weekly sets),\h\h the research is conflicting on whether lower\h or higher frequency training is better.\h\h Some find higher frequency to be better, others\h lower frequency, and some with no differences.\h\h We've more thoroughly examined this in our\h ultimate guide to training frequency video. Nonetheless, it's clear to see for hypertrophy,\h the research fails to demonstrate lower frequency\h\h training is superior. Higher frequency\h training appears perfectly viable. As for strength, a 2018 meta-analysis by Grgic et\h\h al. combined 7 studies and found with\h all other weekly training variables equal\h\h (again, including weekly sets per muscle\h group), training frequency had no impact. All 7 studies had subjects train with a total of\h 12 or fewer weekly sets per muscle group. Thus,\h\h with these volumes, both low and high-frequency\h training appear similarly effective for strength. When performing more than 12 weekly sets per\h muscle group, one study by Bartomolemi et al.\h\h compared training muscles with a frequency\h of 3/4x per week to only once a week. Strength gains were superior\h for the 3/4x frequency group. However, this isn't a consistent finding. 3 other studies indicate with more\h than 12 weekly sets per muscle group,\h\h lower and higher frequencies were\h similarly effective for strength gains. Fascinatingly, returning to the 2018 Grgic\h et al. meta-analysis, the researchers found\h\h when combining studies that did not equate weekly\h sets between lower and higher frequency training\h\h (resulting in the higher frequency training groups\h performing more weekly sets on their exercises),\h\h strength gains were greater\h with higher frequency training. This suggests using higher frequency\h training as a tool to help you perform\h\h more weekly sets may be an effective\h way to produce greater strength gains. In total, the research suggests lower\h frequencies are not superior for strength gains.\h\h Higher frequency training is perfectly viable. In fact, the Grgic et al. meta-analysis\h suggests higher training frequencies,\h\h when used in a way to accumulate more weekly sets,\h can effectively produce more strength adaptations. Moving forward, I wanted to discuss\h one point behind why high-intensity\h\h folks seemingly advocate lower frequencies. I think they assume that the body's\h capacity to recover is very limited. I'm not saying the body can handle\h an infinite amount of training.\h\h There's going to be a point above which\h more training will cause recovery problems. Yet, I feel high-intensity folks significantly\h underestimate where this point may be. After all, the repeated bout effect exists. Ever notice how when you first start\h training, extreme soreness and muscle\h\h performance decrease in the multiple days\h after. But after further weeks of training,\h\h soreness is minimal and no longer is muscle\h performance hampered for multiple days after. This is because of the repeated bout effect, the\h name given to the range of adaptations your body\h\h produces to make you resilient to damage,\h soreness, and force production decreases. It's not clear precisely what creates the repeated\h bout effect, but a 2017 study hypothesized neural,\h\h muscle-tendon, connective tissue, and\h inflammatory adaptations may all play a role. Now, many studies aiming to examine the time\h course of recovery after lifting weights\h\h only do so after a single training session. For example, this study found after trained\h men performed a session consisting of 3\h\h sets of repetitions to failure with a 12\h rep-max load on the bench press and squat,\h\h performance was still not fully\h recovered 48 hours after the session. Some may say this data indicates if your\h training with multiple sets to failure,\h\h more than 48 hours of rest\h is required between sessions. However, this suggestion ignores\h the fact the recovery time course\h\h was only examined after one training\h session. What would happen to the\h\h recovery time course after repeatedly\h training with multiple sets to failure? Due to the repeated bout effect,\h\h we'd expect recovery durations\h to progressively become shorter. My favorite study demonstrating\h this concept is this paper. They had 12 previously untrained perform\h 5 sets of 15 maximal eccentric only leg\h\h extension repetitions on an isokinetic\h dynamometer once a week for 10 weeks. Due to the machines, training loads would\h have increased as subjects got stronger. 5 sets of 15 MAXIMAL eccentric\h repetitions are extremely fatiguing. Eccentric training is known to\h produce more soreness and damage\h\h compared to normal training\h when first exposed to it. The data from the study demonstrates this. After the first training session, Creatine kinase\h\h (an indirect measure of muscle damage) was\h significantly elevated a day later, and muscle\h\h soreness and maximal isometric force production\h were still decreased 5 DAYS after the session. However, as the training weeks progressed,\h the repeated bout effect kicked in and\h\h all markers gradually decreased. This is\h something I feel people underappreciate. By the 10th week, the training\h session produced NO soreness,\h\h NO creatine kinase increases, and NO decreases\h in maximal isometric force in the upcoming days. In other words, subjects were\h recovering within 24 hours of\h\h the intense eccentric training session\h after 10 weeks of consistent training. Again, I'm not saying your body can recover\h from an infinite amount of training,\h\h rather the body can adapt robustly and\h handle a good amount of training over time.\h\h I feel high-intensity training\h regimes underappreciate this. I want to make it clear that by no means\h what this video aim to discredit or hate on\h\h high-intensity training. The goal was to evaluate\h if high-intensity training is supported by the\h\h current literature in the most non-bias way\h I can. I hope I was able to accomplish this. I’d like to say Mike Mentzer's book\h is highly interesting and in my view\h\h extraordinarily well written. I feel Mike\h Mentzer was simply interpreting the data and\h\h knowledge that was available at the time\h he composed the book (the early 2000s). Since then, we have a substantial amount of new\h research, and presumably in the next 20 years,\h\h more will emerge. Nevertheless, I still wanted to discuss aspects\h\h of high-intensity training I\h think are positive in some way. We mentioned training to failure does not\h appear to be essential. Stopping 5-3 reps\h\h from failure seems to be sufficient for maxing\h strength and hypertrophy gains, respectively. Yet, stopping a certain number\h of reps from failure requires\h\h you accurately judge how far from failure you are. This is challenging, and having experience with\h training to failure is likely required to do this. Psychologically, it's easier to train to failure\h when performing only one set per exercise. So high-intensity training can be a great\h\h way to accustom yourself to the\h feeling of training to failure. Progressing on, it's important to\h remember high-intensity training\h\h will unquestionably still build\h a substantial amount of muscle. We've mentioned how performing 3 sets per exercise\h\h tends to be better than 1 set\h for strength and hypertrophy. Yet, performing 3 sets does not\h give you 3x the more strength and\h\h hypertrophy versus performing 1 set,\h rather only marginally more gains. Returning to the Ralson et al. meta-analysis\h\h which found greater strength gains with\h high volume versus low volume training,\h\h the effect size difference was 0.18, which is\h interpreted as being a trivial difference only. As for the Schoenfeld et al. meta-analysis which\h\h found greater hypertrophy with high\h volume versus low volume training,\h\h the effect size difference was 0.24, which\h is interpreted as a small difference only. Now, it's important to remember\h the studies involved in these\h\h analyses largely lasted 12 weeks\h or less, so these trivial to small\h\h gains achieved with 3 sets versus 1 set\h may become more pronounced long-term. Regardless, it's clear you're still going\h build a lot of muscle with low volume\h\h training like high-intensity training.\h Many people, for one reason or another,\h\h may not want to invest extra time in higher\h volume training for slightly more gains. So\h\h high-intensity training can be a great\h time-efficient method for these folks. Finally, and this is a very important point I\h want to emphasize, it might be possible that\h\h some individuals truly grow more with lower\h volume training versus higher volume training. Remember all the research findings\h presented thus far are the average results. Such results are not always\h applicable to an individual. Matter of fact, this study demonstrates this. 16 men and 18 women trained the unilateral\h leg press and unilateral leg extension with\h\h a 7-10 rep-max load, three\h times per week for 12 weeks. With one-leg, subjects trained\h each exercise with only one set.\h\h With the other leg, they trained\h each exercise with three sets. Cross-sectional area of the quadriceps\h was measured before and after the study. The graph shows the individual\h responses for each participant.\h\h The Y-axis shows the cross-sectional area\h increases for the leg that trained with 3 sets,\h\h and the X-axis shows the cross-sectional area\h increases for the leg that trained with 1 set. The results show a near 50/50 split, with 50%\h seeing better gains with 3 sets per exercise,\h\h and the other 50% seeing similar\h or more gains with 1 set. The researchers also looked at strength (they\h averaged out the results from 3 different\h\h strength tests), and the findings\h were similar, a near 50/50 split. These findings truly surprised me, and if\h they can be replicated on a larger scale,\h\h they might suggest many folks experience\h no benefit with higher volumes. However, it's essential to remember\h only 34 subjects were in this study,\h\h so it's very difficult to say this\h exact distribution applies to everyone. Moreover, all these subjects were\h untrained. As mentioned , there's\h\h data showing increasing set numbers in\h trained individuals benefits hypertrophy,\h\h so I'm skeptical these distributions\h hold true for trained individuals. Regardless, it is likely true some individuals\h grow at least the same or even possibly more with\h\h lower volume training, and high-intensity\h training may be great for these folks. Crystalizing everything, the current literature\h\h does not suggest high-intensity training\h is optimal for building muscle or strength. Training to failure isn't essential,\h higher volumes tend to be better than\h\h lower volumes on average, and higher training\h frequencies are also perfectly viable for gains. Still, high-intensity training will build a\h substantial amount of muscle and strength,\h\h and for some individuals, low-volume\h training like this could actually be optimal.

So this paper, which had several good things going for it, found doing triple the number of sets failed to produce greater gains. This study was done on untrained individuals, but there are still numerous examples of untrained individuals growing more from multiple sets versus a single set. Some may say this is yet again an example of science flip-flopping and that you can find any study to support anything. thus rendering science useless. However, these notions stem from a misunderstanding of science. These findings are actually completely compatible with three sets really being superior to one set. I'm fully aware that may sound like an insane thing to say, but I can demonstrate why. Before that, I should emphasize I am not saying low set numbers are bad. It's clear they can absolutely stimulate hypertrophy even in trained individuals. So, can be excellent if you're short on training time. With this new study, we could analyze the methods. We could wonder whether a greater contrast between the low and high sets, a longer duration, or other factors might yield different results. We do this often at the house hypertrophy. Unsurprisingly, it can be a valid way to figure out why studies arrive at different conclusions. But there is an alternative explanation that deserves more attention. It can tell us why even with perfect and identical methods, we can get studies that seem to conflict. In fact, it's something we should expect. Understanding this can reshape how you view single studies. Of course, whenever we run a study, we're trying to figure out at the population level, what training method builds the most muscle. For example, in the billions of untrained people between 18 to 35 years old, or in the millions of trained people between 18 to 35 years old, how does one set compare to three sets on average? We can't run a study on millions or billions of people. So we take samples from our population hoping our results reflect the true population effects. But we always risk obtaining a sample that fails to reflect the overall population by chance. This is especially true with small sample sizes which are common in the exercise science literature. A simple example conveys this. Let's say we have a fair coin. It's quite possible purely by chance that all three flips land on heads which may lead us to incorrectly conclude that the coin is biased towards heads. But as we flip it more times, we get closer to reality. There are many possible sources of error. In the case where we have subjects train one limb with one set and the other limb with three sets, although there are advantages to this design, there are still considerations. Perhaps some had one limb notably smaller to begin with, giving it greater growth potential. Perhaps some were doing things outside the study that impaired the stimulus to one limb over the other. There's also measurement error which by chance could influence one limb more than the other. Finally, a proportion of individuals may genuinely experience similar growth between one and three sets in certain cases, but they may be the exception. We'll discuss individual differences near the end. Again, I can't emphasize enough how these things are more likely to be problematic with small samples. We can use simulations to make this point strikingly clear. Credit goes to James Kger who ran the following simulation. His article is linked in the description. This is based on comparing different groups of people, but it gets the overall point across. Let us make a population with 3 million trained individuals. We're going to say that over a given period, high volumes increase biceps thickness by 3 mm, moderate volumes by 2 mm, and low volumes by 1 mm. Of course, not every single person grows identically. So, let's say each volume condition has a standard deviation of 2 mm. Since we've made all this up, we know for a fact these are the true population effects. But what happens if we simulate five studies comparing low, moderate, and high volumes with 10 subjects per group using statistical software to simulate this? These were the five study results Creger obtained. The studies vary notably. Only study one shows us something that resembles the true population effects. The rest show different patterns. There are instances of a plateau at moderate volumes. high volumes being numerically worse than moderate volumes and moderate volumes being numerically worse than lower volumes. Looking at this, you may be tempted to conclude science is worthless. But larger sample sizes can help overcome this. We can also absolutely make use of small sample size research by combining them into a meta analysis which gives us greater statistical power and likely more accurate insight. Indeed, Creger combined the results of the five papers into a meta analysis and we can see it's pretty close to the true population effects. So mixed results are to be expected. This is why at the house hypertrophy whenever we're overviewing a single study we always try to detail the broader literature in attempt to get closer to the truth. Each study is ultimately a single data point belonging to a future meta analysis. At this point you may be wondering do we have any meta analyses on sets and hypertrophy? Regular viewers will know the answer is yes. Here is the latest meta analysis, specifically a meta regression. More sets tend to cause more hypertrophy with diminishing returns. A proportion saw greater gains with three sets, some similar gains, and a smaller number saw greater gains with one set. Yet, this data may not necessarily prove individual differences due to some points noted earlier, which are even more relevant when interpreting the results of one person. Unfortunately, the study designs necessary to demonstrate true individual differences haven't been done in the muscle growth literature, so nothing conclusive can be said. I will say my best guess is that individual differences exist. Physiological mechanisms could be in play, but also lifestyle factors. If you're going through a stressful period in your life, your response to higher volumes of training may be impaired. Currently, I think the best bet is to use the average effects in the literature as a starting point. It remains possible that they are generalizable to most people, but it's not a definitive training prescription. You can adjust things where you feel it's appropriate. For example, if you're performing a high number of sets and feel underreovered, you can experiment with lower sets.  kol%, H-plplpl coverage, kol-pl coverage, kol-pl coverage, kol-pl coverage, kol-pl coverage, building realm. Some have been dismantled by the scientific literature. Do you still believe them? By the end, we will have separated facts from fiction in five key areas, and you'll have some knowledge to help you along your muscle-building journey. The pump is a temporary increase in muscle size achieved from lifting. Some think of it as a preview of upcoming solidified gains. During intense muscular contractions, a flow of events involving increased blood volume and fluid explains the pump. Some find immense pleasure in the pump. Some say maxing the pump maximizes gains. In fact, popular bodybuilding coach Harney Rambord devised the FST7 program, including components of higher sets and shorter rest to maximize the pump. The belief being this stretches out of the fascia to make room for growth. Multiple high-level bodybuilders have trained with this method. Luckily, this 2023 paper had trained individuals perform an FST-inspired program for the biceps and triceps. The volume was super high and the rest between sets short. One group actually stretched between some of the sets, while another rested passively. The result? Overall arm hypertrophy in both groups was minimal, with multiple non-statistically significant gains. Some even slightly lost size, possibly as the higher volumes led to excessive damage that oriented the protein synthesis response to repair rather than growth. Now, as detailed in some other videos at the house of hypertrophy, higher volumes can produce respectable hypertrophy. But there's good reason to believe the pump's relation to hypertrophy is not strong. When researchers have pharmacologically induced reactive hyperemia, protein synthesis isn't improved. Multiple training strategies also enhance the pump, but not your gains. Higher reps evoke a greater pump, but tend to be similar to lower reps. Although, super high reps can produce a tremendous pump, but inferior gains. Drop sets involve performing multiple bouts of reps to failure with progressively lighter loads. They will produce an incredible pump, but seem to largely be similar to normal sets. A constant tension technique avoids locking out the joints and elicits a great pump, but the majority of the research finds them to be similarly effective to a normal technique. So what does this mean for you? Don't worry about maxing the pump. Think of it as a byproduct of your training, not the goal. This is not to say you can't chase the pump. Many of the techniques that produce a greater pump do not compromise gains. So feel free to enjoy that pump if you like. Time under tension refers to the duration of one of your sets. A longer time under tension or reaching a desired target is often recommended. The popular Mike Mensah even recommended a slow 4 second lifting and 4 second lowering tempo. Tension has been identified as likely the primary initiator of muscle hypertrophy, so you may logically deduce time under tension is important. But what does the scientific literature say? A recent review finds that provided you're training hard and getting to or near failure, slower tempos, which involve higher time under tension, largely produce similar muscle hypertrophy to comparatively faster tempos. On top of this, we've already noted how provided you're training hard and getting to or near failure, the research finds a wide range of rep numbers are similarly effective for stimulating gains. Most of these studies use a 1-2 second lifting and lowering tempo, although reps naturally slow down as you near failure. Either way, time under tension is widely different across this range, but gains are similar. So what's going on? Time under tension shouldn't be mistaken for mechanical tension. The tension we care about is optimized by training hard. Getting to or close to failure forces the body to recruit all the fibers we can and expose them to tension. This kicks off events in all these fibers that conclude in growth. And yes, this means both lower and higher reps can similarly involve high tension. When people prolong time under tension, a lot of that initial time is very far from failure. Accordingly, what we may call time under high tension, which is what matters, ends up being similar. What all this means for you is it's absolutely not essential to prolong or reach a specific time under tension threshold. You can do it if you like since it's not inherently detrimental. This part somewhat links to the pump, as shorter rest time between sets invariably enhances the pump. Despite this, we have well-designed papers finding that resting 2.5-3 minutes between sets actually produces greater hypertrophy than resting for less time. What's going on? Well, transient anabolic hormonal elevations do not appear to be strongly related to the hypertrophy process. In general, it's possible that longer rest more effectively dissipates fatigue that would otherwise limit your ability to expose your fibers to tension. Anyhow, the key takeaway is despite the common practice of bodybuilders, shorter rests between sets are not superior. So if you need to take your time between sets, particularly between compound exercise sets, rest assured you're likely helping, not hurting, your gains. Lifting weight causes micro tears in your muscles. Your body then repairs the damage and enlarges the tissue. This is probably the single most frequent explanation for how muscle growth happens. A consequence of this is many may feel muscle soreness is essential and a valid proxy to know gains will occur. Although, it's interesting to know there are multiple potential causes of soreness. Damage might not just be the only thing going on. Nonetheless, what does the literature say about damage and hypertrophy? There are a few cases in the literature where researchers find that a program with greater average damage just ends up producing similar muscle hypertrophy to a program with lower average damage. Furthermore, your body adapts and reduces the damage you see from training over time, but significant growth still happens. Finally, although there are speculated pathways through which damage causes growth, there are strong counter-arguments to them. None of this is to say damage plays no role in hypertrophy, although it's possible researchers end up discovering it has no role. Hypertrophy was similar between both groups. In the last few videos, we've been going\h into detail with rep ranges. In this video, we'll explore if\h\h performing different rep ranges in your training\h program can help build more muscle compared to\h\h using only one rep range. Theoretically, different\h rep ranges could target different muscle fibers.\h\h Muscles are generally made up of slow twitch and\h fast twitch fibers. Given, slow twitch muscle fibers\h\h are highly resistant to fatigue and produce low\h amounts of power, it's suggested higher repetitions\h\h would grow these fibers more than lower\h repetitions. A meta-analysis by\h Jozo Grgic combined the results of 5 studies\h\h looking at this area. In these 5 studies, the\h higher repetition groups used loads ranging from\h\h 30% to 50% of their one\h rep max on an exercise. rResulting in around 20\h\h to 40 repetitions to failure each set. The lower\h repetition groups used the loads ranging from 75\h\h % to 90% of their one rep max on an exercise.\h Resulting in around 3 to 10 repetitions to\h\h failure each set. Combining the results of the 5 studies, growth of slow twitch muscle fibers was\h\h similar between the higher repetition and lower\h repetition groups. Likewise, growth of fast twitch muscle fibers were similar between the higher\h repetition and lower repetition groups. Now, in this\h\h meta-analysis, the 95% confidence intervals were\h wide. Essentially, meaning we should approach these\h\h results with some caution. More research in the\h future will still be helpful. Nevertheless, the idea\h\h that higher and lower reps do a similar job at\h growing slow twitch and fast twitch muscle fibers,\h\h provided those reps are performed to or very\h close to failure, would make sense. Muscle fibers\h\h are recruited in a progressive sequence. During\h low effort tasks, slow twtich muscle fibers are\h\h recruited. But as your effort increases, faster\h twitch muscle fibers are gradually recruited.\h\h When using heavier loads and therefore lower\h repetitions, many slow twitch and fast twitch\h\h fibers are going to be initially recruited, as your\h effort is high straight away. When using lighter loads\h\h and therefore higher repetitions, the reps\h are going to be fairly low effort initially.\h\h But as you continue and get closer and closer to\h failure, your effort increases. As a result, research\h\h indicates you ultimately end up with many slow\h twitch and fast twitch muscle fibers recruited,\h\h probably similar to what you achieve with heavier\h loads. So, the current evidence leans towards\h\h the idea that higher or lower repetitions\h do not stimulate different muscle fibers.\h\h However, another potential reason behind why\h you may want to use different rep ranges\h\h relates to the activation of proteins. Looking at the\h\h individual data for the vastus lateralis, the\h results are similar. So, except for the triceps,\h\h the varied and constant group experienced similar\h gains. === FILE: Are Isolation Exercises USELESS for Muscle Hypertrophy？ (19 STUDIES) [Qtm1yCpjiPM].en.txt ===

Bro, don't you know isolation\h exercises do nothing? What are you on about? Science has shown adding isolation exercises to a\h\h compound exercise program does\h not produce more muscle growth. Wait, what? You sure this is the correct\h interpretation of the research? Let me check what House of Hypertrophy has to say. Are compound exercises (exercises that train two\h\h or more muscle groups) enough\h for maxing muscle hypertrophy? And are isolation exercises (exercises that\h train one muscle group) just a waste of time? A couple of scientific papers have\h suggested this. Let us examine them. A 2015 Brazillian study by Gentil et al. compared\h lat pulldowns to barbell biceps curls for elbow\h\h flexor growth. The elbow flexors consisted of\h the biceps and brachialis muscles in this case. After 10 weeks of training, increases\h in elbow flexor thickness were similar\h\h between the lat pulldown and biceps curl training. Suggesting an isolation exercise (the biceps curl)\h\h does not produce any more growth to\h a compound exercise (the latpulldown) However, this study does not tell us if\h compared to only performing lat pulldowns,\h\h the combination of lat pulldowns and\h curls could enhance elbow flexor growth. Fortunately, another 2013 Brazillian\h study by Gentil et al. evaluated this. Group one only trained the\h bench press and lat pulldown. Group two performed the bench press\h and lat pulldown with the addition of\h\h a biceps curl and triceps extension. Both groups performed 3 sets of\h 8-12 repetitions to failure on each\h\h exercise per session. This meant training volume\h was not equated between both groups. As group two\h\h performed two additional isolation exercises, they\h would have accumulated higher training volumes. Despite this, after 10 weeks of training,\h\h increases in elbow flexor thickness\h were similar between both groups. Indicating adding biceps curls\h to lat pulldown training does not\h\h enhance elbow flexor growth versus\h only training lat pulldowns. Unfortunately, the researchers did not\h assess triceps growth in this study. In 2015, another Brazillian study by Franca et\h al. further supported these previous findings. Group one trained with the following training\h program, consisting of only compound exericses. Group two trained with all\h the same compound exercises,\h\h but performed two added\h isolation exercises per session. Both groups performed 3 sets of 10-15\h reps for each exercise per session,\h\h again meaning group two would have\h accumulated higher training volumes. After 8 weeks of training,\h increases in arm circumference\h\h were statistically similar between both groups. Suggesting yet again that additional\h\h isolation exercises provide no\h further muscle growth benefit. These three research papers (the ones\h just overviewed) were later included\h\h in a 2017 review study by Gentil et al.,\h in which it was stated "the addition of SJ\h\h exercises to an MJ exercise program does not seem\h to increase gains in muscle size and strength". SJ stands for single-joint,\h\h which are isolation exercises, while MJ stands\h for multi-joint, which are compound exercises. Before moving on, it's worth\h noting that since 2017,\h\h 4 additional studies all published by\h Barbalho et al. further indicate that\h\h additional isolation exercises to a compound\h exercise program do not enhance muscle growth. However, it's recently been established\h much research by Barbalho et al. contains\h\h improbable and atypical data. The data\h in these studies cannot be trusted,\h\h perhaps because the data is illegitimate. Thus, I believe we cannot use these\h studies as additional evidence. Hello There. You're killing your gains. So it's clear some researchers speculate\h compound exercises may indeed max hypertrophy. But as many of you are probably thinking,\h surely there exist limitations and shortcomings. Indeed, I believe there are, and many of\h these limitations were nicely discussed in\h\h a paper by Ribeiro et al. that was directly\h responding to the Gentil et al. review paper Firstly, only growth of the elbow\h flexors and arms were measured,\h\h and only at a single region of these muscles\h (roughly the midpoints of the muscles). This begs the question,\h\h what about other regions of these muscles,\h and what about other muscle groups? Examining the question about other\h regions of the same muscle first,\h\h I believe there's sufficient evidence\h to believe regional hypertrophy exists. That is, an exercise for a muscle does not\h grow all regions of that muscle equally,\h\h rather it grows some regions more than others. For example, Kawakami et al. found after subjects\h trained overhead extensions for 16 weeks,\h\h the triceps mainly increased in cross-sectional\h area in the middle to slightly lower regions.\h\h But in the most upper and lower regions of\h the muscle, little growth was experienced. Likewise, Ema et al. found after\h leg extension training for 12 weeks,\h\h growth not only differed between\h the quadriceps heads but within\h\h each of these muscle heads, growth differed\h between the upper and lower regions of them. This data might suggest that if we wanted to\h maximize growth across as many regions of a\h\h muscle as possible, using a range of exercises\h that biomechanically differ could work. The biomechanically different exercises,\h\h when compared to each other, may target different\h regions of the muscle more so than others,\h\h so collectively they maximize growth\h across the regions of a muscle. Isolation exercises would be\h necessary and pivotal in this. A 2021 Brazillian study by\h Costa et al. supports this. 22 men were allocated into a\h non-varied or varied group. Both groups trained 3 days per week for 8 weeks The non-varied group did train with\h both compound and isolation exercises,\h\h but they performed the exact same\h exercises on the 3 training days per week. The varied group, on each\h of the three days per week,\h\h performed different compound and isolation\h exercises for their muscle groups. Before and after the study, the researchers\h measured the thickness of the upper, middle,\h\h and lower regions of the rectus femoris,\h vastus lateralis, elbow flexors, and triceps. In a couple of measured regions, increases\h were similar between both groups.\h\h However, in other measured regions,\h gains favored the varied group.\h\h Thus, the varied group experienced\h the most regional hypertrophy overall. As a result, this study suggests performing a\h couple of different exercises for a muscle group\h\h (specifically 3 different isolation\h and compound movements per week)\h\h promotes growth across regions of a muscle. Moving forward, other muscle\h groups not examined in the three\h\h previously mentioned studies are likely\h minimally trained with compound exercises. The lateral deltoid abducts the shoulder joint.\h\h No compound exercise significantly involves\h this motion, so isolation exercises that do this\h\h (like lateral raises) are likely required\h to maximally grow the lateral deltoid. The calf muscles plantarflex the ankle, a motion\h that no compound exercise significantly involves.\h\h So plantarflexion exercises\h like seated and standing calf\h\h raises are likely needed to max calf hypertrophy. Compound exercises training the hamstrings\h primarily do so via hip extension movement. However, the hamstrings also flex the knee,\h and there's evidence different parts of the\h\h hamstrings may be recruited during either hip\h extension and knee flexion motion. Thus, knee\h\h flexion exercises (like leg curls) are probably\h needed to max regional hamstring hypertrophy. Compound exercises that train the quadriceps\h seem to grow the vasti muscle heads very well,\h\h but not the rectus femoris. Leg\h extensions and reverse nordic\h\h curls significantly develop the rectus femoris,\h\h so one of these isolation exercises are likely\h necessary to optimally grow all quadricep heads. As for the triceps, two studies\h indicate the bench press fairly\h\h develops the lateral and medial triceps\h heads, but minimally the long head. You see, the long head crosses\h both the shoulder and elbow joints\h\h (the lateral and medial heads\h only cross the elbow joint). And many compound exercises that train the triceps\h (like the bench press, push-up, and even dips)\h\h involve shoulder extension during the lowering\h phase of the exercise, a motion that shortens the\h\h long head and inhibits it from significantly\h producing force during the lifting phase. Isolation exercises such as skull\h crushers, overhead extensions,\h\h and rope pushdowns have all been shown\h to significantly develop the long head. Moreover, recall the Costa et al. study\h found training with a variety of triceps\h\h isolation exercises in a week resulted in\h growth across more regions of the triceps. It’s clear substantial hypertrophy can\h be achieved with compound exercises only. Yet the conclusion compound\h exercises are sufficient for\h\h muscle hypertrophy is likely incorrect. Many muscle groups and regions of a muscle\h group are likely not optimally trained with\h\h compound exercises, hence additional\h isolation exercises are necessary.

These lines of evidence and\h reasoning would go against\h\h the idea that there's something\h special about dumbbell curls. Anyway, logically, dumbbell and barbell curls\h involve more or less identical motions at the\h\h elbow. Most resistance training studies, like the\h Gentil and Mannario studies, have a fairly\h\h small sample size (10-30 subjects). The probability of these two studies\h\h recruiting subjects with a comparable\h ability to gain muscle is unlikely. As a result, the simple fact these two\h studies used different subjects may further\h\h partly explain why the dumbbell curls produced\h greater growth in the Mannario et al. study. So, returning to the core of the\h video, when assessing the two studies,\h\h although it seems that rows are far less\h effective than biceps curls for biceps growth,\h\h lat pulldowns may be similarly\h effective to bicep curls. From this, you may be tempted to think that\h rows and lat pulldowns could be sufficient\h\h for biceps development, given lat pulldowns\h may be itself enough for growing the biceps. However, as alluded to earlier,\h the study by Gentil et al.\h\h finding lat pulldowns produced similar biceps\h growth to bicep curls is limited as it only\h\h measured elbow flexor growth at one region\h (10 centimeters from the cubital fossa). Conversely, the study by Mannario et al.\h\h measured (and then averaged)\h three regions across the biceps\h\h (25%, 50%, and 75% of the muscle's length), making\h it more insightful for overall biceps development. The reason why it is useful to measure\h growth at many regions of a muscle\h\h is that muscles do not appear to grow uniformly. Although Gentil et al. found similar\h growth between the lat pulldown\h\h and barbell biceps curl at one region\h of the muscle, it's quite possible at\h\h other regions, growth responses would\h be different between the two exercises. And this brings us on to probably the\h most important point of the video. The research would appear to suggest that to\h maximize growth across regions of a muscle,\h\h a fair degree of exercise variation is important. This would indicate that rows and lat pulldowns\h are not sufficient for optimal biceps development. A study by Costa et al. demonstrates this nicely. They had 22 detrained men train\h 3 times per week for 9 weeks. One group of subjects trained\h their biceps with lat pulldowns\h\h and barbell bicep curls each session. Another group of subjects varied\h their exercises each week. On day 1 of each week, their biceps\h were also trained with lat pulldowns\h\h and barbell bicep curls. But on day 2 of each week, they trained with lat\h pulldowns behind the neck and preacher curls,\h\h and on day 3 of each week, lat pulldowns with\h a narrow grip and incline dumbbell curls. As a note, both groups trained each\h exercise with 3 sets of 8-12 repetitions. Before and after the study,\h thickness of the elbow flexors\h\h was measured at 50%, 60%, and 70% of\h the upper arm length for both groups. Overall, increases in thickness were\h greater for the group that varied their\h\h exercises, particularly at 50%\h and 60% of the upper arm length. Therefore, front lat pulldowns\h and barbell biceps curl\h\h were inferior to a variety of lat\h pulldowns and curl variations. It's not clear whether it was the variation\h of lat pulldowns, variation of curls,\h\h or even the combination of both that produced\h the superior results for the varied group,\h\h but this study nonetheless demonstrates\h that a fair amount of exercise variety\h\h is beneficial for regional muscle\h growth, likely indirectly indicating\h\h rows and lat pulldowns are not sufficient\h for overall biceps development.

=== FILE: Become Laser Accurate When Leaving Reps in Reserve (New Research) [qmjr8kMaUH8].en.txt ===

Last video, we detailed how the current research,\h\h as well as mechanistic reasoning, imply\h stopping between 0 to 3 repetitions away from\h\h failure can produce similar muscle\h hypertrophy to training to failure. For clarification, when I say stopping\h between 0 to 3 repetitions away from failure,\h\h I'm referring to leaving between\h 0 to 3 repetitions in reserve.\h\h That is, leaving 0 repetitions in reserve\h indicates you stopped at the point where\h\h you feel you cannot perform another full\h repetition, while leaving 3 repetitions\h\h in reserve indicates you believe could\h have performed 3 more full repetitions. Additionally, failure refers to technical failure,\h\h the point at which no more repetitions\h with correct execution can be performed. This definition was essentially\h used in the studies we assessed,\h\h and I believe this is probably the most\h sensible definition as it makes little\h\h sense to significantly deviate from using\h the correct execution for muscle hypertrophy. For example, in a barbell biceps curl,\h technical failure would refer to the\h\h point where you can no longer flex your elbows\h upwards while maintaining a fairly rigid posture,\h\h as your elbow flexor muscles can no\h longer produce the required force. If you were to try to continue\h and start introducing momentum,\h\h either via swinging your back or using your\h legs, your spinal erectors or leg muscles would\h\h be contributing towards moving the weight, your\h elbow flexors would not be doing any more work\h\h (and in some instances, its\h recruitment might actually decrease). Of course, in the real world, your execution\h will likely deviate slightly as you get closer\h\h and closer to failure, but it's likely sensible\h to try your best to minimize any deviation. Returning to the topic of this video,\h as noted, leaving 0 to 3 repetitions in\h\h reserve likely produces similar muscle\h But, there's a potential\h problem with implementing this. A person might be inaccurate at\h estimating how close to failure\h\h they truly are. An individual may think\h they've left 3 repetitions in reserve,\h\h but they might have truly left 5 or\h even more repetitions in reserve. How common is underestimating\h proximity to failure? Moreover, how could an individual ensure greater\h\h accuracy in estimating how\h close to failure they are? A recent 2020 meta-analysis by Halperin\h et al. answers these questions. They combined the results of 12\h studies that examined how well\h\h individuals estimate their proximity to failure. Before detailing the findings, it's worth briefly\h understanding the design of the included studies. The 12 studies had a mix of designs. The studies ranged from having subjects\h perform repetitions to failure with A-50\h\h to 90% one-rep max load. Most of\h the studies used compound exercises,\h\h with the back squat and bench\h press being commonly used. Although, other exercises like leg\h presses, chest presses, trap bar deadlifts,\h\h as well as biceps and triceps isolation\h exercises were also used in a few studies. Some studies had subjects estimate\h how many repetitions they think they\h\h could perform with a given load on an\h exercise before performing the set,\h\h others had subjects estimate at some point during\h the set. For instance, a few studies had subjects\h\h stop at the 10th repetition with a 70% one-rep\h max load to report how many more repetitions\h\h they think they could achieve before they\h went onto complete repetitions until failure. Furthermore, a few studies alternatively had\h subjects report once they felt they reached a\h\h certain number of repetitions in reserve. For\h example, subjects reported once they felt they\h\h hit the point of 3 repetitions in reserve before\h returning and performing repetitions to failure. Let's move on to the results. Combining the 12 studies results,\h\h on average, subjects actually only underestimated\h their proximity to failure by 1 repetition.\h\h Although, as evidenced by the graph,\h there was quite some variation. A fair\h\h few subjects underestimated their proximity\h to failure by 1 to 3 repetitions. However,\h\h some subjects underestimated their proximity\h to failure by as much as 10 to 13 repetitions. Let's now explore some meta-regressions\h performed that can aid an individual\h\h in improving their accuracy at\h estimating proximity to failure. Accuracy increased when subjects gave\h their predictions closer to failure.\h\h This means that studies in which subjects\h reported how many repetitions they thought\h\h they could perform before a set produced less\h accurate estimates compared to studies in\h\h which subjects reported estimates at some\h point during a set. Also, during a set,\h\h making a prediction closer to failure is better\h than making a prediction father from failure. These findings imply that if an individual\h plans to train with repetitions in reserve,\h\h it's likely best to avoid pre-planning how\h many repetitions you think will achieve\h\h this before the set. Instead, you should\h simply perform your repetitions and\h\h end the set only once you truly feel you've\h reached the desired proximity to failure. Accuracy was much better when subjects trained\h with heavier loads that resulted in fewer\h\h repetitions. Using loads that resulted\h in more than 12 repetitions performed\h\h generally resulted in greater underestimations.\h These findings make sense, with higher repetitions\h\h (and thus lighter loads), there's\h a lot more room for error.\h\h Additionally, lighter loads and higher\h repetitions have been shown to produce\h\h greater perceived exertion and discomfort compared\h to using heavier loads and fewer repetitions.\h\h These factors can mask an individual's ability\h to truly delineate their proximity to failure. For muscle hypertrophy, we know\h it's quite likely loads between 30%\h\h to 85% one-rep max are similarly effective at\h building muscle. Therefore, it's probably sensible\h\h for individuals to train on the heavier side of\h this if they wish to use repetitions in reserve. Accuracy slightly improved during predictions\h in later sets compared to earlier sets. This could be for a couple of reasons.\h Firstly, remember that technically the\h\h subjects of the studies took\h all their sets to failure,\h\h they just estimated their proximities to failure\h at certain time points before achieving failure.\h\h As a consequence, those earlier sets to failure\h may have acutely made them more accustomed\h\h and aware of the feeling of failure, thereby\h enhancing their prediction accuracy in later sets. The potential implication of this\h is that if you're someone who\h\h prefers to mix in failure and leaving\h repetitions in reserve in a session,\h\h it might be better to perform\h your failure sets first. For example, let's say you perform 4 sets\h with a certain load on the triceps skull\h\h crusher in a session. Performing the\h first 2 sets to failure may set you\h\h up for being more accurate if you were to use\h repetitions in reserves for the last two sets. Accuracy was slightly worse with lower body\h exercises versus upper body exercises. It's\h\h useful to be aware of this and recognize you may\h have to push slightly harder than you naturally\h\h anticipate if you use repetitions in\h reserve with lower body exercises. Finally, and quite unexpectedly, training\h status minimally impacted accuracy.\h\h That is, on average, having multiple years\h of resistance training experience seemingly\h\h did not significantly enhance an individual's\h ability to predict how close to failure they are. It's not clear why this is. Although I'm not certain, it might simply be\h because many of the trained individuals in\h\h these studies may not have had a fair degree\h of experience with training to failure. It seems reasonable to think if the researchers\h divided the trained individuals into those with\h\h minimal to no experience of training to\h failure and those with a fair degree of\h\h failure training experience, an effect might\h be seen such that those with failure training\h\h experience would be more accurate than\h those with no failure training experience. If true, which I think it probably\h would be as it makes logical sense,\h\h gaining experience and familiarity with\h training to failure should enhance your\h\h accuracy when you use repetitions in reserve. Perhaps you may perform a select few of your sets\h for a given exercise with repetitions to failure,\h\h or you could dedicate occasional blocks where\h most of your sets are performed to failure. In summary, the current literature, although\h there is some variability, intriguing\h\h indicates individuals only underestimate their\h proximity to failure by one repetition on average. Generally, it's best not to pre-plan how\h many repetitions you should perform with a\h\h given load to reach a certain proximity to\h failure, rather simply perform repetitions\h\h with this load and stop only once you truly feel\h you've reached your desired proximity to failure. Training with heavier loads and lower\h repetitions likely makes it easier to\h\h estimate your proximity to failure versus\h lighter loads and higher repetitions. It's worth being aware individuals tend to be\h more accurate with estimates in later sets,\h\h as well as with upper body exercises\h compared to lower body exercises. Finally, it's likely gaining a fair degree\h of experience with training to failure is\h\h beneficial for being accustomed and familiar\h with how failure feels to you, thereby plausibly\h\h enhancing your ability to estimate your closeness\h to failure when you do use repetitions in reserve.

=== FILE: Bench Press OPTIMAL Bar Path to Lift Heavier #shorts [XrgypgL8bpw].en.txt ===

Interesting research by McLaughlin found that during maximal bench press attempts, bar paths differed between novices and elite lifters. They both lowered the bar similarly, a slightly curved diagonal line from above the shoulders to the mid to lower chest region. However, the novices lifted the bar straight up initially, and then back over the shoulders. Conversely, elite lifters pushed the bar back initially, and then straight up. This technique seems to be substantially more efficient in helping you lift heavier loads, likely because it makes the exercise easier on the shoulders. For more details, see the pinned comment in the comment section.

=== FILE: Biceps Curls With NO WEIGHT Build Muscle Optimally (Study) [ipNBCdopegM].en.txt ===

Biceps curls are most commonly performed with\h weights, be it with dumbbells or barbells. However, what if you saw someone doing this in the\h\h gym (show image of lifting no weight),\h bicep curling without any weight? What if I told you that this can build muscle? I'm not just talking about a\h small degree of muscle growth,\h\h rather potentially a similar amount\h to bicep curling with weight. Sounds crazy right? === FILE: Bigger Biceps： This NEW Study Is Interesting [5zxj4rXg4tU].en.txt ===

Welcome to the house of hypertrophy. Is there a best biceps exercise? A brand new study has added to the research comparing biceps exercises, and it's the first study to make a specific comparison. Let's dive in. 15 untrained men were recruited. With one arm, they trained Beijian cable cos, which have the shoulder extended. With their other arm, they trained preacher curls which have the shoulder flexed. Since both the long and short heads of the biceps cross the shoulder, placing the shoulder into extension lengthens the biceps, while placing the shoulder into flexion shortens the biceps. This is the first study to compare shoulder extended versus shoulder flex curls where the resistance profiles were matched. What I mean is that the cables were set up so that both exercises were hardest at roughly 60° of elbow flexion. Subjects trained twice per week for 10 weeks, performing three to five sets of 8 to 12 reps to or very close to failure. Loads were adjusted across sets as well as training sessions to keep subjects training in the 8 to 12 rep range before and after the study. The thickness of the biceps was measured across these three regions, while the thickness of the brachiialis was measured across these two regions. This was excellent since some previous research just measures elbow flexor muscle thickness which is a measurement that does not distinguish between the biceps and brachiialis. So it's great these researchers separated out the biceps and brachiialis. It was found that both exercises grew all regions and there was no statistically significant differences in any region. This may lead some to conclude that the biceps do not benefit from being trained at longer lengths. But is this correct? I think there's a chance this is not. We can see the biceps particularly at the 55% region grew more with the Bayian curls. Also, the lowest brachialis region slightly favors the preacher coals. You may be thinking, so what? It was not statistically significant. In simple terms, this tells us that the differences between conditions was not large enough to be confident in a genuine difference and any difference could be due to error of some kind. This could be true and it's a justifiable response. But here's the thing. Type two errors do occur where we say there's no difference when in fact there is a real difference. Small sample sizes can result in studies being underpowered to detect small to moderate real differences. Here's a quote from a paper titled, "What exercise and sport scientists don't understand. Not significant does not equal no difference. In many cases, it means not enough power." Now, if this was the only study we had to make inferences, I would agree we can't say much. But there's more data that makes me think Beijian curls could really grow the biceps a little more. The evidence that leads me to speculate there could be genuine differences between cable basian curls and preacher curls comes from the literature comparing dumbbell incline curls to dumbbell preacher curls. Incline curls have our shoulder extended while preacher curls of course have our shoulders flexed. Unlike what the researchers achieved with cables, the resistance profile of dumbbell incline and preacher curls are not identical. Incline curls tend to be most challenging at the mid to later point of the curl, while preacher curls tend to be most challenging at the start of the curl. So, keep this in mind. This is highly interesting, although probably not practical as most of you have no intention of spending an hour every day intensely stretching the calves. Although I will mention in our last video, we detailed a case study on a competitive natural bodybuilder with 18 years of experience who combined four sets of straight leg calf raises five times per week with 1 hour of intense calf stretching 6 days per week. Regardless, there might be a more practical way to reap the possible benefits of stretching the calves through stretching between sets. In 2016, this abstract was published online. However, we had a published paper in 2022. Untrained men trained seated and standing calf raises with these variables. One leg immediately descended into a loaded stretch after each set, holding it for 20 seconds and then resting passively for 100 seconds before starting the next set. The other leg just rested passively for the full 120 seconds between sets. Medial gastromus growth was similar between both conditions, while lateral gastromus growth slightly favored the stretching between sets, although some may interpret this as no difference. While solius growth more convincingly favored stretching between sets. Thus, stretching between sets had some benefits. We know science necessitates a large body of evidence to derive strong conclusions. So, I'm not prepared to conclude stretching the cast between sets is absolutely superior. Plus, there is some other research on other muscle groups that does not find a benefit to stretching between sets. Yet, since this does not take any more time, it's something convenient that you could try out, and no study to date has found stretching between sets to impair hypertrophy.
