 ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca ca The triceps can be trained with compound and isolation exercises. Compound exercises involve movement at two or more joints, while isolation exercises primarily involve movement at one joint. An excellent study from 2020 gives us a fascinating insight into how compound and isolation exercises compare for triceps growth. 43 men either train the barbell bench press only, the barbell skull crusher only, the bench press and then the skull crusher, or the skull crusher and then the bench press. These were the training variables used in the sessions. Unsurprisingly, the groups that trained the bench press saw the best pecs for its major growth, but it is highly interesting that training skull crushers before the bench press led to slightly less pecs growth than performing the reverse of this. Presumably, skull crushers fatigued the triceps to where it subsequently became more of a limiting factor in the bench press, thus compromising the pec stimulus. As for the triceps, just training the bench press produced lower gains than the other groups that involved skull crushers. Interestingly, the order in which the bench press and skull crusher was performed didn't have a major impact on triceps growth. Looking at these results, you may say although the bench press grows the triceps, we get much better results from the skull crusher. So there's nothing special about the bench press. However, this isn't necessarily the correct conclusion. Why? Well, the researchers examined growth across each of the three triceps heads. For the long head, skull crushers grew this very well, something the bench press failed to do. For the medial head, both exercises grew this muscle, but the percentages imply its growth was better from skull crushers. But for the lateral head, the bench press actually grew this head very well, something which the skull crusher failed to do. Accordingly, the special thing about the bench press is when compared to a skull crusher at least, although it doesn't develop the long and medial heads as well, it does a better job at growing the lateral head. Now, this data just involves the barbell bench press with a two-time shoulder-width grip. What about closer grips and even other compound exercises? With closer grips, it's possible they enhance overall triceps growth. There's no research comparing wider to closer grip bench pressing for actual triceps hypertrophy. All we have is EMG research that inconsistently observes higher triceps activity with closer grips. Either way, could closer grips change the pattern of growth across the three triceps heads. A 2013 paper delivers potential insight. Subject performed a neutral grip dumbbell bench press. This exercise is performed in the same plane as close grip barbell benching. No, not that plane. I'm talking about plane of movement. Both of them occur in what we call the sagittal plane. Using T2-weighted imaging to infer muscle activity, which has been documented to have some associations with actual muscle hypertrophy. It was found the exercise displayed high lateral and medial head activity. This aligns with the data on wide grip barbell bench pressing that finds similar lateral and medial head hypertrophy. As for the long head, activity was much lower. And indeed, the researchers found after training this exercise for 12 weeks, long head thickness did not increase. Thus, just like the wide grip bench press, closer grips likely fail to meaningfully grow the long head. There's likely a sound reason for this. All three heads of the triceps cross the elbow joint, so can all contribute to elbow extension. But the long head additionally crosses over the shoulder joint, so can partially contribute to shoulder extension and adduction. During the bench press, we need to lift the bar and this involves flexing the shoulder. Since the long head is partially involved in shoulder extension, a strong contraction of it would fight against us trying to lift and flex the shoulder. So it makes sense the nervous system wouldn't highly activate this muscle. This logic extends to all other horizontal pressing compound exercises, machine chest press variations and push-up variations. It even applies to incline presses, decline presses and dips. So all of these exercises probably won't train the long head much. Rather, the lateral and medial heads are likely trained in comparable ways to the bench press. What about vertical presses like overhead presses? Since overhead presses require us to flex and or deduct the shoulder to lift the load, a strong long head contraction may still fight against this and pull the arm down. So perhaps it's also not trained much here, yet. The shoulder angles traversed with vertical presses are different from horizontal presses, and without direct research, I'm unsure if this alters things. As for the lateral and medial heads, I'm unaware of any reason to believe they wouldn't be trained at least fairly decently with vertical presses, but how this compares to horizontal presses remains to be determined by future research. Nevertheless, summarizing this section, compound exercises will absolutely contribute to developing your triceps, and we saw direct evidence horizontal presses are likely great for the lateral head. However, it does seem likely we need isolation triceps exercises to maximize triceps hypertrophy. We saw barbell skull crushers have been documented to grow the long and medial heads quite well, and something we've yet to mention is data suggesting this likely extends to the dumbbell skull crusher. Very quickly, this 2012 paper found the dumbbell variation produced low activity of the lateral head, which aligns with the results of the barbell skull crusher producing minimal lateral head hypertrophy. As for the long and medial heads, the dumbbell skull crusher produced high activity of both, which aligns with the results of the barbell skull crushers producing great hypertrophy of both of them. But what about other triceps isolation exercises? Fortunately, we have some great research here. A 2022 paper out of Japan recruited 21 men. With one arm, they trained overhead extensions. With their other arm, they trained pushdowns. A supinated hand grip was used, and both exercises moved the elbow from 90 to 0 degrees. Here were the training variables used. Subjects progressively overloaded whenever they could to keep training hard with the reps. Subjects were able to lift heavier absolute loads on the pushdown throughout the study. Despite this, long head hypertrophy was better for the overhead extensions. I think it's not a stretch to suggest the strongest explanation for this is stretch. As the researchers implied in the paper, and as seen in previous House of Hypertrophy videos, growing evidence suggests training at long muscle lengths can build more muscle. Remember, although all three heads cross the elbow joint, the long head additionally crosses the shoulder joint. This actually means elevating the arm to an overhead position lengthens the long head, such that overhead extensions train the long head at a relatively more stretched position compared to pushdowns. As for the lateral and medial heads, the researchers had to combine both heads into one measurement due to problems with differentiating between them. It was found this combined lateral and medial head growth was also better with the overhead extensions. This was an unexpected finding, and it's currently not crystal clear what could explain this. After all, the lateral and medial heads just crossed their elbow, so shoulder position isn't really going to influence how much they are stretched. It is also unfortunate that the researchers couldn't differentiate between the lateral and medial heads, as remember skull crushers failed to grow the lateral head much, so it would have been interesting to see how lateral head growth looked with these two exercises. Anyhow, this study nonetheless indicates overhead extensions may be an excellent exercise for the triceps. This study measured muscle volume, which is a three-dimensional measure that considers all muscle regions. But an interesting question is, although overhead extensions seem to produce overall more growth, could there be some differences in the precise regions grown between the two movements? This is where a 2018 Greek paper can assist us. Nine individuals were recruited, and like the last study, one arm trained overhead extensions while the other arm trained pushdowns. But unlike the last study, the elbow angles traversed by both exercises were different. Here were the training variables used, and progressive overload occurred. The researchers only took measurements from the longhead. Longhead thickness at 50% and 60% of approximately the upper arm length leaned towards the overhead extensions. Longhead cross-sectional area at the lower portion also favored the overhead extensions. But quite fascinatingly, cross-sectional area at the upper portion was actually better with the pushdowns. Therefore, these results suggest the two exercises may grow different parts of the longhead. It's important to mention this study has its differences from the previous one, but one similarity is that both papers had each arm trained with one of the exercises. This is actually a great thing to do, since it means the same subjects performed both exercises. This means that all non-training factors that influence muscle growth, such as genetics, nutrition, and outside lifestyle factors were equal between both conditions. After all, your right arm doesn't sleep more or eat more protein than your left arm. But this Greek paper was merely conducted on nine subjects, while the other paper included 21 subjects. The Greek paper was also just six weeks, while the other paper was double this duration. Finally, besides the range of motion differences between the studies, the Japanese paper had subjects alternate which exercise was trained first every session, which is the perfect thing to do. Contrastingly, the Greek paper had subjects perform the pushdowns before the overhead extensions every session. This is a potential problem since the general fatigue from performing the pushdowns first could have slightly impaired the overhead extension stimulus. Therefore, if this study had subjects alternate back and forth which arm was trained first each session, better hypertrophy might have potentially been seen for the overhead extensions. Considering all this, it's quite clear we want to put more stock into the paper from Japan. However, I'm currently not going to write off the regional longhead growth differences between the two movements. Earlier we saw this graph established from skull crushers suggesting it may indeed be true that some regions of a triceps head could display greater activity than other parts. Furthermore, the notion that overhead extensions better develop the lower parts of the longhead might make sense. Remember that overhead extensions place the longhead at a more stretched position, and we have evidence that training muscles at stretched positions better develops the lower portions of the muscle. For example, this paper compared preacher curls with a range of motion that trained the muscle at a shortened position to a range of motion that achieved a relatively more lengthened position. Growth of the biceps at the 50% region was similar between both, but growth at the 70% region was better with a lengthened position. If you only wanted to train with one isolation triceps exercise, I think it's reasonable to recommend overhead extensions based on the data we've overviewed. The scientific papers dissected used cables, but freeway overhead extensions are a possibility. There are no direct comparisons between the two, but based on one small study of five participants, dumbbell overhead extensions resulted in appreciable triceps hypertrophy. Longhead panation angle also increased appreciably, and this measure is believed to represent the addition of contractile units in parallel, which is what a large part of muscle growth is. Now, some of you might be wondering, what about skull crushers? Skull crushers achieve a better stretch of the longhead compared to pushdowns, but overhead extensions achieve a better stretch than both. So in the absence of other research, I suspect overhead extensions may still be better. As for the lateral and medial heads, it's difficult to say how their growth may compare between the two movements. Hopefully future research fills this gap. If you don't like overhead extensions, rest assured you're still going to grow your triceps respectively with skull crushers or pushdowns, so feel free to alternatively train with either. If you're someone who's happy to perform more than one isolation triceps exercise, this could be worthwhile due to the possibility of it resulting in more uniform triceps growth, although we know it had notable limitations. The Greek paper hints at the combination of overhead extensions with pushdowns possibly enabling the complete development of the upper and lower longhead regions. Besides this, the combination of overhead extensions with skull crushers may not be bad either, as something we haven't mentioned about the data on skull crushers is it displayed high longhead activity at the uppermost portion. It is of course not impossible to have all three in a well-constructed program. Something we also can't rule out is potential regional growth differences in the lateral and medial heads between these exercises, making the combination of them possibly ideal for this speculative reason too. There are also other triceps exercises in existence. We've largely focused on these three since they're currently the most studied, but you could experiment with any alternatives you think might work. One final study potentially further supports the effectiveness of training the triceps with a few different exercises. 22 individuals were assigned into either a non-varied or varied group. Both groups trained three times per week for eight weeks. The non-varied group involved just training the triceps pushdown, while the varied group involved training the pushdowns on Monday, cable-seated extensions on Wednesday, and cable kickbacks on Friday. Overall triceps thickness was measured across three regions, and the varied group tended to see better results. The more favorable gains for the varied group could be entirely just a result of the inclusion of the cable-seated extension, which trains the longhead at a more stretched position, rather than the variation itself causing this. Even still, it still nonetheless demonstrates how this combination of isolation movements tended to produce more favorable gains than merely training the pushdowns. I should point out that bench press variations were also trained by both groups, and we can be confident this contributed to some of the growth, but I'm assuming the differences between groups were predominantly driven by the triceps isolation exercises. === FILE: Building Strength First ENHANCES Muscle Growth Later？! (New Study) [w9mAq4TrF3I].en.txt ===

Strength before size? Could aiming to increase\h your strength first, defined as increasing\h\h your one-repetition maximum on an exercise, help\h you build more muscle with that exercise later?\h\h A new study by Carvalho and colleagues explored\h just this. They recruited 26 men with an average of\h\h 4 and a half years of training experience, who\h could score at least 1.5 times their respective\h\h body weight. Subjects were split into pairs based\h on having similar vastus lateralis thickness.\h\h In each pair, one subject was assigned to a\h hypertrophy group, while the other subject\h\h was assigned to a strength plus hypertrophy group.\h Both groups trained twice per week for 8 weeks,\h\h training the back squat and leg press\h each session. The hypertrophy group\h\h for all of their sessions, trained each exercise\h with 4 sets of 8 to 12 reps to failure,\h\h the point at which no more repetitions can be\h performed, and 1 minute of rest between sets.\h\h The strength plus hypertrophy group, for the first\h three weeks, trained each exercise with 4 sets\h\h of 1 to 3 reps to failure and 3 minutes\h of rest between sets This was their strength phase.\h\h For the last 5 weeks, they trained identically\h to the hypertrophy group. So they trained each\h\h exercise with 4 sets of 8 to 12 reps\h to failure and 1 minute of rest between sets.\h\h This was their hypertrophy phase. I should note\h that both the hypertrophy group and strength\h\h plus hypertrophy group, before this 8 week\h experimental protocol, had a 3-week lead-in\h\h period where they both trained identically. But we\h don't really need to worry about this. Measurements\h\h were taken just before the 8-week experimental\h protocol, just after the 3rd week, which remember,\h\h is when the strength phase would have just ended\h for the strength plus hypertrophy group, and just\h\h after the 8 weeks. The measurements were a one-\h rep max test on the back squat and leg press, for\h\h strength gains. And for hypertrophy, thickness of\h the vastus lateralis measured at 60% of the thigh length. Increases in one-rep max\h on the back squat and leg press at the 3rd week and after the 8 weeks were significantly\h greater for the strength plus hypertrophy group\h\h compared to the hypertrophy group. These results\h make sense, the current evidence indicates training\h\h with relatively heavy loads and therefore lower\h repetitions produces the greatest increases in\h\h one-rep max strength. The strength plus hypertrophy\h group spent their first three weeks training with\h\h 1 to 3 reps for both exercises. Furthermore, \h the strength gains developed from this phase\h\h actually allowed them to use heavier loads\h during their following hypertrophy phase.\h\h Remember, during weeks 3 to 8 of the\h study, both groups were training identically.\h\h They used 8 to 12 reps on the back squat and leg\h press. Yet, the strength plus hypertrophy group\h\h used heavier loads on both exercises. Moving on,\h increases in vastus lateralis thickness at week 3\h\h favored the hypertrophy group. However, by the end\h of the 8th week, increases in vastus lateralis thickness were greater for the strength plus\h hypertrophy group. In other words, although the\h\h strength phase did not immediately produce much\h growth for the strength plus hypertrophy group,\h\h it seemed to have boosted the muscle\h growth experienced in the hypertrophy phase.\h\h So much so that the strength plus hypertrophy\h group experienced overall greater gains by the\h\h end of the study. These are some really intriguing\h results. What might explain them? Remember,\h\h during the last 5 weeks of the study,\h both groups trained identically. Despite them\h\h using 8 to 12 reps to failure, the strength plus\h hypertrophy group were able to use heavier loads,\h\h likely thanks to their prior strength phase.\h The author speculated using heavier weights\h\h in the hypertrophy phase meant the strength plus\h hypertrophy group experienced greater mechanical\h\h tension and hence greater muscle growth. In other\h words, heavier loads mean more mechanical tension\h\h and therefore more hypertrophy. However, I'd\h argue this is unlikely and slightly misleading.\h\h Let's explore why. Mechanical tension is currently\h the best understood mechanism of muscle growth.\h\h A large component of this is active tension . Active\h tension is equal to the force generated by the\h\h contractile units of a muscle. Simply put, higher\h levels of muscle fiber recruitment and high levels\h\h of force produced by those recruited muscle fibers\h would mean high levels of active tension. A great\h\h stimulus for hypertrophy. Muscles produce force\h progressively. When your effort is low there are\h\h low numbers of recruited muscle fibers and low\h force produced by some recruited muscle fibers.\h\h As your effort increases, increased muscle fiber\h recruitment and increased force produced by\h\h those recruited muscle fibers occurs. During the\h last 5 weeks, both groups trained with 8 to 12 reps to failure. All subjects would\h have been exerting the same relative effor.t\h\h They all used a load that enabled them to perform\h 8 to 12 reps to failure. So, they all would have\h\h been experiencing high levels of active tension.\h The fact that the strength plus hypertrophy group\h\h used heavier loads does not matter. The relative\h stimulus for both groups was the same. To drive\h\h this point home, imagine we had a complete beginner\h and an individual with three years of training\h\h experience use a load they could only complete for\h 8 reps on the back squat. The beginner would\h\h require a fairly light load, whereas the trained\h individual would be using a much heavier load.\h\h Would the trained individual grow more from doing\h this simply because he's using a heavier load?\h\h Probably not. In fact, this would likely be a much\h better stimulus for the untrained individual, \h\h simply due to the novelty of this event for him.\h There is another potential reason relating to\h\h mechanical tension that could help explain the\h study results. As mentioned, high levels of muscle\h\h fiber recruitment and force produced by those\h recruited muscle fibers are a large component\h\h of mechanical tension. Interestingly, there is some\h research suggesting training with heavier loads\h\h results in greater neural adaptations that\h enable a person to experience greater muscle\h\h fiber recruitment and/or greater force produced\h by those recruited muscle fibers. Therefore, it's\h\h possible the strength plus hypertrophy group in\h the last 5 weeks, despite training with the same\h\h relative effort, would have been able to recruit\h more muscle fibers and/or produce greater force\h\h with the recruited muscle fibers, thanks to the\h neural adaptations from their previous strength\h\h phase. However a limitation of this argument\h is that some evidence suggests that neural\h\h adaptations primarily occur in the early months of\h a person's training career, with little thereafter.\h\h The subjects of the study had an average of 4 and a half years of training experience So it's\h\h questionable whether they would even be able to\h experience meaningful neural adaptations. That said,\h\h I have come across some evidence indicating even\h very trained individuals can still experience\h\h neural adaptations, so ultimately it's not\h completely clear. A final potential reason\h\h that could explain the study results relates to\h re-sensitization. As mentioned, the subjects had\h\h an average of 4 and a half years of training\h experience. Unfortunately, the authors of the study\h\h did not report how the subjects trained previously\h. But, given the popularity of using 8-12 reps,\h\h it's possible they consistently trained with this\h rep range before this study. Taking some time off\h\h from using 8-12 reps and training with 1 to\h 3 reps for a couple of weeks, as the strength\h\h plus hypertrophy group did in their strength phase, could re-sensitize an individual. Meaning that\h\h when they returned to using 8-12 reps in their\h hypertrophy phase, they were more sensitive to\h\h this rep range and gained more muscle as a result.\h But, this is just a hypothesis i'm not aware of any\h\h strong evidence to support this claim. Moving on,\h it's important to remember this is only one study.\h\h Unfortunately, there are no other studies with an\h identical or near identical design to this study. \h\h However, there is research somewhat related that\h would reduce our enthusiasm about the results.\h\h Prestes and colleagues split 20 women with\h at least 6 months of training experience\h\h into a linear or reverse linear group. Both\h groups trained 3 times per week for 12 weeks.\h\h They alternated between workout A and workout\h B. Each exercise was trained for 3 sets.\h\h The linear group throughout the 12 weeks gradually\h progressed from using a load they could perform\h\h 12 to 14 reps with to a load they could\h perform 4 to 6 reps with. So they just\h\h increased the load used and decreased the\h number of reps performed on their exercises.\h\h The reverse linear group did the opposite of this,\h throughout the 12 weeks, they gradually progressed\h\h from using a load they could perform 4 to 6 reps with\h to a load they could perform 12 to 14 reps with.\h\h On weeks 4, 8, and 12 both groups performed 12\h reps on their exercise sets. These weeks were\h\h recovery weeks. they also only trained twice on\h these weeks. the reverse linear group is slightly\h\h comparable to the strength plus hypertrophy\h group in the Carvalho and colleague study. In\h\h that they began with low reps and heavy weight and\h ended with more traditional hypertrophy training.\h\h However, increases in fat-free mass, measured by\h skin fold calipers, were significantly greater for\h\h the linear group versus the reverse linear group.\h Now, skinfold calipers aren't the best measurement\h\h tool for muscle growth. MRI or ultrasound, as\h was used in the Carvalho and colleague study,\h\h is considered much more reliable and\h accurate, so we should keep this in mind.\h\h Nonetheless, this study does somewhat conflict\h with the Carvalho and colleague study. Looking at\h\h other research, if implementing low rep training\h in a hypertrophy oriented program could improve\h\h muscle growth, we would expect alternating your rep\h ranges to produce greater muscle growth than using\h\h only one rep range. But, as we detailed in our last\h video, the research finds no difference between\h\h alternating rep ranges or using a constant rep\h range for hypertrophy, at least in the short term.\h\h 12 weeks or less. The Carvalho and colleagues\h study did only last 8 weeks, so it somewhat\h\h conflicts with this area of research. Moreover, the\h research generally demonstrates that if you use\h\h different rep ranges in your training program,\h the way you organize them does not seem to impact\h\h muscle growth. Again, at least in the short term. A\h meta-analysis by Grgic and colleagues combined\h\h the results of studies comparing linear to daily\h undulating periodization. Linear periodization\h\h ,very generally, involves gradually increasing\h the load you use on an exercise and performing\h\h fewer reps as a result, over many weeks. Conversely,\h daily undulating periodization typically involves\h\h mixing different rep ranges into a weekly\h schedule. The analysis found no significant\h\h difference between the two periodization\h models for increasing measures of muscle growth.\h\h At the end of the day, I don't believe we have\h sufficient data to confidently suggest getting\h\h strong first increases hypertrophy later. Though,\h much of the opposing evidence to the Carvalho and\h\h colleagues study is indirect. I think the idea\h of re-sensitization that we covered earlier is\h\h intriguing. If the strength plus hypertrophy group\h experienced greater hypertrophy because they were\h\h re-sensitized to the 8-12 rep range, technically,\h none of the indirect data we looked at could\h\h refute this. Hopefully future research that is\h identical or near identical to the study emerge.\h\h This should enable greater insight. And of course, if this happens, I do plan to create updated videos.

=== FILE: Can 3-5 Reps Truly Maximize Growth？ (New Study) [GpSR3oicV_I].en.txt ===

Welcome to the house of hypertrophy. How many reps are needed to maximize muscle hypertrophy? A brand new study on trained individuals has been released and I thought it was worth sharing as it leads to an interesting discussion about what the minimum number of reps might be needed per set to optimize hypertrophy. Let's dive into the paper. Okay, I need to work on that dive. 14 individuals with at least two years of training experience were recruited to train the unilateral leg press and leg extension. With one leg, subjects performed 3 to five reps to valitional failure with a heavy load. With their other leg, subjects performed 20 to 25 repetitions to valitional failure with a light load. Both conditions performed three sets per session with 2 minutes of rest between sets. Loads were adjusted when needed to ensure subjects stayed in this rep range across sets and training sessions. They trained twice per week for 9 weeks, although there was a D lo midway where just one session was performed with one set. Muscle thickness of the vasis lateralis was measured at two regions and biopsies from the vasis lateralis were also taken to measure muscle fiber cross-sectional area. Muscle thickness increases were not significantly different between both conditions with average increases of 7.4% at region 1 and 8.5% at region 2. Fascinatingly, despite the fact whole muscle thickness increased for both conditions, neither condition saw increases in muscle fiber cross-sectional area, the author suggest the limitations with biopsies could explain things. Biopsies obviously only extract a relatively small portion of muscle. In this paper, just over 150 fibers were contained per biopsy, but this may fail to represent changes at the whole muscle as the whole muscle contains a ton of fibers. For example, this paper estimated the biceps to contain anywhere between 170,000 to 419,000 fibers. Regardless, as the authors note, the findings largely suggest similar growth between the two different rep ranges. Now, if you're new to the lifting research, the fact that 20 to 25 reps manage to produce growth may surprise you. However, as we'll expand on momentarily, it does appear that provided you're getting to or near to failure, higher reps can be similarly effective for muscle growth. In the spirit of scientific accuracy, there are some key things to keep in mind with this study prior to describing how these findings connect with the rest of the research. 14 subjects is a small sample. Valitional failure was the term used, which can be a little ambiguous, but the researchers did note that strong verbal encouragement was given to the subjects. So, I do suspect subjects were training very hard, but we don't know if it differed between conditions. Finally, it can be tricky to say anything about a specific rep number when a rep range is given. We know one condition trained with three to five reps, but it's reasonable to think there's a difference between all sets of three versus all sets of five. We'll talk more about this soon. It's never been crystal clear what the minimum number of reps might be needed to maximize the growth you can get from a set. So, this is why this new paper involving three to five reps intrigues me. If you've been following the research, you may be thinking, "Haven't we known for a while that provided your training to or close to failure, a wide range of reps produce similar gains. For example, this network meta analysis by Lopez involved 24 studies and found similar hypertrophy across high, moderate, and low loads. This is true. However, if we want to talk about the minimum number of reps needed to maximize the stimulus of a set, it's worth knowing the details of the studies. I have gone through every study. Feel free to pause and skim through if you'd like, but you don't have to, as I'll give you the key details. When looking at the studies, what number we decide to be the minimum number of reps needed to maximize hypertrophy per set is not as clear or obvious as you might think. Some studies, like the new one, report a range of reps performed per group. This is understandable. Researchers may intend subjects to perform exactly four reps, but despite max effort, they may sometimes only hit three reps, or other times may be able to hit five reps. So, it's simpler to give a range. Still, using a range doesn't lend itself well to making claims about an exact rep number. Other studies don't even directly report rep numbers. Instead, they have compared subjects training to failure with a different percentage of their one rep max. The thing is, the number of reps completed for a given percentage can differ between exercises. This meta analysis demonstrated that with an 80% one rep max load, subjects could perform 13 reps on the leg press, but around nine reps on the bench press. Individual differences also exist. You may be able to perform 10 reps with an 80% one rep max load on the bench press, while your friends may only perform eight repetitions despite both of you giving max effort. Additionally, your rep numbers will decrease when training to failure across sets when keeping the same load due to fatigue. Thus, it can be challenging to say things about an exact rep number based on the research. But we can still make approximations as to what the minimum and maximum number of reps could be based on the overall literature. Some say it's 5 to 30 reps, others 3 to 40 reps, but I've previously said the 6 to 35 range better represents the data we have. I'm not going to bore you with the full details of why I selected these numbers, but if you are interested, you can find my explanation in a pinned comment, but has the new study suggesting similar growth between 3 to 5 reps and 20 to 25 reps changed my mind? Before answering that, let's quickly describe what all the other research on five or fewer repetitions suggests. There are these six studies that suggest five or fewer reps may produce similar growth to moderate and higher reps. One of them actually found more growth with three to five reps, but just with one of their measures. But a key consideration is these studies had the five or fewer rep groups perform more sets and or rest longer between sets. These are potential confounders as both these things, more sets and in some cases longer rests can cause more growth. So what about studies using five or fewer reps where sets, rest time, and all other variables are controlled? Well, besides the latest study, we only have two other papers. The first paper found with that all groups performing four sets on the back squat per session and resting 6 minutes between sets training with three to five reps to failure did produce similar quad gains to two other groups training with higher reps. These findings are fairly similar to the new paper. The other paper involved a range of compound exercises with everyone performing three sets per exercise a session and resting 2 minutes between sets. Training to failure in the 2 to four rep range did not produce as much overall growth as training to failure in the 8 to 12 rep range. Of course, two to four reps is not the same as 3 to 5 reps. And this mere difference could explain the discrepancy, but difficult to say. So, the new paper now means we have two studies suggesting 3 to five reps produce similar growth to higher reps with sets and rest time equated. Is that enough to bring down the recommended minimum number of reps needed to maximize hypertrophy? I wouldn't do this yet as two studies is not much. And when we look at the other papers with unequal sets and or rest time, you could make the argument that if three to five reps really was as effective per set, then we should more clearly see three to five reps producing more growth as they were performing more sets and/or resting longer, which we know can cause more growth. As it's a crucial point, it's worth reiterating that since the studies largely use the range of three to five reps with some including two reps at the lower end. It's tough to say anything about an exact rep number. It's quite reasonable to believe that five reps produces more growth than two and three reps, but no study has compared them exactly. Hopefully, future research can shed further light onto this. Finally, we're not overall dealing with a lot of strong data on five or fewer reps anyway. So, the variance demon is always lurking in the shadows. Credit to the guys over at Datadriven Strength who, as far as I know, coined this term. Simply put, the variance demon represents the idea that behind studies, especially studies with small sample sizes, our results can fail to accurately describe reality due to things like measurement error, sampling variance, or other sources of error. For example, we might unknowingly have one group of subjects with better muscle building genetics than another group, which can obscure things. The variance demon can often explain why we have seemingly conflicting and confusing data. I do have a video where I go into more detail on sampling variance. if you're interested. This is why having studies with large sample sizes or simply combining enough small sample size studies into a meta analysis enables us to better separate out the signal from statistical noise. So to be completely clear, I am not saying that 3 to five reps per set does not maximize growth. Rather, I'm saying that the evidence is not strong enough and somewhat confusing to be completely sure. I personally hope that somewhere between 3 to five reps can maximize hypertrophy per set as that just gives us more options, but for now I have more confidence that six and above does likely maximize growth. I'm fully aware this answer may be somewhat disappointing or frustrating, so I apologize, but it's the only honest answer I think there is. Our conversation today has been focused on a very minor detail. Fortunately, the practical recommendations are straightforward. If your goal is to maximize muscle hypertrophy, I think it's a safer bet to train with six or more reps per set. That said, if you've been predominantly training with five or fewer reps and seeing great progress, I wouldn't change a single thing. Also, we have been talking about things in isolation, but in reality, your training program can include a variety of rep ranges, and if you do have a few sets under six reps, that's not a major problem. At minimum, we do know growth can still occur with sets of three to five reps, so they won't be doing nothing. In fact, there is one paper demonstrating that having a few low rep sets might be fine. These researchers had 19 trained men perform a range of exercises each for three sets three times a week for 8 weeks. One group trained with 8 to 12 reps to failure every session, while another group trained with two to four reps on day one of the week, 8 to 12 reps to failure on day two, and 20 to 30 reps to failure on day three. growth was not significantly different between both groups. Some of the numbers favor the varied group, but as one of the authors described in an article, this was probably largely driven by outliers and sampling variance. This is just one study with a small sample. We do have a few other studies comparing direct measures of muscle growth between training with one rep range to training with a variety of reps, finding similar hypertrophy. All groups in these papers largely trained with six or more reps. So, unsurprisingly, training with a variety of rep ranges in your program can absolutely be done. === FILE: Can Repetition Tempo Impact Regional Muscle Growth？ [ePdrCerRRsc].en.txt ===

repetition tempo is probably one of the least thought about variables in a muscle building program repetition temper refers to the duration you perform the various muscle actions in an exercise as a random example you could perform an exercise with a three second eccentric phase zero second isometric and a one second concentric phase i recently came across research exploring if repetition tempo could impact regional muscle growth in other words could different repetition tempos produce different growth on parts of a muscle this could make sense it's possible that performing an exercise with a faster or slower tempo could activate different regions of a muscle more so than others resulting in different regional hypertrophy indeed erp and colleagues compared heavy parallel back squat training using a 75 to 90 one rep max load throughout the study to jump parallel back squat training using a 30 watermax load for a regional growth of the quadriceps muscles the jump parallel back squats were performed very far from muscular failure meaning they were just explosive jumping repetitions whereas the repetitions for the heavy parallel back squat would have been substantially slower as they were training closer to muscular failure heavy parallel back squat training produced greater upper region growth of the vastus lateralis and vastus intermedius compared to jump however jump parallel back squat training resulted in greater lower region growth of the vastus lateralis and vastus intermedius given range of motion was controlled between the groups they both squatted to parallel repetition speed was probably the reason for these differences in regional growth now this study did compare strength hypertrophy style training to power style training what about the use of different repetition tempos in typical strength slash hypertrophy training programs denis and colleagues split 44 untrained women into one of four groups a five second concentric one second eccentric group a one second five second eccentric group a three-second concentric three-second eccentric group or a control group the control group of course did not train and experienced no gains so we won't mention them any further the three training groups performed the knee extension for sets of six reps with A-50 percent warner max load and 180 seconds of rest between sets three times per week for ten weeks weeks one and two had the subjects perform three sets per session weeks three and four four sets per session and weeks five to ten five sets per session the five second one second eccentric We now have two meta-analyses indicating light\h loads can produce similar muscle growth to heavier\h\h loads, provided repetitions are performed to or\h close to failure. Meta-analyses combine the\h\h results of numerous studies looking at the same\h topic. In the two meta-analyses, most studies had\h\h subjects use loads between 30% and 85% of their one\h rep max,roughly equating to repetitions between 35\h\h and 5. But, what about repetitions below 5? Last video, we demonstrated the research suggests\h\h one rep max training is not effective at building\h muscle. This video, we'll evaluate research exploring\h\h repetitions between 2-4 for building\h muscle. On the bottom left and right we'll be\h\h keeping a tally of the study supporting or\h opposing the effectiveness of repetitions\h\h below 5. Starting things off, Schoenfeld\h and colleagues split 19 men with at least\h\h one year of training experience into a heavy or\h moderate group. Both groups trained the bench press,\h\h overhead press, lat pull down, cable row, back\h squat, leg press, and leg extension for 3 sets and 2minutes of rest between sets, 3 times per week for 8 weeks. The heavy group\h\h used a load that allowed them to perform\h 2 to 4 repetitions to failure each set.\h\h The moderate group used a load allowing\h them to perform 8 to 12 repetitions\h\h to failure each set. Both groups aimed to\h progressively overload throughout the study.\h\h Increases in vastus lateralis thickness were\h significantly greater for the moderate group.\h\h Increases in elbow flexor thickness also favor the\h moderate group, while triceps thickness increases\h\h were similar between both groups. So overall, this study indicates 2 to 4 reps is not as\h\h effective as 8 to 12 reps. Weiss and colleagues\h split 44 untrained men into a low rep, moderate\h\h rep, or high rep group. All groups trained 4 sets\h of the back squat with 6 minutes of rest between\h\h sets, 3 times per week for seven weeks. The\h low rep group used a 3 to 5 rep max load\h\h Each set, the moderate rep group used a 13 to 15\h rep max load each set.. The high rep group used a\h\h 23 to 25 rep max load each set. All groups aimed\h to progressively overload throughout the study.\h\h Increases in quadriceps thickness were similar\h between all three groups, suggesting reps below 5\h\h are effective for maximizing muscle\h growth. Managine and colleagues divided\h\h 33 men, with at least two years of training\h experience, into an intensity or volume group.\h\h Both groups trained 4 times per week for\h 8 weeks. The program is listed on screen.\h\h The intensity group performed each exercise for\h 4 sets of 3 to 5 reps with a 90 % one rep max load and 3 minutes of\h rest between sets. The volume group performed each\h\h exercise for 4 sets with 10 to 12 reps with\h a 70% one-rep max load and 1 minute of\h\h rest between sets. Both groups aim to progressively\h overload throughout the study.Increases in rectus\h\h femoris, vastus lateralis, pectoralis major\h, and triceps brachii cross-sectional area were\h\h statistically similar between both groups. But, increases in\h\h arm mass were significantly greater in the\h intensity group. So, 3 to 5 reps were equally\h\h as effective as 10 to 12 reps in most measures and\h actually superior in a lean arm mass measurement.\h\h One limitation of this study was the intensity\h group used 3 minutes of rest between sets,\h\h while the volume group used only 1 minute.\h In our rest interval video, we demonstrate the\h\h research suggests with compound exercises, 2.5 or\h more minutes of rest between sets was superior for\h\h building muscle compared to rest intervals of 1 minute or less. With this in mind, the volume group\h\h would probably have been at a disadvantage. If they\h used a 3-minute rest interval, they could have\h\h experienced greater growth for all measures.\h Another study by Schoenfeld and colleagues\h\h split 17 men with at least one year of training\h experience into a strength group or hypertrophy\h\h group. Both groups trained the same exercises 3 times per week for 8 weeks. The hypertrophy\h\h group used a bodybuilding split schedule, while\h the strength group used a full body schedule.\h\h The hypertrophy group trained each exercise with\h 3 sets of 10 reps to failure and 90 seconds of\h\h rest between sets. The strength group trained\h each exercise with 7 sets of 3 reps to failure\h\h with 3 minutes of rest between sets. Both\h groups aimed to progressively overload. Increases in biceps thickness were similar\h between both groups, supporting the effectiveness\h\h of repetitions below 5 for building muscle.\h However, similar to the previous study, the\h\h strength group used a 3-minute rest interval, while\h the hypertrophy group used only a 90-second rest\h\h interval.Also, the researchers justified equating\h volume load by suggesting volume load was strongly\h\h correlated to muscle growth. Therefore, equating\h it between groups would avoid this potential\h\h confounding effect. However, strong evidence\h indicates with all else equal, reps between 5 and\h\h 35 produce similar muscle growth. Within this range, with the same number of sets performed, volume load\h\h would be dramatically different. To sum up, the majority\h of the evidence supports the idea reps between\h\h 2 and 4 are effective for building muscle. Having said this, of the 5 studies finding this,\h\h 4 either had the low rep group perform\h more sets, in attempt to equate volume load,\h\h and or the low rep groups used longer rest intervals. Based on the reasons provided in the video, these\h\h are probably confounding factors. === FILE: Cheat Reps vs Strict Reps (NEW Study) [ZhOW9ql9x0Y].txt ===

! 25 previously untrained individuals were recruited. They trained unilateral dumbbell curls and pushdowns two times per week for eight weeks. One arm was randomly assigned to cheat on all repetitions, while the other arm used strict technique on all repetitions. To cheat with the curl, participants were instructed to swing the weight up and use external momentum to lift the weight as many times as possible until they reached failure. With the pushdown, they used external momentum and were permitted to flare the elbows and use leg drive until they could no longer perform more repetitions. As for the strict reps, the curl was performed with a stationary body position without any swinging. They simply flexed the elbow until they could no longer complete another strict rep. The same applies to the pushdown, an upright torso with movement just occurring at the elbow until they could no longer extend their elbow down with strict technique. The study's supplementary material provides instructional videos that the subjects saw. Every session, four sets of 8-12 reps were performed, and as we mentioned, those reps were taken to failure for both conditions. Loads were adjusted across time to stay in this rep range. Regular viewers will know this research design of having every subject train both conditions is becoming more common in the literature. There are always a few critiques of this design I see pop up, so I'll quickly address them. People can have one arm stronger than the other, but remember we're not looking at the results of one person. We're looking at the average results of two conditions which typically have a similar number of dominant arms. Some people think that training one arm can directly cause growth in the opposite arm, but this isn't quite true. What is true is that training one arm can cause strength gains in the opposite arm. So this study design is not appropriate for measuring strength, but it is acceptable for measuring hypertrophy. There are also key advantages to this study design. Having 25 subjects each train both conditions is like having 50 subjects assigned to train either one of the conditions. In fact, it's even better since by having the same subjects in both conditions, differences in genetics, nutrition, and outside lifestyle factors are less likely to confound the findings. Muscle thickness of the elbow flexors consisting of the biceps and brachialis and triceps were measured at 55% and 65% regions. It was found that increases in all regions were similar between both conditions. Thus, as the authors describe, the use of external momentum neither helped nor hindered hypertrophy of the target muscles. These findings are truly fascinating and may surprise a number of you. So is that the death of strict reps for hypertrophy, since they provided no growth advantage over cheating? Not necessarily. Many suggest there are other concerns with cheating, safety, and tracking progression. Before critically analyzing these two points, in the spirit of scientific accuracy, we must not let a few key considerations slip our minds. The authors mention it was tricky to standardize form with the cheat reps, so not all subjects cheated identically. It is not implausible that certain cheating styles are worse than others, but this will be tricky to establish. Remember this study wasn't designed to examine cheat reps as an intensity technique. What I mean is you can perform strict reps but then start to cheat as you approach failure to perform more total reps than you could otherwise. Whether this has any worthwhile advantage remains to be tested. Note, cheat reps are the only way to push past typical failure. As the quality and quantity of research we're getting nowadays is increasing, I am optimistic we'll see valuable research on these methods. Besides that, science is ultimately a cumulative process, relying on multiple studies to build a comprehensive understanding of a given topic and get us closer to the truth. The single study at hand just involved untrained individuals training only their biceps and triceps for 8 weeks. Things could be different with any one of these variables altered. Some may be tempted to completely ignore this study since it's on untrained individuals, since they claim untrained individuals grow equally from anything under the sun. While it is undeniably true, we cannot be certain findings on untrained individuals will extend to trained individuals. It is not true untrained individuals grow equally from everything. The literature is abundant with examples of untrained individuals growing more with one thing over another. A few of our videos illustrate this. So studies on untrained individuals are certainly not useless and at the end of the day, it is an informative data point suggesting similar effects between cheat and strict reps. I should also reveal that none other than Jeff Nippard has stated he'll be involved with a cheat rep study on trained individuals. So what about safety and tracking progression? 30 individuals were originally recruited, but 5 dropped out. However, none of these 5 dropped out due to injury. As the authors describe, we don't have strong direct evidence that using external momentum increases injury risk. But absence of evidence is not necessarily evidence of absence. Whether things would change with a longer time frame or more subjects is a question left unanswered for now. As for progress, the cheat condition unsurprisingly trained with heavier weights, but both conditions progressed throughout the intervention. That said, the complication when cheating is as difficult to untangle how much of your progression is driven by you just cheating more. When maintaining strict technique, you have more confidence lifting heavier for the same number of reps is due to you getting stronger, which is assurance you're making gains. Cheat rep proponents may say they're uninterested in untangling what's causing them to lift heavier loads if they're fundamentally seeing no less growth. Ultimately, visual changes over the long term and the general notion that they'll eventually be lifting a load that would have been impossible for them to cheat with back in the day is all that's needed. I think that is a fair perspective, but I know there are many who prefer consistent assurance of progress provided with strict technique. Some individuals thinking outside the box may consider this as a paper on training at long muscle lengths in disguise. Take the normal biceps curl. When cheating and swinging the weight up, you likely increase the tension seen earlier in the curl, where the biceps are at a longer length compared to using a stricter technique with a standard tempo. Since growth was similar between both, you may suggest increasing the demands at longer muscle lengths isn't advantageous. However, since we do have other variables in the mix and it's difficult to know precisely how much tension differed at longer lengths, I wouldn't consider it an ideal study for answering if challenging muscles at longer lengths benefits hypertrophy. I'll also add that as described in our previous video, I believe we should divide the muscle length literature into different categories, as this may tell us when and where training muscles at longer lengths can be beneficial. In this case, changing where the muscle is challenged the most in the motion belongs to the resistance challenge category. We don't have a lot of studies in this category, but the ones we do have failed to show any real benefit of making the exercise harder at longer muscle lengths anyway. Feel free to check out the video for more details. So can we say cheat reps are as good as strict reps? More evidence in a wider context and perhaps some kind of investigation of its safety is necessary before we can be sure. I still think it makes sense for stricter technique to be the default. But depending on how you feel, this study could loosen the strictness you may have towards your reps. It's likely not the end of the world if some degree of deviation and momentum creeps into your sets. There are even advanced options to periodize your training and implement deloads. There are over a quadrillion input combinations on which your plan is based, and with the touch of a few buttons, you can customize things further. === FILE: Comparing Training Splits for Muscle Growth (20 STUDIES) [Sc-QdAadde0].en.txt ===

Dude, I love full body workouts,\h they're amazing for hypertrophy. Nonsense,\h\h everyone knows full body workouts are for newbs.\h Bro-splits are where the real gains are at, bro. Ha! Bro-splits are for\h juice heads, you juicehead. I like push/pull/legs. In this video, we're going extremely\h deep into the science comparing\h\h different training frequencies\h and splits for muscle hypertrophy. Briefly, full-body workouts, needless to\h say, involve training all muscle groups\h\h in one session. Anywhere from 2 to 5 full-body\h training sessions are commonly performed per week. Bro-splits isolate muscle groups\h on different days of the week.\h\h Muscle groups are typically trained with\h a frequency of once or twice a week here. Upper/lower splits train your upper and\h lower body muscles on separate days.\h\h Commonly, 2 upper and lower body\h sessions are performed weekly,\h\h resulting in you training muscle\h groups at a twice per week frequency. Though performing 3 upper and lower body\h sessions each week is also possible,\h\h this results in you training your muscle\h groups with a three times per week frequency. Finally, push/pull/legs train your pushing,\h pulling, and leg muscles on separate days.\h\h Such a schedule means muscle groups are\h hit with a frequency of twice per week. Before diving into the science, let us\h overview some history of training splits. If you do not care about the history,\h feel free to skip to the timepoint shown\h\h on screen where we begin examining\h the training frequency research. Traveling back to the 1900s to 1950s,\h\h surprisingly, full-body\h training seemed to be the norm. It appears Eugen Sandow, often called “the\h father of bodybuilding”, and other legends\h\h within the sport, like Reg Park (an idol of\h Arnold), trained with full-body routines. For example, I stumbled across a newspaper\h article written by Reg Park himself,\h\h detailing his training preparation\h for the 1958 Mr. Universe competition. Part of this prep consisted of\h 3 full-body weekly workouts. By the 1950s-60s and onwards, however, the rise\h of bro-splits was ignited for a couple of reasons. Firstly, it appears the Weider brothers,\h businessmen with their own supplements,\h\h magazines, and bodybuilding competitions,\h are credited with popularising bro-splits\h\h through their magazine's writings. Partly,\h it seems the Weider brother's promotion of\h\h bro splits was to help distinguish themselves\h from other businessmen in the fitness world. Secondly, while evidence exists of occasional\h bodybuilding competitions before the 1930s,\h\h it was in the decades after bodybuilding\h competitions become more regular and prominent.\h\h As an article by BarBend puts it “If\h no bodybuilding competitions exist,\h\h focusing on your biceps peaks\h seems somewhat pointless.”\h\h Thus, the rise of regular and prominent\h bodybuilding competitions likely also\h\h contributed to bro-splits becoming more favorably\h looked upon by bodybuilding enthusiasts. Thirdly and finally, during what’s now sometimes\h called the “golden era of bodybuilding”,\h\h legendary figures like Arnold and Frank Zane\h were known to train and promote bro splits. In Arnold’s encyclopedia of\h bodybuilding, published in 1985,\h\h bro-split routines were detailed. Back to today, the popularity of bro-splits\h seems to remain in the bodybuilding sphere. A 2022 study by Hackett et al. had 235 competitive\h bodybuilders complete an online survey,\h\h and found 85.5% of them used split routines. It may be worth also noting 53.6% of all surveyed\h bodybuilders used performance-enhancing drugs. With regards to upper/lower\h splits and push/pull/leg splits,\h\h I was unfortunately unable to find\h any resources detailing their history. Nevertheless, let us transition\h to examining what the research\h\h has to say on the optimal training\h frequency for muscle hypertrophy. It's very important to note all the\h research to be explored has assessed\h\h how different training frequencies\h impact muscle growth while all other\h\h weekly training variables (including weekly\h sets per muscle group) are kept the same. For example, researchers may get one group\h to train their muscle groups once per week\h\h and compare this to another group of subjects\h training their muscle groups three times per week. Both of these groups ultimately perform\h the same weekly sets on the same exercises\h\h and thus achieve the same weekly\h set numbers per muscle group. Keeping all other weekly training variables\h the same ensures they do not confound our\h\h findings, as we're trying to isolate the\h effect of training frequencies and splits. This is important, as the number of\h weekly sets per muscle group performed can\h\h impact the amount of hypertrophy produced. Nevertheless, some individuals believe in\h the real world, higher training frequencies\h\h are a practical way to increase the number\h of weekly sets performed per muscle group.\h\h This is a fair point, and it's something\h we'll address a little later on. With that out the way, let's\h get on to the literature. In 2016, a meta-analysis by Schoenfeld\h et al. combined the results of all the\h\h existing studies at that time\h point on training frequency. It was found with all other weekly training\h variables equal, training a muscle group twice\h\h per week was better than once a week. Due\h to limited data, the researchers couldn't\h\h speculate on if training a muscle group three\h or more times per week provided more benefit. To this day, many people seem to run\h with this data saying bro-splits are\h\h scientifically inferior, as bro-splits typically\h involve training a muscle group once a per week. Full-body workouts, upper/lower splits, and\h push/pull/legs splits were thought to be superior\h\h as all these involve training a muscle group\h at a frequency of two or more times per week. You might have come across numerous\h Instagram posts expressing these very ideas. Yet, there are major problems here.\h\h This analysis was conducted 6 years\h ago and only involved 7 studies. Fortunately, Schoenfeld et al. conducted\h an updated meta-analysis in 2019.\h\h This is currently the most up to data official\h\h meta-analysis examining training\h frequency and muscle hypertrophy. 13 studies were included in\h the analysis this time around. It was found with all other weekly\h training variables constant,\h\h training frequency did not affect muscle growth.\h\h That is, no particular training frequency\h was superior for muscle hypertrophy. An important point is out\h of the 13 studies included,\h\h 11 had subjects train with a total of 12\h weekly sets per muscle group or fewer. Thus, the most accurate conclusion from this\h analysis is when training with a total of 12 or\h\h fewer weekly sets per muscle group, no particular\h training frequency or split seems to be superior. Bro splits, full-body workouts, upper/lower\h splits, and push/pull/legs splits are all viable. Let's briefly examine a few studies included\h in the analysis underscoring this point. Gomes et al. recruited 23 trained men with\h an average bench press one-rep max of 103kg\h\h and an average squat one-rep max of 132kg. One group used bro-splits that trained muscle\h groups at a frequency of once per week. A second group used full-body\h workouts that trained muscle\h\h groups at a frequency of five times per week. Both groups accumulated 10 weekly\h sets for each trained muscle group. Although, with the triceps and biceps, if you\h count compound exercises in addition to the\h\h isolation exercises, both these muscles\h were trained with 15 weekly sets each. Nevertheless, after 8 weeks of training, increases\h in lean mass were similar between both groups. Another study by Ochi et al.\h recruited untrained subjects\h\h and had them train the leg extension only. One group performed 6 sets on one day per week.\h\h Another group performed 2\h sets across 3 days per week. After 11 weeks of training,\h\h increases in quadriceps thickness\h were similar between both groups. Therefore, this study potentially\h suggests with low weekly set numbers,\h\h training a muscle once a week (as done with\h bro-splits) may be similarly effective to\h\h training a muscle three times per week\h (as done with full-body workouts). Regarding upper/lower and push/pull/legs\h splits, we know these typically train a\h\h muscle at a frequency of twice per week. Again,\h with 12 or fewer weekly sets per muscle group,\h\h there is likely nothing superior or\h inferior with a twice per week frequency. As an example, Yue et al. recruited 18 trained men\h with an average bench press one-rep max of 77kg\h\h and an average squat one-rep max of 103kg. One group trained their muscle groups\h with a frequency of once per week\h\h (except the triceps and biceps which\h were technically trained twice per week),\h\h while another group trained their muscle\h groups with a frequency of twice per week\h\h (except the biceps and triceps which were\h technically trained four times per week). Both groups trained all muscle\h groups with 4-12 weekly sets.\h\h However, if you count compound exercise sets\h toward triceps and biceps weekly set numbers,\h\h the biceps were trained with 16 weekly sets while\h the triceps were trained with 24 weekly sets. After 6 weeks of training, both\h groups did not statistically\h\h differ in vastus medialis and\h elbow flexor thickness gains. So, it seems when performing 12\h weekly sets per muscle group or fewer,\h\h all training splits and frequencies appear viable\h and similarly effective for building muscle. The burning question is what about when training\h with more than 12 weekly sets per muscle group? Does training frequency matter in this situation? Theoretically, there could be a limit to the\h number of effective sets you can perform for a\h\h muscle group per session. Thus, when training a\h muscle group with a fair number of weekly sets,\h\h using a training frequency greater\h than once per week may be required Indeed, two studies published in 2020 by Barbalho\h et al. provided potential evidence for this. Both studies were designed the same,\h\h but one study was done on trained\h men while the other on trained women. Subjects only trained their muscle\h groups at a frequency of once per week. One group trained with 5\h weekly sets per muscle group,\h\h the second with 10 weekly sets, the third with 15\h weekly sets, and the fourth with 20 weekly sets. As subjects trained muscle groups\h with a frequency of once per week,\h\h the number of weekly sets performed\h for a muscle group was equivalent\h\h to the number of sets performed\h for a muscle group per session. Overall, 5 to 10 sets were sufficient\h for increasing muscle size. In fact,\h\h the data of the study shows slightly worse muscle\h size increases when training with 15 to 20 sets. Hence, this data potentially indicates\h on a per session basis (as remember,\h\h the study used a frequency of once per\h week), performing between 5 to 10 sets\h\h per muscle group might be the limit to the amount\h of productive volume you can perform per session. If you want to perform more than\h 5-10 weekly sets for a muscle group,\h\h distributing the weekly sets across a\h higher frequency of days may be necessary. However, we have a problem. These two studies by Barbalho et\h al. have since been retracted,\h\h probably because the data presented\h in the study was not legitimate. It's been established many studies\h conducted by Barbalho et al. contain\h\h atypical and improbable data. So, these Barbalho studies cannot\h help our quest to establish the\h\h optimal training frequency\h with higher weekly volumes. Fortunately, we do have other valid data. Recall in the Schoenfeld et al. 2019\h meta-analysis, 11 of the 13 included\h\h studies in the analysis had subjects train\h with 12 or fewer weekly sets per muscle group. Meaning 2 studies had subjects train with\h more than 12 weekly sets per muscle group. Moreover, since 2019, 3 additional studies\h have been published comparing different\h\h training frequencies when subjects train with\h So in total, we currently have 5 studies. Allow us to overview them. Evangelista et al. recruited untrained men with\h\h an average 60kg bench press one-rep\h max and an average 87kg back squat.\h\h These numbers, particularly the squat numbers,\h are quite impressive for untrained individuals. Anyway, a bro-split routine group trained their\h muscle groups at a twice per week frequency,\h\h while a full-body group trained muscle\h groups at a four times per week frequency. Both groups accumulated 16\h weekly sets per muscle group However, if we include compound exercise sets\h towards the weekly set biceps and triceps counts,\h\h the triceps were trained with\h a whooping 40-48 weekly sets,\h\h while the biceps were trained with 32 weekly sets. Now, although both groups performed the same\h weekly set numbers for their muscle groups\h\h (except for the triceps), exercise selection\h slightly differed between the bro split and\h\h full-body groups. The bro split group\h used a little more exercise variety. Nonetheless, after 8 weeks of training,\h increases in quadriceps, triceps,\h\h and biceps thickness were similar between\h both the bro-split and full-body groups. Suggesting even with higher weekly volumes,\h\h bro-splits may be comparable\h to full body workouts. Brigatto et al. also suggest training frequency\h may not matter much with higher weekly volumes. These researchers recruited trained men whose\h average bench press one-rep max was 94kg\h\h and squat one-rep max was 125kg. Two groups trained with a split routine. One group\h trained their muscle groups with a frequency of\h\h once per week while the second group trained their\h muscle groups with a frequency of twice per week. Both groups accumulated 16 weekly sets per muscle\h group. Though, if we counted compound exercises\h\h toward biceps and triceps weekly set counts, both\h these muscles were trained with 24 weekly sets. After 8 weeks of training, increases\h in triceps, biceps, vastus lateralis,\h\h and anterior quadriceps thickness\h were similar between both groups. Suggesting with higher weekly volumes,\h\h a frequency of once per week may\h be similar to a twice per week. Thus, combining this Brigatto study with\h the Evangelista study, they potentially\h\h indicate training splits and frequency may\h not matter with higher weekly volumes either. However, the remaining three studies\h do not support this conclusion. Zaroni et al. recruited men with an\h average bench press one-rep max of 99kg\h\h and an average squat one-rep max of 109kg. A bro-split group trained their muscle groups at\h a once per week frequency (though the triceps and\h\h biceps would have been trained twice per\h week if we consider compound exercises). A full body trained their muscle group\h at a frequency of five times per week. Both groups accumulated 15 weekly sets for all\h muscle groups. But for the biceps and triceps,\h\h if we count compound exercises, both these\h muscles were trained with 30 weekly sets. After 8 weeks of training,\h increases in triceps, biceps,\h\h and vastus lateralis thickness were superior for\h the full-body group versus the bro-split group. Indicating with higher weekly volumes, full-body\h training may be superior to bro-splits. Yet, another study by Bartolomei et al.\h somewhat directly conflicts with this study. These researchers recruited trained\h men with an average bench press one-rep\h\h max of 96kg and an average\h squat one-rep max of 108kg. A bro-split group trained their muscle\h groups at a frequency of once per week.\h\h Though the triceps, considering compound\h exercises, would have been trained twice per week. A full-body group trained their muscle group\h at a frequency of three to four times per week. Both groups accumulated 15 weekly sets for the\h chest and 20 weekly sets for their quadriceps,\h\h while the trapezius was trained\h with around 25 indirect weekly sets. After 10 weeks of training,\h\h increases in thickness of the chest\h were similar between both groups. But,\h\h increases in thickness of the vastus lateralis and\h trapezius were superior for the bro-split group. Suggesting bro-splits overall to be superior to\h full body training with higher weekly volumes,\h\h thus somewhat conflicting\h with the Zaroni et al. study. Making things even more confusing, we\h have the final study by Lasevicius et al. These researchers recruited trained men with\h an average bench press one-rep max of 79kg\h\h and an average back squat one-rep max of 161kg. An upper/lower split group trained their muscle\h groups with a frequency of twice per week. A full-body group trained their muscle groups\h with a frequency of three times per week. Both groups accumulated 36\h weekly sets for the quadriceps,\h\h and 12 weekly sets for the triceps and biceps.\h However, if we counted compound exercise sets\h\h towards triceps and biceps weekly sets, both of\h these muscles were trained with 24 weekly sets. Suggesting with high weekly volumes, a\h frequency of twice per week (as achieved\h\h with upper/lower splits) is more beneficial\h than a frequency of three times per week\h\h (as achieved with full-body workouts). When combining all of these 5 studies, it's\h utterly confusing as the findings are conflicting. 2 studies suggest training frequency did not\h impact hypertrophy, 1 suggests full-body workouts\h\h are superior to bro-splits, another suggests\h bro-splits are superior to full body workouts,\h\h and the final study indicates upper-lower\h splits are better than full-body workouts. Needless to say, the 5 studies\h were far from identical.\h\h The precise training details\h between the studies differed,\h\h this could go some way toward explaining\h the conflicting results between studies. At this time, it's going to be\h impossible for us to figure this out. Even so, individual differences could also go\h some way to explaining the conflicting data,\h\h and this is a very important point. There's reason to believe different individuals\h\h can respond best to different\h training frequencies or splits. One paper by Damas et al. supports this. 19 untrained men were recruited and had one of\h their legs assigned to a high-frequency condition\h\h and their other leg assigned\h to a low-frequency condition. Both legs were trained on the\h unilateral leg extension with\h\h each session consisting of 3 sets\h of 9-12 repetitions to failure. With the high-frequency leg,\h subjects did this 5 times per week.\h\h With the low-frequency leg, subjects\h did the session 2 or 3 times per week.
