=== FILE: Defending Science-Based Lifting [88bT1no39pM].txt ===

 Welcome to the House of Hypertrophy! In the last few months, science-based lifting has received quite the backlash. There's no doubt that some of the criticisms are quite reasonable and fair, but some of the backlash I've seen has extended to what is an unjustifiable extent. So in this video, I wanted to give my two cents on the matter. We'll be exploring questions such as, is hypertrophy and strength research even valuable? And does science just flip-flop? We'll also be touching on errors in research and whether all this science is just overthinking it. Let's dive in! I want to make it clear that I'll be defending science to the extent that it can be defended, not science-based content creators. In fact, whether people consciously recognize it or not, quite a lot of the criticisms I've seen raised are actually against content creators, not research itself. There's a difference between research and the communication of research. People can say something is supported by science without this being even remotely close to the truth. Some may reference research but interpret it incorrectly or inappropriately extrapolate its findings. For example, across social media, you often see so-called science-based content creators suggesting that maximizing stability is needed to maximize hypertrophy. To the extent they do everything to maximize stability. To some extent, stability is probably important. For example, it's challenging to argue that benching on a swiss ball is a good idea for hypertrophy. But as far as most typical exercises, machines are generally more stable than free weights. Yet, we have meta-analytic evidence suggesting similar hypertrophy between machines and free weights, and this includes research on trained individuals. Related to this, I've seen some believe the bench press is suboptimal, but we just have four studies comparing the barbell bench press to other exercises while measuring muscle growth. Insofar as chest growth, the papers find fairly similar hypertrophy. As for the triceps, it's unsurprising that overall triceps growth was better with skull crushers. But quite fascinatingly, regional differences may exist as this paper found the lateral head of the triceps grew more with the bench press than with skull crushers. Proponents of statements like these frequently base their claims on so-called mechanistic data, and some of them say mechanistic data is superior to outcome data, which I think is very much misguided to say the least. A tacit assumption here is that we know all there is to know about hypertrophy mechanisms, but take a look at this monster review paper and the conclusion it comes to. Investigations in upcoming years will continue to confirm or refute which of the discussed mechanisms are obligatory for, rather than coinciding with, load induced skeletal muscle hypertrophy. This is in stark contrast to the extreme confidence some profess online. Now, some may say the reason the current data actually measuring hypertrophy fails to support their predictions is due to some reason X. That could be true, but the great thing is these are often testable hypotheses, and until it's tested it would be disingenuous to act as though you know what's true. Moving forward, people can make sciencey claims without any references. It's not a guarantee they're wrong, but you should have some healthy suspicion. For example, some people have implied the research demonstrates that isometrics are inferior without any references. So, many were misled into thinking that science says isometrics are inferior, but that simply isn't true. The majority of evidence we have does not find worse hypertrophy with isometrics. An extreme position I've encountered a few times is that research examining hypertrophy and strength is ultimately worthless and hasn't provided anything of value. I think there is a tendency for people to forget about the value that research has already provided. Many people take creatine with the belief that it can increase muscle size and strength, and that it's a safe supplement, but why do they believe this? Many correctly pointed the fact that it's been extensively studied. Although I wouldn't call BCAAsand leucine supplementation useless in all circumstances, many people correctly recognize that they are not essential for maximizing hypertrophy. Again, thanks to the evidence on this topic. Regarding protein consumption, many people aren't as concerned about consuming a protein shake immediately post-workout, since it is clear that protein timing is simply not as important as total daily protein intake. As far as training goes, there are many things that could be said on this front, but as one example, there are many people well aware that resting for short durations between sets is not essential for maximizing hypertrophy. Longer resturations can work and might actually be better in certain scenarios. I think we shouldn't underestimate the potential of research too. There are certain questions that can only reasonably be answered through research. For example, what are the stimuli and sensors that initiate hypertrophy? What exact role does mechanical tension build up of metabolites or muscle damage play? Currently, tension stands out as the most potent stimuli, but as mentioned earlier, there's still a lot to uncover. What is the nature of muscle growth? We all know muscle fibers can get bigger, but there are different ways this could occur. Do different training styles diverge in the way they increase fiber size and might humans truly experience muscle hyperplasia? Continued exploration of this is happening. One certainly reasonable point about much research is that it typically provides the average results, but research has the potential to identify individual differences and perhaps even ultimately explain them in its entirety. For example, there's this review paper examining potential physiological differences between people who may grow more than others. Now, the research in this is very much in its early stages. In my view, some of the best work on individual differences has come in the last year and a half or so, including a paper exploring individual differences with volume. I may cover this in more detail if people are interested enough. A critique I occasionally come across is that science flip-flops. Some say that people who follow research constantly change their training according to the latest study. Other times in my videos I get the comment, just wait until the next study comes out suggesting the opposite. These comments are understandable. It is true that we can get studies that appear to conflict with each other, but as I've argued before, there are often sound explanations for this. Firstly, not all evidence is equal in quality. If there's a study on rats that suggest isometric contractions produce less growth and dynamic contractions, but the human evidence finds similar growth, unless you're a rat, it's clear you should care more about the human data. Secondly, two studies may arrive at seemingly divergent conclusions but can be explained by differences in methods or the populations examined. Thirdly, with hyper-tube strength research, it should actually be unsurprising for studies even with identical designs to arrive at different conclusions. Why? A lot of research on hyper-tube strength training involves small sample sizes. With small samples, we can get results that fail to reflect the true effects due to chance and low power. If you're interested in learning more about this, check out this video where we go into more depth and detail a simulation that drives this point home. Nevertheless, what this means is that we shouldn't place too much emphasis on individual studies. You certainly should not change anything about your training based on them. Fortunately, we can leverage small sample size studies through combining their results with a meta-analysis. In fact, we have meta-analysis on virtually every key training variable, volume, proximity to failure, frequency, rest intervals, and rep tempo. These involve greater statistical power and when done well, provide a much more solid basis to draw conclusions. Now, none of this is to say that what's supported the most by the research never changes. The essence of science is to have no allegiance to a particular outcome, and if the weight of the evidence shifts to support a different conclusion, that should not be viewed as a weakness whatsoever. Of course, such a transition is not something that typically happens overnight. Questionable research practices, statistical errors, and poor methodology aren't hard to find, but researchers are kind of everywhere. Some can reveal problems with the work of others while providing solutions. For example, excellent work by these researchers led to the startling conclusion. 85% of the 20 most highly cited meta-analyses in strengthened conditioning research contained at least one statistical error. They provide advice and recommendations which, when taken on board, should help reduce the incidence of such mistakes. Note that not all these errors are of equal severity. Some may have virtually no influence on the conclusions while others may be more problematic and it could depend on the context. Furthermore, all of the meta-analyses analyzed were published before 2019 with one back as far as 2004, and most were not focused on hypertrophy outcomes. Of course, this is not to say that errors do not occur in more recent meta-analyses focused on hypertrophy. In fact, earlier this year I was re-reading a meta-analysis on protein intake for lean mass changes published in 2022, but I noticed they used DZFX sizes. If you're not familiar with FX sizes, what I'm about to say is going to sound like a foreign language, so just bear with me for a second. What they did is subtract the mean difference in changes in lean mass between a protein and control group, and then divide this by the pool change score standard deviation. Some people don't necessarily mind this, but it was considered an error in the aforementioned paper. When it comes to determining the magnitude of an effect which is what we typically care about, dividing by the pooled pre-standard deviation is more appropriate. I reached out to some very smart people and one of the researchers I contacted, James Steele, has decided to redo this analysis using some highly interesting methods, so we can look forward to a new meta-analysis on protein intake, and I'm excited to cover it when it's out. With all that said, I do believe the quality of meta-analyses is generally improving, and a fair number of the meta-analyses in the hypertrophy space that I was alluding to earlier have been released in the last few years. All of these have been done to what I think is an exceptional standard. I'll likely have some more videos on these in the future where I dive deeper into them, and respond to some criticisms I've seen raised against some of them. Furthermore, the quality of individual studies is also generally improving. For example, we had this excellent paper comparing training to failure versus stopping one to two reps from failure on highly trained individuals. I thought they did an excellent job with the design and methods, and they also provided some training footage. They found similar growth between the two conditions, and you can learn more about this paper in this video. Circling back to the work of James Steele and his colleagues, he was involved in the study comparing different ranges of motions in just under 300 subjects, a sample size far larger than what we typically see. === FILE: Do 5 Reps MAXIMIZE Hypertrophy？ (NEW STUDY) [6yyOi1EPYAk].en.txt ===

For maximizing hypertrophy, should low,\h moderate, or high repetition numbers be used? Well, as we've mentioned in other\h videos, there's a great number of\h\h studies finding loads between 80% one-rep\h max and 30% one-rep max produce similar\h\h muscle hypertrophy, so long as repetitions\h are performed to or very close to failure. Very broadly, this equates to\h performing between 8 and 35 repetitions. But, what about fewer than 8 repetitions? Say 5 repetitions, for example. Could\h this still optimize hypertrophy? For quite a while, I automatically\h assumed there was good evidence showing\h\h 5 repetitions could build muscle optimally. In fact, I've previously said in videos reps\h between 5 and 35 are similarly effective\h\h for hypertrophy, provided repetitions\h are performed to or close to failure. However, a new study by Vann et al. made\h me re-assess this belief and re-examine the\h\h research on rep ranges, and now I'm less certain\h if 5 repetitions could optimally build muscle. Let us overview this study,\h discuss its limitations,\h\h and then detail how it relates to\h the overall rep range research. Vann et al. recruited 15 trained men\h with an average back squat of 167kg.\h\h For these subjects, this equated to\h them squatting 1.9x their bodyweight. Each subject had one leg assigned\h to a high load condition,\h\h and their other leg assigned\h to a high volume condition. Both legs were trained on the unilateral\h leg extension and unilateral leg press,\h\h three times per week for a total of 6 weeks. With the leg assigned to the high load\h condition, they performed 3 sets of 5\h\h repetitions on both exercises every session.\h They also progressed load weekly by 2.5%. During the first week, they trained with\h 82.5% of the pre-study one-rep maxes on both\h\h exercises, and they progressed this load by\h 2.5% each week such that by the 6th week,\h\h they were training with 95% of their\h pre-study one-rep maxes on both exercises. With the leg assigned to the high volume\h condition, they performed the program on-screen. They trained with sets of 10 repetitions with 60%\h\h one-rep max loads. They did not progress\h this load whatsoever throughout the study.\h\h By the 6th week, they were still training\h with 60% of their pre-study one-rep maxes. What they did progress, however, was\h the volume (in the form of sets). During the first weeks, they mainly\h performed 1 to 2 sets per exercise.\h\h But during the later weeks, they mainly\h performed 3 or 4 sets per exercise. Before and after the study, a\h range of measurements was assessed. After the study, the researchers\h found increases in vastus lateralis\h\h cross-sectional area were greater for the high\h volume condition versus the high load condition.\h\h In fact, the high load condition\h saw on average no gains. These findings are highly interesting,\h especially when considering how the two\h\h conditions differed in the set numbers they\h performed and how close to failure they trained. Exploring set numbers first, despite the high\h volume condition progressing their set numbers\h\h across the 6 weeks, they still ultimately did not\h perform as many sets as the high load condition. As for how close to failure they trained, we know\h the high volume condition involved performing sets\h\h of 10 reps with a 60% one-rep max load, and they\h did not progress load at all throughout the study. As you can probably perform\h 20 maximum repetitions,\h\h give or take a few, with a 60% one-rep max\h load, this group would have been training\h\h 10 or so reps away from failure per\h set. This is very far from failure. Opposingly, the high load condition\h performed sets of 5 reps with loads that\h\h likely meant they were largely training\h 0 to 3 reps away from failure per set. Let us now go through some limitations and\h considerations with this Vann et al. study,\h\h and then try and figure out how it\h fits into the rest of the literature. Firstly, we know that by the end of the study,\h the high volume condition saw greater increases\h\h in vastus lateralis cross-sectional\h area versus the high load condition. The table on screen summarizes all\h the current research (I'm aware of)\h\h exploring how 5 or so reps compares\h to higher rep numbers for hypertrophy. Nevertheless, combining the Vann et al.\h study with the rest of this overall data,\h\h it's clear to see it is far from crystal\h clear as to whether 5 reps can truly be\h\h optimal and efficient for hypertrophy. More research is going to be\h highly valuable and insightful. At the end of the day, it's really your choice on\h how you interpret all the data we've overviewed. If your main goal is to maximize hypertrophy, and\h you've been training with 5 reps and experiencing\h\h perfectly fine hypertrophy, I don't think\h there's any solid reason to change anything. === FILE: Do You Gain MORE Muscle Fibers With Training？ (Research Overview) [5fPsnaCMnw8].en.txt ===

In response to resistance training,\h muscles typically increase in size. One of the most commonly accepted and supported\h ways that this occurs is via an increase in the\h\h size of their individual muscle fibers. This\h whole process is called muscle hypertrophy. However, another plausible way\h muscle could increase in size\h\h is through something called muscle hyperplasia. Muscle hyperplasia refers to an increase in\h the number of muscles fibers within a muscle. In theory, this could be achieved by completely\h new muscle fibers being manufactured,\h\h or by pre-existing muscle\h fibers splitting into two. In this video, we'll thoroughly examine the\h existing research on muscle hyperplasia,\h\h with the primary aim of answering if\h muscle hyperplasia truly occurs in humans. Although we'll be assessing\h human research shortly,\h\h animal studies are highly valuable for\h potential insights into muscle hyperplasia. As we'll come to find out, there are major\h methodological and ethical constraints\h\h that limit the quality and validity\h of human research in this area. With studies conducted on animals, these\h constraints become less of a problem. First things first, for researchers\h to explore if muscle fiber number can\h\h increase, they need to train\h the animals in some form. Commonly, this is done in one of three ways:\h\h stretching, synergistic\h ablation, or weight training. Stretching involves using some piece of weighted\h equipment to stretch a muscle of an animal. For instance, on-screen depicts\h how a study by Alway et al.\h\h stretched the anterior latissimus\h dorsi of Japenese quails. Note, I did say anterior latissimus dorsi.\h\h Interestingly, Japenese quails also\h have a posterior latissimus dorsi. In animal studies that use\h stretching to train the muscle,\h\h they either do so chronically or intermittently. In studies that chronically stretch the animal,\h\h they typically stretch the muscle\h for 30 whole straight days. Conversely, in studies that\h use intermittent stretching,\h\h they stretch the muscle for 1 whole\h day, followed by 2-3 days of rest.\h\h This cycle is repeated throughout\h the full duration of the study. As we can see, these stretching protocols\h are extreme. Consequently, we should be\h\h extremely cautious in trying to extrapolate\h results from studies using this to humans. As for synergistic ablation,\h this is undoubtedly more extreme. It involves surgically removing\h a muscle from a muscle group,\h\h thereby overloading the remaining\h muscles in that muscle group. Most commonly, this technique is used in rodents\h\h and involves surgically removing the\h gastrocnemius from the calf muscle group,\h\h thereby resulting in the soleus being\h significantly overloaded during normal tasks. As this is method is highly extreme,\h we also need to be extremely cautious\h\h in trying to extrapolate results\h from studies using this to humans. Finally, weight training involves having animals\h perform exercises in a similar way to humans. For instance, this study by Tamaki et\h al. used a custom piece of equipment\h\h to get rats to squat for 15 sets of 15\h repetitions with a 65-75% one-rep max load. As this method is substantially\h more comparable to what humans do,\h\h studies using this method may be considered more\h applicable to humans than the other two methods. Okay, so now that we've established the various\h ways in which researchers can train the muscles\h\h of animals, let us establish how they can\h measure if muscle fiber number has increased. There seem to be two ways of\h doing this, either via direct\h\h counting or counting from a cross-section. Direct counting involves removing the whole\h muscle and counting every single muscle fiber. Of course, this can only be performed\h once. You can't perform this method before\h\h and after a training duration, as once you've\h removed the muscle, it cannot be put back. Therefore, to determine if the number\h of muscle fibers has increased,\h\h there are two plausible ways used. In the first way, researchers get the\h animals to train only one side of their body,\h\h while their other side of\h the body remains untrained. Then, after a training duration, if the\h number of muscle fibers in the trained muscle\h\h is more than the number of muscle\h fibers in the untrained muscle,\h\h we assume that training\h increased muscle fiber number. The underlying assumption here is\h that before the training period,\h\h the trained and untrained muscles would have\h had a comparable number of muscle fibers.\h\h This may not always be an accurate\h assumption and is thus a limitation. The second way involves using the direct\h counting method to compare the number of\h\h muscle fibers within the muscles of an animal\h that trained to an animal that did not train. After a training duration, if the number of\h muscle fibers in the muscle of a trained animal\h\h is greater than the number of muscle fibers\h within the muscle of an untrained animal,\h\h that before the training duration,\h\h the number of muscle fibers between the trained\h and untrained animals would have been similar. Again, this may not always be an accurate\h Now, one major advantage of this\h method is that as the whole muscle\h\h is removed, all of the muscle fibers are\h counted from the muscle of the animals. However, this also makes it somewhat unpractical\h for researchers, as the dissection of a whole\h\h muscle and counting of potentially ten's of\h thousands of muscle fibers can be difficult. The second method, counting from a cross-section,\h somewhat solves this impracticality. It involves removing only a cross-section from the\h\h muscle and then counting the number of\h muscle fibers in this cross-section. For practical reasons, I believe\h researchers don't take a cross-section\h\h from the muscle of the same animal\h before and after a training duration. Therefore, like the last method, researchers\h either compare the number of muscle fibers\h\h counted between a trained side and untrained side,\h\h or between an animal that trained\h and an animal that didn't train. Counting the number of muscle\h fibers in a cross-section\h\h is potentially more practical,\h as only a sample is required. However, there is a vital\h limitation with this method. It's very possible that the number\h of muscle fibers in a cross-section\h\h could increase without an actual\h increase in muscle fiber number. One example of this is when an increase in\h the pennation angle of the muscle fibers\h\h outpaces the growth of the muscle fibers. Let me explain. Remember, muscles attach to bones in order\h to create movement in the human body. A muscle has two attachment points. Some muscles in the human body do not have\h their muscle fibers run in a straight line\h\h from their two points of attachment. Rather, some muscles have their fibers angled\h slightly between the two points of attachment. The pennation angle is the name given\h to the angle of the muscle fibers. When assessing a particular cross-section of a\h muscle, if an increase in pennation angle outpaces\h\h the growth of the individual fibers, more muscle\h fibers could be observed in that cross-section,\h\h despite there being no actual\h Another example in where more muscle\h fibers could be observed in a cross-section\h\h without an actual increase in muscle fiber number\h relates to an increase in muscle fiber length. Therefore, when assessing a\h particular cross-section of a muscle,\h\h it's possible that a muscle\h fiber could increase in length\h\h to the point where it is now newly\h observed in that cross-section. In general, as a result of these\h potentially vital limitations\h\h when counting muscle fibers from a cross-section,\h a direct count is considered more reliable. Hopefully we've now got a solid\h understanding of how researchers can train\h\h and measure an increase in\h muscle fiber number in animals. Let us now look at the results of such studies. A meta-analysis by Kelley combined the\h results of numerous animal studies. What the analysis found was that muscle fiber\h number increased by 20.95% in studies that had\h\h animals stretch, 11.59% in studies that\h had animals weight training, and 5.44%\h\h in studies that used synergistic ablation. As we noted, given that studies using stretching\h or synergistic ablation are quite extreme and\h\h not applicable to what humans do, the weight\h training data is most relevant and insightful. Specifically, 5 studies were comprised\h in the weight training results. 3 of them\h\h involved counting from cross-sections,\h while 2 involved direct counting. All 5 of these studies found an\h increase in muscle fiber number,\h\h and so this includes the 2\h studies that used direct counting. As mentioned earlier, given direct\h counting is considered more reliable\h\h than counting from cross-sections,\h and the 2 direct counting studies\h\h found an increase in muscle fiber\h number, this adds to our confidence\h\h muscle hyperplasia may indeed increase\h with weight training (at least in animals). Alright, so the animal evidence seems to suggest\h\h that weight training-like stimuli\h may induce muscle hyperplasia. But, results obtained from animals studies\h may not necessarily apply to humans. Unfortunately, there are major\h ethical and practical constraints\h\h when attempting to find out if\h muscle hyperplasia occurs in humans. Recall that the direct method\h of counting muscle fibers\h\h involves removing a whole muscle\h and counting all of the fibers. The first major problem here is that\h I'm not too sure there are many humans\h\h out there willing to have one of\h their muscles completely removed. Even if there were willing human subjects,\h and a researcher could get clearance,\h\h human muscles can contain hundreds\h of thousands of muscle fibers,\h\h making the direct counting of all\h of them extremely impractical. For instance, it's broadly estimated\h that the biceps brachii of humans\h\h contains anywhere from 198,000\h to 419,000 muscle fibers. As far as I'm aware, counting from a\h cross-section has also not been done in humans. I think this because it's too difficult to obtain\h\h a large enough sample from human\h muscles to be considered valid. Despite all of this,\h\h researchers have used other ways in trying to\h find out muscle hyperplasia occurs in humans. There have been 4 cross-sectional studies\h finding potential indirect evidence\h\h that muscle fiber number\h may increase with training. Specifically, these studies\h compared muscle characteristics\h\h between a group of trained bodybuilders or\h powerlifters to a group of untrained individuals. As you'd expect, the bodybuilders and powerlifters\h\h had larger whole muscle cross-sectional\h areas than the untrained individuals. However, the cross-sectional area\h of the individual muscle fibers\h\h assessed was not different between the untrained\h individuals and the bodybuilders or powerlifters. However, there is still a whole\h host of problems with this. One major one is that human\h studies can only assess the\h\h size of a limited number of muscle fibers. This is because to assess the\h size of individual muscle fibers,\h\h a small sample must first\h be taken from the muscle. The muscle fibers in this small sample may not be\h\h identical to muscle fibers\h elsewhere in the muscle. Firstly this data is only from 6 subjects,\h which is an extremely small sample size.\h\h On top of this, the equation\h used to estimate fiber number\h\h is very rough, and there are many\h scenarios in which it can be inaccurate. Indeed, there is evidence from rats\h and crabs that fibers may split\h\h when diffusing oxygen across a\h muscle fiber becomes difficult. To conclude, despite there being\h some interesting hypotheses\h\h behind why the body may\h increase muscle fiber number,\h\h the current research on whether muscle hyperplasia\h occurs in humans from training is far from clear. When overviewing the current animal and\h human research, some may believe it is\h\h promising in suggesting fiber numbers may\h increase, whereas others may think otherwise. Ultimately, due to the major limitation\h in studying whether muscle fiber number\h\h can increase in humans, I'm not sure we're\h going to get a conclusive answer anytime soon. Perhaps if non-invasive technologies can\h be developed to accurately count muscle\h\h fiber numbers in the future, we'll\h be able to make firmer conclusions.

=== FILE: Does SuperSlow Training Produce Super Fast Gains？ (Research Analysis) [HV8xg0w9BHw].en.txt ===

In this video, we aim to establish whether you're\h\h missing out on superfast gains by\h not performing superslow training. Traveling back to the 1980s, it's claimed an\h individual named Ken Hutchins, upon conducting\h\h resistance training research on older women with\h fragile bones, developed superslow training. Super slow resistance training seemed\h to be ideal for this demographic,\h\h as one article claims Hutchins stated "these women\h were so weak we were afraid for their safety". What precisely is superslow training? I ran across a PDF authored by Ken Hutchins,\h on which he makes a distinction between\h\h superslow training as a protocol and\h superslow training as a philosophy. As a protocol, superslow training simply\h refers to performing exercises with a\h\h 10-second lifting duration and\h a 4-10-second lowering duration. As a philosophy, superslow training\h appears to be a whole training methodology.\h\h Ken notes sessions should not exceed 30 minutes,\h 3-7 days of rest are required between sessions,\h\h among a few other factors. Environmental factors are also mentioned,\h\h with Ken, quite intriguingly, believing\h training sessions should be devoid of music. Other sources also state that superslow workouts\h typically only comprise one set per exercise. Though superslow training seemingly\h has formal origins in older women,\h\h Wikipedia states, something like\h the superslow training was used\h\h by bodybuilders and powerlifters to\h break plateaus well before the 80s. Of course, these claims are difficult to verify. Now, there are indeed many similarties\h between superslow training,\h\h Arthur Jones' high-intensity training,\h and even training recommendations from\h\h other individuals such as Dr. Dough\h McGuff's stuff from "Body by Science". In the future, I do plan to assess these\h other training methodologies in more depth. But in this video specifically, we'll be\h focusing on the protocol of superslow training.\h\h That's the 10-second lifting and 4-10-second\h lowering repetition tempo recommended. When I say superslow training from hereafter, know\h I'm merely referring to THIS repetition tempo. So, is superslow training a superior way\h to develop muscle hypertrophy and strength? Allow us to explore the existing literature.\h First, we'll examine superslow training's\h\h effectiveness for strength development, and then\h its effectiveness for hypertrophic adaptations. A 2001 Westcott et al. study is often cited as\h\h evidence for superslow training being\h a potent strength-building stimulus. In the paper, two studies are described. Both studies involved just over 70\h previously untrained men and women\h\h (their ages ranged from 25-82). They were assigned into either\h a superslow or regular group. Both of these groups trained\h a range of nautilus machine\h\h exercises 2-3 times per week for a total of 8\h weeks (in study 1) or 10 weeks (in study 2). The exercises performed each session were the leg\h extension, leg curl, leg press, neck flexion, neck\h\h extension, pullover, chest press, chest crossover,\h lateral raise, biceps curl, and triceps extension. The regular group, each session, performed\h each exercise with 1 set of 8-12 repetitions,\h\h with each repetition consisting of a\h 2-second lifting and 4-second lowering tempo. The superslow group, each session,\h performed 1 set of 4-6 repetitions,\h\h with each repetition consisting of a 10-second\h lifting and 4-second lowering duration. Both groups, throughout the study duration,\h\h attempted to gradually increase the load\h they used on their exercise sets within the\h\h variables prescribed to them (in other\h words, they progressively overloaded). Before and after the study, the\h regular group's strength was tested via\h\h measuring the maximum load they\h could lift for 10 repetitions,\h\h Conversely, the superslow group's\h strength was tested via measuring\h\h the maximum load they could\h lift for a single repetition,\h\h with that repetition consisting of a\h 10-second lifting and 4-second lowering tempo. In study 1, these tests were done\h with all of the trained exercises.\h\h In study 2, these tests were\h done only with the chest press. In both studies, on average, the superslow group\h experienced greater strength gains. As noted by\h\h the authors, the superslow group saw roughly 50%\h more strength gains versus the regular group. So, there we have it. Superslow training is\h optimal for evoking strength adaptations. Not so fast. As with all studies, limitations exist,\h and there is one very notable limitation. As many of you likely noticed, the strength\h tests were different between both groups\h\h (in terms of repetition numbers\h and the repetition tempos used). Generally, most people think of strength as the\h maximum load a person can lift on an exercise\h\h without using any deliberate tempo, rather the\h person just attempts to lift as much as they can\h\h (this is typically called a\h person's one-repetition maximum). This begs the question: how would typical\h one-repetition maximum strength gains\h\h look between the superslow and regular groups? Fortunately, another study by\h Keeler et al. examined this. 14 previously untrained women (with an average\h\h age of 32) were allocated into\h a superslow or regular group. Both groups trained a range of\h exercises 3 times per week for 10 weeks. The exercises performed each session were the\h leg extension, leg curl, leg press, bench press,\h\h seated row, biceps curl, triceps\h extension, and lat-pulldown. The regular group,\h\h each session, performed each exercise for 1 set\h of 8-12 repetitions with an 80% one-repetition\h\h max load, with each repetition consisting of a\h 2-second lifting and 4-second lowering tempo. The superslow group, each session, performed\h\h each exercise for a single set of 8-12\h repetitions with A-50% one-rep max load,\h\h with each repetition consisting of a\h 10-second lifting and 5-second lowering tempo. Both groups, throughout the study, attempted\h to increase the load they used to maintain\h\h their respective relative loading (again, an 80%\h one-rep max load for the regular group and A-50%\h\h one-rep max load for the superslow group). Before and after the study, one-repetition\h maximum while not using any deliberate tempo\h\h (just trying to lift the maximum weight) on all\h trained exercises were evaluated for both groups. For 5 of the 8 exercises, the regular group\h experienced much greater strength gains.\h\h For the other 3 exercises\h (the row, triceps extension,\h\h and biceps curl), strength gains were not\h statistically different between both groups.\h\h Though, it's still worth noting the percentages\h still appear to favor the regular group. Therefore, this study indicates for\h increasing one-repetition maximum strength,\h\h superslow training is suboptimal. These findings are logical. Superslow training, because of the very slow\h repetition tempos, would require you to train\h\h with relatively light loads (that is, a lower\h percentage of your one-repetition maximum). This matters as the current data\h indicate training with heavier loads\h\h (80% one-repetition maximum or heavier)\h evokes greater one-repetition maximum\h\h strength gains compared to\h training with lighter loads. Such findings are intuitive. If you want\h to increase the maximum load you can lift,\h\h training with heavy loads should\h promote this more than lighter loads. As such, I think for individuals wishing to\h maximize their one-repetition maximum strength,\h\h simply training with heavier loads, and\h aiming to move them as fast as you can,\h\h is a sound recommendation. Now, this does not mean super slow training is\h utterly useless for anything strength-related.\h\h Recall the Westcott et al. study found\h that for increasing the maximum load\h\h you can lift WHILE using a 10-second\h lifting and 4-second lowering tempo,\h\h training with this very tempo was\h extremely effective at accomplishing this. Consequently, if an individual wish to maximize\h the loads they can lift with a superslow tempo,\h\h superslow training is probably going\h to be the best way to accomplish this.\h\h This information may be particularly useful\h for those who simply cannot train with very\h\h heavy loads (due to underlying conditions or\h as they simply dislike heavy load training). Progressing on, is superslow training\h superior for muscle building? As of right now, I'm only aware of one\h study by Schuenke et al. exploring this. 19 previously untrained women (with an average\h\h age of 21) were assigned to\h a superslow or regular group. Both groups trained the leg\h press, squat, and leg extension.\h\h Each for 3 sets, 2-3 times per week for 6 weeks. The regular group performed each exercise set\h with 6-10 repetitions, using an 80-85% one-rep\h\h max load, with each repetition consisting of a\h 1-2-second lifting and 1-2-second lowering tempo. The superslow group performed each exercise set\h with 6-10 repetitions, using a 40-60% one-rep\h\h 10-second lifting and 4-second lowering tempo. Both groups rested for 2 minutes\h between sets. Also, if subjects\h\h could perform more than their prescribed\h repetition numbers, loads were increased. By the end of the study, growth of fast and\h slow-twitch muscle fibers from the vastus\h\h lateralis (part of the quadriceps)\h was greater for the regular group. Correspondingly, this data interestingly\h\h suggests superslow training might be\h suboptimal for evoking hypertrophy. Some may be thinking this is likely\h due to the use of the light loads\h\h (40-60% one-rep max loads) by the superslow group.\h However, as we've examined in previous videos,\h\h loads between 30% and 80% one-rep max\h produce similar muscle hypertrophy\h\h when repetitions are performed very close or to\h failure (as was more or less done in this study). Due to this, the use of the light\h loads per se, by the superslow group,\h\h likely would not be sufficient\h to explain these results. So what does? There is another potential explanation,\h we'll explore this shortly. But first, I wanted to critically examine\h a rationale superslow training proponents\h\h sometimes put forth as to why they believe\h superslow training is superior for hypertrophy. Namely, they claim superslow training creates\h more tension in a muscle for a given workload. Tension (that's mechanical tension) is equal\h to the force generated by muscle fibers. Something called mechanosensors within\h muscle fibers can detect these forces\h\h and transduce them into a signaling cascade\h that results in muscle fiber hypetrophy. Based on this, to maximize overall muscle\h growth, we'd want to recruit as many\h\h muscle fibers as possible and have them sustain\h fairly decent forces for a sufficient duration. Superslow training proponents believe a\h superslow tempo accomplishes this best,\h\h due to the force-velocity relationship. The force-velocity relationship states\h that faster muscle contractions result\h\h in less force production, while slower muscle\h contractions result in greater force production. Consequently, a superslow tempo,\h due to the slow muscle contraction,\h\h maximizes the amount of force a\h muscle can produce. Put another way,\h\h it maximizes mechanical tension and\h thus is superior for building muscle. However, I believe this is a misapplication\h of the force-velocity relationship and\h\h is more than likely misleading.\h Let's establish why I think this. It's essential to recognize\h the conditions in which the\h\h force-velocity relationship was established. It can be established with unfatigued isolated\h muscle fibers contracting a single or few times\h\h at different velocities. For example, when\h maximally stimulating a fiber at different\h\h shortening velocities, force outcomes are in\h line with the force-velocity relationship. It can also be established when comparing\h\h unfatigued muscle contractions at\h different forces or velocities. As a simple example, compare performing one\h rep with a 90% one-rep max load to with a\h\h 30% one-rep max load. Despite you trying to\h move both of these loads as fast as you can,\h\h your muscles will generate more force and\h contract slower against the 90% one-rep max load.\h\h This is in line with the\h force-velocity relationship. However, these aforementioned conditions in which\h the force-velocity relationship applies are very\h\h different from lifting a constant light load\h to or very close to failure, and they do not\h\h mean that lifting this constant light load slowly\h will result in greater muscle force production. Henneman's size principle helps us understand why. Different types of muscle\h fibers exist within a muscle.\h\h These different types of muscle fibers can\h likely be categorized across a spectrum. On one end are slow-twitch muscle fibers,\h\h which generally produce low forces\h but are highly fatigue resistant. On the other end are fast-twitch muscle fibers,\h\h which generally produce high\h forces but are highly fatigable. Henneman's size principle indicates\h when muscle force requirements are low,\h\h only recruitment of slower-twitch muscle fibers\h is necessary. But, as force requirements increase,\h\h or you near failure while attempting\h to sustain a given force output,\h\h those faster-twitch muscle fibers\h are incrementally recruited. Here's the thing, with a given light load, lifting\h it slower actually reduces the force requirements. Force is equal to mass multiplied by acceleration.\h In our case, mass mainly refers to the load used.\h\h Using a slower tempo will reduce your\h acceleration during a repetition,\h\h thus resulting in lower force requirements. A study by Schilling et al. demonstrates this. They found when a national weightlifter\h performed the back squat with 170kg,\h\h using a 10-second lifting\h and 4-second lowering tempo\h\h produced lower mean and peak propulsive forces\h compared to using a maximal lifting speed Consequently, lifting light loads with a slower\h\h repetition will actually result in\h low mechanical tension INITIALLY. However, notice I said initially.\h\h Using slower repetition tempos is not\h necessarily suboptimal for hypertrophy. Recall not only do force requirements\h determine the number of muscle fibers recruited\h\h (as well as the force produced\h by recruited individual fibers),\h\h but your proximity to failure while trying\h to sustain a given force output does as well. With a given light load, although\h using a slower repetition tempo\h\h will involve less force production\h compared to using a faster tempo,\h\h as you continue to perform repetitions\h and get closer and closer to failure,\h\h the recruitment of more muscle fibers (as well\h as probably increased force production by some\h\h recruited individual fibers) must occur for you to\h try and sustain repetitions with this given load. As a result, regardless of whether a\h faster or slower repetition tempo is used,\h\h so long as repetitions are\h performed very close or to failure,\h\h you likely end up recruiting a similar\h number of muscle fibers and potentially\h\h exposing the individual recruited\h fibers to comparable levels of force. Put another way, mechanical tension\h likely ends up being similar. So, to summarize this\h hypertrophy discussion so far,\h\h it's very likely superslow training DOES\h NOT produce more mechanical tension. Rather, it's likely so long as repetitions\h are performed very close or to failure,\h\h slower repetitions tempos would be similarly\h effective to faster repetition tempos. However, if this is true, why did the Schuenke\h study find superslow training to be suboptimal? First and foremost, it's worth\h noting this was only a single study.\h\h Also, limitations and\h considerations exist within it.\h\h As one example, the subjects were previously\h untrained women, meaning it's not clear\h\h if the results obtained would apply to\h individuals outside of this demographic. Even so, let us put forth a\h potential hypothesis behind\h\h why superslow training could\h be suboptimal for hypertrophy. As noted moments ago, it's likely so long\h as repetitions are performed very close or\h\h to failure, slower repetitions tempos would be\h similarly effective to faster repetition tempos. In most cases, I believe this\h statement is true. For example,\h\h a meta-analysis by Schoenfeld et al. found that\h individual repetition tempos between 0.5 to 8\h\h seconds produced similar muscle hypertrophy when\h repetitions were performed to or close to failure. However, there might be a problem with\h using individual repetition tempos\h\h beyond the 8-second range (which\h is done with superslow training). This problem is central fatigue. Remember, the reason your muscles produce\h force is thanks to the electrical signals\h\h they receive from the central nervous\h system (the brain and spinal cord). Central fatigue refers to fatigue during exercise\h that decreases the number of electrical signals\h\h sent to the muscle. At the level of the\h muscle, this means a reduction in muscle\h\h fiber recruitment and/or a reduction in the\h force generated by recruited individual fibers.\h\h Put another way, central fatigue\h can lower mechanical tension. Contrary to what most people seem to believe,\h light load and longer-lasting contractions\h\h generate more central fatigue versus higher\h load and shorter-lasting contractions. As an example, Yoon et al.\h et al. had 9 men and 9 women,\h\h on separate days, perform a contraction\h of their biceps at either 20% of their\h\h maximum voluntary contraction force or 80%\h of their maximum voluntary contraction force.\h\h They held each contraction until force\h declined by 10% of the target force. On average, subjects held the 20% contraction\h for around 14 minutes before they could no\h\h longer produce the required force, whereas the 80%\h contraction was only held for around 25 seconds. But, the 20% contraction produced greater\h central fatigue than the 80% contraction. Now, as we've already noted in this video,\h\h loads as light as 30% one-rep max produce\h similar hypertrophy to 80% one-rep max loads,\h\h when repetitions are performed\h very close or to failure. Moreover, much of these studies had subjects\h use a 2-4 second individual repetition tempo.\h\h Thus, we can likely conclude any\h central fatigue generated within\h\h these training variables does not interfere\h with muscle hypertrophy and is perfectly fine. Similarly, we've also already noted that\h individual repetition tempos between 0.5 to\h\h 8 seconds are similarly effective for hypertrophy\h when repetitions are performed very close or to\h\h failure. In these studies, it seems mainly\h 50% to 80% one-rep max loads were used.\h\h Thus, we can also likely conclude any\h central fatigue generated within these\h\h training variables does not interfere with\h muscle hypertrophy and is perfectly fine. However, and this is the key\h point, perhaps superslow training\h\h (due not only to the light loads but probably more\h so the superslow repetition tempo of 10-second\h\h lifting and 4-10 seconds of lowering that would\h significantly extend the set duration) ultimately\h\h evokes excessive central fatigue levels that\h do indeed interfere with muscle hypertrophy. Perhaps this explains the Schuenke study findings. It's worth again emphasizing this is merely\h a hypothesis based on the findings of a\h\h single study. At the end of the day, future\h research would be needed to substantiate this.

=== FILE: Does the 3⧸7 Method Build More Muscle？ [PtFbsZ3pfXY].en.txt ===

When training to build strength or muscle, most people use a sets and reps structure. For instance, you may perform 3 sets of 6 reps on the bench press in a session. However, something called the 3/7 method seems to be gaining some degree of popularity in recent years. This method appears to have originated from a 2005 French Fitness book. The 3/7 method has you select a 70% one-rep max load (which equates to a load you can generally perform a maximum of 12 repetitions with). With this 70% one-rep max load, you perform 3 reps, rest for 15 seconds, perform 4 reps, rest for 15 seconds, perform 5 reps, rest for 15 seconds, perform 6 reps, rest for 15 seconds, and then perform a final 7 reps. Generally, the first 3 and 4 rep sets are quite easy. But, the 5, 6 and 7 rep sets are pretty much near or to failure. Could doing this be superior for muscle or strength gain? Let us examine the evidence. A study by Stragier et al. had 43 previously untrained men train a machine biceps exercise twice per week for 8 weeks. A normal group, each session, performed the exercise with 8 sets of 6 repetitions with a 70% one-rep max load, using 2.5 minutes of rest between sets. A 3/7 group, each session, with a 70% one-rep max load, performed the 3/7 method for 2 bouts, separated by 2.5 minutes of rest between bouts. Just to emphasize this, they repeated the 3/7 method twice in a session, with a 2.5-minute rest interval between them. For both groups, if a subject was unable to complete their respective prescribed protocol, assistance was provided. On the other hand, if a subject could complete their respective prescribed protocol for two sessions in a row, they increased the load they used by 2.5-5%. After the 8 weeks of training, increases in one-rep max on the machine biceps exercise were greater for the 3/7 group. Furthermore, increases in biceps long head thickness (which was averaged out from an upper, middle, and lower region) were also greater for the 3/7 group. Before exploring these hypertrophy results further, I think it's first worth looking at the strength results a little further. Despite the study finding greater increases in one-rep max with the 3/7 method, the results do not necessarily suggest the 3/7 method is optimal for strength gains. Remember, 2 bouts of the 3/7 method were compared to 8 sets of 6 reps with a 70% one-rep max load. For maximizing your one-rep max on an exercise, training with heavier loads is likely better. For example, Schoenfeld et al. found training sets on the bench press and back squat with 2-4 reps with a roughly 90% one-rep max load produced greater one-rep max gains on the bench press and back squat compared to training them with 8-12 reps with a roughly 75% one-rep max load. Therefore, if the 3/7 method was compared to training with 90%+ one-rep max loads, I think it's highly likely the 3/7 method would be inferior. Let us now dive into the hypertrophy results. As we noted, the 3/7 group experienced more gains than the normal group. However, some of you may be questioning the normal group's training program. 8 sets of 6 repetitions with a 70% one-rep max load sounds a little odd and doesn't really sound like something you would do to build muscle. Perhaps if the 3/7 method was compared to a more traditional hypertrophy protocol, say 3 to 5 sets of 8-12 repetitions performed to or near failure, the results would not have been so favorable for the 3/7 group. This was actually my initial thought when I first read the study. However, upon closer analysis, 8 sets of 6 reps with a 70% one-rep max load is probably quite effective for building muscle, meaning this may not be a problem. Firstly, a 70% one-rep max load is perfectly fine for building muscle, as we've explored in previous rep range videos. With a 70% one-rep max load, you can generally perform around a maximum of 12 repetitions to failure. The normal group only performed 6 reps per set, meaning their 1st set would have been roughly 6 reps away from failure. Now, due to the effects of cumulative fatigue, the following sets would have been closer Let us assume that each successive set puts a subject 1 rep closer to failure than the previous set. Of course, this is far from perfect. But for our purposes, it will work. When broken down in this way, it's hard to call this protocol meaningfully suboptimal for building muscle. The reason I say this is because training to failure does not appear to be neccessary for hypertrophy. A fair few papers demonstrate that training 3 to 1 rep away from failure per set is as effective for hypertrophy to training to failure. Out of the 8 sets for the normal group, 5 sets would likely have been within 3 reps from failure. Furthermore, as we'll explore in future videos, there actually is some evidence training 5 reps away from failure could also be as effective as training to failure for hypertrophy. So, perhaps even more of the normal group's sets could be classified as optimal for building muscle. On the basis of all of this, I think this study probably did find the 3/7 method to truly have some sort of enhanced benefit for muscle hypertrophy. Why could this be? Could there be something special amount incrementally performing more reps with a given load while using short rest durations. The authors of the study speculated the 3/7 method superiority could be explained by it producing more metabolic stress. Metabolic stress is the build-up of metabolites (which are products of cellular processes) such as lactate within muscles. However, I'm skeptical of this simply because the role of metabolic stress in muscle growth is far from clear. There are numerous cases in which more metabolic stress does not result in more muscle hypertrophy. All in all, I don't know if there are any legitimate reasons as to why the 3/7 method could build more muscle. Moving on, it's essential to recognize this is only a single study. There are no other studies, as far as I'm aware, exploring the effects of the 3/7 method on muscle hypertrophy. A single study is nothing near definitive and conclusive evidence. Because of this, we simply cannot be anywhere close to certain that the 3/7 method truly builds more muscle. Furthermore, the study was conducted on previously untrained individuals and so we do not know if this study can be replicated in trained individuals. The closest thing I can think of to the 3/7 method is rest-pause training. Rest-pause training involves performing reps to failure with a given load, then resting for 15 to 20 seconds, and performing further repetitions to failure with that same load. This can be repeated however many times you wish. Of course, the similarity to the 3/7 method lies in the short rest between repetition bouts. Could the rest-pause training research provide greater insight into the potential hypertrophic effects of the 3/7 method? By my count, there are only two studies that have technically explored rest-pause training. Enes et al. had 19 men with at least 2 years of training experience perform the back squat, leg press, and leg extension, twice per week for 8 weeks. A normal group trained each exercise per session with 4 sets of 12 repetitions with a 70% one-rep max load, using 2 minutes of rest between sets. A rest-pause group performed 10 repetitions with a 75% one-rep max load, rested 20 seconds, and then performed 6 further repetitions with the same load. For each exercise, they performed 3 of these rest-pause sets, with 120 seconds of rest between sets. At the fifth week of training, both groups increased their training loads by 5%. By the end of the study, increases in lateral thigh thickness (which includes the vastus lateralis and vastus intermedius), at 30%, 50%, and 70% of the thigh bone length were statistically similar between both groups, suggesting rest-pause provides no muscle growth benefit. Having said this, the rest-pause group did not take their repetitions to failure, and only one extra bout of repetitions was performed per set, so this is potentially a limitation. Another study by Prestes et al. has 18 individuals with at least 1 year of training experience perform a range of exercises four times per week for 6 weeks. A normal group performed each exercise per session with 3 sets of 6 reps with an 80% one-rep max load, using 2-3 minutes of rest between sets. A rest-pause group, for each exercise per session, performed reps to failure with an 80% one-rep max load, and then rested 20 seconds before performing further reps to failure. They did until they reached a total of 18 reps. After the 6 training weeks, increases in chest and arm thickness were similar between both groups, but increases in quadriceps thickness were greater for the rest-pause group. So the results of this study partially suggest rest-pause training can enhance muscle hypertrophy. However, there is a limitation. It seems the normal group did not apply progressive overload. Recall they were performing 3 sets of 6 reps with an 80% one-rep max load. In the early stages of the study, this likely would have meant subjects were roughly 3 to 1 reps away from failure per set, which we know is fine for muscle hypertrophy. However, as they get stronger from these initial training sessions, this 80% one-rep max load would no longer have actually been their true 80% one-rep max, rather less. Given no progressive overload was applied, meaning they did not readjust their 80% one-rep max load, they were probably training with more than 3 reps away from failure per set as the study progressed. On the other hand, given the rest-pause group was performing all their repetitions to failure, progressive overload would naturally have been applied. Due to this limitation, this study should be considered with caution. So all in all, the rest-pause research seems too limited and insufficient to provide us with any further clues on the 3/7 method. To conclude the video, a single study does seem to suggest the 3/7 method can build more muscle. However, given it is only a single study, we cannot be certain the 3/7 method truly builds more muscle, hopefully future research can provide us with more clarity. Ultimately, there probably is no terrible downside to experimenting with the 3/7 method if that's something you'd think you like to do. One thing I've yet to mention is the 3/7 method can be considered quite time-efficient. By my calculations, in the stragier et al. study, excluding the warm-up, the 3/7 group would have been training for 5-6 minutes per session, while the normal group would have been training for 19-20 minutes each session.

 prolaphataphataphat, prolifataphat, prolifataphat, prolifataphat, prolifataphat, Welcome to the house of hypertrophy. How many sets should you perform for your muscles? What types of exercises should you train with? And how can you build muscle with quicker training sessions? Three new studies add to our knowledge of these areas. We'll briefly review these new studies, understand how they fit into the overall scientific literature, and then explain what this may mean for your training to maximize muscle hypertrophy. Let's dive in. Much research on set numbers has been done on the quads, triceps, and biceps. This new study is exciting as it's explored another muscle group, the calves, a muscle many report struggling to grow. As with all studies, it's not flawless, but its findings nonetheless nudges along the path to fully understanding the relationship between sets and muscle hypertrophy. 61 untrained women trained this straight leg calf raise exercise three times per week for six weeks. One group performed two sets per session, thereby totalling six sets for the calves in a week. A second group performed three sets per session, thereby totalling nine weekly sets for the calves. A third group performed four sets per session, thereby totalling 12 weekly sets for the calves. All groups trained with 15 to 20 reps to momentary failure each set, with two minutes of rest between sets. Weights were increased as subjects got stronger to stay in the 15 to 20 rep range. Medial gastrocnemius, lateral gastrocnemius, soleus, and the sum of all these was measured before and after the study. For all measurements, growth tended to be best for the 12 weekly set group, followed by the 9 weekly set group, and then the 6 weekly set group. With the sum of all measures, the 12 weekly set group saw 73.9% greater growth than the 6 weekly set group, and 17.6% greater growth than the 9 weekly set group. Some differences weren't statistically significant, but I've previously discussed how statistical significance is not everything. Now, it's still worth pointing out the 6 weekly set group saw respectable gains. Plus, the jump in muscle growth was larger from 6 to 9 weekly sets compared to 9 to 12 weekly sets, suggesting diminishing returns. So how does this fit into the rest of the research? This meta-analysis combined the results of multiple other studies examining sets and gains. It indeed found performing 9 or more weekly sets for a muscle produced greater growth and fewer than 9 weekly sets. So the new study perfectly aligns with these results. Just in case you're confused, don't forget we're talking about the total number of sets you perform for each muscle per week. For example, 9 weekly sets for a muscle group, such as the quads, may include you performing 3 sets on each the squat, leg press, and leg extension in a week. Returning to the meta-analysis, it's still worth pointing out that, again, fewer than 9 weekly sets still build muscle. So lower set numbers are not useless, it's just that you do tend to see better gains with more sets. Summoning the spirit of scientific accuracy, we must not forget this new study was done on previously untrained women and did not exceed 12 weekly sets. In fact, much of the data behind the meta-analysis was likewise conducted on untrained individuals and did not exceed more than 12 weekly sets per muscle group. So what about data in trained individuals and more than 12 weekly sets? We've dissected this data in a previous video, feel free to check that out. But the gist is this, trained individuals can likely still grow from fewer than 9 weekly sets. But muscle growth does seem to be known to be better and potentially even optimized with 12 to 20 weekly sets per muscle group. It's not clear if going beyond 20 weekly sets produces even more growth. Some studies do not find this. But as seen in another one of our videos, some research finds in certain cases, it can provide additional gains. So in general, a solid recommendation is to perform at least 9 to 12 weekly sets for each muscle group. It is perfectly fine to train with fewer than this if you're not looking to maximize the growth of the muscle or muscles in question. Also, if you're happy to train more in the hope of maximizing your gains, pushing nearer to 20 weekly sets or perhaps even beyond for at least some of your muscle groups could be a worthwhile experiment to see how you respond. There are endless options of exercises you could select to be in your training program. But one factor, the length at which a muscle is trained appears to be quite important. Let us review this new study and then we'll explain this further. 42 previously untrained men were recruited. To understand the design of this study, I need to explain a fact about muscles and a certain training style. Your muscles are a lot stronger when lowering a weight, approximately 40% stronger in general. You have probably felt this. In any curl, the lifting is much harder than the lowering part. This fact relates to a certain training style. Lowering Overload Training Here, we'll define lowering overload training as lowering a weight that would be too heavy or difficult for you to lift. How on earth can you do this? Well, in this new study, one group trained Nordic curls. This is a bodyweight hamstring exercise. Many people aren't strong enough to lift themselves up, so the subjects in the study just performed controlled lowering-only repetitions. Subjects progressed through a weighted vest. A second group performed this bending over seated leg curl. How was lowering overload training done with this? Firstly, just remember that the lifting phase of a seated leg curl is where we bend our knees, and the lowering is when we're straightening our knees. To make this lowering overload training, subjects performed the lifting of the weight with two legs and then switched to one leg on the lowering phase to achieve overloaded lowering for that leg. Once they finished the reps with this one leg, they switched over to training the other leg. Sets and reps were equal between both groups. It was found that overall hamstring's hypertrophy was 63.6% greater for the seated leg curls. Muscle length is perhaps the strongest explanation for these findings. Let me briefly explain. The hamstrings consist of four muscles, all cross over the knee joint, so bend the knee, but three of them also cross the hip joint, and this design means they can be stretched more, that is, at a longer length, when the hip is flexed. Seated leg curls involve our hips flexed, while Nordic curls involve virtually no hip flexion. Accordingly, these three hamstring muscles are trained at longer muscle lengths with seated leg curls, and all three of the heads grew better with this exercise. As for the muscle, the biceps femoral short head, which is trained at a similar muscle length between both exercises, it fascinatingly grew better with a Nordic curl. The researchers suggest since Nordic curls may not stimulate the other three hamstring muscles as much, the biceps femoral short head increases its involvement. Alternatively, it's still possible muscle length plays a role. More precisely, as the biceps femoral short head just crosses the knee, it's at a longer length when the knee is straight, but at a shorter length when the knee is bent. Seated leg curls are more challenging when the knee is bent, while Nordic curls are most challenging when the knee is straighter, the point where the biceps femoral short head is at a longer length. Finally, the sartorius and gracilis muscles also grew better with the Nordic curl. You may be unfamiliar with these muscles, but they assist the hamstrings in knee bend. But due to their precise anatomy, they are actually trained at a longer length with the Nordic curl, so this is a strong explanation for the results. So what does this study tell us? Summoning the spirit of scientific accuracy, this research is still emerging and developing, so it's not definitive proof training muscles at longer lengths produces more growth in all circumstances. Rather, just consider training muscles at longer lengths as a potentially promising strategy that you may wish to try out in your training. Also, all of the studies have currently been done on untrained individuals. Fortunately, though, there's upcoming research on trained individuals, and we will be updating you with the findings. How can you shorten your training session duration while not hurting muscle growth? Supersets are one proposed way. They involve performing two exercises with minimal rest and then resting before performing however many more sets you desire. Antagonist supersets are quite popular. These involve supersetting two exercises that train opposing muscle groups, such as a biceps and triceps exercise. Previous research suggests antagonist supersets do not hurt your training performance. That is, you can perform approximately a similar number of total repetitions on your exercises to normal sets, even though the work is in a smaller amount of time. We also have two studies suggesting antagonist supersets produced similar hypertrophy to normal sets. However, these two studies just involved two exercises, and the subjects were untrained. Luckily, this brand new study examined antagonist supersets with multiple exercises in trained subjects. 43 trained individuals were recruited to train these exercises twice per week for eight weeks. Four sets of 8 to 12 reps to momentary failure were performed for each exercise every session. A normal group performed all sets on one exercise before moving on to the next exercise. They rested two minutes between sets. A superset group supersetted the lat pull-down with the smith machine bench press, the leg curl with the leg extension, and the biceps curl with the push-down. It took them around 20 seconds to transition between the supersetted exercises, and they rested two minutes between sets. This resulted in the training session being approximately 36% shorter. Training performance was not meaningfully different between both sessions, although subjects rated the superset as being harder. Thus, the supersets did not reduce the number of reps they could complete to failure even though it felt harder overall for the subjects. It's worth mentioning the superset group did report more nausea than the normal group, but this did reduce over time. As a result, the researchers suggest slowly introducing supersets into your routine. === FILE: Faster Muscle Growth： This New Study Is Epic [wT3SGXW-_B4].txt ===

 Welcome to the House of Hypertrophy. Is there an optimal range of motion to maximize muscle hypertrophy? We yet again have a brand new study on trained individuals exploring this question, and quite importantly, it assessed growth at two different muscle regions, enabling us to see if some regions might grow more with one range of motion or another. To ensure we're all on the same page and to familiarize new viewers, a full range of motion moves the joints in an exercise through their full potential. A length and partial moves through a part of the range of motion where the muscle is at along the length. This is usually the first half of the lifting part of the movement. A short and partial moves through a part of the range of motion where the muscle is at a shorter length. This is usually the final half of the lifting part of a movement. Let us assess the new paper, and then understand how it fits into the rest of the scientific literature exploring range of motion for muscle hypertrophy. Let's dive in. 13 trained individuals with an average of approximately 6 years of experience were recruited. The subjects trained unilateral machine preacher curls, twice per week for 8 weeks. With one arm, subjects trained with a full range of motion, moving the elbow joint from 0 to 140 degrees of flexion. With their other arm, subjects trained with a length and partial, moving the elbow joint from 0 to 70 degrees of flexion. Both arms performed 5 sets of 10 to 15 reps to momentary failure, with 2 minutes of rest between sets. Loads were adjusted over time so subjects continued reaching failure in this rep range. Muscle thickness of the elbow flexors, which contained both the biceps and brachialis, was measured at 50% and 70% of this distance. It was found that growth at the 50% region was virtually similar between both ranges of motion, while growth at the 70% region tended to be greater for the length and partials. For those familiar with Bayesian statistics, the Bayes factor quantifying evidence for greater growth from the length and partials at the distal region was 4.87, which is interpreted as providing moderate evidence for greater growth from the length and partials. So, we're not necessarily talking about a crystal clear and large effect, but, aligned with the authors, I am interpreting this as slightly greater hypertrophy at the 70% region from length and partials. Some may be wondering if the greater growth at the distal region could ultimately end up making your muscles look weird. I'm not convinced this is the case. You can find my full analysis of this in the pinned comment. Nevertheless, do these results mean length and partials are superior for overall growth? This is just one study with a small sample size, so alone it's not robust evidence. So, let's briefly review the rest of the range of motion literature. For a while, it was thought that a four range of motion is superior for building muscle largely based on comparisons to short and partials, but in the last few years, studies comparing length and partials to a four range of motion have challenged this idea. This new study means that our total of six studies comparing full range of motion to length and partials, with three studies on untrained individuals and the other three on trained individuals. All three studies on untrained individuals find overall more muscle hypertrophy with a length and partial. Interestingly, one of them by Pedroza and colleagues examined growth across multiple regions, and it tended to show that for the vastest lateralis, there was a greater numerical difference between the full range of motion and length and partial at the distal region. Supporting the idea length and partials might be quite good for the distal regions of a muscle. As for the three studies on trained individuals, we already know the findings of the new one, but the other two, including one with quite a large sample size, tend to find similar growth between a full range of motion and length and partial. Perhaps importantly, these two studies only examined growth around the mid regions of a muscle, so we're left wondering how distal growth may have looked. Another way to describe this overall research is that length and partial seem to be at least as good as a full range of motion, with the possibility of length and partials building a bit more muscle in some cases. Of course, we're still not talking about hundreds or even tens of studies here, so you may still have some reservations about length and partials. Overall, the range of motion research has been developing quite nicely in the last few years, but there's still a lot to learn. For example, would the results of the new study be the same if they instead used a three-week preacher curl or another biceps exercise? And how effective my length and partials be with compound exercises that involve training a range of muscles? I think having a reserved viewpoint is perfectly fine, so it's absolutely justifiable for you to continue training with a full range of motion if that's your preference. Clearly, you'll still grow, but if you're someone who likes the idea of length and partials and wishes to experiment with them in some way, I say go for it and see how you get along. Of course, it's not an either or. You could include both in your training program and there's a ton of flexibility in how you could do this. Maybe you find length and partials more enjoyable on some exercises, but a full range of motion more enjoyable on other exercises. Maybe you perform length and partials on the final set of some exercises, or maybe you have some sets we alternate between a full range of motion and a length and partial. There are also certain exercises where once you reach failure with a full range of motion, you're able to squeeze out some extra reps with length and partials. We've explored research on this way of implementing length and partials in a recent video. I thought it would be informative to have a quick discussion on short and partials, as I want to make it clear that short and partials aren't tragic. We have 10 total studies involving a comparison between short and partials and a full range of motion or a length and partial. In general, overall muscle growth is a bit worse with short and partials, but it still produces growth and has sometimes been documented to produce similar growth around the mid regions to length and partials or a full range of motion. For example, this paper compared short and to length and partials on a dumbbell preacher curl. Growth of the biceps at the 70% region was greater for the length and partials, but growth at the 50% region was similar. Additionally, if we extend short and partials a bit more, they might become a bit better. Let me explain what I mean. This paper compared squatting to 60 degrees to squatting with 120 degrees of knee flexion. Growth across multiple regions was greater with 120 degrees. However, what if we extend the partial bit by going down to 90 or 100 degrees of knee flexion? Well, this study compared squatting to 90 degrees versus 140 degrees of knee flexion, and fascinatingly found similar quadriceps hypertrophy. A second paper compared leg pressing with 100 degrees of knee flexion to an average of 154 degrees of knee flexion, and found both produced similar overall regional quad growth. So, extending a typical short and partial might make it a little better. That said, if we return to this particular study comparing 90 to 140 degree knee flexion squats, though quad growth was similar, they also measured glute max and adductor hypertrophy, which was better with 140 degrees. So, we don't want to make the mistake of thinking short and partials do nothing, they can still deliver results. But given that most evidence suggests slightly worse overall hypertrophy, I would largely stick to training with a full range of motion or length and partial.
