=== FILE: How Many Sets for Muscle Growth？ (New Study) [21m6wO96KEM].txt ===

 Welcome to the House of Hypertrophy. How many sets are necessary to maximize muscle hypertrophy? This is arguably one of the most debated questions in the world of fitness, but we have a brand new study that I consider to be quite important for understanding the current research in this area. In this video, we'll first provide some background on the contentious literature on sets and hypertrophy, then we'll examine the new study and discuss its implications. This will lead us to a clear outline of what I believe the research truly suggests about the relationship between sets and hypertrophy. Finally, we'll wrap up with some training recommendations. Let's dive in. We need to go back to October 2023, when one of the most controversial papers on muscle growth was published. The researchers recruited 31 well-trained individuals to train the back squats at leg press and leg extension twice a week. In the first training week, every subject performed 22 sets, so that 11 sets per session split between the three movements. A fixed group continued to perform 22 sets every week for the remainder of the study. A 4-set group added 4 sets every two weeks, resulting in them performing 42 sets in the final week. Again, that was split between two training sessions in a week which looked like this. A 6-set group added 6 sets every two weeks, resulting in them performing a whooping 52 sets in the final week, again split between the two training sessions in a week which looked like this. All sets were aimed to be performed two reps away from failure in the 6-12 rep range, except the final set on each exercise which was taken to what the researchers termed volitional concentric failure. It was found that muscle growth, examined by measuring the cross-sectional area and thickness of the Vastus lateralis, tended to be better with the highest volumes. We'll return to a discussion of strength later, but for those curious, increases in back squats one rep max strength followed a similar pattern. These were some fascinating findings. Even today, the 52 sets reached by the 6-set group remains the highest weekly set volume reported in the scientific literature. Thinking about the training protocols, keep in mind that not only did the 4 and 6-set groups ultimately train with higher average set numbers than the fixed group, they also progressively added sets across the weeks. So, strictly speaking, it is unknown which of these factors contributed to the extra growth. Was it the higher average sets, the act of adding sets, or perhaps both? The idea of progressively adding sets is certainly an interesting one. To make this clear, imagine we have one group that trains with 20 weekly sets per muscle group for a total of 11 weeks. They, of course, average 20 weekly sets per muscle group. But imagine another group started with 10 weekly sets, and progressively added set every week to get them to perform 30 weekly sets per muscle group by the end of the 11 weeks. They also averaged 20 weekly sets per muscle group, but would there be a difference in muscle growth between the two groups? Sadly, the current evidence we have is insufficient to provide anything close to a clear answer, but I do intend to discuss what limited evidence we do have in a future video at the House of Iperturphy. Regardless, it is very much reasonable to conclude that these findings support the idea of higher sets delivering greater gains. But, unsurprisingly, this paper was met with mixed reactions across social media. Some thought this paper pointed to a new upper threshold for volume, but others had their doubts. Some of these doubts have contended that the greater growth seen by the highest volumes might not be real hypertrophy, but muscle swelling. Note, when I say real hypertrophy, we're talking about an increase in muscle size due to the addition of contractile units. The idea that swelling could be involved was certainly not an absurd suggestion. We know that after a sufficiently intense workout, muscles can experience transient increases in size due to factors likely relating to muscle damage. In some papers, such muscle swelling has been documented to be detectable in the multiple days after a workout. We might expect higher sets to cause greater muscle swelling. This all begs the question, in the extreme volume study, were the muscle size measurements after training taken at a time point when swelling might be present? Well, muscle size was measured 72 hours after the final training session, and skeptics were unconvinced this was long enough for swelling to have fully subsided. Talk about swelling would be reignited just over a year later when this meta-aggression was released. Based on combining the data of 35 studies, this relationship between sets and hypertrophy was found. Simply put, more sets produced greater hypertrophy with no sign of a plateau or an inverted U relationship, a finding that surprised many. To this day, I believe this remains our strongest insight into what the research suggests about the relationship between sets and hypertrophy. To ensure we all know what we're looking at, the white axis denotes increases in muscle size, while the X axis shows the number of fractional sets performed per muscle group per week. Feel free to pause and read the description and examples if you're unfamiliar with what this means. Of course, we're not talking about warm-up sets, rather working sets where you're training hard. Here are the visuals summarizing the variables used in the various studies. On average, there were 10 reps per set and most sets were taken to failure. But once again, given much of these studies measured muscle size 48 to 72 hours after the final training session, skeptics proposed that swelling was creating the appearance of more sets producing more growth. In reality, lower set volumes were enough to maximize real hypertrophy. Now, just to be clear, the idea of swelling contributing to the research on sets does date back much further, at least to 2018. But in the last few years, the arguments around swelling predominantly relate to these two papers. The problem is we never had a study actually comparing muscle swelling responses from different sets. So, we never had a great insight into how big swelling differences might be between lower and higher sets, as well as how long it takes swelling from varying set numbers to subside. This is where the new study comes into play. It is the first study to have explored this. Let's see what it found. The researchers recruited 13 trained individuals with an average of 5.1 years of experience to train the back squats, leg press, and leg extension in three workouts separated by a week. The only difference between the three workouts was the number of sets completed. One involved seven total sets, another 14 total sets, and the other 21 sets. These workouts were counterbalanced in a randomized order. Subjects began each exercise with 90% of their 10 rep max and aimed to perform all sets with 8-10 reps. Loads were adjusted when needed to maintain the target rep range. Two minutes of rest was provided between sets and three minutes between exercises. The authors note that subjects were motivated to ensure they exerted maximal effort during each exercise. This was applied uniformly to minimize variability in exertion levels. Muscle thickness and echo intensity of the anterior thigh, which contained both the rectus femoris and vastus intermedius, was measured at two sites before the workout, immediately after the workout, and 24, 48, and 72 hours after the workout. Just to be completely clear, this was not a study designed to compare muscle growth between the different sets. The study just had trained individuals trained with different sets, and muscle swelling was measured in the following hours and days after the workouts. It's also worth pointing out that these levels of set numbers, when executed two to three times per week, which is the most common training frequency in studies exploring sets, would correspond to these weekly set numbers. Thus, the 21 set condition in this study would be representative of a very high set number group. So, what did the researchers find? Fascinatingly, there were actually no significant differences in responses between the different set numbers, and swelling had more or less fully subsided 24 hours after the workout for all set numbers. As the authors describe, our results suggest the residual muscle swelling and or edema is unlikely to be a major confounding factor in hypertrophy assessments, at least when post-training measurements are conducted 24 hours or later after the final training session. In the spirit of scientific accuracy, this is just one study, so it's certainly not definitive proof. I know that some might be tempted to completely discard this paper since it just involved 13 trained individuals. However, remember that this was a crossover design, that is, each subject performed all three conditions, so there is no between-subject variability between conditions. Thus, at any given sample size, a crossover design gives us much greater power. So, a crossover design with 13 subjects is typically better than having 40 subjects split between the conditions. Again, this is not to say the study is conclusive proof. It's just that I believe it should be taken seriously. It is worth knowing there are at least five other studies conducted on trained individuals exploring muscle swelling in the days after a workout. Two of them reported that measurement had returned to baseline 24 hours after the workout, suggesting swelling had subsided by this point. However, the other three suggest some levels of swelling still present 48 to 72 hours after the workout. At first, this might be confusing. How come we have some data finding detectable levels of swelling 48 to 72 hours afterwards? But the new paper as well as these two other papers fail to find this. Ultimately, these studies are not identical and so there are multiple potential explanations for the divergent findings. But remember that none of these five other studies compare different set numbers, rather their focus was on other areas. So, they don't allow us to strongly say that higher set numbers produce meaningfully more prolonged swelling. This is why the new study was important since it was the first study to provide insight into this. All this brings me to my next point. Even though the new paper was important and interesting, it's critical to understand that even if it did find greater swelling from the higher sets and that swelling was still detectable 48 to 72 hours after, it actually would not follow that swelling is influencing the observed relationship between sets and hypertrophy in the literature. Why? Remember that all these studies, including the new one, examined muscle swelling after just one workout. This is an important consideration because in the studies behind the meta regression, subjects obviously trained for multiple weeks on end with muscle size assessed after the end of the whole training program. The question is, how confident are we that swelling observed in studies measuring it after just one workout are representative of the swelling that seen after training for weeks on end? The answer is that we should not be confident about this whatsoever because we have evidence that as you continue training with a program for weeks on end, your body produces a range of adaptations that reduce the muscle damage fatigue and muscle swelling response you experience from training. These adaptations are often referred to as the repeated bout effect. Some of you might object and say all these studies that measured swelling after one workout were conducted on trained individuals, so they already have these adaptations. While it is generally true that trained individuals experience lower damage, fatigue and swelling compared to untrained individuals, this objection fails to recognize that how much you are accustomed to a workout still absolutely matters. The trained individuals in these studies are still unaccustomed to the one workout they execute. Many trained individuals can attest to the fact that if they perform a new exercise or train with a different set of variables, they get more sore than usual. But as the weeks go by and they accustom themselves to this new program, soreness diminishes and recovery improves. There are a number of studies relating to the repeated bout effect, but allow us to overview two particular studies that have great relevance. The first paper had untrained individuals perform 10 sets of 6 maximum eccentric curls. As described in a tremendous in-depth article by Greg Knuckles, which is where I first learned about this particular paper, maximal eccentrics on a dynamometer are no joke. You can produce more force eccentrically than concentrically and a dynamometer ensures that every rep is maximally challenging. So every rep is performed with your moment in time eccentric one rep max. Think about that, performing 10 sets of 6 reps with every rep essentially being an eccentric one rep max. Given the brutality of this, it's unsurprising that substantial signs of damage and swelling persisted for multiple days, with some measures not even returning to baseline 7 days after the workout. Four weeks later, they repeated the session. Markers of muscle damage, including swelling, were substantially reduced. There was no swelling present at 48 to 72 hours after the training. Now, across social media, I've seen suggestions that these adaptations are limited, stating there's not much more that occurs beyond the second workout. But the second paper fails to support this, since it demonstrates how these adaptations continue to occur as the sessions go by. This was actually a paper I described back in 2023. It involved untrained subjects performing 5 sets of 15 maximal eccentric late extension reps, once a week for 10 weeks. So imagine performing 15 eccentric one rep max consecutively and doing that for 5 sets. The first session produced considerable signs of damage and fatigue for multiple days after the workout, with many measures not even recovered 5 days after. However, as the weeks went by and they continued training, there were progressive reductions in all signs of damage and faster recovery of performance. Unfortunately, swelling was not examined. But given that all the indicators of damage and fatigue diminished, I believe we can virtually be certain swelling would have followed the same fate. Circling back to the new study, as it didn't even find differences between the different set numbers, or that swelling was present 48 to 72 hours after the workout, we don't even need to consider the repeated bout effect. But I do believe it was worthwhile reviewing some of the repeated bout effect literature. For one, it's interesting in its own right. But you now also know the issues with people using swelling data after a single workout to make claims about swelling after a program. Also, if we get a future study that finds greater swelling from higher sets after a single workout, it doesn't necessarily mean that swelling is confounding the relationship between sets and hypertrophy. So, considering everything we've overviewed, I think it's very unlikely that swelling is meaningfully contributing to the observed relationship between sets and hypertrophy in the literature. That is, in general, higher sets likely do genuinely produce more hypertrophy. Now, I am being careful with my words. I said it's very unlikely that swelling is meaningfully contributing. This does not necessarily mean there's zero swelling. I mean, swelling could very well have zero involvement. It's just that I recognize the current evidence is not strong enough to assert this particular claim with a high level of confidence. Returning to the meta-aggression, they also explored the relationship between sets and strength adaptations. In sharp contrast to the hypertrophy findings, strength fascinatingly appeared to be maximized at merely five sets per muscle group a week. Across social media, these findings were used to fuel speculation that swelling was confounding the hypertrophy results. The thinking goes that if higher sets genuinely produced greater hypertrophy, the addition of contractile units that comes about with the growth should mean greater strength gains too. But since strength appears to be maximized with around five sets, hypertrophy must also be maximized at five sets. All the extra growth from doing more sets is nothing more than swelling or just sarcoplasmic hypertrophy. I've already mentioned this phenomenal article from Greg Knuckles at Stronger by Science. It does an exceptional job at diving into this area. Here, I'll present some of the key points according to my interpretation. The strength analysis contained nearly double the studies. While there were overlapping studies contributing to both analyses, there were many non-overlapping studies. Much of the non-overlapping studies involved in the strength data involved untrained subjects and found large strength gains with low sets. This is not necessarily surprising as untrained individuals can experience significant strength gains due to learning effects and neural adaptations. If we're interested in precisely exploring whether the extra growth from higher sets is associated with greater strength gains, there might be a better way to analyze the data. What we might want to do is focus on studies that involved trained individuals and took related strength and size measurements. Measuring quad growth in Backspot One Rep Max is an example of this. When analyzing the studies that meet this criteria, it indeed seems that higher sets generally cause both greater size and strength increases. Once again, I can't recommend the article enough for those interested. So it seems higher sets generally cause greater muscle hypertrophy. However, it is imperative for me to state that just because I believe the literature suggests higher sets tend to be better for hypertrophy, it absolutely does not follow that I am telling you to train with very high sets or that you can't experience great gains without higher sets. Unfortunately, many make this erroneous assumption. They think that by presenting this data that I'm literally instructing everyone to train with 40 weekly sets per muscle group, but that is not the case. The reason for this is straightforward. We need to consider other details with the data and you're always going to have to consider your individual situation. Let's get into some of these points. Notice how there are diminishing returns. This tells us that it is certainly possible to see some respectable gains with volumes on the lower side, which is great news for those who aren't interested in maximizing everything. We can see that the credible intervals get wider, especially after 25 weekly sets per muscle group. These wider intervals simply mean there's greater uncertainty with very high sets, owing to the fewer studies. So, while we can be pretty much certain that moderate to highest set volumes are superior to lower set volumes, it is certainly possible that as we get more data, the difference between very high volumes and highish to moderate volumes shrinks. The average duration of the studies was around 10 weeks. That said, the authors of the meta-aggression did have some moderator analyses, and we actually see an even stronger relationship between sets and hypertrophy with longer duration papers. Note, these findings may further oppose the swelling arguments. As we know, thanks to the adaptations your body accrues, swelling responses will diminish as the weeks go by. So, the fact we observe this type of relationship between sets and hypertrophy over longer duration studies may be further evidence against swelling. Nevertheless, there are open questions as to how things may look over many years. One possibility is that over this time frame, moderate volumes can eventually get you to the same place. Upon reviewing the papers behind the regression, a fair few use incomplete training programs where they just train one or a few muscle groups. That said, I will note in some of the studies examining high sets, they do train a larger proportion of the body. So, I'm not necessarily saying it's impossible to train virtually your full body with very high sets. Finally, remember that these results are the average. It is possible that individual differences exist. Some people may genuinely grow more or at least the same with volumes on the lower side. Having described all these points, what do I recommend? Welcome to the house of hypertrophy. Is there a limit to the number of sets you can perform for a muscle group per session? A brand new analysis involving 35 studies with over 1,000 subjects helps answer this question. Let's dive in. Of course, we're not talking about warm-up sets, rather sets that involve taking your reps to or close to failure. Here's the variables behind the studies. On average, there were 10 reps per set, and most sets were taken to failure. The analysis examined the relationship between the number of sets performed per muscle group each session and hypertrophy. But how do we count sets per muscle group each session? The researchers compared three different methods to see if there was a best. Feel free to skip ahead if you're familiar with these since we covered these in prior videos. But if you need a refresher or if this is new to you, it's worth understanding this. The differences lie in how they count direct and indirect sets. A direct set for a muscle is where it's the primary force generator. Think of the biceps in any curl, the triceps in any triceps extension, and the chest in typical bench pressing. An indirect set for a muscle is one where it's somewhat trained, but not primarily, such as the biceps during a row and the triceps during wider grip bench pressing. Here's what the authors considered as direct and indirect sets for each muscle group. Not every muscle group or exercise is shown as these are just the ones involved in the data. The total method simply counts each direct set as one and each indirect set as one. The direct only method counts each direct set as one and does not count indirect sets at all. The fractional method counts each direct set as one and each indirect set as half a set. You could argue an indirect set should be a bit less or a bit more than half a set in different scenarios, but to keep things simple, the researchers stuck with half a set in all cases. Even with this arguable imperfection, it was found the fractional method tended to be better than the direct and total methods, which is pretty logical. Indirect sets still stimulate the muscle to some degree. So, we want to count them, but they don't stimulate the muscle as well as direct sets. We don't want to count them equally to direct sets. So unless otherwise noted, all the set numbers in this video are calculated with the fractional method. Here was the relationship between sets per muscle group each session and growth, showing that higher sets generally produce more growth with no clear sign of a plateau. That said, there were diminishing returns. Each additional set produces more growth, but the amount of extra growth decreased with each added set. If for whatever reason you dislike the fractional method of counting sets, you may be interested to see these graphs displaying the findings with a total and direct only methods. Moderator analysis showed a similar relationship when focusing on either untrained or trained individuals as well as when focusing on either using shorter or longer rest between sets. This analysis on rest time between sets is quite interesting as a house hypertrophy. We can see that more sets for a muscle group in a week is also associated with more hypertrophy. If this plateaued at a low number of sets, we shouldn't expect higher sets in a single session to be beneficial. So, it makes sense that more weekly sets generally causes more hypertrophy. As for frequency, this analysis answers the question, when the total sets per muscle group each week is kept constant, does spreading that volume across more days per weekly to better hypertrophy? Think of the biceps in any curl, the triceps in any triceps extension, and the chest in typical bench pressing. An indirect set for a muscle is one where it's somewhat trained, but not primarily, such as the biceps during a row and the triceps during wider grip bench pressing. Here's what the authors considered as direct and indirect sets for each muscle group. Not every muscle group or exercise is shown as these are just the ones involved in the data. The total method simply counts each direct set as one and each indirect set as one. The direct only method counts each direct set as one and does not count indirect sets at all. The fractional method counts each direct set as one and each indirect set as half a set. You could argue an indirect set should be a bit less or a bit more than half a set in different scenarios, but to keep things simple the researchers start with half a set in all cases. Even with this arguable imperfection, it was found the fractional method tended to be better than the direct and total methods, which is pretty logical. Indirect sets still stimulate the muscle to some degree, so we want to count them. But they don't stimulate the muscle as well as direct sets so we don't want to count them equally to direct sets. So unless otherwise noted, all the set numbers in this video are calculated with the fractional method. Here was the relationship between sets per muscle group each session and growth, showing that higher sets generally produce more growth, with no clear sign of a plateau. That said, there were diminishing returns. Each additional set produces more growth, but the amount of extra growth decreased with each added set. If, for whatever reason, you dislike the fractional method of counting sets, you may be interested to see these graphs displaying the findings with the total and direct only methods. Moderator analyses showed a similar relationship when focusing on either untrained or trained individuals, as well as when focusing on either using shorter or longer rest between sets. This analysis on rest time between sets is quite interesting, as at the house of hypertrophy, we've previously discussed the possibility that set numbers and rest time between sets interact with each other. But it's apparent the most recent evidence does not support this. If you're curious about the full details behind this and my latest thoughts, you'll find it in the pinned comment. These results may surprise many. The line shows increasing gains up to 20-plus sets per muscle group each session. There are some good points that help contextualize these findings that we'll examine shortly. Generally, these results align with the latest analyses on the relationship between sets performed per muscle group per week and hypertrophy, as well as the relationship between training frequency and hypertrophy. We can see that more sets for a muscle group in a week is also associated with more hypertrophy. If this plateaued at a low number of sets, we shouldn't expect higher sets in a single session to be beneficial. So, it makes sense that more weekly sets generally causes more hypertrophy. As for frequency, this analysis answers the question, when the total sets per muscle group each week is kept constant, does spreading that volume across more days per week lead to better hypertrophy? For example, if we perform 12 weekly sets all to failure for the biceps, is it better to perform it all in one session, spread across 2 days, 3 days, or even more days? Of course, spreading the volume across more days permits fresher sets, but does it matter? According to the results, not really. All frequencies produce similar growth. Numerically, a once per week frequency did produce lower growth, but the differences did not exceed typical error. We'll return to this point later. This aligns with the new data on sets per session in that if we observed a plateau in growth at very low set numbers, higher frequencies should be better. For example, if muscle growth plateaued at 3 sets per muscle group in a session, but there was still a benefit to training with more than 3 weekly sets per muscle group, then more training sessions in a week would be better. So, the fact that muscle growth does not plateau at low set numbers per session, that we see no real effect of training frequency makes sense. Taking a closer look at the volume analyses, is it really true that upwards of 30 weekly sets for each muscle group maximizes hypertrophy? Not necessarily. Although both analyses show numerically more growth up to the highest set numbers, using a specific statistical-based criterion of the researcher's choice, they determined 11 sets per session was the point where there was simply greater uncertainty about more being beneficial, while this was 31 sets for the weekly set analysis. The credible intervals get wider at higher set numbers, further pointing towards greater uncertainty, and we can see there are simply not as many studies examining very high set numbers. Understanding the details of the individual studies behind this analysis also puts the findings into context. This is a point I probably should have done a better job at emphasizing in previous videos, but upon reviewing the individual papers, a fair number of studies use what I'd call incomplete programs, where only one or a handful of muscle groups are trained. Some studies involved training to failure, but the studies vary in their definitions of failure, so I can't rule out that some studies involved subjects training insufficiently hard. The average duration of a study was around 10 weeks. There was a moderator analysis finding that the relationship between sets and hypertrophy remained when looking at longer-duration studies, but as the researchers describe, the moderator analysis should be viewed with a lot of caution as there's not many data points behind them. It's also plausible that over the very long term, moderate volumes ultimately get you to the same place as higher volumes. For these reasons, I'm not truly confident that super high volumes are superior. This doesn't mean the data is useless, because it still convincingly emphasizes diminishing returns and how low volumes can still build muscle but probably won't be optimal for most people. All in all, when considering these findings and the fatigue research, I'm fairly confident that even in the context of a complete training program where all sets are taken to or close to failure, moderate volumes will be superior to lower volumes. Here's my general recommendation that regular viewers may be familiar with. Maximize training quality first. Select exercises that sufficiently train a muscle, and then ensure you train sufficiently hard per set. If you want to do this, I would perform as much as you can practically and consistently. For most, I think this will fall around 10-20 weekly sets per muscle group. This is not a hard cutoff, and this is very much a broad range. But the reason for this is I suspect there is variability. Some people or even some muscles you have may thrive on the lower end, while other people or other muscles you have may thrive on the higher end. If you wish to experiment with even higher volumes, I would not at all object to that. One feasible way to do this for most people is with muscle group specialization, where you lower the number of sets for all your other muscle groups while increasing the number of sets for a few or even just one muscle group. Taking a closer look at frequency, we know that analysis indicates that when the total number of weekly sets is kept constant, how often you choose to train a muscle group in a week doesn't seem to really matter. So you're free to train with whatever split, whether a lower frequency one with something like a bro split, a 2x per week frequency with something like a typical upper and lower split, or even something that involves higher frequency like a full body split. Of course, there are different variations of these splits and even hybrid splits, and although convenient, it's not essential to confine training splits to the 7 days of a week. Having said all that, the sets per session analysis does show greatly diminished returns above 11 sets. So you may be wondering, if you're training with more than 11 weekly sets for a muscle group, perhaps a once per week frequency is going to be inferior. I think this is potentially true. Recall, although the differences did not exceed typical error, a once per week frequency did produce numerically lower growth. 13 weekly sets per muscle group was the average in the data. If the average was higher, perhaps we'd see stronger evidence of once per week being inferior. There was an analysis that still suggested no clear effect of frequency when separating out studies using higher or lower weekly volumes. But importantly, there aren't actually a ton of studies directly comparing different frequencies with higher weekly set numbers. I could be wrong, but I think as we get higher quality studies that include higher weekly volumes, we'll more compellingly see a once per week frequency not being as good. For these reasons, nowadays I would recommend a frequency of at least two times per week, particularly when training with moderate-ish to higher weekly sets. If you're someone who prefers a once per week frequency, it's clear you can still build muscle with this, so stay with that. === FILE: How Much Muscle Can You Gain？ (& What Causes Growth？) [ZWYf_7jAWEM].txt ===

 Welcome to the House of Hypertrophy, a brand new review has been released exploring how much muscle can be gained as well as what drives muscle hypertrophy. Let's dive straight in. How much muscle might you expect to gain across your training career? The researchers first examined data on the typical gain seen in studies lasting a few months, and then combined this with other data to infer long-term growth potential. Starting with the former, this meta-analysis reported the effects of resistance training on proxies of muscle hypertrophy in healthy adult males. We'll soon return to how things may change for females. Fat-free mass was the most commonly reported metric. It was found that the average response to training was a gain of 1.5 kilograms in around 10 weeks. Keep in mind that fat-free mass is not synonymous with skeletal muscle mass. There are many non-skeletal muscle mass components included in fat-free mass, but the assumption here is that skeletal muscle mass is what primarily drives changes in fat-free mass, especially over the long term. When the meta divided the studies by training status, trained individuals unsurprisingly saw numerically lower increases. Although interestingly, the differences were not statistically significant. Nevertheless, trained is a broad category. Needless to say, we'd expect someone with 10 years of training experience to see much lower increases in fat-free mass than someone with 2 years of training experience. Using the range of values reported from the studies, the researchers also considered responsiveness. In 10-12 weeks, a higher responder might see a 3 kilogram increase while a lower responder might see a 0.4 kilogram increase. Considering the entirety of a lifting career, the researchers decided to make inferences from examining the range of fat-free mass index values in natural bodybuilders. For those unaware, fat-free mass index is calculated by dividing fat-free mass by the square of an individual's height in meters. Let's say you're 85 kilograms with 15% body fat at a height of 1.8 meters. Doing the math and we get 22.3. The researchers referenced data from natural bodybuilders reporting ranges of fat-free mass index between 22.7 to 25. Using these fat-free mass index values, along with typical heights and baseline fat-free mass levels, we can estimate the amount of fat-free mass change in the long term, which amounts to 12.5 to 20.2 kg in total, or 2.5 to 4 kg on average over a 5-year period. Putting all this together, the researchers provide this schematic illustration. A high responder may wind up with a 21 kg increase in fat-free mass, an average responder with a 12 kilogram increase, and a low responder with a 5 kilogram increase. For females, it may come as a surprise to some, but there's good evidence that they gain muscle at a similar relative rate to males. That is, their percentage increase is very similar. However, they do tend to see lower absolute increases since they tend to start out with less muscle. The details on screen should make the distinction between absolute and relative increases clear. Using these precise numbers, the researchers provide the rough estimate that absolute fat-free mass gains in females may be 70% of those observed in males, thus arriving at this figure. All in all, I do think this is a generally decent estimate of how things may look over the long term. But remember this is not a fact, since this is arrived at by merging different areas of the literature each with their own limitations. Further, there are debatable assumptions. For example, the x-axis stops at 5 years, and many debate the degree to which muscle size can be increased after numerous years of training. There is also a lot more nuance behind responsiveness, and I would be very careful with labelling someone a true low responder. It's possible that they may respond better with different training variables and or ensuring they're optimizing non-training factors. I'll also mention that reality isn't necessarily going to be as clean as this trajectory suggests. Many may have time periods where they grow more or less than expected for a range of different reasons. I plan to have a more in-depth video on how much muscle might be gained over an entire training career, where I'll detail more research and explore questions such as if there's really a natural fat-free mass index limit, and how steroids could change things. The biological effects of testosterone have been known since antiquity, but it was first isolated around the 1930s. Nowadays, we're well aware that supraphysologic doses of testosterone can notably increase muscle size. Just take a look at this classic paper, which found that injecting 600 milligrams of testosterone in anthe per week, with no training, led to larger increases in some proxies of hyperchefee versus a group lifting weights naturally. Given these effects of testosterone, it's unsurprising that people pay close attention to it, even outside of exogenous administration. One such example relates to temporary increases in natural testosterone that can occur from lifting weights. In fact, various people are also interested in the temporary increases in other systemic anabolic hormones, like growth hormone and IGF-1 that come about from lifting. Some go so far as to construct their training program in an attempt to maximize the post-training spike in anabolic hormones. Doing this typically requires using exercises that train large amounts of muscle mass, performing a large number of sets with moderate loads and short rest intervals. But, do acute changes in systemic anabolic hormones strongly influence muscle hypertrophy? Let's take a look at the evidence outlined in the review. Wilkinson and colleagues had subjects train unilateral leg extensions and leg presses thrice weekly for eight weeks. In the 90 minutes after the workout, there were no changes in systemic anabolic hormone concentrations, yet increases in fiber cross-sectional area were observed. Thus, acute hormonal elevations do not appear to be required to stimulate hypertrophy. However, since there were no comparisons to other training styles, one could still suggest that training styles that do produce greater acute hormonal changes are superior. Is this true? This study by West had a low hormone condition perform a unilateral arm isolation exercise with these variables. A high hormone condition also performed the unilateral arm isolation curl exercise, but followed this up with a high volume of lower body training. As alluded to earlier, exercises that involve large amounts of muscle mass produce greater temporary elevations in anabolic hormones. So, by performing these leg exercises, larger acute anabolic hormone elevations occurred with this condition. Despite this, hypertrophy ended up being similar. Indeed, there are other studies failing to find that training protocols that produce larger temporary anabolic hormone elevations produce superior hypertrophy, as well as papers failing to find correlations between acute anabolic hormone elevations and muscle growth. This led the researchers to conclude, acute increases in testosterone, growth hormone or IGF-1 after exercise do not influence muscle protein synthesis or hypertrophic outcomes in men or women. Perhaps this isn't as surprising as it may first seem when we consider the fact that the changes in endogenous anabolic hormones that occur with lifting are usually well within the daily variations of the hormone and are orders of magnitude less than what we see with exogenous administration. Furthermore, the temporary changes in hormone levels typically last no longer than 90 minutes after exercise. Mechanical Tension refers to the force generated by muscle fibers. This can be active tension, the force generated by a muscle's contractile elements, or passive tension, the force generated by various components when stretched. These forces are sensed by mechanosensors, which transduce the force into signals that can culminate in hypertrophy. As the authors note, mechanical tension is the primary and essential driver of resistance training induced muscle hypertrophy. In a general sense, proximity to failure is closely tied to mechanical tension. As you get closer to failure, muscle fiber activation progressively increases, ultimately exposing more muscle fibers to greater tension. This doesn't necessarily mean you have to always train to failure as stopping one to two reps from failure could be sufficient in certain scenarios. Now, I do think some people go too far with mechanical tension, and unjustifiably base their whole training program on what they think maximizes mechanical tension. For example, they may hypothesize that a certain training style optimizes mechanical tension and subsequently hypertrophy, even though the actual research measuring muscle growth fails to support that training variable being superior. The key consideration here is that there's still a lot we do not know. So, while knowing about mechanical tension is generally interesting, I would still focus on the research we have measuring muscle growth to inform training rather than possible faulty speculations about optimizing mechanical tension. Moving forward, the authors know that the accumulation of metabolites like lactate, inorganic phosphate, and hydrogen ions have been proposed to contribute to hypertrophy. This notion may lead some to construct their training program with the goal of maximizing the buildup of metabolites. But is this really necessary? There are three pieces of evidence noted in the review that I'll address here. Firstly, the authors note that many bodybuilding routines typically involve training with 8-12 reps per set and tend to elicit greater levels of metabolic stress versus heavier low training. Yet, 3-5 reps can still produce similar gains. This is especially true in studies where the 3-5 reps performs more sets to equate total volume load. If you're interested, we have a video on low reps for hypertrophy examining this literature more. Secondly, blood flow restriction training can create a relatively hypoxic environment that increases metabolic stress. Blood flow restriction training has been shown to be highly effective for hypertrophy even with very light loads. Some hypothesized blood flow restriction causes hypertrophy by way of metabolic stress. However, as the researchers mentioned, blood flow restriction results in premature fatigue that leads to earlier recruitment of more muscle fibers. And it might just be the mechanical loading of these fibers explaining the growth and not metabolite accumulation per se. On top of this, one might expect that if metabolic stress is additive to hypertrophy, adding blood flow restriction to regular training with moderate to heavier loads should stimulate more growth. Yet, we have a few studies exploring this in different ways, either implementing the blood flow restriction during this set, within the rest interval or after the training session, but all fail to find more growth with the added blood flow restriction. Thirdly, there are exercise modalities that produce similar or greater metabolite accumulation to lifting, such as high intensity interval training or sprinting. Yet, these likely produce lower overall hypertrophy to lifting. Considering all this, it is clear that metabolic stress isn't the primary driver of hypertrophy. And the current literature questions whether it's additive. The researchers of the review do not mention this, but I want to add that I don't think we can definitively say metabolic stress has zero role in muscle growth. It's an immense challenge to separate out metabolic stress and other stimuli like tension in humans. Furthermore, there are over 4,200 metabolites in human serum, needless to say, not to all of them have been extensively explored. We also can't rule out that some small amount of metabolic stress contributes to growth and virtually all training styles pass this threshold. Or, maybe more extreme levels of metabolic stress not yet explored in the human data benefits growth. Finally, perhaps there are other avenues by which metabolic stress or at least training styles that involve high metabolic stress could benefit hypertrophy. For instance, there is some evidence that capillarization could be beneficial for muscle growth. Thus, although we can draw some reasonable conclusions about metabolic stress from the current literature, there still remains questions. The researchers note another popular proposed mechanism of hypertrophy is cell swelling, which is linked to metabolic stress. The pump has its origins in post-exercise hyperemia and opening of muscular vascular and capillary beds, which, with increased flow, lead to an increase in muscle size. The authors ultimately conclude that there's a lack of evidence supporting a direct hypertrophy benefit of cell swelling. Indeed, we've covered the pump recently in this video, where we note the research demonstrating that training styles that lead to a greater pump do not necessarily cause more hypertrophy. I will say this doesn't necessarily mean the pump is useless. For one, some enjoy the sensations of a pump, and that can be important when it comes to staying consistent with your training. Furthermore, one speculation is that when you're comparing two exercises performed with the same training variables, the exercise that leads to a greater pump at a certain muscle region means that region is seeing more tension and is thus a good indicator of growth. This is a possibility. But as we saw in our recent video, the evidence on this is interestingly a little mixed. The researchers did not touch on muscle damage, which many have proposed is a crucial driver of muscle hypertrophy. However, like metabolic stress, the evidence linking damage to muscle growth isn't promising. We've covered this topic more in prior videos if you want to dig deeper into it. === FILE: How Much Weight Do You Press in a Push-Up？ #Shorts [voWgMHWJlTQ].en.txt ===

An interesting study by Ebben et al. experimentally calculated how much weight you press during different push-up variations. What they found was during a regular push-up, subjects pressed roughly 64% of their body weight. Elevating the feet increases this percentage. A 30cm feet elevation has you press roughly 70% of your body weight, while a 60cm feet elevation had you press roughly 74% of your body weight Opposingly, elevating your hands decreases the percentage pressed. a 30cm hand elevation had you press roughly 55% of your body weight, while a 60cm hand elevation has you press roughly 41% of your body weight. They also looked at kneeling push-ups, these had you press roughly 49% of your body weight.

The second method, the fractional method, considers indirect sets as half the frequency of direct sets. With our example of rows on Monday and curls on Thursday, this is a frequency of 1.5 times for the biceps. The final method, the direct method, doesn't even consider indirect sets. in an isolation exercise more or less all the load is distributed to the isolated muscle group such as the triceps in a skull crusher compound exercises contrastingly are more complex as two or more muscle groups are actively involved in a barbell bench press the nervous system of one individual may distribute 40 percent of the total load to the pectoralis major 40 percent to the triceps and 20 percent to the anterior deltoid of course this is oversimplified for illustrative purposes in reality bones tendons synergistic and stabilization muscles also bear the load to varying degrees throughout an exercise nevertheless is it possible for an individual to change how their nervous system recruits the muscle groups involved in a compound exercise using our oversimplified example could the person alter their barbell bench press recruitment patterns for example such that the anterior deltoid now handles 40 percent of the load the pectoralis major 20 and the triceps 40 percent a fascinating study by stransker and colleagues gives us potential insight i will use the author's terms and interpretations to describe the study however there are notable limitations and considerations with this study so for those interested please watch until the end to understand what i feel to be the best interpretation of the current evidence 27 men with an average barbell bench press of 105.2 kilograms were recruited all subjects could bench at least 120 percent of their respective body weights during two 4 second maximal isometric barbell bench press contractions performed with their elbows flexed to 90 degrees and the upper arm perpendicular to the floor and three reps with an eighty five percent one rep max load on the barbell bench press surface emg which stands for electromyography recorded muscle activation from the pectoralis major anterior deltoid and triceps for each subject the researchers noted out of the pectoralis major triceps and anterior deltoid which one displayed the lowest relative activation on the bench press tests resultantly three groups were formed those with the lowest relative anterior deltoid activation the anterior deltoid group those attenuate after the six training weeks all three groups similarly increased bench press warner at max strength relevant to our discussion all three groups re-measured their activation levels during the isometric and eighty-five percent or one-rep max bench press tests to keep things condensed i'll just present the results of the surface emg recordings from the three reps on the eighty-five percent or warner mx bench press focusing on the anterior deltoid group first compared to before the study they saw a significant increase in anterior deltoid relative activation with a concurrent significant decrease in pectoralis major and triceps relative activation the pectoralis major group compared to before the study saw a significant increase in relative pectoralis major activation with anterior deltoid relative activation stated another way this study indicates performing exclusive targeted isolation training for a certain muscle group ultimately increases its relative activation during a compound exercise with a corresponding decrease or negligible change in the other involves muscle groups however as alluded to limitations and problems exist notice i've implied surface emg measures and muscles activation this is not actually accurate instead surface emg approximately measures neuromuscular excitation which is when neurons transmit electrical signals to the muscle fibers it innervates muscle activation actually refers to when the contractile units are prepared to generate force for those with some muscle physiology knowledge it's when calcium binds to troponin to enable subsequent cross-bridge cycling the problem here is intermediate steps between neuromuscular excitation and muscle activation exist such that it's not sensible to consider them in complete unison so surface emg approximates neuromuscular excitation however notice i've said approximates i say this because research has found when actual neuromuscular excitation is kept constant manipulating the length of a muscle or joint angle produces different surface emg recordings in other words surface emg still does not truly record a neuromuscular excitation the second problem is how the researchers measured and interpreted their surface emg recordings when presenting the results earlier notice how the recordings of each muscle are expressed as a percentage of a maximum isometric contraction the researchers calculate this by first recording the surface emg response to holding a maximum isometric attraction for each respective muscle group these respective values are then used to normalize the surface emg response recorded during the 85 or one rep max barbell bench press let's use an example with the triceps to make this crystal clear imagine during the shown maximal isometric triceps contraction 100 units were recorded from the triceps by surface emg during an eighty-five percent water at max barbell bench press we recorded 85 units from the triceps as a result we say the triceps produced 85 of its the problem here is we're basing the triceps relative contribution to an exercise on a random isometric contraction it's entirely possible if a different triceps isometric contraction was used to normalize our values we would obtain a vastly different relative activation level for instance if a different triceps isometric contraction generates 150 units from the triceps our 85 units measured from the triceps during the barbell bench press would have only equated to a 57 maximum isometric contraction based on all of this information you would see it's not really sensible to compare maximum isometric contraction values between muscles just because in a certain exercise one muscle generates a higher percentage of a maximum isometric contraction compared to the percentage of maximum isometric contraction achieved by another muscle we cannot definitively say that muscle is truly activated or involves more simply because those percentages are based on === FILE: Incline Curls vs Preacher Curls [tlmyJ3ws3Mk].en.txt ===

Incline coes versus preacher coes. This paper assigned 63 previously untrained women to either train with incline coes or preacher coes. Both groups performed three sets of 8 to 12 reps to failure twice a week for 8 weeks. Elbow flexor thickness, which in this case includes both the biceps and brachiialis, was measured across three regions. Growth at the 50% region was greater for the incin cures. Growth at the 60% region was similar, while growth at the 70% region favored the preacher curls. The biceps are predominantly at the 50% region. So incline curls likely grew this area of the biceps more. As we get to the 70% region, we see more brachiialis. So although there's uncertainty, it's possible the better growth from preacher curls in this area is from the brachiialis. The research is still developing, but I'd say the evidence is leaning towards the idea that shoulder extended curls such as incline curls and beijan curls may be particularly good for the biceps, whereas there might be a potential slight benefit of preacher curls for the brachiialis. That said, it's absolutely clear that your elbow flexor muscles will certainly grow well with any curling exercise, provided you're training hard. So, if you'd like to keep things simple, just select whatever curl you prefer.

It was found that growth at the 50% region was greater with the incline curls. Growth at the 60% region was similar between both, while growth at the 70% region was greater with the preacher curls. As we move to the 70% region, the biceps is obviously still there, but we can see the brachialis becomes more apparent. So it's tough to know if the greater growth at this region from the preacher curls was from the biceps brachialis or both. Having said that, the second study may give us the answer. This study isn't officially published yet. It was presented at a conference and is only available as an abstract online. The authors of this paper have been involved in multiple well-designed published studies, so I consider this study worthy of mentioning. Finally, overall brachialis volume increases were greater with the preacher curl, with the differences between the two exercises occurring at 70-80% of the brachialis length. Thus, returning to the aforementioned study, it's possible the greater growth at the 70% region from the preacher curls is down to greater brachialis growth. === FILE: Is Adding More Load or Repetitions Better for Hypertrophy and Strength？ [0MenoivXo_U].en.txt ===

Progressive overload is necessary for making\h long-term hypertrophy and strength gains.\h\h Simply, it refers to progressing\h your training sessions in some way. Conceptualizing progressive overload as a cycle\h works well. A challenging training session evokes\h\h muscle and strength gains. These gains enable\h you to apply progressive overload, and in turn,\h\h this application of progressive overload\h sustains a challenging training session. Two popular ways to progressive overload are\h with all other training variables constant,\h\h either increasing the load you use or\h the number of repetitions you perform. However, how do these two progressive overload\h\h forms compare to one another for\h long-term hypertrophy and strength? To my knowledge, there hadn't been\h any studies addressing this. But,\h\h a new study by Nobrega et al. changes\h this. Let's thoroughly examine it. The researchers did not\h actually conduct a new study.\h\h Rather, they used data from two of their\h previous studies to create this analysis.\h\h The researchers justified this as the\h two studies were quite comparable. The data taken from study one\h involved 14 previously untrained men,\h\h while the data taken from study two\h involved 10 previously untrained men. In both studies, subjects trained the\h leg extension for 3 sets of repetitions\h\h to failure per session, with 2 minutes\h between sets, for a total of 24 sessions. In study one, which we'll hereafter\h call the subjects of this study the rep\h\h overload group, the total 24 sessions were\h achieved by training two times per week\h\h (on non-consecutive days) for 12 weeks. Furthermore, this rep overload group used an 80%\h one-rep max load on the leg extension in the first\h\h session and did not adjust this initial load at\h all throughout the full study. As subjects were\h\h performing repetitions to failure every\h set, this would have meant this group\h\h was increasing the number of repetitions\h performed per set across their session.\h\h That is, they progressively overload via\h increasing the number of repetitions performed. Now, I did kind of just lie. During the\h 6th week (corresponding to after the 12th\h\h training session), leg extension one-rep max was\h re-tested to return the rep overload subjects to\h\h training with a relative 80% one-rep max load.\h But this was only done once, and subjects kept\h\h this exact new load with no further adjustments\h for the remaining 6 weeks during which they\h\h would have again been simply progressively\h overloading via increasing repetition numbers. In study two, which we'll hereafter call the\h subjects of this study the load overload group,\h\h the total of 24 sessions was achieved\h by training three times per week\h\h (on non-consecutive days) for 8 weeks. Furthermore, this load overload group\h adjusted their load every set and across\h\h sessions to ensure they performed roughly\h 9-12 repetitions to failure every set.\h\h This means they would have predominantly been\h\h progressively overloading via increasing the\h load used to fall within the 9-12 rep range. As you probably noticed, although both groups\h ultimately performed 24 training sessions,\h\h they did not do so identically. Training\h frequency and total study duration differed.\h\h This is a limitation that\h will be returned to later. Nevertheless, before and after\h the 24 training sessions,\h\h one-rep max on the leg extension\h and vastus lateralis cross-sectional\h\h area at approximately 50% of the\h thigh bone length were measured. Additionally, total volume load (calculated\h as the product of sets x repetitions x load)\h\h accumulated by the end of\h as well as volume load progression across\h the 24 training sessions was measured. By the end of the study, total volume\h load, despite being numerically greater\h\h on average for the load overload group, was not\h statistically different between the two groups.\h\h However, progression of volume\h load across the 24 sessions was\h\h statistically greater for the load overload\h group compared to the rep overload group. PAUSE After adjusting the data based on baseline\h values via an analysis of covariance,\h\h increases in relative and absolute\h leg extension one-rep max were not\h\h statistically different between the two groups. Note, relative increases can be\h thought of as percentage changes.\h\h With this data specifically, the rep\h overload group saw an average 31.4%\h\h increase in leg extension one-rep max, while the\h load overload group saw an average 38.3% increase. Absolute increases can be thought\h of as measurement unit changes.\h\h overload group saw an average 14kg leg\h\h extension one-rep max increase, while the load\h overload group saw an average 15.3kg increase. PAUSE Moving forward, also after adjusting for\h baseline values via an analysis of covariance,\h\h vastus lateralis cross-sectional\h\h area was statistically greater for the load\h overload group versus the rep overload group. So overall, this data potentially\h suggests for increasing one-rep max,\h\h there may be no difference between progressively\h overloading via increasing load or repetition\h\h numbers. But for hypertrophy, increasing load\h may be superior to increasing repetition numbers. Quite interesting, when combining both group’s\h data, although the researchers did not find a\h\h significant correlation between the total volume\h load accumulated by the end of the 24 sessions\h\h and one-rep max or vastus\h lateralis cross-sectional gains,\h\h a significant correlation was\h found for volume load progression\h\h across the 24 sessions and gains in one-rep\h max and vastus lateralis cross-sectional area. As the load overload group saw greater\h progressions in volume load across the\h\h 24 sessions, this led the authors\h to suggest this greater volume\h\h load progression may explain the greater\h hypertrophy experienced for this group. Having detailed all of this, there are\h some extremely important limitations\h\h and counterevidence. Let’s explore this\h to derive some more informed conclusions. Firstly, recall this study combined and\h analyzed two independent studies together,\h\h and as such it was not a\h randomized controlled study. Secondly, it’s interesting that both\h groups saw similar one-rep max gains.\h\h Yet, it’s more than likely all subjects\h trained suboptimally for strength.\h\h Both groups trained with loads that\h enabled 8 or more repetitions per set.\h\h Yet, the current evidence indicates training with\h loads that result in you performing 5 or fewer\h\h maximum repetitions is probably more favorable\h for one-rep max gains. For example, Schoenfeld\h\h et al. found with the back squat and bench press,\h adjusting loads every set and across sessions to\h\h maintain 2-4 repetitions to failure produced\h larger bench press and back squat one-rep max\h\h gains versus adjusting loads every set and across\h sessions to maintain 8-12 repetitions to failure. One question arising from this is what if both\h groups simply started with a 2-4 rep max load,\h\h with one group progressively overloading\h via adding reps from hereafter,\h\h and another group simply adjusting loads every set\h and across sessions to maintain 2-4 repetitions,\h\h would both still be similarly\h effective for promoting one-rep\h\h max gains? Hopefully future\h research explores this. Thirdly, we know that although both groups\h ultimately performed 24 training sessions, they\h\h did not do so identically. The rep overload group\h performed 3 leg extension sets 2x per week for 12\h\h weeks, meaning they performed 6 leg extension sets\h per week. The load overload group performed 3 leg\h\h extension sets 3x per week for 8 weeks, meaning\h they performed 9 weekly leg extension sets. However, using other data, it’s actually\h difficult to say this is a true limitation. The evidence indicates when performing 10 or\h fewer weekly sets for a muscle or exercise (as\h\h both groups were doing), training frequency does\h not seem to matter for strength or hypertrophy.\h\h That is, whether you perform these 10 or fewer\h weekly sets for a muscle all in one session,\h\h or across two or more days does not\h really matter. So neither training two\h\h or three times per week are inherently\h superior to each other in this regard. However, the load overload group did\h perform 9 weekly sets on the leg extension,\h\h while the rep overload group only\h performed 6 weekly leg extension sets.\h\h Based on the current data, it’s\h probably likely that on average,\h\h performing 9 weekly sets for an exercise or muscle\h is better than fewer for hypertrophy and strength.\h\h Thus, on a per week basis, the load\h overload group was likely gaining more.\h\h However, remember the load overload group only\h trained for 8 weeks to reach the 24 sessions,\h\h while the rep overload group trained for\h 12 weeks to reach the 24 total sessions,\h\h thus these study's duration differences likely\h cancel out the per week growth differences.\h\h Ultimately probably meaning that use of different\h training frequencies may not be a major problem. Having said all of this, it’s important to\h note muscle and strength gain are not constant.\h\h Generally, each week an individual would\h incrementally experience fewer gains.\h\h This throws another curveball and\h makes the comparisons pretty confusing. Therefore, overall, it’s truly\h difficult to comment on how these\h\h difference in training frequency and\h study durations between the two groups\h\h impacts the results. It would have been much\h better to have controlled these variables. The fourth limitation is that\h the sample sizes were small,\h\h as is most commonly the case\h with resistance training studies.\h\h 14 subjects were in the rep overload group,\h and 10 subjects in the load overload group. Small sample sizes increase the\h chance of errors. Let me explain. Different individuals, despite training\h with exactly the same training variables,\h\h can have very different outcomes. For example, Hubal et al. had 243 men and\h 342 women train preacher and concentration\h\h curls for 12 weeks. On screen is a graph\h illustrating how the subject's biceps\h\h cross-sectional area was impacted by training.\h Most individuals tended to experience a 10-30%\h\h increase in biceps cross-sectional area,\h but there were individuals experiencing\h\h well above this as well as individuals\h experiencing gains well below this. Here’s the thing, with small sample sizes,\h\h your chance of selecting subjects that vary\h widely in response abilities is increased. Expanding on this, we know the Nobrega data found\h the load overload group experienced higher vastus\h\h lateralis cross sectional area gains versus the\h rep overload group. But it’s entirely possible,\h\h due to the small sample sizes, the load\h overload group consisted of subjects\h\h with an average better muscle building\h ability versus the rep overload group.\h\h Thus, this would explain why the load overload\h group saw greater vastus lateralis gains,\h\h and not necessarily that overloading\h via load increases is superior. The fifth limitation relates to the\h measures and variables used in the study. Vastus lateralis thickness (at\h roughly 50% of the thigh bone\h\h length) was measured). But what about gains\h at other regions of the vastus lateralis,\h\h and even gains at other regions of\h the quadriceps muscles. For instance,\h\h other data indicates leg extension training\h (the exercise trained by subjects) heavily\h\h grows the rectus femoris part of the quadriceps.\h Thus, what did growth look like in this muscle? Only the leg extension was trained,\h what about other exercises? The subjects were also\h previously untrained individuals,\h\h do these results apply to trained individuals? Finally, although I would not\h consider this a limitation,\h\h rather potential counterevidence, it’s quite\h difficult to explain the finding of the load\h\h overload group experiencing greater\h vastus lateralis cross-sectional area\h\h gains compared to the rep overload\h group when considering other data. There’s quite a bit of data indicating\h loads between 30% and 80% one-rep max,\h\h so long as repetitions are performed very close\h or to failure, produce similar muscle hypertrophy. One of the reasons for this is likely because\h when performing repetitions very close or to\h\h failure within this loading zone, you’re going to\h be evoking quite high mechanical tension levels.\h\h More precisely, muscle fiber recruitment and\h force production by the individual muscle fibers\h\h is going to be quite high (these are two parts of\h mechanical tension). The reason this matters is\h\h because mechanical tension is currently the\h best categorized stimulus for hypertrophy. If you start with a given loading, let’s say 80%\h one-rep max, and progress via increasing your\h\h repetition numbers over sessions, the relative\h load you’re training with will technically\h\h decrease. But so long as you’re performing\h repetitions to or very close to failure,\h\h and that relative loading remains\h in the 30 to 80% one-rep max zone,\h\h you would presumably think hypertrophy\h should more or less be optimally stimulated. If you start with a given load that has you\h perform a certain number of repetitions,\h\h and you opt to try and maintain the precise\h relative loading (and subsequently rep range)\h\h every session via increasing the load, provided\h you’re performing repetitions to or very close\h\h to failure, and the relative loading you’re\h trying to maintain is within the 30 to 80% zone,\h\h you would also presumably think hypertrophy\h My point with all this is there currently\h does not appear to be any rationale as to\h\h why progressively overloading through\h increasing load may be superior\h\h to progressively overloading via\h increasing repetition numbers. However, recall the authors\h of the study proposed that\h\h the greater volume load progression\h achieved by the load overload group,\h\h compared to the rep overload group,\h might explain the greater hypertrophy. Put another way, greater volume load progression\h week to week might mean more hypertrophy.\h\h Indeed, the researchers, when combining\h the data for all subjects, did note a\h\h correlation between volume load progression\h and vastus lateralis cross-sectional gains. However, the problem here is that not only\h does correlation not indicate causation,\h\h but other areas of the research suggest volume\h\h load progression is completely\h dissociated from hypertrophy. Schoenfeld et al. had a group of men with 1.5-9\h years of training experience perform a range of\h\h exercises each for 3 sets, 3\h times per week for 8 weeks. One group of subjects (a high rep\h group) performed each exercise\h\h with 25-35 repetitions to failure each set. Another group of subjects (a moderate rep group)\h\h performed each exercise with 8-12\h repetitions to failure each set. Note, both groups adjusted loads every\h set and across sessions to ensure\h\h subjects kept training to failure\h within their respective rep range. Across the 8 weeks, volume load progression was\h greater for the subjects training with 25-35 reps,\h\h versus the subjects training with 8-12 reps. If volume load progression itself\h was truly important for hypertrophy,\h\h training with 25-35 reps should be\h superior to training with 8-12 reps.\h\h Yet, as we’ve mentioned already,\h loads between 30% and 80% one-rep max\h\h (which would include the aforementioned\h rep ranges) are likely comparably effective\h\h for hypertrophy when repetitions are\h performed very close or to failure. Another study by Brigatto et al. either had\h men with 2-8 years of training experience\h\h target a specific muscle all in one session\h (the 1x group), or across 2 sessions a week\h\h (the 2x group). All other training variables\h (including weekly set numbers, exercise selection,\h\h and rest interval duration between\h sets) were the same between both groups. Across 8 weeks of training, volume\h load progression on the exercises\h\h was greater for the 2x group versus the 1x group. Yet, increases in thickness of various\h muscles were similar between both groups,\h\h again indicating volume load progression\h may not be predictive of hypertrophy. Two studies by Souza Junior et al.,\h which we’ve thoroughly evaluated\h\h in a previous video, fundamentally seemed\h to compare progressively overloading via\h\h decreasing rest interval duration\h between sets to increasing load.\h\h Despite volume load progression across\h 8 training weeks being larger for the\h\h subjects increasing load, increases in arm and\h thigh cross-sectional area were similar between\h\h the subjects decreasing rest interval durations\h between sets and the subjects increasing load. Finally, as just mentioned, these two Souza\h Junior et al. studies indicated that as a\h\h form of progressive overload, decreasing\h rest interval durations between sets was\h\h as effective as increasing load. Of course,\h these studies did have their own limitations,\h\h which we’ve addressed in a previous video.\h However, If we took these findings literally,\h\h and combined it with the findings of\h this Nobrega study (that is, we’ll\h\h literally assume increasing load is better than\h increasing repetition numbers for hypertrophy),\h\h using some illegal maths, we would come\h to the conclusion that as decreasing rest\h\h intervals is similarly effective to increasing\h load for hypertrophy, but increasing load is\h\h better than increasing repetition numbers for\h hypertrophy, decreasing rest interval durations\h\h between sets would be better than increase\h repetition numbers for hypertrophy. I’m sure\h\h many would agree this is an odd conclusion.\h The only way to truly assess the validity of\h\h this would be to have further studies comparing\h these different forms of progressive overload. In summary, although this analysis by\h Nobrega et al. was highly interesting,\h\h numerous limitations and potential counter\h evidence exist. As such, I believe we can\h\h be nowhere close to definitively concluding\h that increasing load is better than increasing\h\h repetition numbers for hypertrophy, or that both\h methods are similarly effective for strength. Further research is unquestionably required. Before closing out, I should note I came across\h a post by Menno Henselmann briefly detailing this\h\h Nobrega et al. analysis in an Instagram post,\h on which Brad Schoenfeld (a resistance training\h\h researcher) not only gave his brief thoughts\h but also stated that his team has conducted\h\h a study on this topic, with the results to be\h released soon. When his study does get published,\h\h I 100% plan and look forward to covering\h it on the House of Hypertrophy channel. As always, thank you for watching. I hope\h this video was insightful in some way!
