 kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar kar Note that the calf consists of the gastrocnemius and soleus. The gastrocnemius has a lateral and medial head. In support of the notion that the calves are relatively difficult to hypertrophy, I've seen some reference to this 2004 paper, which found after 9 sets of calf raises, soleus muscle protein synthesis increases were substantially lower than what's commonly reported with the quads. The authors provide two possible explanations. Firstly, the calves are involved in standing and walking, meaning we could consider them to be chronically trained, even in people who don't train, thus giving it lower growth potential. Secondly, the calves, notably the soleus, contain a high proportion of slow-twitch fibers. We have plenty examples of slow-twitch fibers not growing as much as fast-twitch fibers. However, this data is simply not strong evidence. Low-protein synthesis data does not always predict muscle growth. I'd also like to point out that we shouldn't mistakenly think slow-twitch fibers hardly grow. They still can grow quite well. There are multiple instances of slow-twitch fibers growing more than 10% in a matter of 6 to 12 weeks, with an example of this even in trained individuals. Additionally, although the soleus is predominantly slow-twitch, the gastrocnemius contains a more even split of slow-twitch fibers. Therefore, it should come as no surprise that dissecting the scientific literature measuring calf growth after training will give us a better insight of its growth potential. We can assess growth in absolute or relative terms. Absolute changes are the raw changes in muscle size. If we measure muscle thickness, the absolute change would be the increase in centimeters or millimeters. Relative changes are the percentage increase. It is possible to have the same relative change but different absolute changes due to differences in the starting measurement. There are quite a few studies on calf hypertrophy, but to keep things simple, I'll share the findings from 5 different research groups worldwide that provide insight into how much the calves may grow. The first research group from Japan found that the calves tended to increase in size from 2 to 6%. The researchers noted that this growth was lower than what they'd previously found for the triceps and hamstrings. However, if we separately analyze each region of the calves, we see that it was the soleus that didn't grow as much. If we compare lateral and medial gastrocnemius head growth to the growth seen by the hamstring head, we see examples of not too far off or similar absolute and relative changes. The second research group from the USA had trained individuals training the quads and calves in the same study. We can see that the absolute changes in size for the calves, particularly the gastrocnemius heads, were not that far off the quad gains. The relative changes show the same thing. A Brazilian research group found that the calves grew with these values. And here we see the soleus actually grew pretty well. These values are quite similar to what they observed with the biceps and brachialis in another study with similar subjects and training details. A Norwegian research group found that the medial gastrocnemius grew with these values, which are similar to what they observed with the quadriceps in another study with the exact same subjects and similar training details. Fifth, and finally, a German research group found that the medial and lateral gastrocnemius grew with these values, which are similar to what they observed with the pectoralis major in another study with similar subjects and training details. In the spirit of scientific accuracy, science requires a substantial body of evidence to form confident conclusions. So a larger number of studies directly comparing the rate of calf growth to other muscle groups will unquestionably refine our understanding. But based on what we do have, it's evident that although there are cases where calf growth is somewhat lower, we're not talking about enormous differences, and we crucially have cases where calf growth is similar to other muscles. As a more general statement, if we factor in studies we haven't mentioned here, we frequently see the calves growing in the range of 6-20%, which is pretty much identical to what we see with other muscles in the overall literature. I fascinatingly came across two case studies on highly trained individuals. The first involved an individual with over 10 years of experience and accustomed to calf training. He performed three sets of straight leg calf raises thrice per week for six weeks. One leg trained with a full range of motion, while the other alternated between a lengthened partial and shortened partial every session. Interestingly, the leg alternating between the two different range of motions didn't really grow, but the leg training with a full range of motion experienced a 4.14% increase in medial gastrocnemius cross-sectional area, which considering the short time frame and training experience is notable. Although, the researchers did not report typical measurement error, so it's difficult to know if the increase in size is confounded by this. The second case study involved a competitive bodybuilder with 18 years of training experience and accustomed to calf training. He performed four sets of straight leg calf raises five times per week in addition to one hour of intense calf stretching six times per week for a total of 12 weeks. Increases in thickness across a range of calf regions ranged from 7% all the way up to 23%, although there was some variability and fluctuations in the measures. But I'd still say there were signs of genuine increases in size. Since these case studies are merely conducted on one person, they may not necessarily be generalizable to the broader population. Still, my interpretation of the overall evidence is that it appears the calves can respond robustly to training, so I think are certainly worthwhile training. In our next video, we will describe how you may go about training to maximize calf hypertrophy, with the help of the latest scientific research. Before wrapping up, there is one final question worth addressing. Does the soleus grow less than the gastrocnemius? Recall that two studies overviewed earlier point towards lower soleus growth compared to gastrocnemius growth, and there is another study supporting this conclusion. Yet, we did see one paper finding the soleus numerically grew more in absolute terms but fairly similar in relative terms to the gastrocnemius. There are four other studies also finding similar or better growth in the soleus. So the available evidence is mixed. In the bodybuilding world, it's not uncommon\h to see a constant tension technique being used. Typically, this is done by avoiding\h locking out the joints in an exercise,\h\h resulting in the muscle producing continuous\h tension for the full duration of a set. It's hypothesized that compared to locking\h out the joints in an exercise and allowing\h\h the muscles to briefly rest, keeping constant\h tension on the muscle is a more powerful stimulus. Although it's far from crystal clear,\h some research indicates these events\h\h may play some role in muscle hypertrophy. So, what does the research say - can\h constant tension enhance muscle growth? A study by Goto et al. does suggest that\h constant tension builds more muscle. 44 men with at least 1 year of training experience\h were assigned to a partial or full group. Interestingly, with these variables,\h\h this group also ultimately performed\h Now, some may be thinking\h the use of different loads\h\h and repetition tempos between\h groups is confounding. Furthermore, repetition durations\h lasting from 0.5 seconds,\h\h all the way up to 8 seconds, are also\h Therefore, the use of different loads and\h repetition tempos is probably not an issue. The constant tension group performed the\h exercise from 90 to 0 degrees of knee flexion,\h\h used A-50% one-rep max load and a 3-second lifting\h and 3-second lowering phase without any pauses. This actually resulted in constant\h tension on the quadriceps. This is because the leg extension is somewhat\h unique, locking out the knee in this movement\h\h still results in considerable quadriceps\h tension. Moreover, at the bottom of the exercise,\h\h so long as you don't pause, your\h quadriceps are still contracting. Therefore, the constant tension group\h was able to achieve a constant tension\h\h while still performing a near full\h range of motion on the leg extension. The normal group also performed the movement from\h 90 to 0 degrees of knee flexion. But they used an\h\h 80% one-rep max load, with a 1-second lifting,\h 1-second lowering, and a 1-second pause phase. This pause phase at the end of repetition\h\h allowed the subjects to momentarily rest\h and take tension off the quadriceps. Increases in quadriceps cross-sectional area\h were statistically similar between both groups. To summarize, when using a constant tension that\h does not significantly reduce range of motion,\h\h the current evidence suggests it is similarly\h effective to a full range of motion. When using a partial range of motion that applies\h a constant tension, the research isn't clear. Goto et al. suggest it is superior\h to a full range of motion,\h\h whereas Pinto et al. suggests it is\h inferior to a full range of motion. However, these aren't the only two studies\h\h exploring the effectiveness of a partial\h range of motion that uses constant tension. In the last video, we detailed a\h fascinating new study by Pedrosa et al.\h\h finding that a leg extension performed with a\h partial range of motion at long muscle lengths,\h\h produced greater muscle growth than\h a full range of motion leg extension. A partial range of motion at long muscle lengths\h\h is technically a constant tension\h technique a lot of the time. Therefore, this might suggest that a constant\h tension technique, that is applied via a\h\h partial range of motion at long lengths,\h could be the optimal way to build muscle. If you're interested in more details\h regarding the Pedrosa et al. study,\h\h I highly recommend you check out the video on it. Nevertheless, as discussed in that video, more\h research is without a doubt required before fully\h\h concluding that a partial range of motion at long\h muscle lengths is the optimal way to build muscle.

=== FILE: Is Maxing Out Effective for Building Muscle？ (One-Rep Max Training) [jQ-JcDrztj8].en.txt ===

Maxing out regularly, so performing a one\h rep max lift, isn't completely uncommon,\h\h especially in the strength world. For instance\h, the bulgarian method, based on my limited reading, appears to have involved maxing out daily on the\h snatch, clean and jerk, as well as squat variations.\h In the powerlifting world, it seems modifications\h of the bulgarian method exist. In this scenario, maxing out is done with the back squat, deadlift, and bench press. Some reasons as to why regular one\h\h rep max training may be great for strength gains\h, involve improved motor learning with heavier loads\h\h and greater neural adaptations. But, what about\h muscle hypertrophy? We often associate numerous\h\h repetitions being effective for building muscle.\h But could one rep max training still be effective? Two research papers can help us here. Let us begin\h with a study by Danekel and colleagues. 5 men,\h\h with at least one year of training experience,had\h one arm assigned to a one rep max arm and their\h\h other arm assigned to a volume arm. They trained\h both of their arms for 21 days straight. With the\h\h one rep max arm, they worked up to a one rep max\h on the unilateral dumbbell biceps curl each day.\h To prevent momentum, their backs and shoulders were\h kept against a wall. They also performed a maximum\h\h isometric contraction of the biceps at 60 degrees\h of elbow flexion, using a dynamometer. This was done\h\h for two contractions each lasting three seconds.\h With the volume arm, they did exactly what was\h\h done with the one rep max arm,so working up to a\h one rep max on the unilateral dumbbell biceps curl\h\h and performing the maximum isometric contraction.\h However, in addition to this, the arm performed\h\h three sets of 10 reps on the unilateral dumbbell\h biceps curl with a 70% one rep max load. Before\h\h , on day 8, day 15, day 21, and three days after\h the 21st session, thickness of the elbow flexors\h\h , which would have included the biceps brachii and\h brachialis, was measured at 50% 60% and 70% of the upper arm length. Additionally, through the\h training protocol itself, one rep max on the dumbbell\h\h unilateral curl and maximal isometric contraction\h strength on the dynamometer was noted. Increases\h\h in one rep max strength and maximal isometric\h contraction strength were similar between both\h\h arms. However increases in elbow flexor thickness\h at all measured regions throughout the 21 days\h\h favored the volume arm versus the one rep max\h arm. Looking more carefully at the data, it's quite\h\h evident the one rep max arm experienced virtually\h no growth. Therefore, one rep max training for 21\h\h days straight on the dumbbell biceps curl does\h not appear to be effective for building muscle.\h\h Adding some volume, in this case three sets of 10 reps on the dumbbell biceps curl, appeared to be\h\h necessary for inducing muscle growth. Now, this\h study had subjects trained daily and the study\h\h was only 21 days in duration. What about rest days\h in between and a longer duration study? Mattocks\h\h and colleagues can help us. 17 men and 21 women, all\h untrained, were assigned to either a testing group\h\h or a hypertrophy group. Both groups trained\h the unilateral knee extension (they did train\h\h both legs) and chest press, twice per week for eight\h weeks. The hypertrophy group each session performed\h\h 4 sets to failure with an 8-12 rep max load and\h 90 seconds of rest between sets for each exercise,\h\h the testing group, each session, warmed up and\h worked up to a one-rep max for each exercise. 90\h\h seconds of rest was given between attempts. One rep\h max on the unilateral knee extension for both legs\h\h and chest press was measured before and after for\h both groups. Also, thickness of the anterior thigh\h\h and lateral thigh was measured at 50%, 60%, and 70% of the thigh\h\h length before and after for both groups. Note, the\h anterior thigh would have included the rectus\h\h femoris and vastus medialis, while the lateral\h thigh would have included the vastus lateralis.\h Increases in unilateral knee extension one rep max\h for both legs and chest press one rep max were\h\h statistically similar between both groups. For all\h measures of anterior and lateral thigh thickness, the results favor the hypertrophy group.\h However, for all measures done on the legs\h\h for the lateral thigh, the differences were\h not classified as statistically significant.\h Similarly, at 60% and 70% of the anterior thigh\h for the dominant leg, differences were also not\h\h classified as statistically different. Even so, it's evident that overall, the hypertrophy group\h\h experienced much greater growth than the\h testing group. The before and after changes\h\h for each group further demonstrate this. Looking at the testing group results, we\h\h can see that for nearly all measures, there were\h virtually no increases, rather slight decreases.\h\h Conversely, the hypertrophy group experienced\h increases across virtually all measures.\h To sum up, the study by Dankel and colleagues\h and Mattocks and colleagues appear to suggest\h\h that one rep max training, although effective for\h strength gain, isn't effective for building muscle.\h\h These findings would support the idea that one\h rep max training likely produces significant\h\h strength gains through neural adaptations and/or\h improved motor skills, rather than muscle growth.\h For building muscle, the current evidence indicates\h that reps between 5 and 35, roughly equating to\h\h loads between 85% one rep max and 30% one\h rep max produce similar muscle growth, provided\h\h repetitions are performed to failure. Which is\h the point at which no more repetitions can be\h\h performed. Interestingly, there does exist some\h research exploring the use of heavy sets of 2 to 4\h\h for hypertrophy. === FILE: Is Overtraining Easier Than We Think？ [mB9znHdMvIg].en.txt ===

Welcome to the house of hypertrophy. How much do you need to train to overtrain? And are you close to overtraining? Today, we'll be overviewing the scientific literature to answer these questions. Let's dive in. We can think about our response to a lifting program on a continuum. Undertraining, maintaining, effective training, functional overreaching, non-functional overreaching, and overtraining. The first three are familiar to most. Undertraining is where the training isn't even sufficient to maintain your size and strength. Maintaining is enough to keep your current strength and size. And effective training is enough to increase your size and strength. As for the next three, people have varying definitions, but I'll use the definitions provided in the scientific literature. Functional overreaching is a performance decrease lasting no more than days to a few weeks followed by performance improvements. Non-functional overreaching is where performance is decreased for weeks and when you recover there are no improvements. Overtraining is a decrease in performance with or without symptoms that requires months to recover and again no improvements occur once eventually recovered. What kind of training program needs to be performed to overtrain or even non-functionally overreach? This review paper is our best insight into this. It identified 22 studies that aim to induce overreaching or overtraining. Fascinatingly, 10 failed to even induce any sustained performance decrease. This immediately tells us that it doesn't seem easy to overtrain. Here's one striking example. 18 trained individuals were recruited to initially train normally for 4 weeks with these variables. Thereafter, they engaged in an intense training program for 2 weeks. They continued performing this exact upper body routine and the leg holds. But for their quads, they performed hack squats and leg presses for six days and front squats and back squats on the seventh day, each for three sets of six maximum reps. Thus, they were performing over 40 sets in a week for their quads. There were signs of fatigue during this and testosterone levels dipped down a little. One subject also experienced patella tendon pain during this. Yet neither overtraining or non-functional overreaching occurred since leg press strength actually improved four days after the final session with non-significant increases on the leg curl and bench press. Testosterone levels also return to normal in the short time frame. So what gets us overtrained? This paper from the '90s seems to have successfully induced it just about. They had 11 trained men perform 10 sets of one rep maxes 6 days a week on a squat machine for 2 weeks. In other words, they did 60 one rep max attempts in a week. This resulted in strength decreases with follow-up surveys revealing it took subjects 2 to 8 weeks to be able to get back to lifting their normal loads. So, just about what we may consider overtraining. The authors also note two subjects were medically diagnosed with overuse syndrome of the knees by the end of the protocol. Despite this, it is interesting to know that the max number of reps they could perform with 70% one rep max on the squat machine was not reduced and testosterone levels were unchanged. This point is worth expanding on. There are many potential markers that could relate to overtraining, but they just seem to be inconsistent. This seems to be why the literature tends to focus on the time frame of performance recovery to define overtraining and not other symptoms or markers. As another potential example of borderline overtraining, this paper recruited trained individuals to train with four three-week blocks with these exercises. The most intense block involved performing six sets per exercise 6 days a week, thereby totaling 36 sets per exercise a week. The other blocks involved training much less. Strength on the power clean was decreased after this intense training block, and it still failed to recover following 3 weeks of reduced training as well as 3 weeks of complete rest. Yet I am skeptical that this is even overtraining as some degree of dtraining may have occurred in the 3 weeks of rest. Additionally, another study using the exact same protocol reported that squat strength returned virtually back to baseline levels after the 3 weeks of reduced training. All the other papers in the review that found performance decreases found that recovery occurred in a week. So aren't overtraining. Thus, it is exceptionally difficult to overtrain. The protocols that get you overtrained are far from what most people would ever do. For some, joint or tendon issues could arise before reaching overtrained states. It is also important to recognize the potential difference between suddenly performing a ton of training versus gradually progressing to high amounts of training. It is possible that some cases of overtraining or extreme levels of fatigue are due to doing too much too soon and are not inherently an issue with the training protocol. There are some notable examples of this in the literature. This paper had six untrained men perform five sets of 10 eccentric only biceps curls with a 110% one rep max load. Of course, you're able to handle heavier loads during the eccentric. So this is why subjects were able to train with multiple reps and sets with a load that they could not actually perform a concentric with. Also, eccentric only training with this intensity is highly damaging when you're unaccustomed to it. So although five sets of 10 may not sound like much, it is certainly something when all those reps are heavy eccentric only reps. The data demonstrates this as there were substantial signs of damage, soreness, and swelling lasting around a week. What was highly intriguing was that elbow flexor muscle size decreased below baseline and remained at this smaller size for numerous weeks thereafter potentially due to partial or total destruction of some fibers. I also came across this paper reporting a series of case reports which notes that after two sets of 25 maximal eccentric curls, a small number of subjects experienced prolonged strength loss lasting longer than 43 to 47 days with extreme swelling of the arm lasting weeks. One subject was clinically diagnosed with rabdtomyolysis. In a way, this is non-functional overreaching or even borderline overtraining reached through a single training session. It's important to mention that this is rare. The paper observing muscle loss was conducted on merely six subjects. The case report paper reported a 3% incident rate in the past year. And there are many examples in the literature of untrained subjects training with a similar or even more intense eccentric only protocol and not experiencing muscle loss or excessively prolonged fatigue. Even so, this is an example of how it's possible for some to do too much too soon. It is likely that if these subjects started out with less or used lighter loads and then gradually progressed across the weeks, no signs of muscle loss or excessive prolonged fatigue would occur. This is thanks to the repeated bowel effect, which refers to a range of adaptations that your body produces to reduce damage and fatigue. We've seen in prior videos that over the long term, it can be quite powerful. This is why if you're going to increase the amount you train, it is probably your safest bet to do so gradually and not all at once. We have evidence in the form of two papers of people doing quite well when they gradually progress training to quite high levels. The two papers had many similarities though the first paper was conducted on trained men while the second on trained women. Both papers after an acclimating phase had subjects train the back squat, leg press and leg extension twice per week for 12 weeks. In the study on men, in the first week, all subjects performed 22 weekly sets for the quads divided approximately equally across the exercises. A control group maintained this level of volume until the end of the study. A four set group added four sets every 2 weeks, totaling 42 sets by the final week and an average of 32 sets. A six set group added six sets every 2 weeks, totaling 52 sets by the final week and an average of 37 sets. In the study on trained women, a control group performed 22 sets every week. A two set group started with 16 sets and added two sets every two weeks, totaling 26 sets by the final week in an average of 21 sets. A four set group started with 18 sets and added four sets every 2 weeks, totaling 38 sets by the final week in an average of 28 sets. In both studies, they aimed to keep two reps in reserve on all sets, except the final sets on each exercise per session, which was taken to valitional failure. Increases in strength was best for the groups that worked up to the greatest number of sets. Size gains also tended to be greater for the groups working up to the most sets. There were no dropouts related to injuries or reports of joint problems. Although the subjects in the men's paper performing the highest number of sets did report excessive perceived fatigue in the final weeks. Given they just train the quads, this is not proof that super high volumes are universally superior for growing. If you're interested in how many sets I generally recommend, feel free to check out this recent video afterwards. I should note though that both papers did have all groups perform a constant eight sets per week for the hamstrings and subjects were free to train other muscles as they wished, but how much they performed for other muscles isn't presented. So these papers could speak to the potential of muscle group specialization phases where you slightly reduce or maintain normal training for other muscles while increasing the amount you train one or two muscle groups. There are differences in recovery capabilities between people. For example, some older individuals may not always recover as quickly as younger individuals. And there's interesting evidence from the endurance training literature that those with a greater proportion of fast twitch fibers may be more likely to overtrain versus those with more slow twitch fibers. Yet, there are also likely differences in how well you may recover at different times in your life. We've seen that your recovery generally improves as you become accustomed to a program. Some other factors may also matter. Regarding food, some say there's no such thing as overtraining, only undereating. There is some degree of truth to this as evidence from the endurance training research suggests some cases of overtraining might be confounded by insufficient energy intake. But that doesn't mean overtraining doesn't exist. The papers we overviewed earlier demonstrating borderline overtraining or non-functional overreaching involved sufficient energy and protein intakes. As for stress, some evidence finds those with greater psychological stress may experience slower recovery. On the flip side, a positive mindset could help. We've previously analyzed some fascinating research that trick subjects into thinking they're taking anabolics when they actually just received placebo pills. Along with reporting greater increases in strength, subjects also reported increased vigor, speaking to the idea of how mindset potentially influences your perceived energy levels. Feel free to check out this video for more details on this research. It is possible to train too much. The point where you tip over from effective training to non-functional overreaching and then overtraining will differ between people and can shift throughout your life due to different factors. But as a general statement, although overtraining is possible, it is improbable for most. Ultimately, the body can tolerate quite a lot, especially if you gradually progress yourself across time. Once you've got some training experience under your belt, the only way you'll truly overtrain is likely if you actively push yourself to extreme levels. Remember, we're talking about overtraining in the sense that it takes months to recover. We're not talking about shorter durations of fatigue. This can be more common, but this should be resolved by just taking a few days of rest or having a couple of easier training sessions. If you're searching for further guidance on programming to obtain your desired physique, it can be tricky and timeconuming. However, our highquality partner, the Alpha Progression app, can help you generate an evidence-based training program that's 100% custom to your needs in less than 3 minutes. Simply specify the equipment you have, how often, and how long you want to train for, and if you want to focus or neglect certain muscles. There are even advanced options to perodize your training and implement D losses. There are over a quadrillion input combinations on which your plan is based. And with a touch of a few buttons, you can customize things further through analyzing your past performance. === FILE: It’s Finally Here! This NEW Study on Muscle Growth is Epic [6i7wHWITWeY].txt ===

ölkerstor doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc doc The scientific literature tends to find that partials at short lengths aren't as effective as a full range of motion or partials at long lengths. And when comparing a full range of motion to partials at long lengths, we fascinatingly have three studies suggesting partials at long lengths built more overall muscle. However, these studies were done on untrained individuals. I'm thrilled to say we finally have the first study in trained individuals comparing a full range of motion to partials at long lengths. Let's dive straight in. 25 trained individuals with an average of 4.9 years of experience were recruited. Here are some real-life photos of some of the subjects. They trained these exercises twice per week for 8 weeks. One side of their body trained with a full range of motion on all exercises, while the other side of their body trained with a partial at long lengths on all exercises. I've mentioned this in previous videos, but the design of having one side of the body trained in one way and the other side of the body trained in another way is fantastic, as it means the same subjects were in both conditions. Thus, differences in genetics, nutrition, and outside lifestyle factors are much less likely to confound the results. After all, the left side of your body hopefully doesn't sleep more or eat more protein than the other side. Both sides trained to momentary failure with a defined range of motion. Muscle thickness of both the elbow flexors and triceps was measured at 45 and 55 percent of the humeral bone length. It was ultimately found growth at all regions was similar between both types of training. Thus, partials at long lengths weren't any better than a full range of motion, but it wasn't any worse, which I believe is still a very impressive finding. It was once thought that using a full range of motion to achieve both the stretch and peak contraction was essential, but these findings demonstrate partials at long lengths might be an appropriate alternative. It seems that the peak squeeze achieved by a full range of motion may not deliver additional gains. Having said this, there are some crucial things we need to keep in mind, but before detailing that, I feel something is worth mentioning. === FILE: Leaving More Than 3 Reps in Reserve vs Training to Failure (Research Overview) [nP1-3Wb1YlA].en.txt ===

In a recent video, we detailed how there's good evidence leaving 3 to 0 repetitions in reserve produces similar muscle hypertrophy to training to failure. Leaving 0 repetitions in reserve indicates you could not have done another full repetition while leaving 3 repetitions in reserve indicates you could have performed another 3 full repetitions. Also, we're defining failure as technical failure, the point at which you fail at performing another full repetition with correct execution. This was essentially the definition used in the studies we examined, and for muscle hypertrophy, it makes little to deviate from using the correct execution, as doing so would typically not benefit the tension experienced by the muscles you're trying to train. For instance, in a biceps curl, deviating from correct execution via excessively swinging your back will recruit the spinal erector muscles. But this won't enhance elbow flexor recruitment. It might decrease elbow flexor recruitment in certain circumstances. With those clarifications out the way, as noted, leaving 3 to 0 repetitions in reserve likely produces similar hypertrophy to training to failure. But what about leaving more than 3 repetitions in reserve? Could leaving 4, 5, 6, or even more repetitions in reserve still optimize muscle hypertrophy? By my count, 4 regular longitudinal studies have technically examined how leaving more than 3 repetitions in reserve compares to training to failure for hypertrophy. Let's analyze them. Martorelli et al. allocated 89 previously untrained women into one of three groups: a failure, non-failure equal set, or non-failure +1 set group. All three groups trained the barbell biceps curl twice per week for 10 weeks. The failure group performed the exercise with 3 sets of repetitions to failure with a 70% one-rep max load each session. The non-failure equal set group performed 3 sets of 7 repetitions with a 70% one-rep max load each session. With a 70% one-rep max load on the barbell biceps curl, the data provided in the study suggests subjects could perform a maximum of 12-13 repetitions. Meaning this non-failure equal set group would have been leaving rouglhy 5 to 6 repetitions in reserve on their first set. However, their 2nd and 3rd sets, due to cumulative fatigue, would have probably had them leave roughly 4-2 repetitions in reserve. The non-failure +1 set group performed 4 sets of 7 repetitions with a 70% one-rep max load each session. This group would have also been training with roughly between 6 to 2 repetitions in reserve, the only difference being they performed an extra set per session. All groups rested 2 minutes between their sets in a session. Moreover, one-rep max was retested on the 5th week to readjust the 70% one-rep max training loads used for all groups. By the end of the study, increases in elbow flexor thickness seemed to be greatest for the failure group. Therefore, this study suggests regardless of whether an individual performs the same number of sets, or performs one extra set, leaving more than 3 repetitions in reserve for the majority of your sets may be inferior for hypertrophy. Do the other studies support this conclusion? Let's find out. The second study by Lasevicius et al. assigned 25 previously untrained men into either a high load or low load group. All subjects performed the unilateral leg extension twice per week for 8 weeks. The high load group used an 80% one-rep max load. With one leg, which we'll call the high load failure leg, they performed 3 sets of repetitions to failure every session. Ultimately, this leg performed 12 repetitions on average in each set. With their other leg, which we'll call the high load non-failure leg, they performed 60% of the average repetitions achieved each set with the high load failure leg. Moreover, they performed additional sets to equalize the overall volume load (the product of sets x reps x load) to the high load failure leg. Ultimately, this leg performed an average of 5-6 sets of 7 repetitions, meaning they would have been leaving an average of 5 repetitions in reserve while performing 2-3 extra sets versus the high load failure leg. The low load group used a 30% one-rep max load. With one leg, which we'll call the low load failure leg, they performed 3 sets of repetitions to failure every session. Ultimately, this leg performed 34 repetitions on average in each set. With their other leg, which we'll call the low load non-failure leg, they performed 60% of the average repetitions achieved each set with the low load failure leg, and they performed additional sets to equalize the overall volume load to the low load failure leg. of 5-6 sets of 20 repetitions, meaning they would have been leaving an average of 14 repetitions versus the low load failure leg. All subjects rested 2 minutes between their sets in a session. Moreover, one-rep max was retested during the 4th week to readjust the 30% and 80% one-rep max training loads used for the respective groups. By the end of the study, except for the low load non-failure leg, all the other legs experienced similar increases in quadriceps cross-sectional area. As a result, given the low load-non failure leg experienced the least growth, this suggests leaving an average of 14 repetitions in reserve may be unable to optimize muscle hypertrophy, despite them performing 2-3 extra sets compared to the failure legs. However, given the high load non-failure leg experienced similar growth to the high load and low load failure legs, this suggests leaving an average of 5 repetitions in reserve might actually be fine for muscle hypertrophy, so long as 2-3 extra sets are performed. Stated another way, performing 5-6 sets while leaving roughly 5 repetitions in reserve may be as effective as performing 3 sets of repetitions to failure. This is interesting, perhaps on a set equated basis, performing 3 sets of repetitions to failure would be superior to performing 3 sets of leaving 5 repetitions in reserve (as somewhat supported by the Martorelli study). However, performing extra sets while leaving 5 repetitions in reserve compensates for this. Having said this, the third study by Karsten et al. questions this. 18 men with 2-5 years of training experience were assigned into a failure or non-failure group. Both groups trained a range of exercises twice per week for 6 weeks. The failure group aimed to perform every exercise each session with 4 sets of 10 repetitions to failure while using 2 minutes of rest between sets. When needed, the load was increased if they could do more than 10 repetitions on a set, or if they could not complete the 10 repetitions, 30 seconds of rest was given to enable them to complete this number. The non-failure group aimed to perform every exercise each session with 8 sets of 5 repetitions that left roughly 5 repetitions in reserve, with 1 minute of rest between sets. When needed, this group adjusted the load each set to maintain roughly 5 repetitions in reserve. By the end of the study, increases in thickness of the vastus medialis and elbow flexors tended to be greater for the failure group, whereas anterior deltoid thickness increases were similar between both groups. As a result, this study conflicts with the Lasevicuis study, as it largely suggests despite performing extra sets (4 in this case), leaving roughly 5 repetitions in reserve was unable to optimize muscle hypertrophy. Why the conflicting findings between these two studies? For one, the Laseviciuis study used previously untrained men, while the Karsten study used men with 2-5 years of training experience. Maybe this implies leaving 5 repetitions in reserve, and performing extra sets, only works in untrained individuals and not those with greater training experience. Secondly, as we noted, if the failure group in the Karsten study could not complete 10 repetitions on a set, they were given a 30-second break to enable them to then achieve this number. This is somewhat like rest-pause training. Frustratingly, the researchers did not state how frequently subjects did this, but if it was frequent, perhaps this could somehow explain the conflicting results between the two studies, as the Lasevicuis study merely had the failure groups perform their repetitions to failure (nothing more, nothing less). Thirdly, in the Lasevicuis study, all subjects rested 2 minutes between their sets in a session. Opposingly, the Karsten study had the failure group rest 2 minutes between sets and the non-failure group rest only 1 minute between sets. This potentially confounds the Karsten study, as it's likely resting for 2 minutes between sets is better than resting for 1 minute between sets for hypertrophy, at least with compound exercises. Therefore, the largely inferior results for the non-failure group might not necessarily be because they left 5 repetitions in reserve, rather because they only rested 1 minute between Unfortunately, it's difficult to say which of these three explanations, was it down to the differences in training experience, the potential rest-pause style in the Karsten study, or rest intervals that explains the conflicting findings of the Lasevicius and Karsten studies, more research is undoubtedly required. *PAUSE* The last regular longitudinal study I'm aware of that has examined how leaving more than 3 repetitions in reserve compares to training to failure comes from Carroll et al. 15 men with an average of 7.7 years of training experience were allocated into a relative intensity or rep max group. Both groups trained three times per week for 10 weeks. Quite an intricate periodized training plan was used for both groups. The link to the full study can be found in the description for those after more details, but I'll simplify the main points. Both groups performed the same exercises (mainly compound exercises, with some isolation work) for the same number of sets and roughly the same number of repetitions. The rep max group used rep max loads for their sets. For example, they may have performed an exercise for 3 sets of 8-12 repetitions with a 10 repetition maximum load. The researchers stated this group reached failure on the last set of each exercise. Moreover, I think it's probably likely their other sets would have left 3 or fewer repetitions in reserve, which we know is fine for muscle hypertrophy. The relative intensity group used around 70-90% of the rep max loads for an exercise. For instance, if someone in the relative intensity group could perform 3 sets of 8-12 repetitions with a 100kg load on an exercise, and this 100kg load was their 10 rep-max load, using an 85% relative intensity resulted in them performing 3 sets of 8-12 repetitions with an 85kg load. Based on some calculations, this relative intensity group would have been leaving around 2 to 6 repetitions in reserve on two of the training days per week, and between 4-14 repetitions in reserve on the 3rd day of each week. By the end of the study, increases in vastus lateralis anatomical cross-sectional area favored the relative intensity group. In other words, with all other training variables equal, largely leaving more than 3 repetitions in reserve (which is what the relative intensity group did) was more favorable for growth compared to training to or closer to failure (which is what the rep max group did). Having said this, there is a potential confounding factor in this study. Both groups performed additional sprint training twice per week. Training to failure is more fatiguing than leaving repetitions in reserve, and thus added sprint training may have impaired the rep max group's recovery capacity, thereby possibly explaining why they experienced suboptimal growth versus the relative intensity group. If true, perhaps this study indicates if an individual performs additional high-intensity training (like sprint training) or frequent cardiovascular training sessions of any type, leaving more than 3 repetitions in reserve might be better for managing fatigue and thus promoting muscle growth. Although, I still feel more research is needed to verify this. I think it'd be useful to see simpler and cleaner designed studies comparing muscle growth between training with various proximities to failure (such as 3 repetitions in reserve, 5 repetitions in reserve, or failure training) while all subjects perform additional cardio or high-intensity training. In summary, Martorelli et al. indicate with all other training variables equal, largely does not optimally build muscle in previously untrained women. Lasevicius et al. indicate that provided an individual performs 2-3 more sets for an exercise than usual, leaving an average of 5 repetitions in reserve can build muscle optimally in previously untrained men. However, a study by Karsten et al. suggests in men with 2-5 years of training experience, despite performing 4 extra sets, leaving 5 repetitions in reserve largely failed to optimize muscle growth. Although there were some confounders in this study. Finally, Carroll et al. indicate when an individual performs additional sprint training sessions, training with more than 3 repetitions in reserve may be superior for promoting muscle growth compared to training to or closer to failure with all other training variables equal. Overall, it's clear to see this current evidence is limited, somewhat conflicting, and overall far from clear. As a result, we unfortunately cannot conclude if leaving more than 3 repetitions in reserve can optimize muscle hypertrophy. Now, for those who have seen our previous video in which we detailed how the current research indicates leaving 3 to 0 repetitions in reserve is similarly effective to training to failure for muscle hypertrophy, you may recall at the end of this video, I stated there's some velocity based research that indicates leaving more than 3 repetitions in reserve may be able to optimize muscle growth. However, after recently digging a lot more into this research and even planning a whole 6,000-word video on it, I eventually realized that this research has far too many considerations and practical limitations. More specifically, due to the design of the studies, a lot of math and extrapolation was required to figure out the repetition in reserve numbers, which ultimately made it very inaccurate, such that it's just not entirely clear what repetition in reserve numbers was used in those studies. As I result, I came to the conclusion it was not worth detailing this research. On the basis of this, as well as the research detailed in this video, because it's simply unclear if leaving more than 3 repetitions in reserve can still optimize muscle hypertrophy, I think it's probably best to err on the side of caution and aim to leave 3 or fewer repetitions in reserve if your aim is to build muscle as best as you can.

=== FILE: Lifting Weights Does NOT Increase Testosterone...or Does It？ [Sj6exknHlss].en.txt ===

Testosterone is probably the most\h discussed hormone in the fitness industry,\h\h largely due to its role in hypertrophy. Firstly, it's worth\h establishing some basic details. Under normal conditions, It's very broadly\h estimated around 70% of total testosterone\h\h is strongly bound to SHGB (that is,\h sex-hormone-binding globulin), 20-30%\h\h weakly bound to albumin, and the remaining 1-2%\h is bound to nothing, and called free testosterone. Testosterone strongly bound to SHBG cannot have\h an active effect on tissues. Testosterone bound\h\h to albumin, due to the binding being\h weak, can actively impact tissues.\h\h Free testosterone, of course, is\h freely capable of exerting effects too. When administered exogenously to evoke\h sustained elevations above normal levels,\h\h we know it can powerfully enhance hypertrophy\h adaptations in response to lifting weights. However, what about the somewhat inverse of this? Does lifting weights increase testosterone? In a previous article, we saw that lifting weights\h can temporarily spike testosterone concentrations.\h\h But In this particular video,\h we'll be focusing on if lifting\h\h weights can chronically increase\h your resting testosterone levels. This seems like a straightforward question. Yet,\h\h closer inspection would reveal an\h array of factors worth considering. Are we talking previously untrained or trained\h individuals, young or older individuals?\h What are the baseline testosterone\h levels of the person in question?\h What were the training\h variables and exercises used?\h Finally, are we talking about total testosterone,\h free testosterone, or bioavailable testosterone\h\h (note, bioavailable testosterone refers to\h both albumin-bound and free testosterone)? Accordingly, as we dissect the\h current existing literature,\h\h we'll do our best to ensure\h these factors are considered. Let's dive in. Two Meta-Analyses\h Firstly, a recent 2021 meta-analysis by Potter et\h\h al. combined findings of 9\h randomized control trials,\h\h all conducted on previously un resistance-trained\h men ranging from 18-75 years old. The normal total testosterone range\h for men roughly lies between 270ng/dl\h\h to 1070 ng/dl, and the subject's average levels\h in these 9 studies fell within this range. Most studies had subjects perform 2-3 full-body\h workouts a week, with mainly compound exercises\h\h comprising the program, with movements like\h the leg press, bench press, and lat pulldown\h\h commonly used. Largely 6-12 weekly sets were\h performed for the trained muscle groups, with\h\h repetitions performed to or very close to failure\h with loads between 50% and 80% one-rep max. Below are the approximate results,\h indicating lifting weights had\h\h no significant effect on resting\h total testosterone concentrations. A 2018 meta-analysis by Hayes and Elliot further\h supports this conclusion, with older men. 17 randomized and unrandomized control trials\h conducted on previously un resistance-trained\h\h men at or above the age of 60, with\h the large majority of subjects still\h\h within the normal total, bioavailable, or\h free testosterone ranges, were combined. Like before, most studies included 2-3 full-body\h workouts per week, with mainly compound exercises\h\h Below are the findings, indicating lifting\h weights did not have a significant effect on free,\h\h bioavailable, or total testosterone\h resting concentrations. What About Other Individuals? So, the two detailed meta-analyses indicate\h\h in men of varying ages, lifting weights does\h not impact resting testosterone concentrations. However, it's worth reiterating all\h this data was derived from previously\h\h untrained men who were largely\h within normal testosterone ranges. What about trained men, or men with\h low total testosterone concentrations\h\h (roughly defined as below 270ng/dl)? Could lifting weights impact resting\h concentrations in either of these demographics? Individuals With Below Normal Testosterone Levels Exploring the low testosterone demographic first,\h\h 3 comparable randomized trials out of Denmark\h recruited men between 60-78 years old,\h\h with low bioavailable testosterone concentrations\h\h (the average levels were around 129ng/dl) and a\h waist circumference greater than 94 centimeters. These studies set out to examine the\h effects of exogenous testosterone treatment\h\h (in the form of gel) with resistance training.\h\h However, they were groups that only\h resistance-trained with a placebo gel. Subjects trained 2-3 times per week for 10 weeks. They trained leg presses,\h knee extensions, leg curls,\h\h chest presses, lat pulldowns, back extensions,\h\h and crunches for 2-3 sets with reps very likely\h to or close to failure with 6-10 rep-max loads. In all three studies, the placebo group\h that resistance-trained did not experience\h\h increases in bioavailable testosterone. Indicating\h even in older men with low testosterone levels,\h\h lifting weights may have no effect on\h resting testosterone concentrations. Trained Individuals As for trained individuals,\h\h a couple of studies provide insight. Schwanbeck et al. had 15 men with\h an average of around 2.5 years of\h\h training experience perform a free\h weight or machine-only program. The respective group's programs are on-screen.\h\h Each exercise was trained\h for 3-4 sets of 4-10 reps. This study assessed free testosterone, with\h baseline measures being in the normal range.\h\h After the training period, neither group\h experienced any changes in resting concentrations. Mangine et al. had 33 men with 2 years of average\h training experience perform a range of exercises. One group trained each exercise for 4 sets\h of 3-5 reps with 90% one-rep max loads,\h\h while another group used 4 sets of\h 10-12 reps with 70% one-rep max loads. Subjects were within the normal total\h testosterone ranges. After the study,\h\h neither group experienced any changes in\h resting total testosterone concentrations. Mccall et al. recruited men\h with prior training experience\h\h (no further details were given) who were\h within the normal total testosterone ranges. They trained 4 biceps\h exercises and 4 other exercises\h\h (again, no further details were given)\h for 3 sets with a 10-rep max load. After 12 training weeks, resting total\h testosterone concentrations were unchanged. Finally, Ostrowski et al. had 35 men\h with 1-4 years of training experience\h\h train a range of exercises for sets\h of 7-12 repetitions to failure. Some subjects trained each exercise for 1 set\h (the low volume group), some 2 sets per exercise\h\h (the moderate volume group), and the rest used\h 3 sets per exercise (the high volume group). Neither group experienced\h statistically significant\h\h changes in total testosterone resting\h concentrations as a result of training. I should note the data of this\h study was kind of all of the place,\h\h as you can see with the numbers provided\h below. The data was highly variable\h\h (as indicated by the standard deviations),\h making it difficult to decipher anything. Studies Finding an Increase\h in Resting Testosterone Levels\h So, all the data assessed so far indicates\h lifting weights has no impact on resting\h\h testosterone concentrations. Yet, I'm\h aware of two studies contrasting with this. Izquierdo et al. had Spanish nation team basque\h ball players with resistance training experience,\h\h and within the normal total testosterone ranges,\h\h train the parallel squat and bench\h press twice per week for 11 weeks. Subjects were either allocated to\h a failure or non-failure group. During the first 6 weeks, the\h failure group trained each\h\h exercise with 3 sets of reps to\h failure with a 10 rep-max load,\h\h while the non-failure group used 6\h sets of 5 reps with a 10 rep max load. Throughout this period, neither group experienced\h\h changes in resting total\h testosterone concentrations. During the next 5 weeks, the failure group trained\h each movement with 3 sets of reps to failure with\h\h a 6 rep-max load, while the non-failure group\h used 6 sets of 3 reps with a 6 rep-max load. Throughout this period, the failure group's\h resting total testosterone concentrations remained\h\h unchanged, but the non-failure group's resting\h total testosterone concentrations were increased. Thus, perhaps compound exercises with heavy\h loads, but only performing a few repetitions,\h\h alters total testosterone resting concentrations. However, it's difficult to verify this claim as\h there are no similar studies as far as I know.\h\h The closest paper was the previously mentioned\h Mangine et al. study, which found in one\h\h group of subjects training a range of compound\h exercises for 3-5 reps with 90% one-rep max loads,\h\h resting total testosterone\h concentrations remained unaltered. Still, differences between these two studies,\h\h such as the precise training\h variables and participants exist. As for the second study, Kraemer et al.\h had 8 young men (with an average age of\h\h 30) and 9 older men (with an average age of\h 62), within the normal testosterone ranges,\h\h train a range of exercises with the loads used\h varying across the three training days per week. Throughout 10 weeks of training, neither the\h young nor older men experienced increases in\h\h resting total testosterone concentrations.\h But, the young men did experience increases\h\h in resting free testosterone concentrations,\h this was not the case for the older men. Despite this finding, a comparably designed\h study by Petrella et al. conflicts. 13 young men ( between 20-35) and 13 older\h men (between 60-75) trained the leg extension,\h\h leg press, and squat each for 3 sets of 8-12\h repetitions, three times per week for 16 weeks. Neither the young nor older\h men experienced an increase in\h\h resting total or free testosterone concentrations. Though, it's still worth noting exercise\h selection did differ between this study\h\h and the one by Kraemer, so it's not clear\h if this may explain the divergent outcomes. Summary\h In summary, the majority of evidence indicates in\h a wide range of individuals, lifting weights does\h\h not appear to increase resting total, free,\h or bioavailable testosterone concentrations. Yet, it's worth considering this data does\h not necessarily prove lifting weights never\h\h increases resting testosterone concentrations. It remains plausible that\h training variables could matter.\h\h Virtually all of the data we assessed\h had subjects train with full-body splits,\h\h but what about something like bro-splits.\h Moreover, minimal data explore the effects\h\h of training with loads above 80% one-rep max,\h as well as different proximities from failure. Finally, virtually all of the data\h assessed lasted 12 weeks or less.\h\h What about many months or even years? For example, Hakkinen et al. found after\h following up on elite weightlifters for 2 years,\h\h their resting total testosterone\h concentrations had elevated.\h\h However, there are two problems with this data. Firstly, they were weightlifters, and as such\h would have been regularly training Olympic lifts,\h\h which is not what most recreational or\h competitive individuals after muscle\h\h hypertrophy or typical strength gains would do.\h It's not clear how this would influence things. Secondly, although the researchers stated\h they were not taking anabolic steroids\h\h before or during the 2 years, I'm a little\h skeptical of this as they were established\h\h champions or record holders in\h Finland with impressive numbers.

 drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought drought need to know about the exercises required to optimize muscle hypertrophy. Yet another great study has been released that helps us out. It has put the leg press up against the leg extension and the straight leg calf raise against the bent leg calf raise. We'll also reveal how the findings of this study potentially relate to other muscles like the triceps and biceps. Let's dive in. 28 trained individuals were recruited. One leg was assigned to train the leg press while the other trained the leg extension. One leg also trained straight leg calf raises and the other bent leg calf raises. This study design is powerful as all 28 subjects trained all four exercises. As the same subjects were in all conditions, differences in genetics, nutrition, and outside lifestyle factors were controlled. After all, your left leg hopefully doesn't sleep more or eat more protein than your right leg. In each session, these were the variables used. Weights were adjusted within and across sessions to keep subjects reaching failure in the 8-12 rep range. The researchers measured the growth of two of the quadriceps' heads. The rectus femoris and vastus lateralis summed across three regions. It was found the rectus femoris grew better with the leg extension, while the vastus lateralis grew better with the leg press. As for the calves, growth of the lateral gastrocnemius, medial gastrocnemius, and soleus was measured each at one region. Medial gastrocnemius growth was clearly greater for the straight leg raise. Lateral gastrocnemius growth also favored the straight leg, although not quite as clearly. Contrastingly, the fatigued growth favored the bent leg, but the benefit was not super compelling, and some may just regard this as similar hypertrophy. There are two key principles that help us to understand the findings of this study, and these principles likely apply to other muscles muscles such as the hamstrings, triceps, and potentially even biceps. The first principle is that biarticular muscles experience suboptimal hypertrophy when one of their functions opposes what happens in a compound exercise. The second principle actually tells us how we might be able to maximize the growth of biarticular muscles. It suggests positioning one of the two joints it crosses to place it at a longer length seems to produce more hypertrophy. Your head may be spinning in complete confusion, but it's simpler than it sounds. Let's break it down. Principle 1 likely explains why the rectus femoris suboptimally grew from the leg press and required the leg extension. Forget about the details of principle 1 for now, and understand that all four quadriceps heads cross over the knee in a way that means they all contribute to knee extension. However, the rectus femoris also crosses over the hip in a way that means it contributes to hip flexion. Since the rectus femoris crosses two joints, we say it's biarticular. The other three quadriceps heads can be described as monoarticular since they only cross the knee joint. Now, during any compound exercise that trains the quads well, such as a leg press and squat, we need to extend our knees and extend our hips to lift the weight. But although the rectus femoris is involved in knee extension, we just saw it's also involved in hip flexion, the opposite of hip extension. So a strong contraction of it would partly pull us down, making it logical that the nervous system would minimize rectus femoris involvement. Thus, all of these compound exercises likely suboptimally grow the rectus femoris. This is principle 1. A biarticulate muscle, such as the rectus femoris, experiences suboptimal hypertrophy when one of its functions opposes what happens in a compound exercise, such as the hip flexion from the rectus femoris opposing the hip extension from these compound exercises. As a result, isolated knee extension training is more effective for rectus femoris growth. Principle 1 likely extends to the other main key biarticular muscles in the human body. I'll briefly detail how this applies to the triceps and biceps, but feel free to check out the pinned comment for details on the hamstrings and gastrocnemius. The triceps consist of three heads, all cross over the elbow joint in a way that means they extend the elbow. But the long triceps head is biarticular because it also crosses the shoulder joint in a way that means it's involved in shoulder extension and shoulder adduction. During any compound pushing exercise, such as the bench press and overhead press, we extend the elbow. But these movements also involve shoulder flexion and or shoulder abduction, which are the opposing shoulder motions the long head contributes to. If you're struggling to see how shoulder flexion or abduction happens in these movements, just focus on the upper arm. Anyhow, a strong long head contraction would partly fight against us lifting the weight, so it makes sense it's not highly involved. Indeed, we have direct data demonstrating that pushing exercises such as the bench press sub-optimally grows the long head of the triceps, but does a better job at growing the lateral and medial heads. Isolated elbow extension exercises have been documented to be very effective for growing the long head, although certain compound exercises such as this pullover extension hybrid likely trains the long head effectively since this involves combined elbow extension and shoulder extension, which both are long head functions. But right now, we don't have direct data on how effective these are, and I'm skeptical they are superior to isolation elbow extension. As for the biceps, this one is quite controversial, and you'll see why. The biceps consist of the long and short head. Both cross the elbow joint and everyone knows they are involved in elbow flexion, but both also cross the shoulder joint in a way that means they can contract during shoulder flexion and shoulder abduction. The biceps can also perform what we call supination at the forearm, and there's also evidence that biceps activity is higher when we're elbow flexing with a supinated grip. Anyhow, during any compound pulling exercise, such as rows, pull-ups, and chin-ups, elbow flexion occurs. But shoulder extension and or shoulder adduction also occur, which are the opposite movements the biceps have at the shoulder. Once again, if you can't see how shoulder extension or adduction happens in these movements, focus on the upper arm. Indeed, we have direct evidence dumbbell rows even with a supinated grip produced much lower elbow flex hypertrophy than dumbbell curls. The reason I said this is controversial is that many people suggest chin-ups are one of the best biceps exercises. The popular Mike Mensah even suggested this. How could this be possible? Well, those who believe the biceps are trained effectively with compound pulling exercises would say what we've detailed is wrong for at least three reasons. Firstly, they may say although the biceps do cross the shoulder joint, there's research suggesting their involvement in shoulder motion is minimal, meaning your nervous system can effectively activate the biceps during these exercises. Secondly, they might also reference this study that fascinatingly found pronated grip lat pulldowns produced similar elbow flexor growth to barbell curls. Finally, some electromyographic research also defines high biceps activity during pull-ups and chin-ups, and so many people feel their biceps are highly involved. I actually believe these three arguments are pretty good, but there are some solid counterpoints. Firstly, although the biceps involvement in shoulder motion is indeed little, it's still partially shortening in these movements, which may mean it nonetheless fails to optimally contribute to pulling exercises. Secondly, as for the study finding similar growth between pulldowns and curls, this was elbow flexor growth, which in this case consists of both the biceps and brachialis. The brachialis is a muscle under the biceps. It's just a monoarticular muscle involved in elbow flexion. Due to this muscle being in the measurement, we can't be certain biceps growth was truly similar between both exercises. Moreover, to be completely transparent, the author of this particular study has been involved in multiple studies with statistical anomalies, so some might question the study's validity. Finally, the electromyographic data is interesting, but as detailed at the house of hypertrophy previously, there are cases where electromyographic data can probably be useful and other cases where it's not. Here, it might not be useful. For example, we've seen the triceps long head minimally grows from compound-pushing exercises, but some electromyographic research finds high triceps long head activity during the bench press, so this is misleading in this circumstance. As for people reporting they feel their biceps highly with some pulling compound exercises, someone might say you're actually feeling the brachialis, not the biceps. So who's right? It would be interesting to hear what you think on this matter, so feel free to drop a comment below. To truly get an answer, I would love to see a study directly comparing chin-ups to a normal biceps curl. Until then, I'm on the fence as to whether principle 1 applies to the biceps. I know, I know, it's frustrating that I remain on the fence, but if it's any consolation, my hypothesis would be that all compound-pulling exercises are not optimal for biceps hypertrophy. If it's not for principle 1, I think it would be because the back musculature is typically the limiting factor in pulling exercises, so your biceps may fail to reach maximal activation and tension. So I think it comes as no surprise that to maximize biceps hypertrophy, direct isolation biceps training is recommended. Let us now move forward to principle 2, which tells us how we could maximize the growth of biarticular muscles. Principle 2 suggests positioning one of the two joints a biarticular muscle crosses to places that a longer length appears to produce greater muscle hypertrophy. We'll understand what this exactly means soon, but this principle likely explains why the gastrocnemius grew better with straight leg calf raises versus bent leg calf raises. Actually, we have another study published in December 2023 which had untrained individuals train bent leg calf raises with one leg and standing straight leg calf raises with their other leg, using these variables. Both lateral and medial gastrocnemius volume increases were better with the straight leg calf raises, while soleus growth was fairly similar between both exercises. So, comparable to the new study, it generally shows better gastrocnemius growth with straight leg raises, and uncompelling evidence the soleus grows much better with bent leg raises. Okay, all three calf muscles, lateral gastrocnemius, medial gastrocnemius, and soleus cross over the ankle in a way that means they perform calf raising. However, the lateral and medial heads are biarticular as they also cross the knee joint. This means they can shorten and contribute to knee flexion. As the knees are flexed in a bent leg calf raise, both gastrocnemius heads are already shortened which likely compromises their force generation. This connects to the idea of active insufficiency, which refers to when a biarticular muscle is shortened at both of the joints it crosses, which limits force. Strictly speaking, some monoarticular muscles could experience meaningfully impaired force at short lengths, but this is a discussion for another day, and we'll stick to this notion of active insufficiency today. With the bent leg calf raise, all the calf muscles are shortened at the top of the calf raise. But since we started with the knees already bent, the gastrocnemius are excessively shortened. Extending our knees will lengthen the gastrocnemius, so straight leg calf raises train the gastrocnemius at longer lengths, which avoids active insufficiency. This is principle 2. Positioning one of the two joints a biarticular muscle crosses to place it at a longer length, such as how positioning the knee in a straight position lengthens the gastrocnemius seems to result in more muscle hypertrophy. If you've been following the house of hypertrophy for a while, you'll know growing evidence suggests training muscles at longer lengths builds more muscle. We've seen it with research suggesting that shortened range of motions fail to grow as much muscle at some regions to a range of motion that reaches longer lengths. And we're also seeing it with selecting exercises that have biarticular muscles at longer lengths, which is what we're focusing on here. Across the web, opinions conflict about the mechanisms behind training muscles at longer lengths. But, in my view, avoiding active insufficiency is one potential mechanism behind why training muscles at longer lengths can be beneficial in some cases. But other mechanisms are almost certainly in play too. Regardless of the mechanisms, we've seen principle 2 with the hamstrings. In the same way that straightening the knee can lengthen the gastrocnemius, the hamstrings can be lengthened by hip flexion. Seated leg curls involve the hips flexed, while lying leg curls do not. Indeed, overall hamstrings hypertrophy was found to be superior with seated leg curls in another paper. So I would certainly recommend seated leg curls over lying leg curls. We've seen it with the rectus femoris. The new study analyzed in this video used normal leg extensions. But leaning back on the leg extension will lengthen the rectus femoris more. And we saw in a recent video this produced greater rectus femoris hypertrophy than normal leg extensions. Feel free to check out that video for the full details of the study and possible alternatives to leaning back leg extensions. We've seen it with the triceps. The triceps long head can be lengthened with shoulder flexion. Overhead extensions involve the shoulders flexed, while pushdowns do not. Long head hypertrophy has been documented to be superior with overhead extensions in another paper. Interestingly, combined medial and lateral head hypertrophy was also greater with the overhead extensions. An unexpected finding. Now, many people do like pushdowns, so I wouldn't completely ditch it if you don't want to. But I would at least recommend a triceps exercise with the shoulders at a more flexed position to cover your bases. As for the biceps, I know there are a few studies currently in the works on them. I'm excited to see what they end up finding, and we'll of course update you whenever they're released. We've seen that Principle 1 likely explains why the rectus femoris grow sub-optimally from the leg press. And Principle 2 likely explains why the gastroponemius heads tend to grow better with the straight leg calf raises. But why was vastus lateralis growth better with the leg press? And why was soleus growth not drastically different between straight and bent leg raises? With the soleus, some mice speculate as gastrocnemius involvement is reduced with bent leg raises. The soleus should increase its involvement and thus grow more. This certainly sounds logical, but according to the results we've seen, it just doesn't seem to happen, at least not significantly. Therefore, straight leg calf raises might be all you need. Although, bent leg raises could be useful for isolating the soleus if you'd like to do that. As for the vastus lateralis, you might speculate, since the rectus femoris is sub-optimally involved in all compound exercises, the other quad heads like the vastus lateralis must increase their involvement and thus grow more. But this is similar to the soleus argument we just proposed which doesn't appear to significantly occur. Though, of course, things could differ between muscle groups. Although, another possible explanation is most compound exercises like leg presses tend to involve more knee flexion than normal leg extensions. This will effectively train and stimulate the vastus muscles at longer lengths, which could explain the greater growth. Nevertheless, to maximize overall quadriceps hypertrophy, it seems a solid recommendation is to have both an isolated knee extension exercise for optimal rectus femoris growth and a quad-focused compound exercise for optimal vastus growth.
