=== FILE: Should You Overhead Press for Muscle Growth？ [o6k8hMa1Z7w].en.txt ===

Welcome to the house of hypertrophy. Are you missing out on gains if you're not training the overhead press? Some say lateral raises are overrated and that overhead presses hit the side delts just as well, while others go so far as to call overhead presses a waste of time. We'll use the literature to examine how different overhead press variations could compare to one another for growing the delts, triceps, and upper pecs. Then we'll see how overhead presses could compare to other exercises. Let's dive in. The overhead press can be performed in different planes. No, I'm not talking about that kind of plane, but rather planes of motion. Overhead pressing can be performed in the frontal or sagittal plane. There are differences between them that likely influence how much the different heads of the shoulders are trained. focusing on the frontal plane. This involves pressing with the arms out by your sides, which happens when using a wider grip on the barbell using the behind the neck variation, having the dumbbells on either side of your head, and with machines that have handles out to the sides. If your upper arms are not aligned with your head, but rather a little more in front, which tends to be the case with some machines and using the front barbell overhead press, you're not exactly in the frontal plane. Rather, you're in what we call the scapular plane. But both have similarities. The motion occurring at the shoulder in both planes is what we can generally call shoulder abduction. We can see that in both planes the side delts have great leverage throughout the range of motion. The front delts also have respectable leverage, especially over 100° of abduction where it matches and possibly surpasses the side delts leverage. The rear delts are not as effective as an abductor as the front and side delts and sometimes may actually function as a shoulder adductor. Note that leverage here refers to a muscle's moment arm, which is the perpendicular distance between the line of force of a muscle and the center of the joint it's moving. There's evidence that a muscle's moment arm relates to how much is activated in a movement. In the spirit of scientific accuracy, there is debate about how useful the leverage literature is for inferring muscle growth. But know that I do think it's useful in many cases. More details and justifications for how I've used it in this video can be found in the pin comment. There are two factors that go some way to slightly enhancing front delt involvement. Firstly, overhead presses have us externally rotated. There is evidence that external rotation increases the front delts leverage for abduction while the side and rear delts leverage is minimally influenced by external rotation. Secondly, overhead presses tend to be quite challenging at higher shoulder angles where the front delts leverage proportionally becomes a lot better. When comparing these different variations, some argue that more stability provided by machines enables greater mechanical tension. It also tends to be why some recommend seated versus standing overhead presses. However, the evidence used to suggest that greater stability equals more tension in my view does not apply to typical resistance training exercises for hypertrophy. We also have evidence in trained individuals finding that seated barbell overhead presses did not elicit greater delta activity than the standing variation. Others argue barbells and dumbbells are better due to eliciting transient elevations in anabolic hormones. However, the overall literature fails to show that temporary elevations in anabolic hormones relate to actual growth. All in all, we generally see that provided you're training to or close to failure, all modalities are capable of producing similar growth. So, it comes down to preference and convenience. Some may prefer the freedom of dumbbells, or you may enjoy the greater stability provided by seated and or machine variations. Now, dumbbell and some machine variations allow us to bring our hands together at the top, but the available literature suggests reaching shorter muscle lengths often fails to confer additional growth benefits. That said, there is another slight movement difference worth noting. This paper fascinatingly found that the side delts were a little more activated during behind the neck barbell overhead pressing compared to front barbell overhead pressing. Testosterone can also bind to a membrane-bound\h receptor to activate something called the\h\h PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, which is quite a well-known\h signaling pathway where a variety of specific\h\h proteins interact in a chain reaction fashion to\h generate an increase in muscle protein synthesis. Considering these events, a spike in circulating\h testosterone evoked via lifting weights could\h\h theoretically increase the likelihood they\h occur, presumably amplifying muscle hypertrophy. Comparably, growth hormone is primarily believed\h to exert its anabolic effects via stimulating\h\h an increase in IGF-1 production from the liver,\h IGF-1 thereafter can activate the PI3K/Akt/mTOR\h\h pathway. Therefore, a spike in growth\h hormone concentrations evoked via lifting\h\h weights could theoretically increase\h the likelihood this event occurs. Aside from these gene expression\h events, there are also nongenomic\h\h roles by which a spike in anabolic hormones\h could heighten long-term muscle hypertrophy. Testosterone can increase the concentrations\h of calcium within muscle fibers.\h\h Calcium plays a fundamental role in\h force-producing events. Due to this, a spike in\h\h testosterone within a workout can boost calcium\h concentrations within muscle fibers, thereby\h\h enhancing force production which could enhance\h the degree of tension experienced by the muscle,\h\h ultimately leading to more muscle hypertrophy as\h mechanosensitive proteins within muscle fibers\h\h detect tension and thereafter convert tension into\h\h a signaling cascade that culminates in\h an increase in muscle protein synthesis. All of these hypotheses sound\h plausible and interesting.\h\h However, do they truly occur in reality? In other words, should you be aiming to\h train in a way that maximally spikes the\h\h anabolic hormone response in order to\h optimally stimulate muscle hypertrophy? From the current literature, I believe there\h are at least 2 ways we could evaluate this. The first way is to evaluate the correlation\h\h between spikes in anabolic hormones\h and long-term muscle hypertrophy. That is, do the individuals that experience the\h greatest spikes in anabolic hormones ultimately\h\h experience the greatest muscle hypertrophy. If\h so, we would have some evidence that temporary\h\h spikes in anabolic hormones evoked via lifting\h weights may be important for building muscle. The second way is to compare a training program\h that generates greater temporary spikes in\h\h anabolic hormones to one that generates lesser (or\h even non-existent) spikes in anabolic hormones.\h\h If muscle hypertrophy is greater with\h a training program that generates\h\h greater spikes in anabolic hormones, we\h would have further potential evidence\h\h indicating temporary elevations\h in anabolic hormones is important. Let us dive into the current literature,\h starting with the correlation data. Intriguingly, two studies have\h indeed observed a correlation\h\h between the magnitude of spikes in anabolic\h hormones and long-term muscle hypertrophy. Mangine et al. had 33 men with an average\h of 5.7 years of training experience perform\h\h a range of exercises 4 times per week for 8 weeks. Every session, subjects trained\h each exercise for 4 sets with 3-12\h\h repetitions with 70-90% one-rep max load,\h using 1 to 3 minutes of rest between sets. Blood samples taken at various time points\h during training sessions on the first\h\h and last week successfully demonstrated\h training immediately temporarily spiked\h\h testosterone, IGF-1, and growth hormone. Moreover, by the end of the 8th week, thickness\h and cross-sectional area of the rectus femoris and\h\h vastus lateralis (measured at approximately\h 50% of the thigh bone length) increased. Most relevant to our discussion, a thorough\h analysis of the data indicates there was a\h\h relationship between the temporary spikes in\h testosterone and muscle hypertrophy. In other\h\h words, it appears the subjects that experienced\h the greatest temporary increases in testosterone\h\h concentrations as a result of training ultimately\h experienced the highest increases in thickness and\h\h cross-sectional area of the rectus femoris\h and vastus lateralis. The temporary spikes\h\h of other hormones, including growth hormone,\h did not seem predictive of muscle hypertrophy. However, another study by Mccall et\h al. somewhat conflicts with this data. 11 men with prior resistance training experience\h performed a range of exercises each for 3 sets\h\h with a 10 rep-max load, using 1 minute of rest\h between sets, three times per week for 12 weeks. Blood samples taken at various time\h points during training sessions in\h\h the 4th and 8th week demonstrated that training\h successfully temporarily elevated growth hormone\h\h concentrations, but had little impact on\h testosterone and IGF-1 concentrations. Measurements taken before and after\h the 8 training weeks revealed training\h\h increased whole biceps cross-sectional\h area and cross-sectional area of slow\h\h and fast-twitch fibers obtained from the biceps. Relevant to our discussion, the temporary\h spikes in growth hormone correlated with\h\h increases in slow-twitch as well as fast-twitch\h fiber cross-sectional area gains. In other words,\h\h those that experienced the highest temporary\h elevations in growth hormone evoked via training\h\h tended to experience the most growth of the\h fast and slow-twitch fibers of the biceps. There were no other correlations, implying\h contrary to the Mangine study, there was no\h\h association between testosterone spikes and\h hypertrophy. However, recall testosterone\h\h concentrations were virtually unaffected via\h training, and so this may explain this finding. Overall, the results of this Mcall et al. study\h are a little difficult to wrap our heads around.\h\h Although a correlation between growth hormone\h spikes and slow and fast-twitch fiber growth\h\h was noted, there was no correlation\h between growth hormones spikes and\h\h increases in whole biceps cross-sectional\h area, which is difficult to reconcile. What's also difficult to reconcile is IGF-1\h concentrations were virtually unimpacted\h\h via training, and as we noted earlier,\h it's thought growth hormone primarily\h\h exerts its anabolic effects via stimulating an\h increase in IGF-1 production from the liver. Nonetheless, these two studies by Mangine and\h Mcall, despite conflicting to some degree and\h\h having some inconsistencies, broadly indicate\h some relationship between temporary hormones\h\h spikes generated via lifting weights\h and long-term muscle hypertrophy. However, 4 other studies find very weak or\h non-existent associations between temporary\h\h spikes in anabolic hormones and\h long-term muscle hypertrophy. West and Phillips found that after 56 men\h (untrained at least in the last 8 months\h\h before the study) trained a variety of exercises\h each for 2-4 sets of 6-12 reps 5 times per week\h\h for 12 weeks, there was no correlation between\h temporary spikes in free testosterone and growth\h\h of slow and fast-twitch fibers from the vastus\h lateralis, nor was there a correlation between\h\h temporary spikes in IGF-1 and growth of slow and\h fast-twitch fibers from the vastus lateralis. However, there was a weak correlation between\h temporary spikes in growth hormone and slow and\h\h fast-twitch fiber growth, but again\h these relationships were very weak.\h\h There was also a weak correlation between cortisol\h temporary spikes and fast-twitch fiber growth,\h\h but not slow-twitch fiber growth. It's worth mentioning cortisol is actually\h catabolic, it increases muscle protein breakdown\h\h and as such, is considered counteractive\h to hypertrophy, so this relationship\h\h (again, which was weak) between cortisol\h spikes and fast-twitch fiber growth does\h\h not readily make much sense, and perhaps\h may be best interpreted as a coincidence. Another study by Fink et al. found after 20\h men (untrained at least in the last 2 years\h\h leading up to the study) trained a variety of arm\h exercises each for 3 sets with 8-20 repetitions\h\h and between 30 seconds and 3 minutes of rest\h between sets, there was no correlation between\h\h temporary spikes in growth hormone (measured\h during a training session in the second week)\h\h and increases in arm cross-sectional area. No\h other hormones were assessed in this study. Thirdly, Mitchell et al. found after\h 23 men (untrained at least in the year\h\h leading up to the study) trained a range of\h exercises each for 2-4 sets with 6-12 reps,\h\h using 60-120 seconds of rest between sets\h for four times per week for 16 weeks,\h\h there was no relationship between any temporary\h spikes in the main anabolic hormones evoked via an\h\h acute training loading protocol (which occurred\h during the first and last weeks of training)\h\h and growth of slow and fast-twitch\h muscle fibers from the vastus lateralis. Finally, Morton et al. found after 49 men (with\h at least 2 years of training experience) trained\h\h a range of exercises for 3 sets of 8-25 reps\h to failure 4 times per week for 12 weeks,\h\h there was no relationship between all temporary\h spikes in the anabolic hormones evoked via an\h\h acute training loading protocol (which\h occurred before and after the training\h\h period) and growth of slow and fast-twitch\h muscle fibers from the vastus lateralis. So in total, the majority of the\h current literature fails to find\h\h a correlation between temporary spikes evoked\h via training and long-term muscle hypertrophy. Now, this is only correlational data, and it\h still does not necessarily inform us how a\h\h training with a program that generates significant\h temporary spikes in anabolic hormones compares to\h\h a program that generates lesser (if any) spikes in\h anabolic hormones for direct muscle hypertrophy. The best way to assess this is to directly analyze\h the current literature that has looked at this. Quite interestingly, one study by Ronnestad et\h al. indicates long-term muscle hypertrophy may\h\h be enhanced with a program that generates\h high temporary spikes in anabolic hormones. 11 previously untrained men had one arm\h assigned to a low hormone condition and their\h\h other arm assigned to a high hormone condition. Both arms were trained\h twice per week for 12 weeks. Each session, the low hormone arm trained the\h biceps curl, hammer curl, and reverse curl each\h\h for 2 sets with a 6-10 rep-max load. This training\h session, due to involving low amounts of muscle\h\h mass, failed to evoke any significant temporary\h spikes in testosterone or growth hormone. The high hormone arm, each session, performed\h exactly what the low hormone arm did,\h\h but before doing so, performed\h the leg press, leg extension,\h\h and leg curl each for 3 sets with a 10 rep-max\h load using 60-90 seconds of rest between sets.\h\h Due to these additional leg exercises which\h involve large amounts of muscle mass, as well\h\h as the short rest intervals between sets of them,\h this lower-body training generated significant\h\h spikes in testosterone and growth hormone during\h the subsequent biceps exercises, with the growth\h\h hormone spike remaining further elevated\h after the completion of the biceps exercises. By the end of the study, increases\h in cross-sectional area of the elbow\h\h flexors at two proximal sites were\h similar between both conditions,\h\h but at two distal sites, increases\h were greater for the high hormone arm. Therefore, this data suggests preceding biceps\h exercises with lower body training that evokes\h\h spikes in testosterone and growth hormone may\h ultimately enhance overall biceps hypertrophy. This is quite fascinating, however,\h\h a different study by West et al.\h somewhat conflicts with these findings. 12 previously untrained men\h had one arm assigned to a low\h\h hormone condition and their other arm\h assigned to a high hormone condition. Both arms were trained one to\h two times per week for 15 weeks. Each session, the low hormone arm performed an\h arm curl (they weren't specific on which arm\h\h curl) for 3-4 sets of 8-12 repetitions with a 95%\h 10 rep-max load. Due to the low amounts of muscle\h\h mass trained, this exercise failed to temporarily\h spike free testosterone, growth hormone, or IGF-1. The high hormone arm, each session, performed\h exactly what the low hormone arm did,\h\h but thereafter performed 5 sets\h of 10 repetitions on the leg press\h\h and 3 sets of 10 repetitions on a\h leg extension/leg curl superset,\h\h both were performed with a 95% 10 rep-max load.\h Due to these lower body exercises performed after,\h\h this session successfully provoked spikes\h in testosterone, growth hormone, and IGF-1. Despite this, by the end of the study,\h increases in cross-sectional area of the\h\h elbow flexors at all measured regions\h were similar between both conditions.\h\h Moreover, increases in slow-twitch and\h fast-twitch fiber cross-sectional area\h\h from the elbow flexors were also\h similar between both conditions. What could explain the conflicting findings\h between the West and Ronnestad studies? The West study had the high hormone condition\h perform the lower body exercises that evoked\h\h spikes in anabolic hormones after the biceps\h exercise, whereas the Ronnestad study had\h\h the high hormone condition perform the lower\h body exercises before the biceps exercises. Perhaps performing the lower body exercises\h that generate spikes in anabolic hormones\h\h prior to the biceps exercises, due\h to resulting in you performing the\h\h biceps exercises under elevated\h anabolic hormone concentrations,\h\h somehow potentiates long-term biceps\h hypertrophy via some mechanism. One such mechanism might relate to enhanced\h testosterone and androgen receptor content. More precisely, creating an elevated anabolic\h environment via performing lower body exercises\h\h prior to biceps training may not only elevate\h circulating testosterone concentrations\h\h but also androgen receptor\h content within the biceps itself.\h\h Such events would presumably enhance\h the likelihood testosterone can bind to\h\h androgen receptors to thereafter provoke\h an increase in muscle protein synthesis. I speculate this because one study by\h Spiering et al. found that performing\h\h a range of compound upper body exercises\h each for 4 sets with a 10 rep-max load\h\h (which temporarily spiked testosterone) before\h performing 5 sets with a 5 rep-max load on\h\h a knee extension and flexion dynamometer\h increased androgen receptor content within\h\h the vastus lateralis 180 minutes after\h exercise. This was in contrast to only\h\h performing 5 sets with a 5 rep-max load on\h the knee extension and flexion dynamometer,\h\h which failed to spike testosterone and androgen\h receptor content within the vastus lateralis. Stated another way, performing exercises that\h spike anabolic hormones before training a certain\h\h muscle may ultimately increase the androgen\h receptor content within that certain muscle. Having said all of this, some data challenges\h these aforementioned ideas and results. There exist studies finding\h that despite a training\h\h protocol evoking temporary spikes in testosterone,\h\h androgen receptor content actually downregulates\h in the hours after (that is, it decreases). Additionally, if spiking anabolic\h hormones prior to training a muscle\h\h enhanced its hypertrophy long-term, we\h would expect training compound exercises,\h\h due to spiking anabolic hormones as they\h involve large amounts of muscle mass,\h\h prior to single-joint biceps and triceps exercises\h to enhance biceps and triceps hypertrophy. However, this does not appear to be the case. Three studies have found biceps and/or\h triceps hypertrophy was similar regardless\h\h of if compound or biceps and triceps isolation\h exercises were performed first in a session.\h\h If anything, the results of these studies\h might favor performing the biceps and triceps\h\h isolation exercises first, therefore\h conflicting with the Ronnestad study. On the basis of this data, I believe we cannot be\h certain the results of the Ronnestad study can be\h\h truly confirmed, the results might just be random\h and related to the small sample size of the study. Moving forward, two further areas of\h the literature indicate a program that\h\h evokes higher spikes in anabolic hormones\h does not confer additional hypertrophy. Firstly, Schwanbeck et al. found in men,\h performing free weight squats and bench\h\h presses temporarily spiked free testosterone more\h than smith machines squats and bench presses.\h\h Yet, after an 8 week training period, a\h free weight program (including the free\h\h weight squat and bench press) produced similar\h increases in quadriceps and biceps thickness to\h\h an exclusive machine program (that included\h the smith machine squat and bench press). Secondly, as we noted much earlier in this video,\h using shorter rest intervals between sets (90\h\h seconds or less) tends to evoke greater spikes in\h anabolic hormones (particularly growth hormone)\h\h compared to training with longer\h rest intervals (2.5 minutes or more).\h\h However, as we've thoroughly described in\h our complete guide to rest intervals video,\h\h it seems with compound exercises and all\h other training variables equivalent, resting\h\h for 2.5 minutes or more generates more muscle\h hypertrophy than resting for 90 seconds or less. Therefore, this free weight vs machine literature,\h as well as the rest interval literature,\h\h together further support the idea that\h programs that evoke higher temporary spikes\h\h in anabolic hormones do not necessarily\h produce greater long-term hypertrophy. Combining all of the current\h evidence assessed thus far,\h\h and its apparent training in a way designed to\h maximally spike anabolic hormones is unnecessary. Not only are there weak (virtually non-existent)\h correlations between the magnitude of temporary\h\h spikes in anabolic hormones and muscle\h hypertrophy, but programs that generate\h\h higher temporary spikes in anabolic hormones\h do not appear to enhance muscle hypertrophy. Why might this be? The earlier mechanisms we outlined, that\h spikes in anabolic hormones could increase the\h\h likelihood of hormone-receptor interactions that\h culminate in increased muscle protein synthesis,\h\h seemed pretty logical. But evidently,\h this seems to not be occurring in reality. There are a few reasons I can think of\h that could potentially resolve this. Firstly, receptor content could\h just downregulate (that is,\h\h decrease in number) despite spikes in anabolic\h hormones, thereby counteracting the increase in\h\h anabolic hormones and making it no more likely\h hormone receptor interactions would be enhanced.\h\h Supporting this, and as I noted earlier\h already, there's evidence despite training\h\h evoking a spike in testosterone,\h androgen receptor content decreased. Secondly, it's important to recognize these\h temporary spikes in anabolic hormones are\h\h typically not very substantial, and it's\h quite possible these transient elevations\h\h are just too insignificant to influence muscle\h hypertrophy. Of course, we know that chronic\h\h supraphysiological elevations of anabolic hormones\h (achieved via exogenous administration, that is,\h\h you use steroids), very powerfully enhance muscle\h hypertrophy. Yet, the very transient elevations\h\h achieved via training naturally generally\h do not reach supraphysiological levels. Thirdly, it's quite plausible\h the temporary spikes in anabolic\h\h hormones may just simply be a response to the\h build of metabolites (like lactate) within a\h\h muscle and/or be more so oriented towards\h mobilizing fuel for muscle contraction,\h\h rather than promoting an increase in\h muscle protein synthesis post-exercise. At this time, I don't believe we have\h enough evidence to comment on which of\h\h these three reasons (if any) explains the\h current observations of the literature. Nonetheless, at the end of the day,\h I think everything outlined in this\h\h video more or less indirectly\h demonstrates that for natural\h\h individuals that are within the normal\h physiological anabolic hormones ranges,\h\h local factors within the muscle are more important\h for muscle hypertrophy than any systemic factors. What I mean by this is training sufficiently\h to stimulate the full spectrum of muscle fibers\h\h (which would enable mechanosensitive\h proteins within the fibers to detect\h\h tension and subsequently initiate a signaling\h cascade the results in an increase in muscle\h\h protein synthesis), and then fuelling your\h muscles correctly via sufficient caloric\h\h and protein intake (depending of course\h on your goals) is far more important for\h\h muscle hypertrophy than any transient spike\h in systemic anabolic hormone concentrations. As always, thank you for watching.\h I truly hope you found the video\h\h interesting and informative in some way!

=== FILE: Stretch Between Sets for More Hypertrophy？ (New Research) [9dlwvYq26NA].en.txt ===

For those of you who have been following this channel for a while, you might know that approximately 13 months ago, I created a video on whether stretching in between sets could enhance muscle hypertrophy. In the video, we explored a study by Evangelista et al. that essentially found in previously untrained men, performing 30 seconds of pain-free static stretching between sets for the main muscle in an exercise resulted in greater increases in muscle thickness measurements. At the time that video was published, that was the only single published study examining stretching in between sets. Since then, 2 new studies have come out adding to the literature on stretching in between sets and hypertrophy. One study by Nakamura et al. examined the outcomes of static stretching between sets in previously untrained men, while the second study by Wadhi et al. assessed the outcomes of weighted stretching between sets in trained men. Let us first overview the study by Nakamura et al. 16 untrained men had one leg assigned to a stretching condition and their other leg to a traditional condition. They trained the bilateral squat with an inertial flywheel for 3 sets of 10 repetitions, using 3 minutes of rest between sets, twice per week for 5 weeks. For those unaware, an inertial flywheel actually overloads the lowering (termed eccentric) phase of the movement. With the leg assigned to the stretching condition, during the 3-minute rest interval between sets, they stretched the quadriceps for 30 seconds, rested for 30 seconds, stretched the quadriceps for a further 30 seconds, and then rested for the remaining 90 seconds before commencing the next set. With the leg assigned to the traditional condition, it performed no stretching and rested for the 3-minute rest intervals between sets. Before and after the study, muscle thickness of the vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, rectus femoris, lateral region of the vastus intermedius, and medial region of the vastus intermedius were each measured at an upper and lower region. Furthermore, thickness of the hamstrings and gluteus maximus was each measured at a single region. The researchers found that for all regions and muscles measured, changes in thickness were statistically similar between the stretching and traditional condition, indicating that stretching in between sets may not enhance muscle hypertrophy. As a result, this study does not agree with the original findings by Evangelista et al. Let us progress to overviewing the second study by Wadhi et al. 26 men with an average of 3 years of training experience were allocated into a stretching or traditional group. Both groups trained twice per week for 8 weeks. Each session, the flat bench press and incline bench press were trained. Throughout the 8 weeks of training, they progressed from performing 3 sets per exercise to performing 5 sets. On training day one of each week, they aimed to perform 4-6 repetitions that were approximately 2 repetitions away from failure each set. Although the final set on the incline bench press was executed to failure. On training day two of each week, they aimed to perform 8-10 repetitions approximately Although, again, the final set on the incline bench press was executed to failure. When necessary, the load was adjusted on each set and over sessions to ensure subjects continued to train within the prescribed repetition ranges, and at the same proximity from failure. The traditional group rested passively for 2 minutes between their sets in a session. The stretching group similarly rested for 2 minutes between sets in a session. However, for the first 30 seconds of this rest interval, they performed a loaded chest stretch on a cable machine, using approximately 15% of the load they just used on the prior set. Also, subjects were instructed not to produce any active tension from the chest, rather let the chest be maximally be stretched by the load. Before and after the study, thickness of the pectoralis major at the belly, and at a lateral portion, was measured. What the researchers found was that increases at both regions of the pectoralis major were statistically similar between the stretching and traditional groups, suggesting weighted stretching between sets may not enhance muscle hypertrophy. So, combining these two new studies with the Evangelista study, and it now seems the ever so slight majority of the evidence indicates that stretching in between sets might not help you build more muscle. Having said this, there still are some important considerations. These three studies, although generally looking at the effectiveness of stretching in between sets, are quite different from one another. The Wadhi study examined weighted stretching in between sets in trained men, whereas the other two papers by Nakamura and Evangelista examined unload static stretching between sets in previously untrained men. Furthermore, if we more directly compared the Nakamura and Evangelista studies, which have conflicting results, there are some potentially noteworthy differences. Firstly, the Nakamura study used an inertial flywheel squat exercise, which as we've noted applies eccentric overload, whereas the Evangelista study used typical free weight and machine exercises, like the leg extension. Could these different exercise modalities somehow explain the conflicting results? Secondly, in the Evangelista study, in which stretching was found to benefit muscle hypertrophy, they had subjects stretch for 30 seconds during the rest intervals. Contrastingly, the Nakamura study had subjects stretch for 2 bouts of 30 seconds during each rest interval, totaling 60 seconds of static stretching in between sets. The reason this could matter is that longer duration static stretching appears to reduce muscle force production, and this could negatively influence the hypertrophic stimulus. For example, Siatras et al. found that stretching the quadriceps for 60 seconds resulted in greater decreases in quadriceps force output versus stretching for 30 seconds. As a result, perhaps the reason the Nakamura study failed to find a benefit to static stretching in between sets was that subjects stretched for a total of 60 seconds between sets. Perhaps a 30-second stretch instead, as used in the Evangelista study, is the ideal duration to induce enhancements in muscle growth. However, it's worth remembering that the Wadhi study, in which weighted stretching was employed, did use a 30-second stretching duration between sets, yet found no benefits for hypertrophy. All in all, it's clear to see that future research will still be of great benefit for trying to tease out the details on if and how stretching in between sets could enhance muscle growth. Now, it's potentially worth discussing the fact that all the current three studies that have examined stretching in between sets have measured muscle growth via muscle thickness. Muscle thickness only measures one dimension of the whole muscle. How would the results of these studies look if they used an alternative muscle growth measurement? What if researchers measured cross-sectional area, (which measured two dimensions), volume (which measures three dimensions), or even something like fascicle length. I think the fascicle length measurement is an interesting one. As we've described in a previous video, an increase in fascicle length likely reflects an increase in the length of muscle fibers, as muscle fibers are within fascicles. As we saw in that video, it appears stretching stimuli can induce increases in muscle fiber length. Furthermore, although not a unanimous finding in the research, some human evidence indicates intense static stretching protocols produce increases in fascicle length (which presumably reflects an increase in muscle fiber length). This brings up the interesting question, could stretching in between sets be a tool to help increase muscle fiber length? Hopefully, future research can examine this. - As a final section for this video, viewers may be interested in how stretching in between sets impacts strength adaptations. Many people would think, and justifiably so, that given static stretching can decrease the force output of a muscle, stretching in between sets would reduce the strength adaptations you experience. However, the long-term research does not appear to strongly support this. In the Evangelista study, they found similar increases in bench press and leg extension one-rep max between the group that stretched pain-free for 30 seconds between sets and the group that rested passively. In the Nakamura study, they decided to look at one-rep max on the leg press, peak concentric, eccentric, and isometric torque on a leg extension dynamometer. Except for isometric torque, increases in these strength measures were statistically similar between the stretching and traditional conditions. Intriguingly, the isometric torque increases were greater for the stretching condition. Finally, in the Wadhi study, increases in bench press one-rep max were similar between the group that weighted stretched between sets and the group that rested passively. Therefore, the majority of the current data indicate stretching in between sets might not deleteriously influence strength adaptations, at least within the confines of the protocols used in the respective studies. To conclude the video, since the publication of the study by Evangelista, suggesting stretching in between sets could enhance muscle growth, two new studies now indicate stretching in between sets may not help build more muscle. However, these three studies are fairly heterogeneous, meaning that future research will be of great value for teasing out if and how stretching in between sets could actually enhance muscle hypertrophy. I am aware of at least one study currently being conducted examining the outcomes weighted stretching in between sets. According to the author, it should be published by the end of 2021. So, hopefully, I'll be creating an updated version of this video in the future. Thank you for watching. As always, I hope you found the video helpful or informative in some way.

As a brief review, and for those who haven't seen\h the previous videos, let us first establish what\h\h myofibrillar hypertrophy, myofibrillar packing,\h as well as sarcoplasmic hypertrophy, are. Myofibrils are where the magic\h of muscle contraction happens,\h\h they consist of an array of sarcomeres. Sarcomeres are what generate muscle force. As per the science and\h practice of strength training,\h\h the response of a biological object to\h a constant stimulus decreases over time. Despite this study's findings,\h I think it's worth touching on\h\h three potential considerations with\h changing exercises every session. Firstly, many exercises (particularly\h compound exercises) are skills. Regular practice of an exercise is required to\h achieve smoother and more efficient movement,\h\h something that would ensure we're stimulating\h the intended muscles most effectively. Changing exercises every session can\h prevent or significantly delay exercise\h\h skill acquisition. This may be more so a problem\h for individuals with minimal training experience. Secondly, changing exercises every\h session might require longer recovery\h\h durations than training with fixed\h exercises, at least in the long term. Allow me to explain. The amount of muscle damage present is one factor\h\h that determines whether you're\h recovered between sessions. When you first expose yourself to a novel training\h routine, the amount of muscle damage produced\h\h afterward is quite high. But as you continue to\h expose your body to the same training routine\h\h week after week, the amount of muscle damage\h produced afterward incrementally decreases. This is thanks to a range of adaptations within\h the muscles called the repeated bout effect. The repeated bout effect is going\h to be greater when performing the\h\h same weekly exercises in your training routine. Most people have experienced this. When\h performing the same weekly training routine,\h\h the amount of soreness you experience gradually\h diminishes over many weeks of training,\h\h and you're overall recovery\h capacities become better. However, If you're changing the\h exercises you perform every session,\h\h the repeated bout effect likely occurs to a lower\h extent. It's likely your recovery durations are\h\h going to always be longer compared to\h training with the same weekly routine. Now, in the Baz-Valle et al. study, evidently\h recovery was not a problem for the variation\h\h group, as the variation and fixed group's gains\h were not statistically different from one another. But it's worth noting the study\h used an upper/lower split,\h\h in which the same muscle\h was trained 72 hours apart. However, what if something like\h a full-body split was used,\h\h in which the same muscle is mostly\h trained 48 hours or quicker apart?\h\h Would the variation group appropriately\h be able to recover long-term? It's difficult to say without future research. Another point worth adding is there's evidence\h gradually increasing the number of weekly sets\h\h you perform for a muscle group might be\h an effective way to get past plateaus.\h\h We overviewed this evidence in\h our ultimate guide to sets video. Of course, increasing set numbers requires you can\h tolerate and recover from this increased volume.\h\h This might be harder to do when\h changing exercises every session. The third consideration with changing exercises\h every session relates to tracking progression. When performing the same weekly exercises,\h so long as you're able to progressively\h\h overload them in some form (either via\h increasing load or repetition numbers),\h\h you have proof you're progressing. Furthermore, if you're not progressing with your\h fixed exercise selection in the way you expect,\h\h this can be an indicator something's wrong,\h\h and it allows you to re-assess your\h training plan and make adjustments. In other words, fixed exercise selection\h can help you individualize and optimize\h\h your training routine in the long\h term via more meticulous tracking. When changing exercises every session,\h you can simply perform repetitions to\h\h or very close to failure on them, which\h ensures you've provoked a good stimulus.\h\h However, the fact is it's very difficult to\h tell if you're making progress week to week.\h\h If you hit a plateau, it's going\h to be difficult to establish this. We currently have one study by\h Baz-Valle et al. finding changing\h\h exercises every session was comparable for\h muscle growth to training with fixed exercises. Despite this, I think there are some potential\h issues with changing exercises every session. Firstly, for those with minimal training\h experience, changing exercises every session\h\h can prevent or at least significantly delay the\h development of form and skill with exercises. Secondly, over the long-term, changing exercises\h every sesion probably requires longer recovery\h\h durations than training with the same exercises,\h this might make it unpractical when training\h\h with full-body splits that require you\h to recover within 48 hours or less.\h\h Moreover, it may also make it challenging\h to increase volume in the long term,\h\h and increasing volume may be\h helpful for getting past plateaus. Finally, changing exercises every\h session makes it difficult to track\h\h progression and very challenging to\h establish if you've hit a plateau.

=== FILE: The BEST Chest Exercises for Building Muscle (33 Studies) [qsDleTVaKhk].txt ===

  Before getting into the heart of our analysis, the chest refers to a few muscles, but we're focusing on the pectoralis major. It covers the most area and is what most mean when they say the chest. Furthermore, dividing the pectoralis major into different heads isn't bro science. Various scientific analyses have divided it into a clavicular and sternocostal head, each with a unique nerve supply. In fact, we could even go a step further and consider there to be three distinct regions. For simplicity, we'll just refer to the upper, middle and lower pecs. Commencing our analysis, the flat barbell bench press is one of the most famous exercises in the galaxy, seen in powerlifting, pro sport and maybe even your dreams if you're anything like me. Some say barbell benching sucks for chest gains, but the fact is the literature would not agree. Multiple papers establish the pectoralis major growth very well from flat barbell benching, seeing similar or even slightly more average growth than the expected rate of hypertrophy. For instance, this Japanese paper had previously untrained men trained the exercise with these variables and we can see mid-pec thickness increase throughout the study, ending up seeing a 43% increase in thickness. As for how flat bench pressing impacts other pec regions, two studies shed light onto this. This 2022 Australian study had trained folks train the flat barbell bench press across eight weeks. A normal group performed four sets of five reps with an 85% 1 rep max load. A cluster group used the same variables, but they rested 30 seconds between each repetition in a set. The cluster group didn't see gains galore, which isn't a surprise as the rest between repetitions would have resulted in them training quite far from muscular failure, which isn't ideal. The normal group experienced impressive hypertrophy across all three pectoralis major regions, and this is the key finding. Flat benching appears to grow all pec regions well. This Japanese study is the second paper. Untrained men trained the flat barbell bench press with these variables. A normal group trained every week across 24 weeks, while a break group took a three-week break every six weeks. Both groups experienced substantial and similar pectoralis major hypertrophy across three regions. Thus, this study suggests taking a three-week hiatus every six weeks didn't compromise gains. A remarkably fascinating finding, something talked about in previous videos. Anyhow, the key is these results again reveal flat benching grows the pecs well across its regions. This begs two questions. Do we really need dedicated upper and lower pec training when flat benching appears to evoke pectacular percentage gains across all regions? Stay tuned for some upcoming videos where we'll unravel the answer to this question. But in this video, we'll decode the second question, which is since these papers didn't compare flat barbell benching to other exercises, how does it stack up to other exercises? What's going on? This is Vince with VFRED.com. Now if I was your trainer… BELL RINGS On the one hand, some say barbell bench pressing is undefeatable since we can use heavy loads and easily progressively overload in the long term. On the other hand, others may say the dumbbell's freedom renders it superior or that the stability with machine variations is the secret source to maximum muscle fiber recruitment and thus hypertrophy. Who's right? Luckily, we have research comparing chest hypertrophy between some of these exercises plus electromyographic research. Research actually measuring chest hypertrophy is supreme since it's the real thing we care about, but we'll sprinkle in the EMG data where appropriate. For those unaware, EMG uses electrodes to record a muscle's electrical activity, so it does not actually directly measure muscle activation. But as electrical activity precedes muscle activation, some say this makes EMG a perfect tool. Is this true? Not quite. There are steps in between electrical activity and muscle activation, so there's not always a one-to-one relationship. And notably, EMG doesn't always measure electrical activity accurately in the first place. Noise and technical errors can mess things up. We even have studies failing to find an association between EMG and actual muscle hypertrophy, although some indirect papers find a relationship. So overall, the relationship between EMG and hypertrophy isn't straightforward. We need to be cautious, and some EMG studies are also better designed than others. I'll do my best to describe this along the way. Beginning with machine chest presses versus the flat barbell bench press, One EMG paper finds greater pec and triceps activity with the barbell bench press, yet two others find similar activity, with this paper finding these two machine chest press variants produce comparable activity of all three pec regions, the front delts, and triceps to flat barbell benching. Most critically, this recent study directly compared pec-traced major hypertrophy between this machine chest press and the flat barbell bench press. Hypertrophy was quite similar between both. Therefore, I believe we can contend various machine presses probably have the capability of producing similar pec gains to flat benching. Delving into the push-up, this Japanese paper compared high-rep push-ups to high-rep bench pressing, and similar chest hypertrophy as well as triceps hypertrophy was seen between both. Perhaps some are pondering, hold on a moment, aren't the high reps in this study a crucial drawback? It is not. Regular house hypertrophy viewers will be more than aware that reps approximately between 6 and 35 can produce similar hypertrophy, provided reps are performed to or close to failure. Even so, weighted push-ups are a possibility. And this rather well-constructed EMG analysis compared load-equated weighted push-ups to flat barbell bench pressing. It found comparable pec, triceps, and even front deltoid activity between them. Push-ups can even be progressed via harder variations. This study had subjects do just this in predominantly the 4-8 rep range using these variations. Another group just overloaded the flat barbell bench press in the 6-8 rep range. Fascinatingly, chest growth leaned towards the push-up group. But this study was merely 4 weeks and nothing reached significance. At the very least, I'd merely state this indicates the barbell bench is not undeniably superior. Thus, overall, push-ups seem to possess the capacity to produce similar pec gains to flat benching. But this is contingent upon successfully progressing push-ups long term, so you can continuously train hard in the 6-35 rep range. Transitioning to the Smith Machine Five EMG studies have compared Smith Machine to barbell bench pressing, and the majority find similar pec, triceps, and front deltoid activity between them. Considering this is EMG data, and there's an absence of any studies directly measuring hypertrophy, my tentative hypothesis is Smith Machine Benching may be comparable to barbells for the pecs. And it may be worth mentioning EMG might be more reliable when comparing exercises that are similar to one another, which is the case here. Progressing to Dumbbells Let's first focus on the triceps as I think it's quite interesting. Three studies have compared triceps activity between dumbbell and barbell bench pressing, and all discovered slightly lower activity with a dumbbell. Why could this be? It may be because during the barbell bench press, although vertical forces are produced to lift the load, some degree of lateral forces are naturally produced, and the triceps are likely heavily involved in these lateral forces. With the dumbbell, however, lateral forces cannot be produced. Attempting to do so would result in the dumbbells falling either side of you. As for the pecs and front delts, four studies have made the comparison between dumbbell and barbell benching, and the majority find similar pecs and front delts activity between both. However, there is a trap with EMG that we must be aware of. EMG doesn't measure the passive forces muscles generate when they're stretched, but emerging research suggests these importantly contribute to muscle hypertrophy. Dumbbells have the potential to permit a deeper pec stretch compared to the barbell and even other variations. For this reason, it's potentially numero uno. But there are some complications. Firstly, larger dumbbells will obstruct your ability to actually attain a deeper stretch, and in general, I think most naturally don't execute the movement in a way that maximizes the stretch. Secondly, it's even plausible that any extra stretch simply fails to translate into more gains. It is true multiple studies suggest training muscles at stretched positions is better for building muscle than shortened positions. But this data doesn't necessarily mean getting an extra deeper stretch above an already solid stretch leads to more hypertrophy. Some studies allude to this. This Japanese paper compared 90 degree to 140 degree knee flexion squats. Glute max and adducted hypertrophy was indeed better with a deeper range of motion, but quad hypertrophy was similar between both. Yet another Japanese paper compared these partial triceps skull crushers to a full range of motion which attained a better stretch, but triceps hypertrophy was actually better for the partial. This study is somewhat of an outlier, as it's the only one to date to find that reaching a better stretch led to worse hypertrophy. In any case, these are just two studies on the quads and triceps, and there are currently no studies on the pecs, but they at least present the concept that a greater stretch may not always equal greater gains. Having said all this, others might suggest the convergence of the dumbbells at the top is advantageous. But there's not much tension at this point, and most studies suggest the contracted top position isn't that stimulatory for gains. For all these reasons, I hesitate to say dumbbells are clearly superior. Rather, it may be more reasonable to conclude they're largely similar for now. Last but not least, what about dips? No, not that guacamole dip, I'm talking about these dips. There are currently no officially published studies measuring EMG or hypertrophy, comparing dips to other different exercises. I know this paper involved a comparison of EMG between different dips, with the ring and normal dips producing decent levels for the chest, front delts and triceps. Not much can be drawn from this, so we can't really make any firm conclusions surrounding dips. But in an upcoming video on the lower chest, we'll dive into dips a little more. Disregarding dips, we've seen the entirety of the evidence appear to suggest all variations may be comparably effective for chest hypertrophy. How could this be given some of the arguments presented earlier? Although the barbell bench press can be trained with heavier loads, heavier loads are not a prerequisite for maximizing the hypertrophy stimulus. Instead, training to or near muscular failure is what does this. This can be done with lighter loads, which is likely why higher reps with lighter loads can produce similar muscle growth to lower reps with heavier loads. As for the barbell bench press having great progressive overload potential, although progressive overload is certainly important for sustaining long-term gains, we simply can't say that exercises easier to progressive overload are superior. Very partial squats have great potential to be progressively overloaded, but they are not great for hypertrophy. As for the suggestion, machines are the ticket to the city of gains thanks to their great stability. Greater stability has indeed been linked to enhanced muscle fiber recruitment, but the context of this research should not be overlooked. For illustration, this paper manipulated stability levels on a leg extension by strapping down the leg and torso. The generalizability of this research is questionable, and when push comes to shove, the research measuring hypertrophy will always reign supreme to indirect mechanistic speculation. And we have a few other analyses finding machines produce similar hypertrophy to free weights. Note, the number of dominant legs was equally divided between the conditions, and subjects alternated which leg was trained first to every session. I'd say there's some underappreciated reasoning behind this, and this reasoning also links to the multiple different training strategies that are available for you to maximize muscle growth. It also links to whether we should consider increasing sets or training frequency as progressive overload. How is this achieved? Achieving a high level of muscle fiber recruitment and tension are key for stimulating muscle hypertrophy. How is this achieved? Simply by taking your repetitions too or very close to failure. Stopping a few reps short of failure can be fine in many cases, as seen in our last video. By training close to failure, we're going to stimulate adaptations. These adaptations mean we can do more than we could before. We can lift a heavier load for the same number of reps, or we can perform more repetitions with the same load. In both of these cases, we're effectively maintaining being close to failure, and by extension, we maintain high muscle fiber recruitment and tension. So in essence, increasing load or reps fundamentally accomplishes the same thing. Thinking of progressive overload as a cycle works well. A hard training session stimulates adaptations. These adaptations enable us to increase load or reps, and doing this maintains a hard training session. Considering this, progressive overload isn't really training harder than last time. Rather, progressive overload keeps us training as hard as usual to continually stimulate growth. Moreover, progressive overload isn't a result of you digging to progressively deeper and deeper depths of effort. Instead, successful progressive overload is proof gains are happening. Now, there is an important detail we must not neglect. The current literature suggests reps between 6 to 35, provided they perform too or close to failure, produce similar muscle hypertrophy. Reps below 6 probably involve too little time at high tension, while reps above 35 probably involve excessive fatigue that impairs muscle fiber recruitment and tension. With this in mind, there is only so much you can increase reps. If you somehow get to the point of performing more than 35 reps, increasing the load is recommended. And overall, a combination of both increasing load and reps over the long-term is what's going to happen in most cases. For instance, exercises involving smaller amounts of muscle mass are harder to progressive overload, and constantly increasing load across your training sessions on these is far from always possible, unless you have access to very light microplates. === FILE: The BEST Rep Speed For Size (New Study) [2sys7keMuy4].txt ===

 Welcome to the House of Hypertrophy. Is there an optimal tempo to maximise muscle hypertrophy? I'm glad to say we have a new meta-analysis exploring this. Let's dive straight in. The researchers aim to identify all the studies that compared faster and slower tempos on either the concentric and eccentric phase and met these criteria. So, to be clear, studies that had one group train with both a slower concentric and eccentric to another group that trained with both a faster concentric and eccentric tempo were not included because the new analysis just included studies that independently manipulated eccentric and concentric tempo. The meta-analysis ended up including 14 studies with a total of 278 subjects. These were the average and range of tempos for the fast and slow eccentric and concentric. Let's start with the eccentric data which answers the question. When using a given concentric tempo, is a fast or slower eccentric tempo superior for hypertrophy? Here's the results. I thought it'd be worth ensuring we all know what we're looking at here. This is what's known as a forest plot. It's a graphical representation of the individual results of each study included in the meta-analysis together with the combined meta-analytic results. As a fun fact, forest plots go back at least to the 1970s. The name refers to the forest of lines produced. For each individual study, we see the effect estimate shown with a dot and the value of it on the right. A positive value in this case means the gains are greater for faster tempos. We also see a 95% credible interval with the upper and lower bounds of the interval noted on the right. Credible intervals quantify the uncertainty in our estimate. To make this clear, remember that each study is trying to estimate the true possible difference between faster and slower tempos, but our estimate is not necessarily perfect. For example, if we wanted to measure the average arm size of adults in England, it would be quite impractical to measure every single person, so we take a sample instead. But the average we get from our sample isn't guaranteed to be equivalent to the true population average, so we have uncertainty with our results. Of course, the larger the sample, the less uncertainty there will be. The way we interpret 95% credible intervals is simple. We say that we believe it is 95% probable that the true effect falls within this interval. Of course, wide credible intervals indicate a lot of uncertainty, whereas narrow credible intervals suggest our estimate is quite precise. We also see a posterior distribution. All you need to know for our purposes is that the areas with greater height are considered to be more plausible than areas with lower heights. The overall meta-analytic effect is the main result, but it is also still an estimate and thus has its own 95% credible interval. For this particular analysis, we see that the effect favors faster tempos with the standardized mean difference of 0.06, which is fairly hard to make sense of if you're not a researcher. Fortunately though, thanks to Greg Knuckles' excellent work over at Stronger by Science, there's a rough but good enough way to convert this number into something more interpretable. A 0.06 effect size roughly translates into a 0.9% difference. Note, this is an additive percentage difference. So if slower tempos produced an increase in muscle size of 5%, faster tempos produced an increase in muscle size of 5.9%. In terms of a multiplicative percentage difference, this roughly equates to 18%. So we're not really talking about a large effect. Moreover, notice the uncertainty we see with the credible interval, with the difference of 0 comfortably being in the interval. Given this, despite the estimate slightly favoring faster tempos, I do think the best description is no clear advantage for either tempo. That said, there is a subgroup analysis worth discussing. With this eccentric data, the researchers split the data into those that had subjects trained to failure and those that did not train to failure. With the failure data, the estimate was in favor of slower tempos, while with a non-failure data, the estimate was in favor of faster tempos. The reason I thought this is perhaps notable is because three of the five studies in the non-failure data had subjects trained with isokinetic dynamometers, which matches the subject's effort and maintains a set velocity, which is not identical to normal training. Whereas with this failure data, six of six studies had subjects trained with regular freeway or machine exercises which most people train with. Thus, there's a case to be made that this analysis is the most generalizable to normal training. So, slower eccentric tempos could have a possibly small advantage, but once again, we have to grapple with the fact this estimate is far from precise, so I don't think it's unjustifiable to once again just say this data shows no clear advantage for either tempo. Let's move on to the concentric data, which answers the question. When using a given eccentric tempo, is a faster or slower concentric tempo superior for hypertrophy? Here, we see that the estimate favors faster tempos, but there's a great degree of uncertainty. Given the limited data here, no further analyses were done with this concentric data. So, what conclusions can we take away from this meta-analysis? The somewhat boring point is that the uncertainty we see in the data demonstrates that additional studies will help us obtain more precise estimates, plus we currently do not have much research on trained individuals, so it would be premature for me to definitively rule out a possibility of genuine effects. On the bright side, the research is developing quite nicely, so I'm hopeful we'll get more precise estimates. Of course, we can't wait, we have to train now. So, when looking at this data, I think the most sensible interpretation is that there's no strong evidence for a clear advantage for either tempo. I'll also add that the researchers did an extra analysis, exploring the gains achieved by faster tempos and slower tempos, with the effect sizes being in the range of 0.34 to 0.43, which roughly equates to 5-6%. But what is the typical magnitude of muscle growth? Fascinatingly, this 5-6% increase is right in line with the typical muscle size increase seen in the literature. Specifically, this excellent meta-analysis included 111 studies and observed muscle size to increase by approximately 5%. I'll add this was quite a precise estimate. Thus, we can have no doubt that you can grow well with either faster and slower tempos. It is clear that rep tempo is far from the most important training variable for muscle hypertrophy. From this, we can probably infer that if there is a difference between slower and faster tempos, the difference is likely not going to be large. So, for now, I would select your preference and this of course can vary between exercises if you wish. There is also further evidence against the notion that tempo has a meaningful impact on hypertrophy. Recall that only studies that independently manipulated concentric and eccentric tempo were included. But there are studies comparing faster concentrics and faster eccentric to slower concentrics and slower eccentrics. These papers tend to find no significant differences in hypertrophy. Indeed, we've had an older meta-analysis and some more recent reviews emphasizing some of this literature and ultimately concluding that provided you're training 2 or close to failure, repetition tempos across a wide range of durations are probably similarly effective for building muscle. That said, it is possible that super slow training might not be ideal for hypertrophy. This paper had untrained women train the back squats, leg press, and leg extension with these variables. A normal group took each set to failure with a 1-2 second concentric and eccentric tempo, with an 80-85% one rep max load. While a super slow group aimed to take each set to failure with a 10-second concentric and full-second eccentric tempo, with a 40-60% one rep max load, increases in slow and fast-switch fibrocyzes from the vastest lateralis favored the normal group. The super slow group did use lighter loads, but it's tough to argue this is what's to blame, since we've seen plenty of times at the house of hyperchve that loads as light as 30% one rep max can be similarly effective for building muscle. But now, this is one study, so it's anything but proof. But in the absence of other data, I think it's best to err on the side of caution and avoid super slow tempos if the aim is to maximize hypertrophy. === FILE: The Bench Press Grows These Triceps Heads #Shorts [pevqsw8WNfc].en.txt ===

How well does the bench press develop the triceps? Brandao et al. had previously untrained men perform the barbell bench press with a 2x shoulder-width grip for 3 to 5 sets of repetitions to failure with an 80% one-rep max load, twice per week for 10 weeks. They experienced pretty good growth of the lateral head, fairly decent growth of the medial head, but very little growth of the long head. Wakahara et al. found similar results with a dumbbell bench press. They had subjects perform the dumbbell bench press with a neutral hand position and found that activation of the long head, measured by T2 weighted imaging, was much less than that of the medial and lateral heads. Therefore, bench pressing is likely good at growing the lateral and medial heads, but poor for the long head.

=== FILE: The Best Exercise for Muscle Hypertrophy (What Science Says) [JVyLnLWpbxE].en.txt ===

It's far from uncommon to run\h across content claiming to\h\h detail the best exercises or best\h workout programs for hypertrophy. For example, you might have heard certain\h compound exercises such as back squats or\h\h conventional deadlifts being described as\h the most effective for building muscle.\h\h Other times, they are called\h the "king of all exercises". However, I want to describe why I think when\h overviewing the current exercise selection\h\h literature, as well as the literature on\h muscle hypertrophy stimuli, the concept of\h\h there being the best exercise, or the best couple\h of exercises, for hypertrophy makes little sense. For one, there does not appear to be an\h optimal exercise modality for hypertrophy. A recent meta-analysis by\h Heidel et al. established\h\h free weights and machine exercises were\h comparably effective for hypertrophy. Adding some extra detail, one study by Schwanbeck\h et al. compared an exclusive free weight program\h\h (consisting of exercises such as back squats\h and e-z bar curls) to an exclusive machine\h\h program (consisting of exercises such as smith\h machine back squats and machine biceps curls). After 8 weeks of training, increases in thickness\h\h of the biceps and quadriceps were\h similar between both programs. Bodyweight exercises are\h likely no less effective too. Kikuchi and Nakazato found that\h bodyweight push-up variations and a 40%\h\h one-rep max flat barbell bench press\h evoked similar pectorlais major and\h\h triceps thickness increases\h after 8 training weeks. Note, a 40% one-rep max load is perfectly fine\h for muscle hypertrophy, Quite a bit of evidence\h\h indicates loads between 30% and 85% one-rep max\h produce similar growth, provided repetitions are\h\h performed to volition failure (which was\h done in the Kikuchi and Nakazato study). Moreover, though notable limitations with\h muscle excitation studies exist, a number of\h\h them find when push-ups are load equated to bench\h presses (either via comparing light load bench\h\h pressing to bodyweight push-ups, or via comparing\h weighted push-ups to heavier load bench pressing),\h\h both exercises similarly generate excitation\h of pectoralis major, triceps, and front delts. The findings of these various\h studies make sense. Let me explain. The current literature on the\h stimuli of muscle hypertrophy\h\h indicates mechanical tension may be\h the primary hypertrophy stimulus. Mechanical tension is equal to the force generated\h by muscle fibers. Components within muscle fibers,\h\h called "mechanosensors" can detect the\h force produced by a muscle fiber and\h\h thereafter transduce these forces into a signaling\h cascade the results in muscle fiber hypertrophy. Following on from this, to\h maximize a muscle's growth,\h\h we'd want to recruit as many muscle\h fibers as possible and have them\h\h sustain at least decent amounts of their\h respective forces for a fair duration. The key point here is this\h can be accomplished with\h\h any exercise modality. Your body possesses no\h mechanism to know if free weights, machines,\h\h or body weight is being utilized to stimulate\h muscle fiber recruitment and force generation. So long as you perform between roughly 5 and\h 35 repetitions (and those repetitions are\h\h performed with 3 or fewer reps in reserve) with\h a free weight, machine, or bodyweight exercise,\h\h the aforementioned conditions are likely\h achieved. That is, the working muscles in\h\h the exercise likely experience maximal muscle\h fiber recruitment, and the individual muscle\h\h fibers likely sustain at least decent amounts\h of their respective forces for a fair duration. Before moving on, there is another component\h to mechanical tension worth touching on.\h\h This is passive tension. When muscle fibers are sufficiently stretched,\h\h a component within it called titin\h produces passive tension while elongating. A rubber band can help you conceptualize\h passive tension. When stretching a rubber band,\h\h it produces tension (analogous to force) to try\h and resist stretch. Titin operates comparably. Mechnosensors, potentially within titin\h itself, can detect this passive force\h\h and transduce it into a signaling cascade\h that produces muscle fiber hypertrophy. Generally, exercises that involve a\h good stretch of the working muscle\h\h or muscles can involve high\h amounts of passive tension. Numerous free weight, machine, and\h bodyweight exercises can involve a\h\h good stretch of the working muscle or muscles.\h For example, a barbell back squat, hack squat,\h\h or pistol squat all accomplish a good stretch\h of the quadriceps and gluteus maximus. Another reason why the concept of the best\h exercise or exercises makes little sense is\h\h for optimizing growth across many regions of a\h muscle, exercise variety is likely important. Costa et al. allocated 22 detrained men\h\h (they had not trained in the previous 6\h months) into a non-varied or varied group. Both groups trained for 8 weeks.\h The non-varied group performed\h\h the exact same exercises for their\h muscle groups three times per week. The non-varied group, across the 3 days, performed\h different exercises for their muscle groups. Both groups trained each exercise\h with 3 sets of 8-12 repetitions,\h\h using 90-120 seconds of rest between sets. Before and after the study, thickness\h of the upper, middle, and lower regions\h\h of the rectus femoris, vastus lateralis,\h elbow flexors, and triceps were measured. Overall, although increases in thickness\h were similar between both groups at a\h\h couple of regions, increases at other\h regions favored the varied group. Accordingly, this data demonstrates performing\h around 3 different exercises per muscle group\h\h each week results in greater growth\h across more regions of a muscle. This is logical. Typically,\h different regions of a muscle,\h\h or the different muscles in a muscle\h group, do not function in complete unison. Rather, the different regions of a muscle,\h or the different muscles in a muscle group,\h\h are activated to different degrees during\h movements that contrast in some way. For example, Nunes et al. established performing\h calf presses with the feet rotated outwards\h\h results in preferential growth of the medial\h gastrocnemius, while calf presses with the\h\h feet rotated inwards evoked preferential\h growth of the lateral gastrocnemius. As for example on the muscle group level, although\h back squats seem to do a great job at stimulating\h\h the vasti muscles of the quadriceps (that is, the\h vastus medialis, intermedius, and lateralis), they\h\h fail to meaningfully target the rectus femoris.\h Yet, leg extensions or reverse nordic curls (which\h\h involve more isolated knee motion with little hip\h motion) preferentially grow the rectus femoris. On the account of all this, by training a\h certain muscle group with a few different\h\h exercises that vary in some way (either\h via the angle used, joint positioning,\h\h or hand orientation), you most likely\h end up growing more regions of a muscle. Therefore, saying there's a single best\h exercise for a muscle misses the notion\h\h different exercises collectively contribute\h towards more uniformly growing a muscle. The final reason I think is worth discussing\h on why the concept of the best exercise or\h\h exercises makes little sense\h relates to individual differences. With the same exercise,\h\h not all individuals recruit and stimulate\h the same musculature to the same degree. Stronska et al.'s data indicate the relative\h recruitment of the pectoralis major,\h\h triceps, and anterior deltoid differed between\h individuals on the bench press. Some individuals\h\h preferentially recruited the pectoralis major,\h some the anterior deltoid, and others the triceps. Likewise, Boyer et al. observed during\h nordic curls and stiff-legged deadlifts,\h\h recruitment of the various hamstring\h muscles differed amongst individuals. These findings highlight the notion that just\h because one individual grew a certain way with\h\h one exercise, this does not necessarily\h guarantee the same will occur for you. As a final point, I should emphasize\h that by no means am I saying every\h\h single exercise in existence\h is optimal for building muscle. Unquestionably there exist factors that\h would result in certain exercises being\h\h more favorable for hypertrophy. It's just\h that even with these factors in mind,\h\h a whole host of exercises are still\h highly effective for hypertrophy. Even so, let us briefly overview\h factors that could make an\h\h exercise more or less effective for hypertrophy. If the muscle you're attempting to train\h is not the limiting factor in an exercise,\h\h chances are it's a suboptimal movement. Take a bosu ball pistol squat. Your\h balance and stability are probably\h\h going to limit your performance more than\h force production from the main muscles.\h\h Consequently, a whole host of other\h exercises that provide a more stable\h\h environment are more optimal, be it back\h squats, hack squats, or assisted pistol squats. Another factor relates to achieving a stretch.\h The current evidence is increasingly leaning\h\h towards the idea that exercises that achieve a\h good stretch of the working muscle or muscles\h\h may be a more powerful hypertrophy stimulus versus\h\h exercises that only train the\h muscle in a shortened length. There are an array of exercises for\h each muscle that involve good stretches. Finally, personal preferences for one\h reason or another may be important too.\h\h If certain exercises, either due to\h your natural anatomy or injury history,\h\h are uncomfortable or painful, chances are\h you're better off performing other movements. In a different scenario, if you're someone who\h utilizes the mind-muscle connection, and you find\h\h you're able to best achieve this with an exercise\h like the dumbbell curl as opposed to barbell curl,\h\h hypertrophy outcomes could potentially\h be better with the dumbbell variation. That brings us to the end of the video. As always,\h\h thank you for watching, I hope you found the\h video interesting and informative in some way!
