=== FILE: Time Under Tension Is OVERRATED...or Is It？ (10 studies) [_RVjlfyyjow].en.txt ===

When it comes to maximizing muscle growth, it's far from uncommon to hear that time under tension is an important component. Time under tension refers to the duration you place a muscle under strain. Typically, it's represented as the duration of a set for an exercise. For instance, performing 10 reps on the biceps curl with each rep consisting of a 2-second lifting phase and a 2-second lowering phase results in a total time under tension of 40 seconds. It's often claimed a longer time under tension maximizes hypertrophy. It's thought longer durations place the muscle under more strain, resulting in a more powerful stimulus for hypertrophy. For example, numerous sources claim around 30-60 seconds of time under tension per set is optimal for building muscle. In this video, with help from scientific research, we'll critically assess these claims. Indeed, some evidence indicates a longer time under tension may enhance muscle growth, but the details are important. Usui et al. divided 16 untrained young men into a slow or normal speed group. Both groups trained the back squat to around 90 degrees of knee flexion for 3 sets of 10 reps with A-50% one-rep max load, three times per week for 10 weeks. The slow speed group performed each rep with a 3-second lowering phase and a 3-second lifting phase. The normal speed group performed each rep with a 1-second lowering phase and a 1-second lifting phase. Thickness of the rectus femoris and vastus intermedius was measured at 30, 50, and 70% of the thigh length, while thickness of the vastus lateralis and vastus medialis was measured at 50% of the thigh length. The normal speed group experienced virtually no growth at all measured areas, while the slow speed group experienced significant increases at 70% of the thigh length of the rectus femoris as well as 50 and 70% of the thigh length for the vastus intermedius. Taken at face value, this study indicates slower repetition speeds result in greater muscle growth. However, there is a noteworthy limitation with this study. Both groups performed 3 sets of 10 reps with A-50% one-rep max load on the back squat each session. The slow speed group would have actually been training closer to failure. Failure is defined as the point at which you cannot perform any more repetitions with a given load. This is because, with a given load, slower rep speeds mean you perform fewer reps. You can imagine this for yourself. When keeping load and repetition number constant, using slow rep speeds would be more fatiguing compared to faster rep speeds. As a result, we don't know if the greater muscle growth observed for the slow speed group was actually because of the longer time under tension or because they were training closer to failure. As far as I'm aware, there are only two other studies in the research supporting the idea slower repetition tempos produce greater increases in measures of muscle growth. But both of these studies share the same limitation in that the slower repetition conditions were Watanabe et al. had a group of untrained men perform 3 sets of 8 reps with A-50% one-rep max load on the knee extension and leg curl, twice per week for 12 weeks. A slow speed group performed each exercise with a 3-second lowering and 3-second lifting phase, while a normal speed group used a 1-second lowering and 1-second lifting phase. Increases in quadriceps and hamstring thickness were significantly greater for the slow speed group. However, all subjects trained with 3 sets of 8 reps with A-50% one-rep max load. Consequently, the slow speed group was training A second study by Watanabe et al. had untrained men train the knee extension for 3 sets of 12 reps with a 30% one-rep max load, twice per week for 12 weeks. A slow speed group performed the exercise Increases in quadriceps cross-sectional area favored the slow speed group. Both groups trained with 3 sets of 12 reps with a 30% one-rep max load, again meaning the slow speed group would have been training closer to failure. Collectively, although in these three studies, the slow speed groups experienced greater muscle growth, we cannot be certain the greater growth was because they trained with a longer time under tension or because they trained The only way we can know is to look at studies that not only had groups use different repetition speeds, but also had subjects perform their repetitions to failure. Let us evaluate a recent study by Lacerda et al., which I believe to be the best study to date exploring if a longer time under tension enhances muscle growth. 10 untrained men had one leg assigned to a 2-second condition, and their other leg assigned to a 6-second condition. Both legs trained the unilateral knee extension for 3-4 sets to failure with A-50-60% one-rep max load, 2-3 times per week for 14 weeks. The leg assigned to the 2-second condition performed the exercise with a 1-second lifting phase and a 1-second lowering phase. The 6-second condition leg performed the exercise with a 3-second lifting phase and a 3-second lowering phase. I should emphasize again that both conditions involved performing repetitions to failure with their respective repetition speed. On average, the 6-second condition involved a time under tension of between 37 to 52 seconds, whereas the 2-second condition involved a time under tension between 25 and 38 seconds, so some of their sets were performed under the 30-second threshold which numerous sources recommend. However, both conditions produced similar increases in rectus femoris and vastus lateralis cross-sectional area. Therefore, when repetitions are performed to failure, a longer time under tension does not appear to enhance muscle growth. Another recent study by Chavez et al. supports these findings. Untrained men performed the unilateral knee extension for 3 sets to failure with a 70% one-rep max, twice per week for 8 weeks. Some subjects trained one leg with a 2-second lifting and 2-second lowering phase, called the 4-second condition, and their other leg with a self-selected repetition speed. On average, subjects performed a 0.9-second lifting and 0.9-second lowering phase with this leg. Again, I should emphasize both conditions involved performing repetitions to failure. However, increases in vastus lateralis cross-sectional area were similar between both conditions. Now, these are not the only two studies assessing the impacts of different time under tension durations on direct measures of muscle growth when subjects carry out their repetitions to failure. A meta-analysis by Schoenfeld et al. sums up the other studies. For those unaware, meta-analyses are studies that combine the results of numerous individual studies looking at the same topic. Combining the results of 4 studies, increases in measures of muscle growth were similar between fast and medium repetition speeds. In this analysis, fast rep speeds were classified at repetitions that lasted between 0.5 to 4 seconds, whereas medium rep speeds were repetitions that lasted between 4 and 8 seconds. Therefore, this analysis indicates that provided repetitions are performed to failure, there is no difference in muscle growth between performing reps with a 0.5-second duration or 8-second duration. Interestingly, there is a study not included in this analysis suggesting that super slow rep speeds may actually be inferior for building muscle. Schuenke et al. had untrained women perform the leg press, squat, and knee extension for 3 sets, 2-3 times per week for 6 weeks. Some subjects performed each exercise to failure with a 1-2 second lifting phase and a 1-2 second lower phase using an 80-85% one-rep max load. This was the traditional strength group. Other subjects performed each exercise to failure with a 10-second lifting phase and a 4-second lowering phase using a 40-60% one-rep This was the super slow group. Increases in vastus lateralis slow-twitch and fast-twitch fiber cross-sectional area were significantly greater for the traditional strength group compared to the super slow group. Now, this is only one study, so I believe we cannot be truly confident repetition tempos longer than 10 seconds are suboptimal. More research is needed. So, when overviewing the current evidence, it appears repetition durations lasting from 0.5 seconds up to 8 seconds produce comparable muscle growth, opposing the notion a longer time under tension enhances growth. Now, all of these studies were conducted on untrained subjects. That includes the 4 studies in the Schoenfeld et al. meta-analysis. One might argue that in trained individuals, a longer time under tension would enhance muscle growth. To my knowledge, there aren't any papers with trained subjects in this area unfortunately. However, physiologically, I believe it seems unlikely a longer time under tension would enhance muscle growth, provided repetitions are performed to or very close to failure. I say this because, irrespective of repetition speed, mechanical tension would likely be adequately high provided repetitions are carried out near failure. Mechanical tension is currently the best-categorized mechanism of muscle growth. Mechanical tension is equal to the force produced by a muscle. One key component of how much force a muscle produces is the number of muscle fibers recruited. In a very general sense, muscles consist of slow-twitch fibers and fast-twitch fibers. Slow-twitch fibers are highly resistant to fatigue but produce low amounts of power, whereas fast-twitch fibers are less fatigue resistant but produce high amounts of power. Generally, when force requirements are low, slow-twitch muscle fibers are recruited, but as force requirements increase, faster-twitch muscle fibers are recruited. High levels of muscle fiber recruitment, so high levels of slow-twitch and fast-twitch fiber recruitment, is one important component for inducing muscle growth. Regardless of time under tension, performing repetitions to or very close to failure likely results in sufficiently high levels of muscle fiber recruitment. A study by Morton et al. demonstrates this. A group of men with at least 2 years of training experience performed the leg extension for 3 sets with 4 different conditions. One condition involved performing repetitions to failure with an 80% one-rep load using a 1-second lifting, 1-second pause, and 1-second lowering phase. On average, the time under tension for this condition was 26 seconds per set. The second condition involved performing repetitions to failure with an 80% one-rep max load too, but using a 3-second lifting, 1-second pause, and 3-second lowering phase. condition was 31 seconds per set. The third condition involved performing repetitions to failure with a 30% one-rep max load using condition was 54 seconds per set. The fourth condition involved performing repetitions a 3-second lifting, 1-second pause, and 3-second condition was 76 seconds per set. The researchers found that all four conditions resulted in similar recruitment of slow-twitch and fast-twitch fibers from the vastus lateralis. Note, recruitment was measured via glycogen depletion of the fibers. Put differently, regardless of load or repetition speed, overall muscle fiber recruitment was likely similar. This supports the idea that provided repetitions are carried out near to failure, mechanical tension is likely sufficiently high regardless of the repetition tempo used. The research on rep ranges provides further evidence that a longer time under tension does enhance muscle growth. Two meta-analyses indicate that reps between 5 and 35 produce similar muscle growth, again, provided those reps are performed to or very close to failure. This includes research done on trained subjects. For instance, Morton et al. found that in men with at least 2 years of training experience, there was no difference in vastus lateralis fast-twitch and slow-twitch fiber growth after training the leg press and knee extension with either 8-12 reps to failure or 20-25 reps to failure. Of course, performing 20-25 reps means you experience a longer time under tension versus performing 8-12 reps, yet this did not matter. Finally, I should mention that theoretically, there may be a minimal time under tension threshold per set required for optimal hypertrophy. For instance, we've detailed in a previous video that one-rep max training does not produce muscle growth. Therefore, accumulating some reps and consequently some time under tension is likely needed to elicit optimal adaptations. As we've mentioned already, reps between 5 and 35 are likely similarly effective for muscle growth, when reps are carried out to or near failure. Therefore, the time under tension accumulated with 5 normal speed reps may be the minimal time under the tension threshold per set. Although, as we've discussed in a previous video, reps as low as 3 could build muscle effectively, so the threshold could be even lower. Ultimately, it would be interesting to see more research evaluating the minimal time under tension threshold for muscle growth per set. In conclusion, I believe there is sufficient evidence to suggest that a longer time under tension does not enhance muscle growth. Furthermore, the numerous recommendations that sets should last from 30-60 seconds are not substantiated. However, this should not be misinterpreted to say that using a longer time under tension is useless. Slowing your repetition speeds could be a way of applying progressive overload. For instance, in one session you may perform 3 sets of 8 reps with 20kg on an exercise using a 2-second lifting and 2-second lowering phase. Next session, you may use the same load, reps, and sets but use a 3-second lifting and 3-second lowering phase. Additionally, using a variety of repetition speeds in your training program could potentially be one effective way of ensuring more balanced growth across a muscle, as there is some evidence that different repetition tempos produce different regional muscle growth. We've covered the research on this in a previous video.

=== FILE: Train EASIER for Size & Strength？ This NEW Study Is Interesting [JbU6sO9q3bs].en.txt ===

Welcome to the house of hypertrophy. When thinking about the most important variables for muscle growth, there's a strong case to be made that how close to failure you train is up there. Simply put, getting to or very close to failure ensures you maximize muscle fiber recruitment and tension, which are likely crucial for maximizing hypertrophy. The recommendation to train with two or fewer reps away from failure is definitely solid. However, what if some of your sets are a bit further from failure? Does it hurt, help, or have a neutral effect on growth? A brand new study on trained individuals has explored this. It is actually the first study comparing varying proximities to failure to training with a fixed proximity to failure for muscle growth. Let's dive in. 31 trained individuals with 2 to n years of experience were recruited. They trained with this upper lower program. There were two four-week blocks. One group aimed to leave one rep in reserve every single set. The second group varied in how close to failure they trained across the program. During both four-week blocks, they aim to leave four reps in reserve on all sets in the first week, three reps in reserve on all sets in the second week, two reps in reserve on all sets in the third week, and one rep in reserve on all sets in the final week. There was a de lo in between the two four-week blocks and at the end of the last block where frequency and volume were halved and all sets were performed with one rep in reserve. Some may be thinking, "How can we be sure the subjects were reasonably accurate in estimating their reps in reserve?" The researchers tested it. They had subjects perform repetitions to failure on the back squat and bench press with an 80% one rep max load. During both, the subjects shouted out when they thought they had three reps left as well as one rep left before continuing on with reps to failure to see how accurate they were. So, there were four measurements here. The subjects were fairly accurate with the largest average error being negative - 1.5 with their three rep in reserve estimation on the squat. This means that if a subject shouted out they had three reps left, they actually went on to perform 4.5 more reps. All the other estimations had lower average errors. The researchers did retest this after the study and it was nice to see there were average numerical improvements for both groups. The largest average error was now around negative -1 and there was virtually no average error with a few other measures. Moving on to the main findings, cross-sectional area of the vasis lateralis and thickness of the triceps were assessed and it was found there was no significant differences in growth between both groups. Fascinatingly, triceps growth does lean towards the varied group. One rep max on the bench press and squat were also assessed and there was also no significant difference in strength gains between groups. This time though for the men, the bench press gains favor the fixed group. Overall, this was a pretty cool study. Taken at face value, the findings suggest having a portion of your training further from failure may be perfectly fine. But in the spirit of scientific accuracy, there are some important things to keep in mind. The study did not have another group training to failure. So in the strictest sense, we don't know how that could affect fared. Although if other research suggests no difference between leaving one rep in reserve and training to failure, we could infer that a group training to failure would not have seen superior gains. We'll summarize the research on training to failure shortly. The study was only partly supervised. The researchers fully supervised just the fourth week of training with the subjects unsupervised in all other weeks. To the researchers credit, they had subjects fill out extensive weekly training logs and film a set on the bench press and squats twice. We know subjects were on average fairly accurate in estimating their reps in reserve. However, if we look at the individual data points, we can see some deviated from the average a fair bit. Also remember these tests were just done on the bench press and squat, but there were multiple other exercises in their program, so we can't be certain how accurate they were on them. It wouldn't surprise me if estimation accuracy was a little worse on the Bulgarian split squats, but virtually perfect with something like an incined dumbbell curl. Finally, we mustn't forget this is just one study with a small sample size. So, these results are far from strong evidence. This is also why I'm not reading too much into the triceps growth favoring the varied group or the men's bench press measures favoring the fixed group. Before discussing this new paper further, let's quickly summarize the overall literature on failure for size and strength for muscle growth. When considering the collective research and the details of some well-designed individual papers, my current view is that if you're training with low volumes, training to failure might be superior. Whereas, if you're training with moderate to higher volumes, which are generally superior for growth anyway, training with one to two reps in reserve is likely sufficient. For strength, things are a little different. Proximity to failure has a much lower impact. Training much further from failure seems to be perfectly fine for getting stronger. There are nuances here that I could expand on in a future video if you like. Let me know how many of you are interested in the research on strength gains and how it may compare to training for exclusively size. Returning to the new study, we know it suggests that as long as you have some sets very close to failure, having some other sets a little further from failure may be fine. So, does that mean you should right now go ahead and include three or four reps in reserve sets in your program? If your primary goal is strength, I think it's indeed perfectly fine for you to have sets further from failure. Since, as just alluded to, there's enough overall evidence demonstrating that strength gains are not impaired when training further from failure. If your primary goal is muscle growth, I think you can definitely experiment with this if it's appealing to you and see how you get along. But I will say I currently don't have a large degree of confidence in this for growth since we're just dealing with one study on a small sample. So for now, I think the safer bet is still to have all sets in the 0 to2 reps in reserve range for muscle growth. And this will remain as my default recommendation. But again, you're always free to explore around. And there are certain scenarios where I think having some sets a little further from failure could lend itself well. for example, the evidence is still developing, but there is some evidence that very high volumes could have benefits for growth. So, if you're someone who's experimenting around with very high volumes, even if that's just with muscle group specialization, where you just train one or two muscle groups with very high volumes, it is going to be more manageable to have a portion of those sets a little further from failure, at least initially, when you're progressing and acclimatizing yourself to the higher volume. and then you can see if you want to maintain those sets further from failure or push them closer to failure. Finally, some days you may have limited energy. On days like these, you may find it more manageable to just train a bit further from failure than normal as opposed to skipping the workout entirely. These early results may give you a little more comfort in doing this occasionally. === FILE: Training BEYOND Failure - This NEW Study is Epic [13LiLwBZfa8].en.txt ===

Welcome to the house of hypertrophy. Can you build muscle faster by training beyond failure with some of your exercises? A brand new study is the first ever to explore a distinct way of training beyond failure in trained individuals. Firstly, what distinct way of training beyond failure did they investigate? Some exercises are most challenging at the final part of the lifting phase where the muscles are at a shortened length. For example, calf raises are hardest at the final top position. Pulling exercises like rows and pull downs are also hardest at the final position. Free weightight shoulder raises are hardest at the top. And certain leg curl and leg extension machines are hardest at the final position. We'll call these shortened position challenged exercises. If you train to failure on them, you fail at the shortened position, but you could go beyond by squeezing out as many partial repetitions as you can, resulting in you more effectively challenging the muscles at longer lengths. I've called these lengthened supersets in the past, but today I'll stick with the researchers terminology and call them post-failure partials. A study last year demonstrated the potential effectiveness of post-failure partials. Untrained individuals trained the car phrase. One condition trained to failure with a full range of motion, stopping when they couldn't reach the top position. The other condition also trained to failure with a full range of motion but kept going through squeezing out as many partials as possible aiming to fail at the most bottom position. That is they used post-failure partials. Medial gastromus growth was greater with the postfailure partials. However, there is a potential alternative to postfailure partials and this paper which also had untrained subjects train car phrases demonstrates it. One condition trained with a full range of motion. A second with a lengthened partial where you move through the half of the range of motion where the muscle is more lengthened and a third condition with a shortened partial where you move through the half where the muscle is more shortened. Gastromas growth was greatest with a lengthen partials. Thus, instead of post failure partials with shortened position challenged exercises, you could just use lengthen partials entirely. This raises the intriguing question, how do they compare? This is what the brand new study on trained individuals explored. Let's dive into it. 23 trained individuals with an average of 7.3 years of experience were recruited. All subjects trained four sets of car phrases on a Smith machine two times per week for 8 weeks. With one leg, subjects trained to failure with purely lengthened partials in the 10 to 20 rep range, stopping when they could no longer raise to 0°. With their other leg, subjects trained to failure with a full range of motion and then continued beyond this by performing partial repetitions and stopped when they could no longer raise to 0°. Note that loads were adjusted accordingly so that per set the post failure condition performed 5 to 10 full range of motion reps and 5 to 10 partial reps which was done to match the number of reps completed by the length and partials per set. Loads progressed over time as subjects got stronger to continue reaching failure in the prescribed rep ranges before and after the study. Medial gastromus thickness was measured. It was found that growth tended to be greater for the length in partials. These results are highly intriguing. Even though post failure partials involved hitting failure twice in a single set, they were not superior to exclusively using length and partials. In the spirit of scientific accuracy, this is just one study on 23 trained individuals. Also, although they had an average of 7.3 years of experience, they generally tended to train their calves with low volumes. The statistical analysis actually failed to provide anywhere close to strong support for the lengthened partials being better than the post failure partials. The researchers also reported relatively high measurement error. Thus, this paper is absolutely not what I deem robust or incontestable evidence. That said, I do suspect lengthen partials are great with car phrases. In the intro, the paper that found post failure partials grew the medial gastrochemis more than a full range of motion found a relative difference of 43.3%. While the other paper that found lengthened partials grew the medial gastrochemis more than a full range of motion found a relative difference of 126.9%. This might serve as further indirect evidence of lengthened partials being better than post failure partials. Also, this hints at a possibility we'll detail shortly, but there's evidence that the gastromus generates greater contractile tension at longer lengths. As the authors of the new study describe, the fact that postfailure partials involve a greater proportion of time at shorter lengths where contractile tension is lower could mean it isn't as good as lengthen partials. All in all, I'd say it's a solid move to train the calves with lengthen partials. But what about other exercises and muscles? allow us to explore three possibilities around lengthen partials. Firstly, regardless of whether we're talking about shortened position challenged exercises or other exercises, could lengthen partials just be the best range of motion to build muscle? We've already seen this study in 42 untrained women finding greater medial and lateral gastromus growth from lengthened partials versus a full range of motion and shortened partial. There's a second study on 45 untrained women finding with leg extensions lengthened partials tended to produce greater quad growth than a full range of motion and shortened partial. The biggest differences tended to be at the distal regions of the muscle. That's the regions closer to the knee joint. A third unpublished abstract finds in 34 untrained individuals greater overall glute and hamstring volume increases from lengthened partials compared to a full range motion with a machine hip extension exercise. But regular viewers of the House of Hypertrophy will know that more recent data doesn't look as promising. A paper by Wolf and colleagues last year recruited 25 well-trained individuals to perform an upper body program. One condition trained with a full range of motion on everything while the other condition trained with lengthened partials on everything. Biceps and triceps growth was comparable between both. A second paper had a large sample of 297 trained individuals perform a full body program. One group trained with a full range of motion on everything while the other group trained with a length and partial on these select exercises. Arm and thigh gains were clearly not different between groups. So length and partials may not be superior on everything. In the spirit of scientific accuracy, I don't believe we can confidently say this is 100% case closed. There is some controversy about the standardization of the length and partials in the paper by Wolf. The other paper, although having an impressively large sample size, did involve quite low volumes. Both papers also measured growth at the mid regions of the muscle, but there's some indication that lengthen partials may be particularly effective for the distal regions of a muscle. So, there are still open questions. The second possibility opposes the idea that lengthen partials are superior on everything and instead suggests lengthen partials only work on specific exercises. We noted how there are some considerations with both the Wolf paper and this paper. But notice how they did involve exercises that aren't shortened position challenged such as bijian curls, triceps overhead extensions, and incline curls. These are moderate to lengthened position challenged exercises. Conversely, the three papers that find a lengthened partial to beat out a full range of motion generally uses more shortened position challenged exercises. Thus, perhaps lengthened partials beat out a full range of motion only with shortened position challenged exercises. Overall, this might be a real possibility, and there's no super strong evidence currently to refute or confirm it. The third possibility goes a little deeper and suggests lengthened partials are only superior with specific muscles, and the calves are a prime example. Earlier we alluded to how the force generating components of the calves cannot generate as much tension at short lengths which is not necessarily the case for other muscles. So avoiding the shortened position for the calves through lengthened partials permits greater tension and subsequently growth. Based on the limited evidence we have the traps and pegs may also be like the calves. So with something like rows which tend to be most challenging at shortened positions lengthen partials may better develop the traps. As for the pecs, many exercises that train them are already challenging at moderate to lengthened positions, even with a full range of motion. So, lengthen partials may not be needed. Overall, this is a fascinating hypothesis, but it remains just that, a hypothesis. So, what's the overall verdict? To get as close to the truth as possible, we require a large quantity of quality data. But we're unfortunately not there yet. This frustratingly leaves us unable to conclusively say which possibility is true. Even with this being the case, I think there are some general and flexible recommendations we can arrive at. Based on what we have, I feel fairly confident that training the calves with lengthened partials is a good idea. But for other muscles, the first option is just to stay with a standard way of training all other exercises with a full range of motion. The second option is to experiment with length and partials where you personally wish to. Remember that no study to date has actually found lengthen partials to be inferior. So they may very well be compatible with maximizing hypertrophy. This doesn't necessarily have to be every sets or exercise, perhaps in just some sets. The third option is to experiment with post failure partials. Of course, we've just seen evidence that post failure partials may not be superior with the calves, but since we don't have data with other shortened position challenge exercises, it remains a possibility that post failure partials are useful, and they generally can be quite convenient in some cases. For example, on the final set of rows, pull downs, or lateral raises, it can be quite satisfying to squeeze out several extra partial reps. No other app gets close to creating personalized programs as comprehensive and well-rounded. The training philosophy is based on the latest scientific literature, but further customizations can easily be done. Reorder, swap out, remove, or add exercises. === FILE: Training to Failure Is a MUST for Hypertrophy (Or Is It？) [4OIsnpVs7Kc].en.txt ===

Failure is defined as the inability to perform\h another full repetition of an exercise. How close an individual gets to failure\h with their repetitions is probably one\h\h of the more hotly debated training variables. Some propose achieving failure is\h critical for muscle hypertrophy,\h\h as it ensures maximal muscle fiber\h recruitment and force production. In this video, we'll assess the soundness\h of this claim via the current training\h\h to failure literature as well as the\h mechanistic research on muscle hypertrophy. Kicking things off, 4 well-designed\h papers have compared training to\h\h failure to stopping a couple of reps\h shy of failure for muscle hypertrophy. Let's briefly overview them. A 2018 Brazillian study by Lacerda et al. had 10\h previously untrained men train the unilateral leg\h\h extension for 3-4 sets with a 55-60% one-rep\h max load, 2-3 times per week for 14 weeks. With one leg, subjects performed their\h repetitions to failure every set. With their other leg, they ended up stopping\h 2 reps away from failure in the first set in\h\h a session, 1 rep away from failure in the second\h set, and 0 reps away from failure in the last set. By the end of the study, increases in rectus\h femoris and vastus lateralis cross-sectional area\h\h were similar between both legs,\h suggesting stopping 2-0 reps away\h\h from failure is as effective as\h training to failure for growth. The second study by Nobrega et\h al., conducted in Brazil in 2017,\h\h allocated each leg of 32 previously untrained men\h into one of four conditions: a high load failure,\h\h high load non-failure, low load failure,\h and low load non-failure condition. All four conditions involved training the\h unilateral leg extension for 3 sets per session,\h\h twice per week for 12 weeks. The high load failure condition\h involved performing repetitions\h\h to failure every set with an 80% one-rep max load. The high load non-failure condition, also with\h an 80% one-rep max load, involved performing\h\h repetitions to just before they felt they were\h going to fail. Based on the data provided,\h\h it's likely this ended up being 1 to 3\h repetitions away from failure per set. The low load failure condition\h involved performing repetitions\h\h to failure every set with a 30% one-rep max load. The low load nonfailure condition,\h with a 30% one-rep max load,\h\h involved performing repetitions to just\h before they felt they were going to fail.\h\h Again, this likely ended up being 1 to\h 3 repetitions away from failure per set. By the end of the study, increases in vastus\h lateralis cross-sectional area were similar\h\h between all four conditions, indicating regardless\h if an 80% or 30% one-rep max load is used,\h\h stopping 3 to 1 reps away from failure is no less\h effective than training to failure for growth. As a separate point, it's worth noting this\h Nobrega study nicely demonstrates a point we've\h\h covered in other videos, that loads as light as\h 30% one-rep max can build muscle very effectively. Moving on to the third paper, a 2015\h Australian study by Sampson & Groeller\h\h had 28 previously untrained men\h perform a bicep curling-like exercise\h\h for 4 sets with an 85% one-rep max\h load, three times per week for 12 weeks. One group of subjects performed all their\h sets with repetitions to failure with a\h\h 2-second lifting and 2-second lowering speed.\h This group ended up averaging 6 reps per set. A second group performed only\h 4 repetitions per set with a\h\h 2-second lowering and maximal lifting\h speed. Based on the numbers provided,\h\h this group would have been an average of\h 2 repetitions away from failure each set. A third group also performed\h only 4 repetitions per set,\h\h but they used a maximal lowering\h and maximal lifting speed.\h\h This group would have also been an average\h of 2 repetitions away from failure each set. Although not major, there are some\h slight limitations with this study. As you likely noticed, the three different\h groups used different repetition speeds,\h\h which is potentially confounding. However,\h as described in our time under tension video,\h\h individual repetition speeds between 0.5-8 seconds\h appear similarly effective for muscle growth,\h\h so the use of different repetition speeds in\h this study is probably not a major concern. Also, groups two and three, who both stopped\h roughly 2 reps away from failure each set,\h\h actually performed an additional one\h set of repetitions to failure each week.\h\h However, I doubt this would\h significantly impact the outcomes. Anyway, by the end of the study, increases in\h elbow flexor cross-sectional area (consisting\h\h of the biceps and brachialis) were\h similar between all three groups,\h\h suggesting stopping 2 reps away from failure can\h be comparably effective to training to failure. As a small summary thus far, these three\h studies overviewed indicate stopping 3\h\h or fewer repetitions from failure can be\h equivalently effective for building muscle\h\h versus training to failure. However, all three of these studies were\h conducted on previously untrained individuals.\h\h One could suggest these results should be expected\h in untrained individuals, as they would be highly\h\h responsive regardless of how close they get to\h failure with their repetitions on an exercise.\h\h They may suggest that different results\h may arise in trained individuals. Fortunately, the fourth paper, a 2020 Brazillian\h study by Santanielo et al. was conducted on 14 men\h\h with an average of 5.1 years of\h training experience. They had an\h\h average body weight of 74.4kg and could leg\h press an average of 237.5kg before the study. Subjects trained both the unilateral\h leg press and unilateral leg extension,\h\h twice per week for 10 weeks. A great thing about this study was the\h researcher's individualized set numbers.\h\h More precisely, the researchers noted how many\h sets per week the subjects performed for the\h\h quadriceps before the study, and then the subjects\h performed 20% more for the study's duration. For example, if a subject performed 15 weekly\h sets for the quadriceps before the study,\h\h they performed 18 weekly sets (a 20%\h increase) for the quadriceps in this study.\h\h These 18 weekly sets were equally divided\h between the leg press and leg extension. With one leg, subjects performed\h every set with repetitions to failure. With their other leg, they performed every\h set with repetitions to a point before\h\h failure. The data provided suggest\h they mostly ended up stopping their\h\h sets around 3 to 1 repetitions away from failure. By the end of the study, increases in vastus\h lateralis cross-sectional area were similar\h\h between both legs, suggesting stopping 3\h to 1 repetitions away from failure is still\h\h similarly effective to training\h to failure in trained individuals. So, considering the totality of the current\h literature, it appears in previously untrained\h\h and trained individuals, training to failure\h is not a must. Stopping 3 to 1 repetitions\h\h away from failure appears equivalently\h capable of eliciting muscle hypertrophy. Indeed, these results make sense mechanistically. Mechanical tension is currently the\h best-categorized stimulus for muscle hypertrophy,\h\h and it's quite likely stopping 3\h to 1 repetitions away from failure\h\h elicits sufficient mechanical tension levels. Let me explain. Mechanical tension is equal to the\h force generated by muscle fibers. Components within muscle\h fibers, called mechanosensors,\h\h detect forces produced by the muscle fiber and\h transduces these forces into a signaling cascade\h\h that results in muscle protein synthesis (which\h are the proteins that make our muscles bigger). It's worth exploring the concept of\h motor units to further understand\h\h overall mechanical tension and why\h training to failure may not be necessary. A motor unit refers to a single motor neuron\h and the multiple muscle fibers it innervates.\h\h When the single motor neuron sends an electrical\h signal through to the muscle fibers it innervates,\h\h those muscle fibers produce force. Within a whole muscle, a variety of motor\h units with different characteristics exist. In general, these characteristics\h likely lie across a spectrum,\h\h with low threshold motor units on one end, and\h high threshold motor units on the other end. Typically, a low-threshold motor unit consists of\h a small motor neuron that innervates slow-twitch\h\h muscle fibers that produce low amounts of force\h but are highly fatigue resistant. Due to this,\h\h low-threshold motor units are described as\h highly fatigue resistant but low force-producing. A high-threshold motor unit generally consists of\h a large motor neuron that innervates fast-twitch\h\h muscle fibers that produce high amounts of\h force but are highly fatigable. Therefore,\h\h high-threshold motor units are described\h as high-force producing but very fatigable. For maximizing overall mechanical tension (and\h thus the stimulus for overall muscle growth),\h\h we'd want to recruit as many motor\h units as possible during an exercise\h\h (from the low-threshold motor units all the\h way up to the high-threshold motor units). Furthermore, we'd likely want the individual\h motor units to produce at least decent degrees\h\h of their respective force capacities for a fair\h duration. The precise details of this will differ\h\h depending on the motor unit in question. Remember,\h low-threshold motor units have overall low-force\h\h producing capacities but can sustain these forces\h for a long time. Conversely, high-threshold motor\h\h units have overall high-force producing capacities\h but cannot sustain these forces for very long. Here's the main points: Firstly, It's not clear when you\h reach maximal motor unit recruitment,\h\h and the motor unit literature indicates\h this can differ between muscles. However, the literature indicates this is\h likely achieved a fair while before failure. For instance, one study suggests maximal\h motor unit recruitment for the shoulder\h\h and trap muscles may be obtained\h 3-5 repetitions before failure. Secondly, by the time you've reached failure,\h\h it's quite likely many motor units\h (particularly the high-threshold motor units)\h\h are past producing their highest\h forces and are instead just fatiguing. Remember, it's tension (analogous to force)\h\h that's categorized as a prime stimulus for muscle\h hypertrophy. The idea that more motor unit fatigue\h\h is beneficial for muscle hypertrophy is\h not supported by the current literature. A motor unit modeling study by Potvin and\h Fuglevand demonstrates our points nicely. Their model included 7 different motor\h units, ordered in terms of thresholds. Motor unit 1 was the lowest threshold motor unit,\h\h while motor unit 120 was the\h highest threshold motor unit. The graph on-screen depicts the\h contribution of each motor unit to A-50%\h\h maximal isometric contraction held until failure.\h The total contraction lasted 100 seconds. Except for motor unit 120, all of the other motor\h\h units were recruited from\h the onset of contraction. Motor units 1, 20, 40, and 60 produced steady low\h forces throughout the full contraction duration.\h\h This makes sense, these would be\h considered the low-threshold motor units\h\h (which produce low forces but\h are highly fatigue resistant). Motor unit 80, a higher-threshold motor\h unit, produced its most force for the\h\h set at the start of the contraction,\h where it thereafter gradually fatigued. Motor unit 100, a higher-threshold motor\h unit, continued to increase its force\h\h contribution up until the 65-second\h mark, and thereafter began to fatigue. Motor unit 120, the highest-threshold motor\h unit, was recruited at the 70-ish second mark,\h\h and steeply increased its force contribution\h up until the 95-ish second mark,\h\h where it then steeply fatigued. This data demonstrates motor unit recruitment,\h\h as well as the maintenance of at least decent\h amounts of respective force production from\h\h the individual motor units, is achieved\h before failure. At the point of failure,\h\h no additional motor units nor enhancements\h in individual motor units force occurred. This probably explains why\h training 3 to 1 repetitions\h\h away from failure is sufficient for muscle growth. I should restate this data was from\h modeling isometric contractions. Recruitment patterns and strategies\h likely differ between isometric\h\h and the isotonic contractions that\h occur during your typical exercises. However, I'm unaware of any reason to\h believe that the main point (that failure\h\h offers no additional motor unit recruitment or\h enhancements in individual motor units force)\h\h would not also be the same\h with isotonic contractions. In summary, the current literature,\h as well as mechanistic rationale,\h\h likely indicate stopping 3 to\h 1 repetitions away from failure\h\h is similarly effective to training\h to failure for muscle hypertrophy. Now, some may be thinking in the real world,\h\h away from the laboratory in which\h researchers can verify proximity to failure,\h\h an individual may not actually be able to\h accurately estimate how close to failure they are. For example, an individual may think they've\h stopped 3 repetitions away from failure,\h\h but in actuality, they may have been 5 or\h even more repetitions away from failure. This is a very solid point. In the next video,\h we'll explore some interesting recent research\h\h that can help an individual become more accurate\h at predicting how far from failure they are. In the video after that,\h\h we'll be exploring something that many may have\h been thinking about throughout this video. That\h\h is, could stopping more than 3 repetitions away\h from failure still optimize muscle hypertrophy? Specifically, there's some really\h intriguing velocity-based research\h\h that potentially indicates,\h under certain conditions,\h\h training farther than 3 repetitions away\h from failure could optimize hypertrophy.

=== FILE: Unilateral vs Bilateral Training for Muscle Growth [6lsCo8B-mPI].txt ===

 Welcome to the House of Hypertrophy. Is training one limb at a time the secret to maximizing muscle growth? How many reps do you need to maximize hypertrophy? And how can you maximize quad hypertrophy? Three new studies add to our knowledge in these areas. Let's dive straight in. The first paper explored whether small muscle mass exercises couldn't enhance hypertrophy by comparing unilateral and bilateral training. Some may be wondering, why would we expect there to be a difference in hypertrophy? After all, if we're comparing a unilateral to a bilateral dumbbell curl, we're ultimately performing the same movement pattern. However, some have suggested that exercises that train a smaller amount of muscle mass, like unilateral exercises, could be superior for muscle hypertrophy for a variety of reasons. For example, as the authors described in the introduction, there is some evidence that the force produced when both limbs contract simultaneously is lower than the summed force from each limb contracting one at a time, a phenomenon known as the bilateral force deficit. One hypothesis behind this is that with exercises that involve smaller amounts of muscle mass, greater neural drive to the muscle and thus potentially higher muscle fiber recruitment can occur. Furthermore, exercises with smaller amounts of muscle mass tend to involve lower cardiovascular demand, which can permit greater local muscle fatigue. On the basis of these reasons, the authors hypothesized that unilateral training would be superior for muscle growth. Let's see if they ended up being right. The researchers recruited 54 untrained women to train three times per week for eight weeks. A bilateral group performed bilateral dumbbell curls, while a unilateral group trained unilateral dumbbell curls. That is, they trained one arm first and then moved on to training the other arm. Both groups trained their exercise for two sets of 8-12 reps to what the authors termed concentric task failure. Loads were adjusted when necessary to ensure subjects kept reaching failure in the 8-12 rep range. The unilateral group alternated which arm was trained first every session. Strength was measured by assessing bilateral dumbbell curl one rep max strength as well as unilateral dumbbell curl one rep max strength on both arms. Muscle growth was assessed through changes in thickness at 60 and 70% regions of the elbow flexors, which contained both the biceps and brachialis. Starting with strength, increases in bilateral dumbbell curl one rep max strength were not significantly different between both groups. Increases in unilateral right arm dumbbell curl one rep max strength was significantly greater for the unilateral group, while unilateral left arm strength was not significantly different, but did favor the unilateral group. This might be explained by the unilateral group ultimately lifting a heavier load per arm. Specifically, during the first session, the dumbbell load used by the bilateral group was a little more than the dumbbell loads used by the unilateral group. In other words, there was no apparent bilateral deficit between groups. But in the last session, the unilateral group trained with slightly heavier loads. As for muscle growth, changes in muscle thickness at both regions were not significantly different between both groups. Therefore, the findings do not support the notion that unilateral training is superior for muscle growth. In the spirit of scientific accuracy, this is merely just one study on untrained women utilizing the dumbbell curl. So, I would be cautious in over extrapolating these findings. In the discussion, the authors mentioned that while unilateral curls involve half the muscle mass compared to bilateral curls, the absolute difference is quite small given that the elbow flexors are not particularly large. So, they leave open the possibility that differences could exist between exercises that involve a larger difference in muscle mass. However, when looking at other areas of the literature, I am skeptical that exercises that involve small amounts of muscle mass are superior for muscle growth. We do have other studies that tend to find similar hypertrophy between unilateral and bilateral training. What's more, as described previously at the House Fypertrophy, we have a paper comparing glute max hypertrophy between back squats and hip thrusts. Back squats train a larger amount of muscle mass versus hip thrusts. Yet, the paper ultimately observes similar glute max hypertrophy between both exercises. Furthermore, we'll see how some of the data we're about to examine next also relates to this area. Nevertheless, with all this in mind, I currently think that whether an exercise is bilateral or unilateral isn't a critical consideration for hypertrophy. I would select things considering your preferences and goals. For instance, unilateral training requires you to train each limb independently, which, with all else equal, takes longer. But unilateral training could have potential benefits when it comes to reducing size imbalances. We have another study comparing heavier to lighter loads for muscle hypertrophy, and its design provides insight into some other questions. For example, it's not uncommon for some to suggest that they can grow certain muscles easier than others. This new study provides insight into the question. Do people who grow their arms well also tend to grow their legs well? Twenty previously untrained men were recruited to train three times per week for 10 weeks. Subjects had one arm and leg randomly assigned to train with heavier loads, while the contralateral arm and leg trained with lighter loads. They trained the unilateral leg extension and unilateral dumbbell preacher curl each for three sets per session. The side of the body training with heavier loads performed 8-12 reps, while the side of the body training with lighter loads performed 20-25 reps. Reps were performed to what the researchers termed volitional failure, and loads were adjusted when necessary across sets to continue reaching failure in the prescribed rep ranges. Strength was assessed both through one rep max on the unilateral leg extension and dumbbell preacher curl, as well as isometric knee extension and elbow flexion strength. Muscle growth was assessed through a range of measures. Thickness and cross-sectional area of the biceps and vascular lateralis were measured, fat and bone-free lean mass and muscle fibro cross-sectional area with fibres just from the vascular lateralis were also examined. Starting with strength, the increases across all measures were not significantly different between the heavier and lighter load conditions. When looking at the rest of the research, it is clear that lighter loads can still increase strength, but we do tend to see that heavier loads produce greater increases. I think the reason this study did not observe this is since it had within-subject design. The thing is, there can be a transfer of strength gains across limbs which can confound the results. Note, there is no transfer in muscle growth between limbs, so this study design is appropriate when the aim is to examine muscle growth. Speaking of muscle growth, changes in all the measures of growth were not significantly different between the heavier and lighter load conditions. If you are a regular viewer at the house viperchiphy, you will know these results align with the rest of the research, even research conducted on trained individuals. That is, provided your training to or close to failure, a wide range of loads, thus repetition numbers, produce similar muscle hypertrophy. For more details on how low you can go rep number wise, check out this fairly recent video. It is notable to mention that both slow and fast twitch fiber size increases were not significantly different between conditions. I bring this up since it has long been speculated that lighter loads and higher reps may build slow twitch fibers better, while heavier loads with fewer reps may build fast twitch fibers better. But this study, along with a couple others we have exploring this, fail to support this notion. Aggregating the arm measures, as well as the leg measures, the researchers ranked individuals on how much they grew both the arms and the legs. There was a correlation between the two. That is, high responders for the legs generally tended to be high responders with the arms. Technically, there was around 50% variant still unexplained. Moreover, do remember that this is just one study with a small sample size of 20, and the measures were largely just from the biceps and vastus lateralis. I do like that the researchers explored this, and hopefully future research continues providing insight about whether it's possible for certain individuals to be high responders with only certain muscle groups. Finally, we know that on average, growth was similar between higher and lighter loads. But could some people grow more with one over the other? Well, aggregating the hypertrophy measures, the researchers ranked responsiveness with the different loads. We generally see that those that grew well with the high loads also tended to grow well with the lighter loads. However, we do see some data points that would seem to suggest certain individuals may experience better growth with lighter loads and others higher loads. Although, as hinted at in recent videos, there are nuances when it comes to determining individual differences, I intend to have a future video diving deeper into this. In conclusion, this is yet another study suggesting that there's no superior rep range for muscle hypertrophy. Provided your pushing reps to or close to failure, a wide range of loads and thus repetition numbers can be highly effective. So, feel free to train according to your preference, and that can certainly include training with a variety of rep ranges. Over the last few years, we've seen an increase in the number of studies comparing different exercises for muscle hypertrophy. A few months ago, we had another study adding to this, comparing back squats to leg extensions. 63 untrained women were recruited to train twice per week for 8 weeks. One group trained Smith machine back squats, while another group trained machine leg extensions. Both groups trained their exercise for three sets of 8-12 reps to momentary muscular failure, with loads adjusted when necessary to stay in this rep range. Strength was assessed via three rep max on both the back squats and leg extension, while muscle growth was assessed by measuring thickness of the rectus femoris and vastus lateralis across three regions. Starting with strength, unsurprisingly, increases in back squat strength were greater for the back squat group, while interestingly, there was no statistically significant difference in leg extension strength between both groups. This suggests that the carryover from back squats to leg extensions may be better than the carryover from leg extensions to back squats. Regarding hypertrophy, rectus femoris growth across all three regions were greater for the leg extensions. Vastus lateralis growth at the proximal and middle regions were not significantly different, but growth at the distal region was greater for the back squat group. If you're a frequent viewer, you'll likely be aware that these findings generally align with the other research we have on the quadriceps. That is, compound exercises that involve simultaneous knee and hip extension, such as squats and leg presses, seem to be highly effective for growing the vastus heads of the quads, but fail to optimize development of the rectus femoris. This is likely explained by the fact that the rectus femoris crosses over two joints. It crosses over the knee and hip joints in a way that means it's involved in knee extension and hip flexion. During exercises like the squats, knee extension but also hip extension occur, so if the rectus femoris strongly contracted, it would partly fight against hip extension, so it makes sense that the nervous system would try to minimize the overall involvement of the rectus femoris. Conversely, isolated knee extension exercises, like leg extensions, better engage the rectus femoris and have been documented to effectively grow it. Note that reverse Nordics and city squats also involve isolated knee extension. While we have minimal data on these movements, I do think it's likely they grow the rectus femoris well. Now, this new paper was conducted on untrained women, but we do have evidence of this idea in trained individuals. Specifically, this paper on trained individuals compared leg presses to leg extensions. Again, rectus femoris growth was greater for the leg extensions, while vastus lateralis growth, interestingly across all three regions, favored the leg press. Circling back to the idea proposed by some that small muscle mass exercises could be superior via hypertrophy, the fact that squats and leg presses may grow the vastus lateralis little more than leg extensions is further evidence against this notion. That is, squats and leg presses train a larger amount of muscle mass than leg extensions, but are not in theory of foregrowing the vastus heads of the quads. To acquire your goal physique, there's no question that effective training is necessary. If you'd like assistance with this all while supporting what I do at the House of Hypotrophy, our highly rated partner, the Alpha Progression app, can generate a comprehensive program 100% custom to your needs. Choose your goal, specify if there's muscles you want to focus on more, and let it know how often and how long you want to train for. This process can take less than a minute. There are well over a quadrillion input combinations on which your plan is based on. Furthermore, the training philosophy is based on scientific literature. During workouts, the algorithm analyzes your past performance to derive progressive overload recommendations, thereby fostering long-term progress. Improve your understanding of your response with progression charts on a range of key metrics. The exercise database continues to grow, with just under 800 exercises. Each exercise has simplified instructions and further basic information. Try out all this free for two weeks with a link in the comments and description. And if you like it and continue, the link provides 20% off a subscription. Feel free to let me know what you think about the app anytime. Thank you for making it to the end. === FILE: Volume Load Does NOT Drive Muscle Hypertrophy (Science Overview) [QhQs4o0v1UU].en.txt ===

It's not uncommon to hear that\h volume drives muscle hypertrophy. Specifically, it's thought more volume\h could produce more muscle hypertrophy,\h\h probably up until a certain point. However, volume is quite a broad term. In\h general, it refers to how much work you perform. This can be quantified in a variety of ways,\h including the number of sets you perform for\h\h an exercise or muscle group, the product of\h the number of sets and repetitions you perform,\h\h the product of the number of sets,\h repetitions, and loads you use,\h\h or even the product of the number of sets,\h repetitions, load, and range of motion you use. Volume load is the product of the number of sets,\h repetitions, and loads you use. For example,\h\h if you perform 3 sets of 10 repetitions on\h the barbell bench press with a 100kg load,\h\h this equals a volume load\h of 3000kg for this exercise. It's not uncommon to see individuals state that\h volume load is what drives muscle hypertrophy.\h\h I've even come across numerous researchers\h who have suggested this in their papers. In this video, I'll detail why this is a mistake,\h\h and why I believe volume load is\h actually unrelated to muscle hypertrophy. First, we'll evaluate some research that may lead\h you to believe volume load drives hypertrophy,\h\h then we'll then look at numerous other papers\h\h which demonstrate volume load\h is not related to hypertrophy. Finally, we'll briefly touch on what form of\h\h volume likely drives hypertrophy. Let us begin with the research that\h\h may lead you to assume volume\h load drives muscle hypertrophy. One example comes from the research on rep ranges. Schoenfeld et al. had 17 men with at least\h\h 1 year of training experience\h perform a range of exercises. One group of subjects, who we'll call a\h strength group, performed each exercise for\h\h 7 sets of 3 repetitions to failure (the point\h at which no more repetitions can be peformed). Another group of subjects, who\h we'll call the hypertrophy group,\h\h performed each exercise for 3\h sets of 10 repetitions to failure. The reason the strength group performed more sets\h\h per exercise was to equate the\h volume load between both groups. Both groups attempted to increase the load\h they used within their rep range every week. After 8 weeks of training, the\h total volume load performed on\h\h each exercise was similar between both groups.\h\h Moreover, increases in a biceps growth\h measurement were similar between both groups. Therefore, given volume load was similar\h between both groups, and both groups seem to\h\h have experienced similar hypertrophy, you may\h think volume load may be driving hypertrophy. Another example comes from the\h research on rest intervals. Schoenfeld et al. had 13 men with at least 6\h months of training experience perform a range of\h\h exercises each for 3 sets of repetitions to\h failure with an 8-12 rep-max load, three times per\h\h week for 8 weeks. All subjects aimed to increase\h the load used within the rep range every week. One group of subjects, who\h we'll call a long rest group,\h\h performed this while resting\h for 3 minutes between sets. Another group of subjects, who\h we'll call a short rest group,\h\h for 1 minute between sets. Throughout the 8 weeks of training, the long\h rest group was achieving greater volume loads on\h\h all their exercises versus the short rest group.\h This makes sense, as resting for longer between\h\h sets enables you to perform more repetitions\h to failure, thus increasing the volume load. By the end of the study, increases in\h growth measurements for the elbow flexors,\h\h triceps brachii, anterior quadriceps, and\h vastus lateralis favored the long rest group. Therefore, as the as the long rest\h group peformed higher volume loads,\h\h and experienced greater muscle growth,\h\h the results would lead you to assume higher\h volume loads drive more muscle hypertrophy. So, the two examples we've just given support\h the idea that volume load may drive hypertrophy. If studies like these were\h the only ones that existed,\h\h the evidence would be indeed promising that\h volume load is a driver of hypertrophy. However, there does exist many other\h studies in which volume load appears\h\h to be unrelated to hypertrophy. If we examined the research on rep\h\h ranges in more depth, we'd find great evidence\h volume load does not drive muscle hypertrophy. As explored in previous videos, there's quite\h a bit of evidence that with all other training\h\h variables equal, performing repetitions to\h or very close to failure with a 30% one-rep\h\h max load is as effective for muscle hypertrophy as\h\h performing repetitions to or very close\h to failure with an 80% one-rep max load. As a note, an individual can roughly perform\h 30-ish repetitions to failure with a 30%\h\h one-rep max load, and roughly 8 to 12 repetitions\h Now, here's the thing, the volume load\h you achieve with a 30% one-rep max load\h\h is greater than the volume load you\h achieve with an 80% one-rep max load. For instance, Lim et al. had 21\h previously untrained men train the\h\h leg press and leg extension each for three\h sets, three times per week for 10 weeks. One group of subjects performed repetitions\h to failure each set with a 30% one-rep\h\h max load, while another group of subjects peformed\h\h repetitions to failure each set\h with an 80% one-rep max load. However, growth of slow-twitch\h and fast-twitch fibers from the\h\h vastus lateralis muscle was similar between\h training with a 30% and 80% one-rep max load. Therefore, the rep range research\h demonstrates that higher volume loads do\h\h not neccessarily produce more muscle hypertrophy. Additionally, the rep range research also\h demonstrates that your ability to increase\h\h the volume load you perform overtime probably\h doesn't relate to muscle hypertrophy either. Illustrating this, Schoenfeld et al. had a group\h of men with between 1.5 to 9 years of training\h\h experience perform a range of exercises each\h for 3 sets, three times per week for 8 weeks. Opposingly, the moderate rep\h group, compared to the first week,\h\h increased their volume load performed\h for all exercises only by 10,714kg. However, as we know from other data, both the\h high rep and moderate rep groups would likely have\h\h experienced similar muscle hypertrophy, indicating\h your ability to increase volume load overtime is\h\h likely not related to muscle hypertrophy. Progressing further, the research on\h training to failure further supports\h\h the idea volume load is not a\h driver of muscle hypertrophy. So, if volume load is not the form of volume\h that relates to muscle growth, what is?. It seems the number of sets you perform for your\h\h muscle groups is what appears to\h be related to muscle hypertrophy. That's close to nothing. There's no denying that's true, but the researchers did two important things. Firstly, each subject trained both conditions. Also, there is no transfer in growth between limbs, and there was an even balance of dominant arms in each condition, meaning that the overall results are not confounded by this.  ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج ج 24 trained individuals with an average of 7.1 years of experience were recruited. Each subject had one arm randomly assigned to train dumbbell lateral raises and the other arm assigned to train cable lateral raises. Interestingly, the researchers had subjects use cuffs to minimize grip fatigue. This design of all subjects training both exercises is great, as differences in genetics, nutrition, and outside lifestyle factors are less likely to confound the findings. I've said it before, but it's not like your right arm eats more protein or sleeps more than your left arm. With both the dumbbell and cable, subjects moved from 0 to 90 degrees of shoulder abduction straight out to the sides in what's known as the frontal plane. Some subjects did have pain, so instead, both exercises were raised in between the frontal and scapular planes. The cable was positioned so that the arm and cable formed a roughly 90-degree angle at the start. This results in the exercise being hardest at this position, where the side delts are at a longer length. With the dumbbells, we know they provide the greatest challenge when the arms are straight out, where the side delts are at a relatively shorter length. They train 2 times per week for 8 weeks. Each exercise was trained with 5 sets per session with repetitions to momentary muscular failure in the 12 to 16 rep range, with progressive overload applied to stay in this rep range across sessions. Side delts thickness was measured at a proximal and distal region. It was ultimately found that growth in both regions was similar between both exercises. Therefore, as the authors note, the findings suggest both dumbbells and cables present similarly effective options for eliciting hypertrophy of the side delts in trained individuals. Before describing how this study may fit into the overall literature on training muscles at long lengths, in the spirit of scientific accuracy, we need to keep some things in mind. Firstly, a single study is never definitive proof. Let's say we have a coin with A-50% chance of landing on heads. Although unlikely, it is still possible to flip heads 5 times in a row, which may lead you to think this coin is biased towards heads. But as we flip it more times, things will eventually reflect the truth. In the same way, a single study can find things that don't reflect reality due to chance, so additional studies are necessary to know we're on the right track. Nevertheless, this study is certainly a data point suggesting no meaningful difference between a dumbbell and cable lateral raise. Secondly, the amount of hypertrophy seen by both conditions was fairly small and not far off measurement error. This isn't too surprising as we're dealing with an 8-week study on already well-trained individuals. So we can't rule out the possibility this study was underpowered to detect potentially small growth differences between the exercises. Thirdly, remember range of motion was the same between the dumbbells and cables. But you can actually bring your arm across your body with cables to lengthen the side delts even more. It remains possible doing this does yield greater growth, we don't know, at least not yet. Fourth and finally, participants aim to maintain a similar rep tempo. But both conditions increased acceleration at the bottom as they approached failure. With the dumbbells, this will increase the tension at longer side delts lengths. Whether this influenced the findings is up to debate. When considering the literature on training muscles at long vs short lengths, I think we should split the data into three categories. Resistance challenge, range of motion, and biarticular muscles. With resistance challenge, with all else equal, we're comparing exercises that are harder at longer vs shorter lengths. The new lateral raise data belongs to this category. The only other study in this category was conducted on untrained subjects in 2020, comparing barbell preacher curls, which are harder near the start of the curl where the biceps are at a longer length, to cable preacher curls, which are harder later in the curl where the biceps are relatively shorter. Similar to the Seidel data, this study failed to find any difference, as biceps growth measured around the mid-region was comparable between both exercises. As for the range of motion category, with any given exercise, you can train with a full-range motion which moves the joints through the largest capacity possible. A shortened partial which moves through the half where the muscle is at a shorter length, or a lengthened partial which moves through the half where the muscle is at a longer length. It was once thought a full-range motion was best, but this was predominantly based on comparisons with shortened partials. Three studies, all on untrained individuals, fascinatingly found length and partials build overall more muscle than a full-range motion. However, two studies in 2024 on trained individuals, including a paper on just under 300 subjects that I detailed in our 2024 summary, largely found length and partials to be similar to a full-range motion. This isn't case closed due to some nuances, but it does seem clear that length and partials are not unequivocally superior, and both a full-range motion and length and partial are options on the table. With biarticulate muscles, these are muscles that cross over two joints. With these muscles, we can change the position of one of the joints to lengthen the muscle more. For example, the rectus femoris is the only head of the quads that crosses both the knee and hip. The rest of the quad head just cross the knee. Leaning back on the leg extension, which puts the hip joint in a more extended position, lengthens the rectus femoris part of the quads. This grew the rectus femoris more than normal leg extensions in one study, while growth of the vastus lateralis, which is trained at the same length between both, was similar. Many probably don't think about it in this way, but it also applies to the gastrocnemius heads of the calves, which cross both the ankle and knee. Compared to bent-legged calf raises, straight-legged calf raises have our knees extended which lengthens the gastrocnemius heads. The two papers found better gastrocnemius growth with a straight leg, while soleus growth, which is trained at the same length between both, was similar. Similar concepts may apply to the biceps, triceps, and hamstrings. However, nearly all of these studies have been done on untrained individuals. Does it apply to trained individuals? The spirit of scientific accuracy would haunt me if I said I was certain, so I'm not certain. But my suspicion is this is the category where trained individuals will see better growth from longer muscle lengths. Indeed, one of the papers finding straight leg calf raises built the gastrocnemius more involved trained individuals. Moreover, this study on competitive bodybuilders found they experienced greater overall rectus morse activity with leaning and lying back leg extensions versus normal leg extensions. The measure of activity used in this paper has been found to relate to muscle growth in a few studies. So right now, it tentatively seems except for the biarticulate muscle category, making the exercise harder at longer muscle lengths as well as using a lengthened partial may largely not be superior in trained individuals. But they crucially do not appear to be any worse either, so you have the freedom to choose what works best for you. All of this is very much a developing area of research. The quantity of quality research we're getting is increasing. In 2024, we had seven studies relating to training at different muscle lengths, with four being the first ever set of studies on trained individuals directly measuring hypertrophy in this area. I'm excited to see how our knowledge progresses in this area and other areas of muscle growth. It can be frustrating because we desperately want to know everything now, but we do know a lot more than 20 years ago. And if the literature has shown anything so far, it is that there are many different paths to growing muscle. For example, if we provisionally accept the findings of the latest study, if you've been training with dumbbell lateral raises, you haven't been missing out.
